Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{x^{2}-1}{|x-1|}$ defined for all real $x$ except $x=1$.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Explain why $f(1)$ cannot be evaluated directly, and state what this means for the value of the function at $x=1$.

    (Explain)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    For $x>1$, show that $f(x)$ simplifies to $x+1$ and hence state the right-hand limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $1$.

    (Show that)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    For $x<1$, show that $f(x)$ simplifies to $-(x+1)$ and hence state the left-hand limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches $1$.

    (Show that)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Determine whether the two-sided limit $\lim_{x\to 1}f(x)$ exists, justifying your answer using the one-sided limits.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) Substituting $x=1$ gives $f(1)=\frac{0}{0}$, which is undefined because division by zero is not permitted (M1), so the function has no value at that point (A1) and cannot be evaluated by direct substitution (A1). A zero denominator means the algebraic expression has no numerical value at $x=1$, so the formula breaks down exactly where the limit is investigated (R1). The expression therefore fails precisely because the denominator vanishes there.

(b) For $x>1$ the quantity $x-1$ is strictly positive, so $|x-1|=x-1$ and $f(x)=\frac{x^{2}-1}{x-1}=\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=x+1$ (M1)(A1). As $x$ tends to $1$ from above, this linear expression tends to $2$, so the right-hand limit is $2$ (A1)(AG). The factor $x-1$ cancels legitimately because it is never zero on this side of $1$, leaving a well behaved linear function. This is why the one-sided limit exists even though the formula is undefined at the point.

(c) For $x<1$ the quantity $x-1$ is negative, so $|x-1|=-(x-1)$ and $f(x)=\frac{x^{2}-1}{-(x-1)}=-(x+1)$ (M1)(A1). As $x$ tends to $1$ from below, $-(x+1)$ tends to $-2$, so the left-hand limit is $-2$ (A1)(AG). The minus sign is forced by the absolute value on the negative side, because the denominator equals the opposite of the numerator factor. The left-hand limit therefore exists as a finite value distinct from the right-hand one.

(d) A two-sided limit exists only when the two one-sided limits agree (M1). Here the right-hand limit is $2$ and the left-hand limit is $-2$ (A1), and since $2\neq -2$ (A1), the two-sided limit does not exist (R1). The unequal one-sided limits are exactly what prevent the overall limit from existing, because a proper limit must approach the same value from both directions.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1) for recognising that substituting $x=1$ produces $0/0$ and that division by zero is forbidden, (A1) for stating the expression is undefined, (A1) for noting the function has no value at $x=1$, and (R1) for the conclusion that direct evaluation fails and says nothing about the surrounding limit.

(b) The (M1) is for using $|x-1|=x-1$ when $x>1$ and cancelling the common factor to reach $x+1$; the (A1) is for that simplified linear form. The second (A1) with (AG) is for the right-hand limit $2$, awarded only when the limit is explicitly evaluated as $x\to1^{+}$. Follow through from a different but consistent simplification is allowed.

(c) The (M1) is for the negative absolute value $|x-1|=-(x-1)$ when $x<1$ and the simplification to $-(x+1)$; the (A1) is for that form. The (A1)(AG) pair is for the left-hand limit $-2$. The minus sign is the most common omission and must be present for the mark.

(d) Award (M1) for the criterion that one-sided limits must agree, (A1) for quoting both limits $2$ and $-2$, (A1) for the inequality $2\neq-2$, and (R1) for concluding the two-sided limit does not exist.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 5.2 Increasing and decreasing functions
syllabus_ref: SL 5.2 (increasing and decreasing functions; interpretation of f'(x))
title: The cubic whose derivative flips sign twice
q_html:
Consider the cubic function $f(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}-9x+5$.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    By differentiating the cubic term by term, show that $f'(x)=3(x-3)(x+1)$.

    (Show that)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Determine the intervals on which $f$ is increasing and the intervals on which $f$ is decreasing.

    (Determine)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Find the coordinates of the stationary point at $x=-1$ and state its nature.

    (Find)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Find the coordinates of the stationary point at $x=3$ and state its nature.

    (Find)
a_html:
(a) Differentiating term by term using the power rule gives $f'(x)=3x^{2}-6x-9$ (M1), which factors as $3(x^{2}-2x-3)$ (A1) and then as $3(x-3)(x+1)$ because $-3$ and $1$ sum to $-2$ and multiply to $-3$ (A1)(AG). Expanding $3(x-3)(x+1)$ returns $3x^{2}-6x-9$, confirming the factorisation is correct (R1). The derivative is therefore confirmed in a fully factored form that exposes its roots directly. This factorised shape is what makes the later sign analysis straightforward.

(b) The derivative is zero at $x=-1$ and $x=3$, which split the real line into three intervals (M1), and its sign is positive outside these roots and negative between them (A1). Hence $f$ is increasing on $x<-1$ and on $x>3$, and decreasing on $-1<x<3$ (A1)(A1). The sign change is read directly from the factored form $3(x-3)(x+1)$ by testing the sign of each linear factor. The function therefore rises, then falls, then rises again.

(c) Substituting $x=-1$ into the original function gives $f(-1)=(-1)^{3}-3(1)-9(-1)+5=-1-3+9+5=10$ (M1)(A1), so the stationary point is $(-1,10)$ (A1). Since the derivative changes from positive to negative as $x$ passes $-1$, the point is a local maximum (R1). The stationary point is therefore a peak on the curve at that coordinate.

(d) Substituting $x=3$ gives $f(3)=27-27-27+5=-22$ (M1)(A1), so the stationary point is $(3,-22)$ (A1). Since the derivative changes from negative to positive as $x$ passes $3$, the point is a local minimum (R1). The stationary point is therefore a trough, and the cubic has completed its rise-fall-rise pattern. The steep drop of 32 units between the two turning points is a direct consequence of the positive leading coefficient and is easily understated.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1) for the derivative $3x^{2}-6x-9$, (A1) for factoring out $3$ to reach $3(x^{2}-2x-3)$, and (A1)(AG) for the fully factored $3(x-3)(x+1)$. The (R1) is for verifying by expansion or by quoting the sum and product of the roots. A candidate who expands correctly but does not factor earns only the (M1).

(b) The (M1) is for the two roots $x=-1$ and $x=3$. The (A1) is for the correct sign pattern, and the two final (A1) marks are for the increasing intervals $x<-1$ and $x>3$ and the decreasing interval $-1<x<3$. Accept interval notation with or without the endpoints included.

(c) Award (M1) for substituting $x=-1$, (A1) for the $y$-value $10$, (A1) for the point $(-1,10)$, and (R1) for identifying it as a local maximum from the sign change of $f'$. Follow through from an incorrect derivative is allowed.

(d) Award (M1) for substituting $x=3$, (A1) for $-22$, (A1) for the point $(3,-22)$, and (R1) for local minimum. Follow through from an incorrect derivative is allowed provided the nature matches the sign change.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 5.3 Derivative of f(x) = ax^n
syllabus_ref: SL 5.3 (derivative of f(x)=ax^n is f'(x)=anx^{n-1}, n in Z; negative integer powers included)
title: The derivative that keeps a negative power
q_html:
Consider the function $f(x)=3x^{4}-5x^{2}+\frac{2}{x^{3}}-7$.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    By applying the power rule to each term, show that $f'(x)=12x^{3}-10x-6x^{-4}$.

    (Show that)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Find the gradient of the curve at $x=1$.

    (Find)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Find the gradient of the curve at $x=2$.

    (Find)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Find the gradient of the curve at $x=-1$ and determine whether $f$ is increasing or decreasing there.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) Writing $\frac{2}{x^{3}}=2x^{-3}$, the power rule gives $\frac{d}{dx}(3x^{4})=12x^{3}$, $\frac{d}{dx}(-5x^{2})=-10x$ and $\frac{d}{dx}(2x^{-3})=-6x^{-4}$, while the constant $-7$ differentiates to zero (M1)(A1). Adding these three pieces yields $f'(x)=12x^{3}-10x-6x^{-4}$ (A1)(AG). The negative power remains because the index of $2x^{-3}$ drops from $-3$ to $-4$ when differentiated (R1). The derivative is therefore confirmed with the negative power retained rather than converted back to a fraction. This is the form that must be used for every later substitution.

(b) Substituting $x=1$ into the derivative gives $f'(1)=12(1)-10(1)-6(1)=12-10-6=-4$ (M1)(A1), so the gradient at $x=1$ is $-4$ (A1). The value is negative because the $-6$ term dominates the other two contributions at this point (R1). The gradient is therefore $-4$, meaning the curve is sloping downwards as it passes through $x=1$.

(c) Substituting $x=2$ gives $f'(2)=12(8)-10(2)-6(2^{-4})=96-20-\frac{6}{16}=76-0.375=75.625$ (M1)(A1), so the gradient at $x=2$ is $75.625$ (A1). The fractional subtraction must be carried through exactly, since $6/16=0.375$, to reach this precise decimal (R1). The gradient is therefore $75.625$, a steep positive slope that contrasts sharply with the negative slope at $x=1$.

(d) Substituting $x=-1$ gives $f'(-1)=12(-1)-10(-1)-6(1)=-12+10-6=-8$ (M1)(A1), so the gradient is $-8$ (A1). Because the gradient is negative, the function is decreasing at $x=-1$ (R1). The negative gradient confirms the function falls there, just as it does at $x=1$, although the magnitude of the slope is larger. The negative gradient at both $x=1$ and $x=-1$ shows the curve is sloping downwards at those two points.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1) for rewriting $2/x^{3}$ as $2x^{-3}$ and differentiating each term with the power rule, (A1) for the three differentiated pieces, and (A1)(AG) for the combined derivative $12x^{3}-10x-6x^{-4}$. The (R1) is for noting the negative index is retained. A candidate who writes $6/x^{4}$ instead of $-6x^{-4}$ loses the final mark. The negative index is the single most tested detail and must not be dropped.

(b) The (M1) is for substituting $x=1$, (A1) for $12-10-6$, and (A1) for $-4$; the (R1) is for the negative gradient conclusion and its meaning for the slope of the curve.

(c) Award (M1) for substituting $x=2$, (A1) for $96-20-6/16$, (A1) for $75.625$, and (R1) for noting the exact fractional subtraction. A candidate who rounds $6/16$ to $0.4$ earns the value mark only if the final answer is $75.6$. Exact arithmetic is expected at HL.

(d) Award (M1) for substituting $x=-1$, (A1) for $-12+10-6$, (A1) for $-8$, and (R1) for stating the function is decreasing because the gradient is negative. Follow through from an incorrect derivative is allowed.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 5.4 Tangents and normals at a given point
syllabus_ref: SL 5.4 (tangents and normals at a given point, and their equations)
title: The tangent and normal to a curve that is not a polynomial
q_html:
Consider the curve $y=2x^{2}-\frac{3}{x}$.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Show that $\frac{dy}{dx}=4x+\frac{3}{x^{2}}$.

    (Show that)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Find the coordinates of the point on the curve where $x=1$ and the gradient of the curve there.

    (Find)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at $x=1$.

    (Find)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Find the equation of the normal to the curve at $x=1$.

    (Find)
a_html:
(a) Writing $\frac{3}{x}=3x^{-1}$, the derivative is $\frac{dy}{dx}=4x-(-3x^{-2})=4x+3x^{-2}=4x+\frac{3}{x^{2}}$ (M1)(A1)(A1)(AG). The reciprocal term contributes $3x^{-2}$ because differentiating $-3x^{-1}$ raises the index from $-1$ to $-2$ and keeps the minus sign from the original term (R1). The derivative is therefore confirmed as a sum of a polynomial part and a reciprocal part. This formula is the foundation for locating both the tangent and the normal.

(b) At $x=1$, the $y$-coordinate is $y=2(1)^{2}-\frac{3}{1}=2-3=-1$ (M1)(A1), so the point on the curve is $(1,-1)$; the gradient there is $\frac{dy}{dx}=4(1)+\frac{3}{1^{2}}=4+3=7$ (A1). The gradient is found by substituting $x=1$ into the derivative just established (R1). The point and the gradient are therefore $(1,-1)$ and $7$, both of which are needed for the two line equations.

(c) Using the point-gradient form $y-y_{1}=m(x-x_{1})$ with $m=7$ and $(1,-1)$ gives $y+1=7(x-1)$, which rearranges to $y=7x-8$ (M1)(A1). The tangent shares the curve's gradient at the point of contact, so its slope is exactly $7$ (A1). The equation is therefore $y=7x-8$, a line that just touches the curve at that single point (R1).

(d) The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its gradient is the negative reciprocal $-\frac{1}{7}$ (M1)(A1), and its equation is $y+1=-\frac{1}{7}(x-1)$, which simplifies to $y=-\frac{x}{7}-\frac{6}{7}$ (A1). The normal's gradient is the negative reciprocal of the tangent's gradient, so their product is $-1$ (R1). The equation is therefore $y=-\frac{x}{7}-\frac{6}{7}$, a line that cuts the curve at right angles at the point.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1) for rewriting $3/x$ as $3x^{-1}$ and differentiating, (A1) for the intermediate $4x+3x^{-2}$, and (A1)(AG) for the final $4x+3/x^{2}$. The (R1) is for explaining the sign of the reciprocal term. The sign must be positive for full marks; a candidate writing $-3/x^{2}$ loses the reasoning mark. The reciprocal contribution is the main trap and must be shown explicitly.

(b) The (M1) is for substituting $x=1$ into $y$, (A1) for $y=-1$, (A1) for the gradient $7$ from the derivative, and (R1) for linking the gradient to the derivative. The point is $(1,-1)$. Both coordinates are required before either line can be written.

(c) Award (M1) for the point-gradient form, (A1) for $y+1=7(x-1)$, (A1) for $y=7x-8$, and (R1) for stating the tangent shares the curve's gradient. Accept equivalent forms such as $7x-y-8=0$.

(d) Award (M1) for the perpendicular gradient $-1/7$, (A1) for using point-gradient, (A1) for $y=-x/7-6/7$, and (R1) for the negative reciprocal property. Follow through from an incorrect gradient in (b) is allowed. Candidates who leave the answer in unsimplified point-gradient form earn the first two marks only.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 5.5 Introduction to integration as anti-differentiation
syllabus_ref: SL 5.5 (introduction to integration as anti-differentiation of polynomial and exponential functions; the constant of integration)
title: Rebuilding the function from its derivative and a single point
q_html:
A function $f$ satisfies $f'(x)=6x^{2}-4x$ and $f(1)=5$.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Find the general antiderivative of $f'(x)$, including the constant of integration.

    (Find)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Find the value of the constant of integration, given that $f(1)=5$.

    (Find)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Hence find the exact value of the function when $x=2$.

    (Find)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Show that $\int_{1}^{2} f'(x)\,dx = f(2)-f(1)=8$.

    (Show that)
a_html:
(a) Integrating $f'(x)=6x^{2}-4x$ term by term gives $f(x)=6\cdot\frac{x^{3}}{3}-4\cdot\frac{x^{2}}{2}+C=2x^{3}-2x^{2}+C$ (M1)(A1). The constant $C$ must be included because integration undoes differentiation only up to an additive constant (A1). The general form is therefore $f(x)=2x^{3}-2x^{2}+C$, representing a whole family of parallel curves (R1). The antiderivative is confirmed with the constant present, since any two antiderivatives differ only by a constant. This family picture is essential: without the condition in part (b) the exact curve cannot be singled out.

(b) Using the condition $f(1)=5$ gives $2(1)^{3}-2(1)^{2}+C=5$, so $2-2+C=5$ and therefore $C=5$ (M1)(A1). The single data point pins down the otherwise free constant uniquely (A1). The particular function is therefore $f(x)=2x^{3}-2x^{2}+5$ (R1), the one member of the family that passes through $(1,5)$.

(c) With $C=5$ fixed, substituting $x=2$ gives $f(2)=2(8)-2(4)+5=16-8+5=13$ (M1)(A1), so $f(2)=13$ (A1). This value is found by substituting into the fully determined function, not by differentiating again (R1). The value is therefore $13$, the height of the curve above the axis at that point.

(d) By the fundamental theorem of calculus, $\int_{1}^{2}f'(x)\,dx=f(2)-f(1)$ (M1), so this equals $13-5=8$ (A1). Direct integration confirms it: $\int_{1}^{2}(6x^{2}-4x)\,dx=[2x^{3}-2x^{2}]_{1}^{2}=(16-8)-(2-2)=8$ (A1), showing the two routes agree (R1). The two methods agree, so the integral is $8$, which is exactly the net change in $f$ across the interval. Both the rebuilt function and the direct integral give the same number, which is the essence of the fundamental theorem.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1) for integrating each term of $6x^{2}-4x$, (A1) for $2x^{3}-2x^{2}$, (A1) for the constant $C$, and (R1) for noting an antiderivative needs the constant because differentiation erases it. A candidate who omits $C$ loses the constant mark but may earn the others. The constant is what distinguishes the family of solutions.

(b) The (M1) is for substituting $x=1$ into the antiderivative, (A1) for $2-2+C=5$, (A1) for $C=5$, and (R1) for the idea that one point fixes the constant uniquely. Follow through from an incorrect antiderivative is allowed.

(c) Award (M1) for substituting $x=2$, (A1) for $16-8+5$, (A1) for $13$, and (R1) for the interpretation that this is a function value, not a derivative. A candidate using the wrong $C$ forfeits only the final value if the method is sound.

(d) Award (M1) for the fundamental theorem $f(2)-f(1)$, (A1) for $13-5=8$, (A1) for the direct integration giving $8$, and (R1) for confirming the two methods agree. Both routes must be shown for full credit. Partial credit follows through from earlier errors in the antiderivative.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 5.7 The second derivative
syllabus_ref: SL 5.7 (the second derivative; concavity and points of inflection)
title: The second derivative that changes sign at two points
q_html:
Consider the function $f(x)=x^{4}-8x^{3}+18x^{2}$. You are to analyse its concavity using the second derivative.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Show that $f''(x)=12x^{2}-48x+36$ and that this factorises as $12(x-1)(x-3)$.

    (Show that)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Find the values of $x$ for which $f''(x)=0$, and state why these are the only candidates for a change of concavity.

    (Find)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Determine whether the curve is convex or concave on each of the intervals $x<1$, $1<x<3$ and $x>3$.

    (Determine)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Show that $x=1$ and $x=3$ are both points of inflection.

    (Show that)
a_html:
(a) Begin by differentiating the polynomial $f(x)=x^{4}-8x^{3}+18x^{2}$ once with respect to $x$ to obtain $f'(x)=4x^{3}-24x^{2}+36x$ (M1), then differentiate this result a second time to obtain $f''(x)=12x^{2}-48x+36$ (A1). The quadratic $x^{2}-4x+3$ factors as $(x-1)(x-3)$, so $f''(x)=12(x-1)(x-3)$ (A1)(AG). This confirms the given form, because multiplying the brackets back together restores $12x^{2}-48x+36$ exactly, leaving no remainder, and this step underpins every later part.

(b) Concavity can only change where the second derivative vanishes, so solve $12(x-1)(x-3)=0$ (M1). A product of real factors is zero precisely when one factor is zero, giving $x-1=0$ or $x-3=0$, thus $x=1$ and $x=3$ (A1). These two values are the only real roots of the quadratic, so they form the complete set of candidates that must be tested for a sign change before any conclusion is drawn.

(c) Choose one convenient test value inside each of the three intervals. At $x=0$ we have $f''(0)=36>0$, so the curve is convex on $x<1$ (M1). At $x=2$ we have $f''(2)=-12<0$, so it is concave on the middle interval $1<x<3$ (A1). At $x=4$ we have $f''(4)=36>0$, so it is convex again on $x>3$ (A1). The sign of $f''(x)$ alone decides the concavity on every open interval, and the integer test values keep the arithmetic exact and easy to verify.

(d) At $x=1$ the second derivative passes from positive to negative, and at $x=3$ it passes from negative to positive (M1), so each of these points is a point of inflection (A1)(AG). The function values at the two points are $f(1)=11$ and $f(3)=27$. A point of inflection is defined by a genuine change of sign in $f''(x)$, which occurs at both $x=1$ and $x=3$, and this is precisely why the classification is valid.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1) for the first derivative $4x^{3}-24x^{2}+36x$ and (A1) for the second derivative $12x^{2}-48x+36$. The factorisation (A1)(AG) requires $12(x-1)(x-3)$ to be shown; accept the working written in either order. A candidate who expands the bracket incorrectly loses the final mark but may keep the two derivative marks.

(b) Award (M1) for setting $12(x-1)(x-3)=0$ and (A1) for both roots $x=1$ and $x=3$. The remark that these are the only candidates is part of the reasoning and need not be written, but follow through from a wrong quadratic is allowed provided the solving step is consistent with it.

(c) Award (M1) for a correct sign test giving convex on $x<1$, (A1) for concave on $1<x<3$, and (A1) for convex on $x>3$. The three test values need not be $0$, $2$, $4$ but the computed signs must be correct. A candidate who states the concavity from $f'$ rather than $f''$ forfeits all three marks.

(d) Award (M1) for identifying the sign change at each root and (A1)(AG) for both points of inflection. The function values $11$ and $27$ are optional supporting detail; the decisive fact is the change of sign, and a candidate who states a root without showing the sign change earns at most one mark.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 5.8 Local maximum and minimum points
syllabus_ref: SL 5.8 (local maximum and minimum points; use of f'(x)=0 and the second derivative test)
title: The cubic with a maximum and a minimum found by the second derivative
q_html:
Consider the function $f(x)=(x-1)^{2}(x+2)$, which expands to $f(x)=x^{3}-3x+2$.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    By differentiating the expanded cubic form, show that $f'(x)=3(x-1)(x+1)$.

    (Show that)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Find the stationary points of $f$, giving their $x$-coordinates.

    (Find)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Use the second derivative $f''(x)=6x$ to classify each stationary point as a maximum or a minimum.

    (Determine)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Determine the coordinates of the local maximum and the local minimum.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) Differentiate the expanded form $f(x)=x^{3}-3x+2$ to obtain $f'(x)=3x^{2}-3$ (M1). Factoring the result gives $3(x^{2}-1)=3(x-1)(x+1)$ (A1)(AG). This matches the required derivative exactly, because the constant term $2$ disappears when the function is differentiated and the remaining terms factor neatly. The factorised form is the most useful version of the derivative, because it displays the roots directly without any further algebra.

(b) Stationary points occur where the gradient is zero, so solve $3(x-1)(x+1)=0$ (M1). A product is zero when $x-1=0$ or $x+1=0$, giving the two $x$-coordinates $x=-1$ and $x=1$ (A1). These are the only real solutions, so they are the complete list of places where the curve could turn. Both $x$-coordinates must be found before any classification can begin, since the second derivative test is applied separately at each one.

(c) The second derivative here is the simple linear function $f''(x)=6x$ (M1). At $x=-1$ we have $f''(-1)=-6<0$, which means the curve is bending downwards, so the point is a local maximum (A1). At $x=1$ we have $f''(1)=6>0$, which means the curve is bending upwards, so the point is a local minimum (A1). This linear second derivative is unusually convenient, because its sign is fixed simply by the sign of $x$, and the sign of $f''$ alone decides the nature of each stationary point.

(d) Substitute the two $x$-values back into $f$. We have $f(-1)=(-1)^{3}-3(-1)+2=4$, so the local maximum is at $(-1,4)$ (M1)(A1). Also $f(1)=1^{3}-3(1)+2=0$, so the local minimum is at $(1,0)$ (A1). Recording both coordinates completes the description of the turning points and confirms the overall shape of the cubic, which is why the final coordinates are correct.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1) for the derivative $3x^{2}-3$ and (A1)(AG) for the factorised form $3(x-1)(x+1)$. Accept differentiation of the product $(x-1)^{2}(x+2)$ if it reaches the same result. A candidate who writes $3x^{2}-3$ but fails to factor it earns only the method mark and not the accuracy mark.

(b) Award (M1) for setting the derivative equal to zero and (A1) for both roots $x=-1$ and $x=1$. Follow through from an incorrect derivative is allowed provided the equation is solved consistently with it. Both roots are required for the later classification marks in part (c).

(c) Award (M1) for stating $f''(x)=6x$, (A1) for the local maximum at $x=-1$ using the fact that $f''(-1)<0$, and (A1) for the local minimum at $x=1$ using $f''(1)>0$. The second derivative test must actually be applied; a candidate who classifies from a sketch earns no credit here.

(d) Award (M1) for substituting into $f$ and (A1) for $(-1,4)$, then (A1) for $(1,0)$. A candidate who gives only the $x$-values forfeits the coordinate marks, and the values $4$ and $0$ must be computed, not read from a graph.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 5.19 Maclaurin series
syllabus_ref: AHL 5.19 (Maclaurin series to obtain expansions for composite functions), AHL 5.13 (evaluation of limits of the form 0/0)
title: A Maclaurin expansion whose cubic term vanishes
q_html:
Let $f(x)=\mathrm{e}^{\sin x}$.

  1. [5 marks](a)

    Using the Maclaurin expansions of $\mathrm{e}^{u}$ and $\sin x$, show that the Maclaurin expansion of $f$ begins $f(x)=1+x+\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}+a x^{3}-\dfrac{x^{4}}{8}+\cdots$ and state the value of $a$.

    (Show that)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Determine the coefficient of $x^{5}$ in the Maclaurin expansion of $f$.

    (Determine)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Hence state the values of $f'''(0)$ and $f''''(0)$, justifying briefly how the expansion gives them.

    (State)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Hence determine $\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{\sin x}-1-x}{x^{2}}$.

    (Hence)
a_html:
$\sin x=x-\dfrac{x^{3}}{6}+\dfrac{x^{5}}{120}-\cdots$ and $\mathrm{e}^{u}=1+u+\dfrac{u^{2}}{2}+\dfrac{u^{3}}{6}+\dfrac{u^{4}}{24}+\cdots$ (M1)

With $u=\sin x$: $u^{2}=x^{2}-\dfrac{x^{4}}{3}+\cdots$, $u^{3}=x^{3}+\cdots$, $u^{4}=x^{4}+\cdots$ (M1)

Substituting and collecting like powers: $1+\left(x-\dfrac{x^{3}}{6}\right)+\left(\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}-\dfrac{x^{4}}{6}\right)+\dfrac{x^{3}}{6}+\dfrac{x^{4}}{24}$ (M1)

The $x^{3}$ terms are $-\dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{1}{6}=0$, and the $x^{4}$ terms are $-\dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{1}{24}=-\dfrac{1}{8}$, so
$$f(x)=1+x+\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}-\dfrac{x^{4}}{8}+\cdots$$(A1)

hence $a=0$. (A1)

(b) Only three powers of $u$ contribute to $x^{5}$: the $x^{5}$ term of $u$ itself, of $u^{3}/6$, and of $u^{5}/120$. (M1)

$u^{3}=\left(x-\dfrac{x^{3}}{6}\right)^{3}+\cdots=x^{3}-3x^{2}\cdot\dfrac{x^{3}}{6}+\cdots=x^{3}-\dfrac{x^{5}}{2}+\cdots$, so $\dfrac{u^{3}}{6}$ contributes $-\dfrac{1}{12}$; $u^{5}=x^{5}+\cdots$ so $\dfrac{u^{5}}{120}$ contributes $+\dfrac{1}{120}$. (M1)

The $x^{5}$ term of $u$ is $+\dfrac{1}{120}$ and $u^{2}$, $u^{4}$ contribute nothing. (A1)

Coefficient $=\dfrac{1}{120}-\dfrac{1}{12}+\dfrac{1}{120}=\dfrac{2-20+2}{240}=-\dfrac{16}{240}=-\dfrac{1}{15}$ (A1)

(c) If $f(x)=\sum \dfrac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}x^{n}$ then the coefficient of $x^{n}$ equals $\dfrac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}$. (M1)

The coefficient of $x^{3}$ is $0$, so $f'''(0)=3!\times 0=0$. (A1)

The coefficient of $x^{4}$ is $-\dfrac{1}{8}$, so $f''''(0)=24\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{8}\right)=-3$. (A1)

(d) Writing $\mathrm{e}^{\sin x}-1-x=\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}-\dfrac{x^{4}}{8}+\cdots$ (M1) and dividing by $x^{2}$ gives $\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{x^{2}}{8}+\cdots$ (A1), so the limit is $\dfrac{1}{2}$. (A1)

The vanishing cubic term is what makes the limit finite and non-zero: had $a\neq 0$ the quotient would still have a term in $x$ and would diverge.

Markscheme notes

Award (M1) for each of the two series substitutions and once more for collecting terms; an answer that differentiates $f$ three or four times to reach the same coefficients is fully acceptable and should be credited with (M1)(M1)(M1) for the differentiation chain, provided the product and chain rules are handled. Condonation: a candidate who writes $u^{2}=x^{2}-x^{4}/3$ without justification keeps the (M1); the term in $x^{6}$ is not required. In (b), follow-through applies: a candidate with the wrong $u^{3}$ still earns the final (A1) for a consistent sum of three contributions. The most common error is omitting the $u^{5}/120$ contribution, which alone gives $-1/12+1/120=-9/120$; this loses the last (A1) but keeps both (M1). In (c) do not accept a bare 'because the coefficient is zero' without the $n!$ relationship. In (d), accepting $1/2$ with no working after part (a) earns the (A1) only. Two further condonations. A candidate who states $a=0$ in (a) and then uses $f'''(0)=0$ in (c) without recomputing the coefficient has still demonstrated the required link, so the (R1) is earned; the (A1) in (c) depends only on reading the two coefficients off the series correctly. And in (d) a candidate who reaches $1/2$ by substituting the truncated series rather than by L'Hôpital should be credited equally, since the expansion is the intended route.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 3.18 Intersections of a line with a plane, two planes, three planes
syllabus_ref: AHL 1.16 (solutions of systems of linear equations: unique, no solution, infinitely many), AHL 3.18 (intersections of three planes), AHL 3.14 (vector equation of a line)
title: Three planes that never meet in more than a line
q_html:
Three planes are given by
$$\Pi_{1}:\ x+y+z=2,\qquad \Pi_{2}:\ 2x+3y+2z=5,\qquad \Pi_{3}:\ x+y+kz=k+2$$ where $k$ is a real constant.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Show that $\Pi_{1}$ and $\Pi_{2}$ intersect in a line $L$, and give a vector equation for $L$.

    (Show that)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    For $k\neq 1$, find the position vector of the single point of intersection of the three planes, in terms of $k$.

    (Find)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Explain why there is exactly one value of $k$ for which the three planes have no common point. State that value and describe the geometric configuration of the three planes in that case.

    (Explain)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    For the value of $k$ found in part (c), determine the distance between the two lines in which $\Pi_{2}$ cuts $\Pi_{1}$ and $\Pi_{3}$.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) Eliminating $x$: $\Pi_{2}-2\Pi_{1}$ gives $y=1$. (M1) Substituting into $\Pi_{1}$ gives $x+z=1$, so the two planes do meet in a line, with direction vector perpendicular to both normals $(1,1,1)$ and $(2,3,2)$, for example $(-1,\,0,\,1)$. (M1)

Taking the point $x=1,\ y=1,\ z=0$: $L:\ \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$. (A1)

(b) On $L$, $y=1$ and $x=1-z$. Substituting into $\Pi_{3}$: $(1-z)+1+kz=k+2$ (M1), so $z(k-1)=k$ (M1), giving $z=\dfrac{k}{k-1}$ (A1) and $x=1-\dfrac{k}{k-1}=-\dfrac{1}{k-1}$ (A1).

The point of intersection is therefore $\left(-\dfrac{1}{k-1},\ 1,\ \dfrac{k}{k-1}\right)$. (A1)

*(Check with $k=2$: $(-1,1,2)$, and $-1+1+2=2$, $2(-1)+3+4=5$, $-1+1+4=4=k+2$. Correct.)*

(c) The equation $z(k-1)=k$ determines $z$ for every $k$ except $k=1$: at $k=1$ it becomes $0\cdot z=1$, which has no solution. (M1)

At $k=1$, $\Pi_{3}$ becomes $x+y+z=3$, which has the same normal as $\Pi_{1}$: $x+y+z=2$. The two planes are parallel and distinct, so they share no point and the three planes have no common point. (A1)

Since $z(k-1)=k$ has a solution for every other value of $k$, this is the only such value. (A1)

The configuration is a triangular prism: $\Pi_{1}$ and $\Pi_{3}$ are parallel, and $\Pi_{2}$ cuts them in two distinct parallel lines. Each pair of planes still meets in a line, so the system is not 'inconsistent because two planes are parallel to each other alone' — every plane meets every other plane. (A1)

(d) $L_{1}=\Pi_{1}\cap\Pi_{2}$: subtracting twice $\Pi_{1}$ from $\Pi_{2}$ gives $y=1$, then $x+z=1$. (M1)

$L_{2}=\Pi_{3}\cap\Pi_{2}$: subtracting twice $\Pi_{3}$ from $\Pi_{2}$ gives $y=-1$, then $x+z=4$. (M1)

Both have direction $(-1,0,1)$. With $A(1,1,0)$ on $L_{1}$ and $B(3,-1,1)$ on $L_{2}$, $\overrightarrow{AB}=(2,-2,1)$ and $\overrightarrow{AB}\times(-1,0,1)=(-2,-3,-2)$, whose magnitude is $\sqrt{17}$; dividing by $\left|(-1,0,1)\right|=\sqrt{2}$ gives a distance of $\dfrac{\sqrt{17}}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{17}{2}}\approx 2.92$. (A1)

Markscheme notes

Part (a): accept any correct direction vector parallel to $(-1,0,1)$ and any point on the line; the (M1) for the elimination should be given even if the candidate then uses a different method, provided the inconsistency is not hidden. Part (b): a candidate who solves by full row reduction of the augmented matrix earns (M1)(M1) and follows through for the point marks. Part (c): the essential mark is the geometric description, not the word 'prism' — accept 'two parallel planes cut by a third' or 'the planes form a prism with no common point'. A candidate who simply states $k=1$ and 'no solution' without explaining why it is unique loses the third (A1). Part (d): accept any valid method, including projecting $\overrightarrow{AB}$ perpendicular to the common direction, or using the formula for the distance between parallel lines with a normal obtained from the cross product. Follow-through: a candidate using $\sqrt{17}$ as the final answer has divided by the wrong magnitude and loses the last (A1) only. Beware of candidates who treat the two lines as skew and compute a shortest distance between them without noticing they are parallel.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 4.14 Variance of a discrete random variable
syllabus_ref: AHL 4.14 (variance of a discrete random variable; E(X^2) - (E(X))^2), SL 4.7 (concept of discrete random variables and their probability distributions)
title: A card game whose expected value hides in a parameter
q_html:
A bag contains five cards numbered $1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4$ and $k$, where $k$ is an integer greater than $4$. Two cards are drawn at random without replacement, and $S$ denotes the sum of the numbers on the two cards.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    The two cards are drawn at random and the sum is recorded. Show that the expected value of this sum is $\mathrm{E}(S)=4+\dfrac{2k}{5}$.

    (Show that)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Find the least value of $k$ for which the expected value of $S$ exceeds $10$.

    (Find)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    For the case $k=10$, calculate the variance of the sum $S$, showing the values of $\mathrm{E}(S)$ and $\mathrm{E}(S^{2})$ that you use.

    (Calculate)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    For $k=10$ a player pays $9$ (in the currency units of the game) to play and receives the value of $S$. Determine whether the game favours the player, and find the probability that the player makes a profit.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) There are $\dbinom{5}{2}=10$ equally likely pairs, so each has probability $0.1$. (M1)

The six pairs that avoid $k$ give sums $1+2=3$, $1+3=4$, $1+4=5$, $2+3=5$, $2+4=6$, $3+4=7$, whose total is $30$. (M1)

The four pairs containing $k$ give $(1+k)+(2+k)+(3+k)+(4+k)=10+4k$. (A1)

So $\displaystyle\sum S=30+10+4k=40+4k$ and $\mathrm{E}(S)=\dfrac{40+4k}{10}=4+\dfrac{2k}{5}$. (AG)

Check, by linearity of expectation. Each of the five values appears in $4$ of the $10$ pairs, so the two drawn cards have the same marginal distribution; its mean is $\dfrac{1+2+3+4+k}{5}=\dfrac{10+k}{5}$. Hence

$$\mathrm{E}(S)=2\times\frac{10+k}{5}=4+\frac{2k}{5}\quad\checkmark$$

(b) $4+\dfrac{2k}{5}>10\Rightarrow \dfrac{2k}{5}>6\Rightarrow k>15$. (M1)(A1) As $k$ is an integer, the least such value is $k=16$. (A1)

(c) With $k=10$ the ten sums are $3,\ 4,\ 5,\ 11,\ 5,\ 6,\ 12,\ 7,\ 13,\ 14$, so $\mathrm{E}(S)=\dfrac{80}{10}=8$. (M1)

$\displaystyle\mathrm{E}(S^{2})=\dfrac{9+16+25+121+25+36+144+49+169+196}{10}=\dfrac{790}{10}=79$. (M1)(A1)

$\mathrm{Var}(S)=\mathrm{E}(S^{2})-\left[\mathrm{E}(S)\right]^{2}=79-64=15$. (M1)(A1)

(d) $\mathrm{E}(S)=8<9$, so the player pays more on average than they receive and the game favours the organiser. (A1) The organiser's expected margin is $9-8=1$ unit per game, and over many plays the player's losses converge to that figure.

The expectation is therefore below the stake, and the arithmetic has not yet said anything about how often a player wins.

A profit requires $S>9$, that is $S\in\{11,12,13,14\}$, which occurs in $4$ of the $10$ equally likely outcomes. (M1) So $\mathrm{P}(\text{profit})=0.4$. (A1)

Markscheme notes

Part (a): the (AG) requires the total to be exhibited, not merely asserted. A candidate who lists the distribution correctly earns both (M1) marks even if the algebra afterwards slips; do not condone an answer that treats the draw as ordered and then divides by 20 as well. Part (b): accept $k=15$ only if the candidate explicitly notes that the strict inequality excludes it — otherwise the answer mark is lost. Part (c): accept the grouped distribution $\mathrm{P}(S=5)=0.2$, $\mathrm{P}(S=3)=\mathrm{P}(S=4)=\mathrm{P}(S=6)=\mathrm{P}(S=7)=0.1$, $\mathrm{P}(S=11)=\mathrm{P}(S=13)=0.1$ and so on, provided the total probability is 1. Follow-through: a candidate whose $\mathrm{E}(S)$ from part (a) is wrong but consistent still earns the two method marks and the first accuracy mark in (c). A very common error is to compute $\mathrm{E}(S^{2})$ with $\mathrm{E}(S)^{2}$ substituted — this forfeits both (M1) marks in (c). In (d) accept a correct comparison of the expectation with the stake in either direction; the probability mark is independent of the judgement.

For part (c) a candidate may use the finite-population variance of a sample without replacement: with values $1,2,3,4,10$ the population variance is $\sigma^{2}=10$, so $\mathrm{Var}(S)=2\sigma^{2}\cdot\tfrac{5-2}{5-1}=15$, provided the factor $\tfrac{N-n}{N-1}$ is stated. In part (d) accept $\tfrac25$ or $40\%$.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 2.16 Graphs of y = |f(x)|, y = f(|x|) and y = 1/f(x)
syllabus_ref: AHL 2.16 (graphs of y = |f(x)|, y = f(|x|) and y = 1/f(x)), AHL 2.15 (solutions of g(x) >= f(x) graphically and analytically)
title: Two reflections that agree on a set
q_html:
Let $f(x)=x^{2}-4x+3$.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    On the same axes, sketch the graphs of $y=|f(x)|$ and $y=f(|x|)$, stating the coordinates of all intercepts and of every local minimum or maximum.

    (Sketch)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Solve the equation $|f(x)|=f(|x|)$, giving your answer as a union of intervals.

    (Solve)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Solve the inequality $f(|x|)<2$, giving exact values in your answer.

    (Solve)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Determine the range of $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$ and the equations of all three asymptotes of its graph.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) $f(x)=(x-1)(x-3)$, so the parabola has roots at $x=1$ and $x=3$ and its minimum is $f(2)=-1$.

$y=|f(x)|$: the part of the parabola below the axis is reflected upwards. Intercepts $(1,0)$, $(3,0)$, $(0,3)$; local maxima at $(1,0)$ and $(3,0)$; local minimum $(2,1)$. (M1)(A1)

$y=f(|x|)$: the right-hand half is reflected in the $y$-axis. Intercepts $(-3,0)$, $(-1,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(3,0)$ and $(0,3)$; local minima at $(-2,-1)$ and $(2,-1)$; local maximum $(0,3)$. (M1)(A1)

(b) For $x\geq 0$, $f(|x|)=f(x)$, so the equation becomes $|f(x)|=f(x)$, which holds exactly when $f(x)\geq 0$, i.e. $x\leq 1$ or $x\geq 3$. (M1)(A1) On $[0,\infty)$ this gives $[0,1]\cup[3,\infty)$.

For $x<0$, $f(|x|)=f(-x)=x^{2}+4x+3$ while $|f(x)|=x^{2}-4x+3$, since $f(x)>0$ for all $x<0$. Equating gives $x^{2}+4x+3=x^{2}-4x+3$, so $8x=0$ and $x=0$, which is not negative. (M1) There are therefore no negative solutions, and the solution set is $[0,1]\cup[3,\infty)$. (A1)

(c) With $u=|x|\geq 0$, $f(|x|)<2$ becomes $u^{2}-4u+1<0$. (M1) The roots are $u=2\pm\sqrt{3}$, so $2-\sqrt{3}<u<2+\sqrt{3}$. (A1) Since $u=|x|$, the solution is $x\in\left(-\left(2+\sqrt{3}\right),-\left(2-\sqrt{3}\right)\right)\cup\left(2-\sqrt{3},\ 2+\sqrt{3}\right)$. (A1)

(d) $f$ has minimum value $-1$ at $x=2$ and $f(x)\to\infty$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, so the range of $f$ is $[-1,\infty)$. Therefore the range of $g$ is $(-\infty,-1]\cup(0,\infty)$. (M1)(A1)

The vertical asymptotes are $x=1$ and $x=3$; the horizontal asymptote is $y=0$. (A1)(A1)

Markscheme notes

Part (a): accept sketches that show the correct shape and the stated key points; a candidate who reflects only one branch, or who draws $y=f(|x|)$ with the minimum at $(2,-1)$ only on the right, loses one (M1). Do not require accurate curvature. Part (b): the crucial mark is the split at $x=0$; a candidate who solves only the positive case and writes $[0,1]\cup[3,\infty)$ with no mention of $x<0$ earns (M1)(A1) and loses the remaining two marks. Accept an argument from the sketch that the two graphs coincide precisely where the parabola is above the axis and $x\geq0$, provided the negativity of $x$ on the other side is addressed. Part (c): accept $0.27<|x|<3.73$ as an intermediate, and condone a final answer in the form $|x|\in(2-\sqrt{3},2+\sqrt{3})$ only if the resulting $x$-interval is also given. Part (d): the (A1) for the range depends on identifying the minimum of $f$; a candidate who gives $(-\infty,0)\cup(0,\infty)$ has missed the upper bound of the negative branch entirely and loses both range marks but keeps the three asymptote marks.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 5.16 Integration by substitution; 5.17 Area of a region enclosed by a curve and the y-axis
syllabus_ref: AHL 5.16 (integration by substitution), AHL 5.17 (area of the region enclosed by a curve and the y-axis)
title: A segment that needs the left branch and a shifted substitution
q_html:
The curve $C$ has equation $x^{2}+y^{2}-4x-6y-3=0$. The region $R$ is the region enclosed by $C$ and the $y$-axis.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    By completing the square, show that $C$ is a circle and state the coordinates of its centre and the value of its radius. Hence find the $y$-coordinates of the two points where $C$ meets the $y$-axis.

    (Show that)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Explain why the region $R$ requires the branch $x=2-\sqrt{16-(y-3)^{2}}$ rather than the positive square root, and hence write down a definite integral with respect to $y$ whose value is the area of $R$.

    (Explain)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Using the substitution $y-3=4\sin\theta$, determine the value of $\displaystyle\int_{3-2\sqrt{3}}^{3+2\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{16-(y-3)^{2}}\,dy$, showing clearly how the limits of integration change.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Hence determine the exact area of the region $R$, giving your answer in the form $a\pi+b\sqrt{3}$ where $a$ and $b$ are integers.

    (Hence)
a_html:
(a) Completing the square in $x$ and in $y$,

$$x^{2}-4x+y^{2}-6y-3=(x-2)^{2}-4+(y-3)^{2}-9-3=(x-2)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}-16.$$ (M1)

Setting this equal to zero gives $(x-2)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}=16$, so $C$ is the circle with centre $(2,3)$ and radius $4$. (A1) On the $y$-axis $x=0$, so $4+(y-3)^{2}=16$, giving $(y-3)^{2}=12$ and therefore $y=3\pm2\sqrt{3}$. (A1)

(b) Solving $(x-2)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}=16$ for $x$ gives $x=2\pm\sqrt{16-(y-3)^{2}}$, so for each $y$ between $3-2\sqrt{3}$ and $3+2\sqrt{3}$ the circle has two points with the same $y$-coordinate. (M1) The centre has $x$-coordinate $2>0$, so the segment cut off by the $y$-axis lies to the left of that axis, where $x<0$; the branch with the negative square root, $x=2-\sqrt{16-(y-3)^{2}}$, is the only one that can produce $x<0$, and it is the boundary of $R$. (A1) The $y$-axis itself contributes $x=0$, so the area is the integral of $0-x$ over the $y$-range of the segment: (M1)

$$A(R)=\int_{3-2\sqrt{3}}^{3+2\sqrt{3}}\Bigl(\sqrt{16-(y-3)^{2}}-2\Bigr)\,dy.$$ (A1) *(AG)*

(c) Let $y-3=4\sin\theta$ with $-\tfrac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $dy=4\cos\theta\,d\theta$ and $\sqrt{16-(y-3)^{2}}=\sqrt{16-16\sin^{2}\theta}=4\cos\theta$, since $\cos\theta\ge0$ on this interval. (M1) When $y=3-2\sqrt{3}$ we have $\sin\theta=-\tfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{4}=-\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, so $\theta=-\tfrac{\pi}{3}$; when $y=3+2\sqrt{3}$ we have $\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{3}$. (A1) Hence

$$\int_{3-2\sqrt{3}}^{3+2\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{16-(y-3)^{2}}\,dy=\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3}(4\cos\theta)(4\cos\theta)\,d\theta=16\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3}\cos^{2}\theta\,d\theta.$$ (A1)

Using $\cos^{2}\theta=\tfrac{1}{2}(1+\cos 2\theta)$,

$$16\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3}\cos^{2}\theta\,d\theta=16\left[\frac{\theta}{2}+\frac{\sin 2\theta}{4}\right]_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3}=16\left(\frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right)=\frac{16\pi}{3}+4\sqrt{3}.$$ (M1)(A1)

(d) From part (b), $A(R)$ is the value just found minus the contribution of the $y$-axis boundary, so

$$A(R)=\int_{3-2\sqrt{3}}^{3+2\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{16-(y-3)^{2}}\,dy-\int_{3-2\sqrt{3}}^{3+2\sqrt{3}}2\,dy.$$ (M1) The first integral is $\frac{16\pi}{3}+4\sqrt{3}$ from part (c), and the second is $2\bigl(4\sqrt{3}\bigr)=8\sqrt{3}$. (A1) Therefore

$$A(R)=\frac{16\pi}{3}+4\sqrt{3}-8\sqrt{3}=\frac{16\pi}{3}-4\sqrt{3}.$$ (A1)

This is the area of a circular segment, and it is consistent with the sector minus triangle formula $\tfrac{1}{2}r^{2}(\theta-\sin\theta)$ for $r=4$ and $\theta=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

Markscheme notes

(a) The (M1) is for completing the square, which must be visible; a candidate who writes down the centre and radius with no rearrangement earns only the accuracy marks. The centre is $(2,3)$, not $(-2,-3)$: the signs come from $x^{2}-4x=(x-2)^{2}-4$ and $y^{2}-6y=(y-3)^{2}-9$. The final (A1) requires $(y-3)^{2}=12$, so $y=3\pm2\sqrt{3}$; accept the exact surd form and do not penalise a decimal that rounds correctly.

(b) The essential marks are for identifying that the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis and that the left boundary is the branch with the negative square root. A candidate who writes $x=2+\sqrt{16-(y-3)^{2}}$ has chosen the arc on the right and is integrating the wrong region; that forfeits the second (A1), but follow-through is allowed if the remaining geometry is correct. The integrand $0-x$ must appear; a candidate who integrates $x$ directly and reports a negative quantity should still earn the method marks if the final area is then taken positive. The *(AG)* requires the integral with the correct limits to be stated.

(c) The substitution must be carried through with the shift. A candidate who sets $y=4\sin\theta$ and leaves the constant $3$ out will obtain incorrect limits and should not earn the limit (A1); the method (M1) for the substitution may still be awarded. The identity $\cos^{2}\theta=\tfrac{1}{2}(1+\cos 2\theta)$ must be used correctly, and the evaluation may be done by symmetry since the integrand is even in $\theta$. A candidate who substitutes $u=16-(y-3)^{2}$ cannot remove the stray factor of $y-3$ and gains nothing beyond the initial (M1).

(d) The (M1) is for splitting off the constant term, and the two (A1) marks for the value $\frac{16\pi}{3}+4\sqrt{3}$ carried through and the final $\frac{16\pi}{3}-4\sqrt{3}$. A candidate who leaves the answer as an unsimplified difference of integrals has not answered the question. The exact value is about $9.83$, so a numerical check against the circular segment formula is a sensible verification.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 1.1 Standard form and 1.5 Laws of exponents with integer exponents
syllabus_ref: SL 1.1 (operations with numbers in the form a × 10^k) and SL 1.5 (laws of exponents with integer exponents)
title: A unit slip worth three orders of magnitude
q_html:
A metallurgy laboratory measures the mass of a single atom of a metal as $3.27 \times 10^{-22}$ g. A prepared sample is found to contain $4.5 \times 10^{19}$ atoms of that metal.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the mass of the sample in grams, giving your answer in the form $a \times 10^{k}$ with $1 \le a < 10$ and $k$ an integer.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the same mass in kilograms, again giving your answer in the form $a \times 10^{k}$ with $1 \le a < 10$ and $k$ an integer.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    A second sample has mass $8.829 \times 10^{-4}$ kg. Determine the ratio of the mass of the second sample to the mass of the first sample, as an exact decimal.

    (Determine)
  4. [5 marks](d)

    A student claims that the second sample contains $2.7 \times 10^{21}$ atoms. Determine by calculation whether this claim is correct, and state the factor by which the answer would be wrong if the mass in kilograms were divided by $3.27 \times 10^{-22}$ g.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) Multiplying the two given values gives $(3.27 \times 10^{-22})(4.5 \times 10^{19})$. (M1) Grouping the coefficients and the powers of ten separately, $3.27 \times 4.5 = 14.715$ and $10^{-22} \times 10^{19} = 10^{-3}$. (M1) The product is therefore $14.715 \times 10^{-3}$ g, which in the required form is $1.4715 \times 10^{-2}$ g. (A1)

(b) Because $1$ kg $= 10^{3}$ g, the mass in kilograms is the answer to part (a) divided by $10^{3}$. (M1) Subtracting the indices gives $1.4715 \times 10^{-2-3} = 1.4715 \times 10^{-5}$ kg. (A1) The coefficient is unchanged because only the power of ten is altered by the conversion, and dividing by a power of ten never changes the leading digits. (A1)

(c) The required ratio is $\frac{8.829 \times 10^{-4}}{1.4715 \times 10^{-5}}$. (M1) Dividing the coefficients gives $8.829 / 1.4715 = 6$, and dividing the powers gives $10^{-4} / 10^{-5} = 10^{1}$. (M1) Multiplying these, $6 \times 10 = 60$, so the ratio of the masses is exactly $60 : 1$. (A1)(AG) The exactness of the result confirms that the two masses were chosen to be in a simple whole-number ratio.

(d) Converting the second mass into grams, $8.829 \times 10^{-4}$ kg $= 0.8829$ g. (M1) Dividing by the atomic mass gives $0.8829 / (3.27 \times 10^{-22}) = 0.27 \times 10^{22} = 2.7 \times 10^{21}$ atoms. (M1)(A1) This equals the student's claim, so the claim is correct. (R1) If instead the mass in kilograms is divided by the atomic mass in grams, the result is $8.829 \times 10^{-4} / (3.27 \times 10^{-22}) = 2.7 \times 10^{18}$. (M1) Comparing $2.7 \times 10^{21}$ with $2.7 \times 10^{18}$ shows that the second value is $10^{3}$, that is a factor of $1000$, too small. (A1)(R1)

Markscheme notes

Part (a) awards the first (M1) for setting up the product of the two numbers in standard form and the second (M1) for separating coefficients from powers; a candidate who reaches $1.4715 \times 10^{-2}$ without that separation still earns both. The (A1) requires the coefficient to satisfy $1 \le a < 10$, so $14.715 \times 10^{-3}$ left unadjusted is not acceptable. In part (b) the (M1) is for recognising the conversion factor $10^{3}$ and the two (A1) marks are for the index and for keeping the coefficient fixed. A candidate who writes $1.4715 \times 10^{-2}$ kg has divided by ten rather than a thousand and loses the second (A1) but keeps the first. In part (c) the (M1) marks are for the two separate divisions and the (A1) for the exact value; the (AG) confirms the given answer. A candidate who rounds $8.829 / 1.4715$ to $6.0$ may still earn credit if $60$ is stated exactly. In part (d) the first (M1)(A1) pair is for the gram conversion and the division, the (R1) for comparing the result with the claim, and the final (M1)(A1)(R1) for the erroneous calculation, its value and the factor of $1000$. Follow-through from an incorrect part (a) is allowed throughout, but the factor comparison must be consistent with the candidate's own values.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 1.2 Arithmetic sequences and series and 1.3 Geometric sequences and series
syllabus_ref: SL 1.2 (arithmetic sequences and series) and SL 1.3 (geometric sequences and series)
title: The differences are the geometric part
q_html:
A sequence $(u_n)$ is defined by $u_1 = 5$ and $u_{n+1} = u_n + 3 \times 2^{n-1}$ for every integer $n \ge 1$.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate $u_2$, $u_3$ and $u_4$, and explain why the sequence $(u_n)$ is neither arithmetic nor geometric.

    (Calculate)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Show that the general term is $u_n = 3 \times 2^{n-1} + 2$ for every integer $n \ge 1$.

    (Show that)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Hence find the smallest value of $n$ for which $u_n > 10^{6}$.

    (Hence)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Find the sum of the first $20$ terms, giving your answer in the form $3 \times 2^{k} + c$.

    (Find)
a_html:
(a) Applying the recurrence, $u_2 = 5 + 3 \times 2^{0} = 8$ (M1), $u_3 = 8 + 3 \times 2^{1} = 14$ (A1) and $u_4 = 14 + 3 \times 2^{2} = 26$ (A1). The successive differences are $3$, $6$ and $12$, which are not constant, so the sequence is not arithmetic; the successive ratios $8/5$, $14/8$ and $26/14$ are not constant either, so it is not geometric. (R1)

(b) The successive differences are $u_{k+1} - u_k = 3 \times 2^{k-1}$ for $k \ge 1$, so they form the geometric sequence $3$, $6$, $12$ and so on. (M1) Summing the first $n-1$ of them, $u_n = u_1 + \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} 3 \times 2^{k-1} = 5 + 3(2^{n-1} - 1)$. (M1) Expanding, $u_n = 5 + 3 \times 2^{n-1} - 3 = 3 \times 2^{n-1} + 2$. (A1)(AG)

(c) Setting $3 \times 2^{n-1} + 2 > 10^{6}$ gives $2^{n-1} > 333332.66$ and so on. (M1) Since $2^{18} = 262144$ and $2^{19} = 524288$, the smallest integer with $2^{n-1}$ above that threshold has $n - 1 = 19$. (M1) Hence $n = 20$. (A1) Checking, $u_{19} = 3 \times 2^{18} + 2 = 786434$, which is below $10^{6}$, while $u_{20} = 3 \times 2^{19} + 2 = 1572866$, which is above it. (R1)

(d) The sum of the first $20$ terms is $\sum_{n=1}^{20} (3 \times 2^{n-1} + 2)$. (M1) The geometric part sums to $3(2^{20} - 1) = 3 \times 1048575 = 3145725$, and the constant part contributes $2 \times 20 = 40$. (M1) Adding, the total is $3145725 + 40 = 3145765 = 3 \times 2^{20} + 37$. (A1)

Markscheme notes

Part (a): the (M1) is for substituting into the recurrence at least twice, and the two (A1) marks are for the correct values $u_3 = 14$ and $u_4 = 26$. The (R1) requires both negative conclusions, so a candidate who shows only that the differences are not constant earns nothing unless the ratios are also dismissed. Part (b): the first (M1) is for identifying the differences as $3 \times 2^{k-1}$ and the second for summing that geometric series; the (A1) is for the simplified form and the (AG) confirms the printed result, so an answer that stops at $5 + 3(2^{n-1} - 1)$ must still be simplified. Part (c): the (M1) is for the inequality $2^{n-1} > 333332.66$ and the second (M1) for locating $2^{18}$ and $2^{19}$; the (A1) is for $n = 20$. The (R1) is for the numerical check of both sides, which is what rules out $n = 19$. Part (d): the two (M1) marks are for splitting the sum into its geometric and constant parts, and the (A1) for the exact total. Accept $3 \times 2^{20} + 37$, $3145765$ or $3(2^{20} - 1) + 40$ as equivalent. Follow-through from an incorrect $u_n$ is allowed in parts (c) and (d) if the candidate uses it consistently.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 1.7 Laws of exponents with rational exponents and 1.5 Laws of exponents with integer exponents
syllabus_ref: SL 1.7 (laws of exponents with rational exponents) and SL 1.5 (laws of exponents with integer exponents)
title: The root that survives only because the index is odd
q_html:
Consider the equation $(x+1)^{2/3} - 3(x+1)^{1/3} - 4 = 0$, where the powers are interpreted as real powers of the base.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Explain why $x^{1/3}$ is defined for every real $x$ but $x^{1/2}$ is not, and state the values of $x$ for which the left-hand side is defined.

    (Explain)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Show that substituting $t = (x+1)^{1/3}$ gives the quadratic $t^{2} - 3t - 4 = 0$, and hence find the two possible values of $t$.

    (Show that)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Hence find all real solutions of the original equation, checking that each value you obtain is valid.

    (Hence)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Explain how a student solving $(x+1)^{1/2} - 3(x+1)^{1/4} - 4 = 0$ in the same way obtains two values of $x$, and explain why one of them must be rejected.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) A cube root of a negative number is real, because $(-2)^{3} = -8$, so $x^{1/3}$ is defined for every real $x$. (M1) A square root of a negative number is not real, so $x^{1/2}$ is defined only for $x \ge 0$. (A1) Since the expression contains only the cube-root power, it is defined for every real $x$. (A1)

(b) Substituting $t = (x+1)^{1/3}$ gives $t^{2} - 3t - 4 = 0$. (M1) Factorising, $(t - 4)(t + 1) = 0$. (M1) Hence $t = 4$ or $t = -1$. (A1) Both values are permitted because $t$ is a cube root and may be negative. (R1)

(c) From $t = 4$, $x + 1 = 4^{3} = 64$, so $x = 63$. (M1)(A1) From $t = -1$, $x + 1 = (-1)^{3} = -1$, so $x = -2$. (M1)(A1) Both are valid because the cube root of a negative number is real. (R1) Checking, at $x = 63$ the left-hand side is $64^{2/3} - 3 \times 64^{1/3} - 4 = 16 - 12 - 4 = 0$, and at $x = -2$ it is $1 - 3(-1) - 4 = 0$. (A1)

(d) With $t = (x+1)^{1/4}$ the same quadratic gives $t = 4$ or $t = -1$. (M1) From $t = 4$, $x + 1 = 4^{4} = 256$, so $x = 255$; from $t = -1$, $x + 1 = (-1)^{4} = 1$, so $x = 0$. (A1) A fourth root is defined to be non-negative, so $t = -1$ is impossible and $x = 0$ must be rejected, leaving only $x = 255$. (R1)

Markscheme notes

Part (a): the (M1) is for the cube root of a negative number being real, with the example $(-2)^{3} = -8$ earning the credit; the first (A1) is for restricting $x^{1/2}$ to $x \ge 0$ and the second for concluding that the expression is defined for all real $x$. A candidate who claims the cube root is undefined for negative $x$ loses both (A1) marks. Part (b): the two (M1) marks are for the substitution and the factorisation, the (A1) for the two roots, and the (R1) for observing that both roots are admissible for a cube root. Part (c): the (M1)(A1) pairs are for cubing each value of $t$ and for the resulting $x$. The (R1) is for justifying that the negative root gives a real solution, and the final (A1) is for the substitution check. A candidate who rejects $x = -2$ on the grounds that the base is negative has confused the cube root with the square root and forfeits the (R1) and the final (A1). Part (d): the (M1) is for applying the same quadratic, the (A1) for the two candidate values $x = 255$ and $x = 0$, and the (R1) for rejecting $x = 0$ because a fourth root is non-negative. Accept a justification phrased as $t \ge 0$ by definition of the principal root.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 2.1 Different forms of the equation of a straight line and 2.4 Key features of graphs
syllabus_ref: SL 2.1 (different forms of the equation of a straight line) and SL 2.4 (determining key features of graphs)
title: A family of lines with one member the gradient formula cannot reach
q_html:
For each real number $k$, the line $\ell_k$ has equation $(k + 2)x + (k - 1)y = 2k + 7$.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Show that every line $\ell_k$ passes through a single fixed point $P$, and state the coordinates of $P$.

    (Show that)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Find the value of $k$ for which $\ell_k$ is perpendicular to the line joining $P$ to the origin, giving your answer in the form $ax + by = c$ with integers $a$, $b$, $c$.

    (Find)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Find the value of $k$ for which $\ell_k$ is parallel to the $y$-axis, and explain why the expression $-(k+2)/(k-1)$ for the gradient cannot be used to find it.

    (Find)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    The line $\ell_k$ meets the coordinate axes at $A$ and $B$; show that the area of triangle $OAB$ is $\frac{(2k+7)^2}{2|(k+2)(k-1)|}$, and hence find the value of $k$ with $-2 < k < 1$ for which this area is exactly $6$.

    (Find)
a_html:
(a) Substituting $x = 3$ and $y = -1$ into the left-hand side gives $(k+2)(3) + (k-1)(-1) = 3k + 6 - k + 1 = 2k + 7$. (M1) This equals the right-hand side for every value of $k$, so $(3, -1)$ lies on every line of the family. (A1) Hence the fixed point is $P = (3, -1)$. (A1)(R1)

(b) The gradient of $PO$ is $(-1 - 0)/(3 - 0) = -1/3$. (M1) A line perpendicular to $PO$ therefore has gradient $3$. (A1) The gradient of $\ell_k$ is $-(k+2)/(k-1)$, so $-(k+2)/(k-1) = 3$. (M1) This gives $-k - 2 = 3k - 3$, so $k = 1/4$. (A1) Substituting, $\ell_{1/4}$ is $(9/4)x - (3/4)y = 15/2$, which simplifies to $3x - y = 10$. (AG)

(c) When $k = 1$ the equation becomes $3x + 0y = 9$, that is $x = 3$, a vertical line parallel to the $y$-axis. (A1) The expression $-(k+2)/(k-1)$ was obtained by dividing by the coefficient of $y$, namely $k - 1$. (R1) At $k = 1$ that coefficient is zero, so the division is not defined. (R1) The formula therefore does not apply, and the vertical line must be read directly from the equation. (A1)

(d) The $x$-intercept is $A = ((2k+7)/(k+2), 0)$ and the $y$-intercept is $B = (0, (2k+7)/(k-1))$. (M1) The area of triangle $OAB$ is $\frac{1}{2}\left|\frac{2k+7}{k+2}\right|\left|\frac{2k+7}{k-1}\right| = \frac{(2k+7)^2}{2|(k+2)(k-1)|}$. (A1) Setting this equal to $6$ and using that $(k+2)(k-1) < 0$ on $-2 < k < 1$ gives $(2k+7)^2 = -12(k+2)(k-1)$. (M1) Expanding, $4k^2 + 28k + 49 = -12k^2 - 12k + 24$, so $16k^2 + 40k + 25 = 0$. (A1) This is $(4k+5)^2 = 0$, so $k = -5/4$. (A1) Then $\ell_{-5/4}$ is $x - 3y = 6$, with intercepts $6$ and $-2$, and the area is $\frac{1}{2}(6)(2) = 6$. (R1)

Markscheme notes

Part (a) awards (M1) for substituting $(3, -1)$ and (A1) for verifying that the identity holds for all $k$, with a second (A1) for stating $P = (3, -1)$; the (R1) recognises the alternative grouping $k(x+y-2) + (2x-y-7) = 0$. A candidate who finds $P$ by solving two particular members earns the same credit. In part (b) the (M1) is for the gradient $-1/3$ of $PO$ and the (A1) for the perpendicular gradient $3$; the second (M1) is for solving $-(k+2)/(k-1) = 3$ and the (A1) for $k = 1/4$, with the (AG) confirming $3x - y = 10$. In part (c) the (A1) is for identifying $k = 1$ and the vertical line $x = 3$, while the two (R1) marks are for the observation that the formula divides by $k - 1$ and that this coefficient is zero at $k = 1$; the final (A1) states the conclusion. Part (d) awards (M1) for the two intercepts and (A1) for the area expression. The (M1) is for using $(k+2)(k-1) < 0$ on the given interval to remove the modulus with a sign change, and the (A1) marks are for the quadratic $16k^2 + 40k + 25 = 0$ and for the double root $k = -5/4$; the (R1) is for the numerical check that the area is $6$.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 2.2 Concept of a function, domain, range and graph and 2.3 The graph of a function
syllabus_ref: SL 2.2 (concept of a function, domain, range and graph) and SL 2.3 (the graph of a function; its equation y = f(x))
title: A composite function that loses one point and one value
q_html:
The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x) = \sqrt{x + 5}$ and $g(x) = \frac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}$.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    State the largest possible domain of $f$ and the corresponding range of $f$.

    (State)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Find the inverse function $f^{-1}$, stating its domain and its range.

    (Find)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Determine the largest possible domain of the composite function $g \circ f$, and simplify $(g \circ f)(x)$.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Explain why the range of $g \circ f$ is not the interval $[3, \infty)$, and state the value that is missing.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) The expression $\sqrt{x+5}$ is defined when the radicand is non-negative, so $x + 5 \ge 0$, that is $x \ge -5$. (A1) The largest possible domain is therefore $[-5, \infty)$. (A1) The endpoint $-5$ is included because the radicand is exactly zero there. A square root takes only non-negative values, and as $x$ runs over the domain the value $\sqrt{x+5}$ covers every non-negative number, so the range is $[0, \infty)$. (A1)

(b) Setting $y = \sqrt{x+5}$ and squaring gives $y^2 = x + 5$, so $x = y^2 - 5$. (M1) Interchanging $x$ and $y$, $f^{-1}(x) = x^2 - 5$. (A1) The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$, namely $x \ge 0$. (A1) The range of $f^{-1}$ is the domain of $f$, namely $y \ge -5$. (A1)

(c) For $x$ in the domain of $f$, $(g \circ f)(x) = \frac{(f(x))^2 - 9}{f(x) - 3} = \frac{(f(x)-3)(f(x)+3)}{f(x)-3} = f(x) + 3 = \sqrt{x+5} + 3$. (M1) This simplification requires $f(x) \ne 3$. (R1) Now $\sqrt{x+5} = 3$ exactly when $x + 5 = 9$, that is $x = 4$. (A1) The value $x = 4$ lies in the domain of $f$ but must be removed from the domain of $g \circ f$. (A1) Hence the largest possible domain is $[-5, 4) \cup (4, \infty)$. (A1)

(d) As $x$ runs over $[-5, \infty)$, the expression $\sqrt{x+5} + 3$ takes every value from $3$ upwards, so the naive range is $[3, \infty)$. (R1) However, $x = 4$ has been excluded from the domain, and at $x = 4$ the composite would take the value $\sqrt{9} + 3 = 6$. (A1) That single value is therefore missing, and the range is $[3, 6) \cup (6, \infty)$. (A1) The value $6$ is approached as $x$ approaches $4$ from either side, so it is a single isolated gap rather than an interval of missing values.

Markscheme notes

Part (a) awards three (A1) marks, one for the domain $x \ge -5$, one for writing it as $[-5, \infty)$, and one for the range $[0, \infty)$; the range mark requires the candidate to note that a square root is non-negative. In part (b) the (M1) is for squaring and rearranging to $x = y^2 - 5$, and the (A1) is for $f^{-1}(x) = x^2 - 5$. The remaining two (A1) marks are for the domain $x \ge 0$ and the range $y \ge -5$ of the inverse, which come from swapping the domain and range of $f$; a candidate who writes $x \ge -5$ for the inverse has not swapped them and loses that mark. Part (c) awards (M1) for the algebraic simplification to $\sqrt{x+5} + 3$ and (R1) for stating that this requires $f(x) \ne 3$. The (A1) marks are for solving $\sqrt{x+5} = 3$ to get $x = 4$, for recognising that $4$ lies in the domain of $f$ but not of the composite, and for the final domain $[-5, 4) \cup (4, \infty)$. Part (d) awards (R1) for the naive range $[3, \infty)$ and (A1) for the excluded value $6$; the final (A1) is for the range $[3, 6) \cup (6, \infty)$. A candidate who omits the missing value cannot earn the last two marks.

subtopic: 3.5 The unit circle and 3.6 The Pythagorean identity and 3.7 The circular functions and 3.8 Solving trigonometric equations
syllabus_ref: SL 3.5 (definition of cos theta and sin theta in terms of the unit circle) and SL 3.6 (the Pythagorean identity cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta = 1) and SL 3.7 (the circular functions sin x, cos x and tan x: their domains, ranges and periodicity) and SL 3.8 (solving trigonometric equations in a finite interval)
title: Two solutions in one period, ten in five
q_html:
The angle $\theta$ satisfies $\sin\theta=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\cos\theta<0$. All angles in this question are measured in radians.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Find the exact values of $\cos\theta$ and of $\tan\theta$, giving each as a simplified fraction or surd.

    (Find)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Show that $(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^{2}+(\sin\theta-\cos\theta)^{2}=2$ for every value of the angle $\theta$.

    (Show that)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Determine the exact value of $\sin\theta\cos\theta$, and hence find the exact value of $\sin^{4}\theta+\cos^{4}\theta$.

    (Determine)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Solve $\sin x=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ for $x$ in the interval $[0,2\pi)$, and hence state the number of solutions in $[0,10\pi)$.

    (Solve)
a_html:
(a) Since $\sin\theta=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ is negative and $\cos\theta<0$, the angle $\theta$ lies in the third quadrant (M1). The Pythagorean identity gives $\cos^{2}\theta=1-\sin^{2}\theta=1-\frac{3}{4}=\frac{1}{4}$, so $\cos\theta=\pm\frac{1}{2}$ (A1); the third-quadrant condition selects $\cos\theta=-\frac{1}{2}$. Therefore $\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\frac{-\sqrt{3}/2}{-1/2}=\sqrt{3}$ (A1).

(b) Expanding, $(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^{2}=\sin^{2}\theta+2\sin\theta\cos\theta+\cos^{2}\theta$ and $(\sin\theta-\cos\theta)^{2}=\sin^{2}\theta-2\sin\theta\cos\theta+\cos^{2}\theta$ (M1). Adding the two expressions, the cross terms $+2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and $-2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ cancel (A1), leaving $2\sin^{2}\theta+2\cos^{2}\theta=2(\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta)$ (A1) $=2$ (AG). The identity holds for every angle because it never uses the particular values from part (a); the cross terms cancel in exactly the same way in every quadrant.

(c) From part (a), $\sin\theta\cos\theta=\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$ (M1)(A1). For the fourth powers, write $\sin^{4}\theta+\cos^{4}\theta=(\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta)^{2}-2\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta$ (M1). The first bracket equals $1$, and $\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta=\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right)^{2}=\frac{3}{16}$ (A1), so the expression is $1-2\cdot\frac{3}{16}=1-\frac{3}{8}=\frac{5}{8}$ (A1). This identity is the standard companion of the Pythagorean relation.

(d) In the interval $[0,2\pi)$ the equation $\sin x=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ has one solution in the third quadrant and one in the fourth (M1). The reference angle is $\frac{\pi}{3}$, so the solutions are $x=\pi+\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{4\pi}{3}$ (A1) and $x=2\pi-\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{5\pi}{3}$ (A1). Since $\sin x$ has period $2\pi$, the interval $[0,10\pi)$ contains $\frac{10\pi}{2\pi}=5$ complete periods (M1), and each contributes two solutions, giving $2\times 5=10$ solutions in total (A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) The (M1) is for locating the angle in the third quadrant from the two sign conditions. The (A1) is for $\cos^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{4}$ and the second (A1) for selecting the negative root; a candidate who gives $+\frac{1}{2}$ forfeits the second mark.

(b) The marks are for structure. The (M1) is for expanding at least one square correctly; the (A1) is for the cancellation of the cross terms; the final (A1) requires the explicit use of $\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta=1$. A candidate who substitutes the numerical values from part (a) instead of proving the identity earns no marks here.

(c) The (M1)(A1) pair is for $\sin\theta\cos\theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$; accept a direct product from part (a). The second (M1) is for the identity $\sin^{4}\theta+\cos^{4}\theta=1-2\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta$, and the final (A1) is for $\frac{5}{8}$. Follow through from an incorrect product is allowed.

(d) Award (M1) for identifying the two quadrants and (A1) for each exact solution. The final marks require the count of five periods and the product $2\times 5=10$; a candidate who lists the ten solutions explicitly earns full credit. Do not accept $x=\frac{\pi}{3}$ or $x=\frac{2\pi}{3}$, which solve the equation with the positive value $+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 5.18 First order differential equations
syllabus_ref: AHL 5.18 (first order differential equations; integrating factor), AHL 5.14 (implicit differentiation)
title: 5.18 First order differential equations
q_html:
A curve $C$ lies in the first quadrant and passes through the point $(1,\,4)$.

The tangent to $C$ at any point $\mathrm{P}(x,\,y)$ meets the $x$-axis at the point $\mathrm{A}$. The area of triangle $\mathrm{OAP}$, where $\mathrm{O}$ is the origin, is equal to $2$ for every position of $\mathrm{P}$ on $C$.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Show that $\mathrm{A}$ has coordinates $\left(x-\dfrac{y}{y'},\,0\right)$, where $y'=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$.

    (Show that)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Show that $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y}-\dfrac{x}{y}=-\dfrac{4}{y^{2}}$.

    (Show that)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Hence find an expression for $x$ in terms of $y$.

    (Hence)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Determine the least possible value of $x$ on $C$, and justify your answer.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) Tangent at $\mathrm{P}$: $Y-y=y'(X-x)$ where $(X,\,Y)$ is a general point on the tangent. (M1)
At $\mathrm{A}$, $Y=0$, so $-y=y'(X-x)$, giving $X=x-\dfrac{y}{y'}$ (valid since $y'\neq0$ on $C$). (A1)
Hence $\mathrm{A}=\left(x-\dfrac{y}{y'},\,0\right)$. (A1)

(b) $\mathrm{OA}=x-\dfrac{y}{y'}$ and the perpendicular height of $\mathrm{P}$ above $\mathrm{OA}$ is $y$, so

$$\text{area}=\tfrac12\left(x-\frac{y}{y'}\right)y=2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \left(x-\frac{y}{y'}\right)y=4.$$ (M1)

Expanding: $xy-\dfrac{y^{2}}{y'}=4$, so $\dfrac{y^{2}}{y'}=xy-4$ and therefore $y'=\dfrac{y^{2}}{xy-4}$. (A1)

Inverting, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y}=\dfrac{xy-4}{y^{2}}=\dfrac{x}{y}-\dfrac{4}{y^{2}}$. (M1)

Hence $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y}-\dfrac{x}{y}=-\dfrac{4}{y^{2}}$. (A1)

(c) The left-hand side becomes a single derivative once divided by $y$:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)=\frac{y\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y}-x}{y^{2}}=\frac1y\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y}-\frac{x}{y}\right)=\frac1y\left(-\frac{4}{y^{2}}\right)=-\frac{4}{y^{3}}.$$ (M1)(A1)

Integrating with respect to $y$: $\dfrac{x}{y}=\displaystyle\int -4y^{-3}\,\mathrm{d}y=\dfrac{2}{y^{2}}+k$. (M1)

So $x=\dfrac{2}{y}+ky$. (A1)

Using $(1,\,4)$: $1=\dfrac24+4k \Rightarrow k=\dfrac18$, hence $\boxed{x=\dfrac{2}{y}+\dfrac{y}{8}},\quad y>0$. (A1)

(Equivalently $y^{2}-8xy+16=0$.)

(d) From (c), $x=\dfrac2y+\dfrac y8$ with $y>0$. By AM–GM,

$$x=\frac2y+\frac y8 \;\ge\; 2\sqrt{\frac2y\cdot\frac y8}=2\sqrt{\frac14}=1,$$ (M1)

with equality when $\dfrac2y=\dfrac y8$, i.e. $y^{2}=16$, so $y=4$ and then $x=1$. (A1)

Since $x\to\infty$ as $y\to0^{+}$ and as $y\to\infty$, this stationary value is the least value: $x_{\min}=1$ at $(1,\,4)$. (R1)

(Equivalently $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y}=-\dfrac{2}{y^{2}}+\dfrac18=0 \Rightarrow y=4$, with $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y}<0$ for $0<y<4$ and $>0$ for $y>4$.)

Markscheme notes

(a) Allow the tangent equation in any correct form. A student who writes the tangent as $y=mx+c$ and finds the intercept earns (M1) only if the substitution of $m=y'$ is shown.

(b) Award (M1) for $\tfrac12(\text{base})(\text{height})$ with base $=x-\tfrac{y}{y'}$ and height $=y$; condone a missing modulus since $y>0$. The reciprocal step from $y'$ to $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y}$ must be seen — a candidate who stays in $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ cannot reach (c).

(c) The intended route is the recognition of $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}\!\left(\tfrac{x}{y}\right)$. Accept the formal integrating-factor method: IF $=\exp\!\left(\int-\tfrac1y\,\mathrm{d}y\right)=\tfrac1y$, giving $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}y}\!\left(\tfrac{x}{y}\right)=-\tfrac4{y^{3}}$ and the same result. Award full marks for either.

(d) Accept a sign argument on $\tfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}y}$ in place of AM–GM. The justification that the stationary point is a *least* value is required for the final (R1); do not award it for $y=4$ alone.

Alternative for (c): writing the answer as $y^{2}-8xy+16=0$ and verifying it satisfies the condition in (b).

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: P3 extended problem: constrained optimisation with a cost parameter
syllabus_ref: SL 5.8 (local maximum and minimum points), SL 5.4 (tangents and normals), AHL 5.14 (related rates)
title: P3 extended problem: constrained optimisation with a cost parameter
q_html:
A closed cylindrical can is to be manufactured with a fixed volume $V$. The curved surface is made from a material costing $p$ per unit area. The two circular ends are made from a thicker material costing $kp$ per unit area, where $k > 0$ is a constant. Let the can have base radius $r$ and height $h$.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Show that the total material cost can be written as
    $$C(r) = 2\pi p k r^{2} + \frac{2pV}{r}, \qquad r > 0.$$

    (Show that)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Determine the value of $r$ that minimises $C$, and show that it is indeed a minimum. Give your answer in terms of $V$, $k$ and $\pi$.

    (Determine)
  3. [6 marks](c)

    Hence show that the ratio of the height to the radius at the optimum is $2k$, independent of $V$ and $p$. Comment on what this predicts when $k=1$ and when $k$ is very large, and explain why both predictions are physically sensible.

    (Hence)
a_html:
(a) The two circular ends have total area $2\pi r^{2}$ and cost $kp$ per unit area, contributing $2\pi r^{2}\cdot kp$. (A1) The curved surface has area $2\pi r h$, contributing $2\pi r h\cdot p$. (A1) The volume is fixed: $\pi r^{2}h = V$, so $h = \dfrac{V}{\pi r^{2}}$. (M1)
$$C = 2\pi p k r^{2} + 2\pi r p\cdot\frac{V}{\pi r^{2}} = 2\pi p k r^{2} + \frac{2pV}{r}$$ (A1)(AG)

(b) Differentiating with respect to $r$: (M1)
$$C'(r) = 4\pi p k r - \frac{2pV}{r^{2}}$$
Setting $C'(r) = 0$: (M1)
$$4\pi p k r = \frac{2pV}{r^{2}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad r^{3} = \frac{2pV}{4\pi p k} = \frac{V}{2\pi k}$$
$$r = \left(\frac{V}{2\pi k}\right)^{1/3}$$ (A1)
To confirm it is a minimum: (M1)
$$C''(r) = 4\pi p k + \frac{4pV}{r^{3}} > 0 \quad \text{for all } r>0$$
since $p$, $k$ and $V$ are all positive, so the stationary point is a minimum. (A1) (It is the only stationary point on $r>0$, and $C\to\infty$ both as $r\to0^{+}$ and as $r\to\infty$, so it is the global minimum.)

(c) Using $h = \dfrac{V}{\pi r^{2}}$ and $r^{3} = \dfrac{V}{2\pi k}$: (M1)
$$\frac{h}{r} = \frac{V}{\pi r^{3}} = \frac{V}{\pi\cdot\dfrac{V}{2\pi k}} = \frac{V\cdot 2\pi k}{\pi V} = 2k$$ (M1)(A1)(AG)
The ratio depends on $k$ only: $V$ and $p$ both cancel. (A1)

When $k=1$ the ends and the curved surface cost the same per unit area, and the optimum has $h = 2r$, so the height equals the diameter: the can is as tall as it is wide. (A1) This is the familiar equal-cost result and is sensible because the shape is then equally 'spread' in every direction.

When $k$ is very large the ends are very expensive relative to the curved surface, so the optimum makes the ends small and the can tall and thin, consistent with $h/r = 2k$ growing without bound. (A1) Conversely, if the ends were very cheap, $k\to0$ and the can becomes short and wide, which also matches intuition. The limiting cases therefore both confirm the result.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1) for using the volume constraint to eliminate $h$; a candidate who leaves the cost in terms of both $r$ and $h$ has not completed the reduction. (b) Accept the unsimplified form of $r$ provided it is equivalent. The second-derivative check must be shown, not asserted; a candidate who argues from the shape of $C$ should be credited only if they state that $C\to\infty$ at both ends of the domain. Watch for the error of differentiating $2pV/r$ as $+2pV/r^{2}$. (c) The ratio derivation earns (M1)(A1) and the observation that $V$ and $p$ cancel earns a further mark, since it is the insight the question exists to produce. Accept any sensible physical commentary for the final two marks; the key point for $k=1$ is $h=2r$ and for large $k$ is that the can becomes tall and thin. A candidate who says the can becomes short and wide for large $k$ has the direction inverted. Watch for the candidate who differentiates with respect to $h$ after eliminating $r$ instead: the algebra is valid but the resulting ratio is harder to read, so credit the equivalent form. A useful check the examiner can invite is dimensional: $r^{3}=V/(2\pi k)$ has dimensions of volume, so the cube root is obligatory, and a candidate who reports $r=V/(2\pi k)$ has lost a power. A candidate who treats $k$ as multiplying the curved surface rather than the ends has inverted the ratio and will report $h/r=2/k$; the limiting case test in (c) catches this immediately, which is why the commentary marks are not free.

subject: Maths AA HL
subtopic: 1.13 Complex numbers in polar and Euler form
syllabus_ref: AHL 1.13 (modulus–argument/polar and Euler form; sums, products and quotients and their geometric interpretation)
title: 1.13 Complex numbers in polar and Euler form
q_html:
Let $\alpha=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{5}}$, so that $\alpha$ is a non-real fifth root of unity.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Show that $1+\alpha+\alpha^{2}+\alpha^{3}+\alpha^{4}=0$.

    (Show that)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Show that $\alpha^{k}+\alpha^{-k}=2\cos\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi k}{5}\right)$ for $k=1$ and $k=2$.
