Two measurements of the same impulse

A trolley of mass $1.20\ \mathrm{kg}$ runs on a level track and rebounds from a rigid barrier fitted with a force sensor. The force sensor was connected to a data logger that recorded the contact force every $10\ \mathrm{ms}$. Two light gates were also used: one measured the speed of the trolley immediately before it reached the barrier and the other measured its speed immediately after the rebound. The uncertainty in each speed measurement is $\pm 0.010\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the mass of the trolley is known to $\pm 0.01\ \mathrm{kg}$. The force sensor records to the nearest $1\ \mathrm{N}$ and the timing of the data logger is accurate to $1\ \mathrm{ms}$. Neither instrument had been zeroed before the run.

The light gates recorded $u = 0.850\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ towards the barrier and $v = 0.250\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ away from it. Take the direction away from the barrier as positive.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Use the force-time data to calculate the impulse acting on the trolley during the collision. State the method you use to find the area under the graph.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the change in momentum of the trolley from the light-gate readings, and estimate the uncertainty in this value.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Determine whether the two results agree within the combined uncertainty. Show your working and state your conclusion clearly.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Suggest a specific instrumental fault that would account for the discrepancy, justifying it from a feature of the data other than the area, and state what should have been done before the run to prevent it.

    (Suggest)
a_html:
(a) The impulse is the area under the force-time graph. With readings every $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ the trapezium rule gives (M1)

$$I = 0.010\left[\frac{1}{2}(1) + 10 + 27 + 38 + 34 + 19 + 8 + 3 + \frac{1}{2}(1)\right]$$

$$= 0.010\left[0.5 + 139 + 0.5\right] = 0.010(140) = 1.40\ \mathrm{N\,s}$$ (A1)(A1)

Counting squares would give the same result to within the resolution of the plot. The impulse acts away from the barrier, so it is positive. (A1)

(b) Taking the direction away from the barrier as positive, $u = -0.850$ and $v = +0.250\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so (M1)

$$\Delta p = m(v-u) = 1.20\bigl(0.250-(-0.850)\bigr) = 1.20(1.100) = 1.32\ \mathrm{N\,s}$$ (A1)

Each speed contributes $m\,\delta u = 1.20(0.010)=0.012\ \mathrm{N\,s}$, and the two speeds are independent, so adding in quadrature gives $\sqrt{2}\,0.012 = 0.017\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. The mass uncertainty contributes $0.01/1.20 = 0.8\%$ of $1.32$, about $0.011\ \mathrm{N\,s}$, so the combined uncertainty is $\sqrt{0.017^{2}+0.011^{2}} \approx 0.02\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. (A1)

(c) The difference is $1.40-1.32 = 0.08\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. (M1) The uncertainty in the force-sensor result is dominated by the resolution of $1\ \mathrm{N}$ acting over the whole $80\ \mathrm{ms}$, giving about $1\times0.080 = 0.08\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ in the worst case, but the resolution errors partly cancel across the interval and a realistic estimate is about $0.03\ \mathrm{N\,s}$; combining with the $0.02\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ from (b) gives a combined uncertainty near $0.04\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. (A1) The discrepancy of $0.08\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ is therefore about twice the combined uncertainty, so the two results do not agree within it. (A1)

(d) The force sensor had not been zeroed: it reads $1\ \mathrm{N}$ at $t=0$, before the trolley has made contact, and $1\ \mathrm{N}$ again at $t=80\ \mathrm{ms}$, after contact has ended. (M1)(A1) A constant offset of $+1\ \mathrm{N}$ acting for the full $80\ \mathrm{ms}$ adds $1\times0.080 = 0.080\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ to the area, which is exactly the size of the discrepancy. (A1) The sensor should have been zeroed with no load applied immediately before the run, and a short section of data recorded before contact to confirm that the baseline was zero. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) Accept the trapezium rule or counting squares; award the method mark for any sensible treatment of the end intervals. Accept $1.38$ to $1.42\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. A candidate who simply multiplies the peak force by the duration earns no marks. (b) Accept $1.32\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ and any uncertainty between $0.01$ and $0.03\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ that is justified. Watch the sign: a candidate who treats both speeds as positive has computed the wrong quantity and should not earn the momentum mark, though follow-through to later parts may still apply. (c) The mark is for comparing the discrepancy with a combined uncertainty, not for asserting agreement. Accept a conclusion of marginal disagreement; a candidate who says the results agree because both are 'about $1.3$' has not made the comparison. (d) The identifying feature is the non-zero baseline at both ends, not the value of the area; a candidate who proposes friction on the track should be asked what it predicts for the baseline, and should not be credited, since friction would not make the sensor read $1\ \mathrm{N}$ before contact.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: C.1 Simple harmonic motion — data-based question
syllabus_ref: C.1 (Simple harmonic motion: period of a mass-spring system) and experimental skills
title: C.1 Simple harmonic motion — data-based question
q_html:
Student investigation: the period of a loaded spring

A student hangs a spring from a rigid support and suspends a mass hanger from its lower end. She pulls the hanger a short distance below its equilibrium position and releases it, so that the system oscillates vertically. She measures the time for 20 complete oscillations using a stopwatch that reads to 0.01 s, and divides by 20 to obtain the period. She estimates her reaction time as 0.2 s at both the start and the stop. She repeats the measurement for seven different loads. The masses are known to the nearest gram, so the uncertainty in the load is negligible.

The student intends to test the relationship $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$ and to determine the spring constant $k$ from her data.

  1. [2 marks](a)

    State the uncertainty in a single value of the period $T$, and explain how you obtained it from the information given about the timing.

    (State)
  2. [2 marks](b)

    Describe how the student could reduce the uncertainty in the period using the same stopwatch, and state one further change to the apparatus that would reduce it more.

    (Describe)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Explain why the student should plot a graph of $T^2$ against $m$ rather than $T$ against $m$, and state what feature of the resulting graph would support the proposed relationship.

    (Explain)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Determine the spring constant $k$ from the data. You should make it clear which points you used to fix your best-fit line and why, and give $k$ with its unit.

    (Determine)
  5. [3 marks](e)

    Evaluate whether the data support the proposed relationship. Identify any anomalous reading, suggest a plausible experimental cause for it, and state what the student should have done at the time.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The reaction time contributes at both the start and the stop, so combining in quadrature gives $\Delta t = \sqrt{0.2^2 + 0.2^2} = 0.28\ \mathrm{s}$ for the timing of 20 oscillations. Since $T = t/20$, the uncertainty in the period is $\Delta T = 0.28/20 = 0.014\ \mathrm{s}$. (M1) for dividing the timing uncertainty by the number of oscillations, (A1) for a value of about $0.01\ \mathrm{s}$ to $0.02\ \mathrm{s}$. Adding the two reaction times directly instead of in quadrature gives $0.4/20 = 0.020\ \mathrm{s}$, which is also acceptable; the stopwatch resolution of $0.01\ \mathrm{s}$ is far smaller than either and can be ignored.

(b) Timing a larger number of oscillations divides the same timing uncertainty by a larger number, so 50 oscillations rather than 20 would give $\Delta T \approx 0.006\ \mathrm{s}$. (A1) A much larger reduction comes from removing the human element: a position sensor or a video recording analysed frame by frame gives a period limited only by the sampling rate. (A1) Note that timing more oscillations is free, which is why it should always be the first thing a student does.

(c) The relationship $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ is not linear in $m$, so a graph of $T$ against $m$ would be a curve and a curve cannot confirm a hypothesis by eye. Squaring gives $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{k}\,m$, which is the equation of a straight line through the origin with gradient $4\pi^2/k$. (M1) The relationship is supported if the plotted points lie close to a straight line (A1) and if that line passes through, or very close to, the origin (A1) — a non-zero intercept would indicate that the spring's own mass is contributing to the inertia of the system.

(d) The point at $m = 0.300\ \mathrm{kg}$ lies well above the trend and must be excluded from the fit (R1); the reason is given in part (e). Using the remaining six points, a least-squares fit of $T^2$ against $m$ gives a gradient of $1.56\ \mathrm{s^2\ kg^{-1}}$ and an intercept of about $0.005\ \mathrm{s^2}$, effectively zero. (M1) Hence $k = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{\text{gradient}} = \dfrac{39.5}{1.56} = 25.3\ \mathrm{N\ m^{-1}}$. (A1) A hand-drawn best-fit line will give a gradient anywhere in the range $1.53$ to $1.60\ \mathrm{s^2\ kg^{-1}}$, so any value of $k$ from $24.7$ to $25.8\ \mathrm{N\ m^{-1}}$ should be credited. (A1)

(e) With the anomalous point removed, the remaining six points lie on a straight line through the origin to within the scatter expected from the timing uncertainty, so the data do support the relationship. (A1) The reading at $m = 0.300\ \mathrm{kg}$ is the anomalous one: the model predicts $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.300/25} = 0.688\ \mathrm{s}$, whereas $0.730\ \mathrm{s}$ was recorded, some $6\%$ high, which is far outside the $2\%$ timing uncertainty at that load. (M1) A plausible cause is that the hanger caught on the support or that an extra mass was left on the hanger for that run. The student should have repeated that measurement immediately, while the apparatus was still set up, rather than processing a single suspicious value. (A1)

Markscheme notes

In (a) accept any value from 0.014 s to 0.020 s; credit the method of dividing by 20 even if the combination of the two reaction times is done by simple addition. Do not credit the stopwatch resolution of 0.01 s alone, which ignores the dominant error. In (b) the first mark is for timing more oscillations; the second must be a change of technique, not simply 'be more careful' or 'use a better stopwatch'. In (c) all three marks are for the linearisation argument: award the first for stating that the untransformed graph is curved, the second for the straight-line prediction, and the third for the through-the-origin test. In (d) allow follow-through from a gradient obtained with the anomalous point included, provided the point is not silently absorbed; a candidate who includes it and comments on the resulting poor fit can still earn the reasoning marks. In (e) the anomaly must be identified by its load, and the suggested cause must be physically plausible rather than 'human error' alone. A candidate who argues that the point should simply be deleted without a reason earns no credit.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
subtopic: E.3 Radioactive decay — data-based question
syllabus_ref: E.3 (Radioactive decay: detection of radiation, counting statistics) and experimental skills
title: E.3 Radioactive decay — data-based question
q_html:
Student investigation: count rate and distance from a source

A student places a sealed gamma source on a metre rule and a Geiger-Muller tube connected to a counter at a measured distance $d$ from it. At each distance she records the count over 100 s and divides by 100 to obtain the count rate. The background count rate was measured separately, over 600 s, as 0.40 counts per second, and has already been subtracted from the values in the table. The distances were set with a metre rule graduated in millimetres. One reading in the table is unreliable.

The student wants to find the exponent $n$ in the relationship $C = \dfrac{A}{d^{\,n}}$, where $A$ is a constant.

  1. [2 marks](a)

    The count recorded at $d = 20.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ over 100 s was 10200. Assuming the counts follow Poisson statistics, calculate the percentage uncertainty in this count rate, and state what the uncertainty would have been had the count been recorded over only 10 s.

    (Calculate)
  2. [2 marks](b)

    Suggest why the background count rate was measured over 600 s rather than 100 s, and explain why subtracting the background before analysing the data matters more at large distances than at small ones.

    (Suggest)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Explain how plotting $\lg C$ against $\lg d$ allows the exponent $n$ and the constant $A$ to be found, and state what the gradient and the intercept represent.

    (Explain)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Determine the exponent $n$ and the constant $A$, making clear which point you excluded and giving the unit of $A$.

    (Determine)
  5. [3 marks](e)

    Evaluate whether the data confirm the inverse-square relationship. Identify the anomalous reading, suggest a plausible cause, and state what should have been done about it.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) For a Poisson count, the uncertainty in the number of counts is $\sqrt{N}$, so with $N = 10200$ the uncertainty is $101$ counts and the percentage uncertainty is $\dfrac{101}{10200} \times 100 = 0.99\%$, which is also $1/\sqrt{N}$ expressed as a percentage. (M1)(A1) Over 10 s the same rate would give $N = 1020$ counts, so the percentage uncertainty would be $1/\sqrt{1020} \times 100 = 3.1\%$. (A1) The uncertainty therefore improves only as the square root of the counting time, which is why long counts are needed for precision.

(b) The background rate is small, so it must be known precisely before it can be subtracted; a 600 s count gives $N \approx 240$ counts and hence a percentage uncertainty of about $1/\sqrt{240} = 6\%$, whereas a 100 s count would give only 40 counts and around $16\%$. (A1) Subtracting the background matters far more at large distances because the corrected rate there is small: at $d = 50\ \mathrm{cm}$ the measured rate is 16 per second, so a background uncertainty of even a few per cent is comparable with the quantity being measured, while at $d = 10\ \mathrm{cm}$ the rate of 403 per second makes the same background correction negligible. (A1)

(c) Taking logarithms of $C = A/d^{\,n}$ gives $\lg C = \lg A - n\,\lg d$, which is the equation of a straight line. (M1) The gradient is $-n$, so the exponent is found directly from the slope (A1), and the intercept on the $\lg C$ axis is $\lg A$, from which $A$ follows as $10^{\text{intercept}}$ (A1). This is the only straightforward way to test the value of an exponent, since a direct plot of $C$ against $d$ is a curve whose shape is very hard to judge by eye.

(d) The point at $d = 30.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ sits clearly above the trend and must be excluded from the fit (R1); part (e) gives the reason. Using the remaining six points, a least-squares fit of $\lg C$ against $\lg d$ gives a gradient of $-1.99$ and an intercept of $4.60$. (M1) Hence $n = 1.99 \approx 2.0$ (A1) and $A = 10^{4.60} = 4.0 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{s^{-1}\ cm^{2}}$, with the unit fixed by the requirement that $A/d^2$ has the unit of a count rate. (A1) A hand-drawn line will give $n$ in the range $1.9$ to $2.1$ and $A$ in the range $3.5$ to $4.5 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{s^{-1}\ cm^2}$; all such values should be credited.

(e) With the anomalous point removed, the remaining six points lie on a straight line of gradient $-2.0$ to within the counting uncertainties, so the data do confirm the inverse-square relationship. (A1) The anomalous reading is at $d = 30.0\ \mathrm{cm}$: the fitted relationship predicts $C = 4.0 \times 10^4/30^2 = 44\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, whereas $57\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ was recorded, roughly $28\%$ high and many times the $1.5\%$ counting uncertainty at that rate. (M1) A plausible cause is that the source was not properly seated against the rule for that reading, so the true distance was smaller than 30.0 cm. The student should have rechecked the alignment and repeated the measurement immediately rather than carrying a suspicious value forward into the analysis. (A1)

Markscheme notes

In (a) accept any value from 0.98 to 1.0 per cent for the 100 s count and 3.0 to 3.2 per cent for the 10 s count; the key relationship being tested is that the uncertainty scales as one over the square root of the number of counts. In (b) the first mark is for linking a longer background count to a smaller percentage uncertainty; the second must refer explicitly to the corrected rate being small at large distances, and 'because the count rate is smaller' on its own is not sufficient. In (c) award the first mark for the logarithmic transformation, the second for the gradient being minus n, and the third for the intercept being the logarithm of A. In (d) allow follow-through from a gradient that includes the anomalous point only if the candidate comments on the resulting poor fit; a silent inclusion earns no reasoning mark. The unit of A must be consistent with the unit of d used, and a candidate who works in metres should have A of order 4.0 per second per square metre, which is equally acceptable. In (e) the anomaly must be identified by its distance, and 'the source moved' is acceptable only if the direction of the resulting error is stated correctly.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: D.4 Switching on a series circuit containing an inductor: the initial rate of rise of the current is set by the e.m.f. and the inductance alone, the final current and the time constant are set by the total resistance including the resistance of the coil itself, and the energy stored rises as the square of the current
syllabus_ref: D.4 Induction (AHL): Faraday's law applied to the coil itself, so that a changing current induces a back e.m.f. in the coil, the time constant of a series circuit containing an inductor, and the energy stored in the magnetic field of the coil
title: D.4 Switching on a series circuit containing an inductor: the initial rate of rise of the current is set by the e.m.f. and the inductance alone, the final current and the time constant are set by the total resistance including the resistance of the coil itself, and the energy stored rises as the square of the current
a_html:
(a) At $t = 0$ the current is zero, so there is no potential difference across either resistance. The whole of the battery's e.m.f. therefore appears across the coil, and the back e.m.f. equals the applied e.m.f. (M1):
$$L\frac{di}{dt} = 12.0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{di}{dt} = \frac{12.0}{0.250} = 48.0\ \mathrm{A\,s^{-1}} \;(A1).$$
This rate depends only on the e.m.f. and the inductance. It does not depend on the $40.0\ \Omega$ resistor, nor on the coil's own $8.0\ \Omega$ resistance, because at that instant neither resistance carries any current and neither therefore produces any potential difference (A1).
(b) After a long time the current is steady, so $\dfrac{di}{dt} = 0$ and the back e.m.f. is zero. The circuit is then simply two resistances in series with the battery, and the coil's resistance is one of them (M1):
$$I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R + r} = \frac{12.0}{40.0 + 8.0} = \frac{12.0}{48.0} = 0.250\ \mathrm{A} \;(A1).$$
The time constant is $\tau = \dfrac{L}{R + r} = \dfrac{0.250}{48.0} = 5.21 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s} = 5.21\ \mathrm{ms}$ (M1)(A1). The coil's resistance must appear in both because it is in the same series loop as the resistor: charge passing through the coil passes through the coil's own resistance too, and there is no way to separate the two contributions to the total opposition in the loop. Using $R = 40.0\ \Omega$ alone gives $0.300\ \mathrm{A}$ and $6.25\ \mathrm{ms}$, both of which are wrong.
(c) The energy stored in the field of an inductor is $U = \tfrac{1}{2}Li^{2}$, so at the steady state
$$U = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.250)(0.250)^{2} = 7.81 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{J} = 7.81\ \mathrm{mJ} \;(M1)(A1).$$
At $t = \tau$ the current is $i = I(1 - e^{-1}) = 0.250 \times 0.6321 = 0.158\ \mathrm{A}$ (M1), so
$$U_{\tau} = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.250)(0.158)^{2} = 3.12 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{J},$$
which is a fraction
$$\frac{U_{\tau}}{U} = (1 - e^{-1})^{2} = 0.400$$
of the final energy (A1). The current has reached $63\%$ of its final value but the energy only $40\%$, because the energy is proportional to the square of the current.
(d) The initial slope of the curve is $\dfrac{di}{dt} = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{L}$, and the asymptote is at $i = I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R + r}$. The tangent line is therefore $i = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{L}t$, and it meets the asymptote where
$$\frac{\varepsilon}{L}t = \frac{\varepsilon}{R + r} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t = \frac{L}{R + r} = \tau \;(A1).$$
The result is not a coincidence of the numbers: the e.m.f. cancels from both sides, so the tangent at the origin of any such rise meets its own asymptote at one time constant (A1). It is a useful way to read $\tau$ off a graph, since the intersection of the tangent with the asymptote is easier to judge than the point at which the curve reaches $63\%$ of its final value.
At $t = \tau$ the current is $0.158\ \mathrm{A}$, so the potential difference across the coil's resistance is $0.158 \times 8.0 = 1.27\ \mathrm{V}$ and across the $40.0\ \Omega$ resistor is $0.158 \times 40.0 = 6.32\ \mathrm{V}$, a total of $7.59\ \mathrm{V}$. The remaining $12.0 - 7.59 = 4.41\ \mathrm{V}$ is the back e.m.f. of the coil (A1). It is still substantial, which is why the current has not yet reached its final value; at the steady state this back e.m.f. has fallen to zero and the whole $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ is shared between the two resistances as $10.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and $2.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for recognising that the whole e.m.f. appears across the coil at $t = 0$, (A1) for $48.0\ \mathrm{A\,s^{-1}}$, (A1) for the statement that the rate is independent of both resistances. A candidate who answers $12.0/40.0 = 0.30$ has divided by a resistance to obtain a rate and scores nothing; a candidate who writes $48\ \mathrm{A\,s^{-1}}$ but attributes the independence to the coil's resistance only, overlooking the external resistor, loses the third mark.
(b) (M1) for adding the coil's resistance to the external resistance, (A1) for $0.250\ \mathrm{A}$, (M1) for the time constant with the same total resistance, (A1) for $5.21\ \mathrm{ms}$. Condonation: $5.2\ \mathrm{ms}$ is accepted. A candidate who uses $R = 40.0\ \Omega$ throughout scores (M1) for the structure of both calculations and nothing else, because both numerical answers are wrong. The explanation must connect the coil's resistance to the series loop; a bare assertion that the coil has resistance scores the numerical marks but not the explanation.
(c) (M1) for $\tfrac{1}{2}Li^{2}$ with the steady current, (A1) for $7.81\ \mathrm{mJ}$, (M1) for the current at one time constant, (A1) for the fraction $0.400$ or the value $3.12\ \mathrm{mJ}$. A candidate who reports the fraction as $0.632$ has used the fraction of current rather than the fraction of energy and loses the last mark; the square is the whole point of the part.
(d) (A1) for forming the tangent line and the asymptote and solving for their intersection, (A1) for noting that the e.m.f. cancels so the result is general, (A1) for the back e.m.f. of about $4.4\ \mathrm{V}$ at $t = \tau$. Accept any answer between $4.3\ \mathrm{V}$ and $4.5\ \mathrm{V}$, and accept a candidate who obtains it as $12.0 - 0.158 \times 48.0$ or by any equivalent route. A candidate who says the back e.m.f. is zero at $t = \tau$ has confused the transient with the steady state and scores the first two marks only.
Follow-through: a candidate whose total resistance is wrong in (b) but who then uses the same total consistently keeps the method marks in (c) and (d). Forfeits: treating the coil as having no resistance; using $i = I(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$ with $\tau = L/R$; and asserting that the current cannot change at all while the switch is closed.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
subtopic: B.3 Testing the ideal gas equation against data; uncertainty and systematic error
syllabus_ref: B.3 (Gas laws)
title: B.3 Testing the ideal gas equation against data; uncertainty and systematic error
q_html:
Student investigation: testing the ideal gas equation

A student traps a fixed amount of gas in a sealed syringe connected to a pressure gauge and placed in a water bath. The pressure, the volume and the temperature of the water bath are recorded for six different settings. The pressure gauge reads to the nearest 1 kPa, the syringe scale to the nearest 1 cubic centimetre, and the thermometer to the nearest 0.5 K. The student wants to know whether the data support the ideal gas equation, and to determine the amount of gas in the syringe.

The readings are shown in the table. Take the molar gas constant as $8.31$ J per mole per kelvin.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the value of $\dfrac{pV}{T}$ for each of the six settings, stating the unit, and hence determine the amount of gas in the syringe in moles.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Estimate the percentage uncertainty in $\dfrac{pV}{T}$ for the first row of the table, using the resolutions given in the method.

    (Estimate)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Identify which row is not consistent with the other five, and state the temperature that would bring it into line with them.

    (Identify)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Suggest a physical cause for the inconsistency, and describe a change to the experimental method that would remove it.

    (Suggest)
a_html:
(a) With $p$ in kPa and $V$ in cubic centimetres, $pV$ is in units of $10^{3}\times10^{-6}=10^{-3}$ J, so the unit of $\dfrac{pV}{T}$ is $10^{-3}$ J per kelvin. The six values are:

$$166.3,\;166.1,\;166.4,\;166.2,\;166.3,\;161.2\quad(10^{-3}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}).$$

(M1)(A1) Excluding the last row, the mean is $166.3\times10^{-3}$ J per kelvin. Since $\dfrac{pV}{T}=nR$, the amount of gas is

$$n=\frac{166.3\times10^{-3}}{8.31}=2.00\times10^{-2}\text{ mol}.$$

(M1)(A1)

(b) For the first row, the fractional uncertainties are $\dfrac{1}{100}=1.0\%$ in the pressure, $\dfrac{1}{499}=0.20\%$ in the volume and $\dfrac{0.5}{300}=0.17\%$ in the temperature. (M1)(A1) Adding these in quadrature,

$$\sqrt{1.0^{2}+0.20^{2}+0.17^{2}}=\sqrt{1.00+0.040+0.029}=1.0\%.$$

(A1)

(c) The last row is the outlier: its value of $161.2\times10^{-3}$ J per kelvin lies about $3\%$ below the others, against a measurement uncertainty of about $0.6\%$ for that row, so the discrepancy is several times larger than the uncertainty and cannot be put down to precision. (M1)(A1) The temperature that would bring it into line is $T=\dfrac{pV}{nR}=\dfrac{200\times332\times10^{-3}}{8.31\times2.00\times10^{-2}}=399$ K, so about $400$ K rather than $412$ K. (A1)

(d) The most likely cause is that the thermometer was not measuring the temperature of the gas. (A1) If the bulb or probe was resting outside the water bath, in the laboratory air, or in direct sunlight, or was touching the bench, then it reads something other than the gas temperature, and the recorded $412$ K is an over-read of about $12$ K. (A1) This is a systematic error, not a random one: it does not average out over repeats, and it grows with the setting, which is exactly what a sunlit probe would do as the water bath is heated. (A1) The change to the method is to immerse the temperature probe in the water bath alongside the syringe and allow enough time for thermal equilibrium before each reading, to shield the bath from direct radiation, and to stir the bath so that it is isothermal; a further improvement is to read the temperature with the probe in the bath rather than from a sensor clipped to the outside of the syringe. (A1)

Markscheme notes

In (a) allow values within one or two units in the last place and accept the unit expressed as kPa cubic centimetres per kelvin, which is equivalent. The amount of gas should be reported as $2.00\times10^{-2}$ mol; allow $0.0200$ to $0.0201$. In (b) allow the uncertainties to be added linearly, giving about $1.4\%$, provided the method is stated; the quadrature answer is $1.0\%$. In (c) the justification must compare the discrepancy with the uncertainty, not merely point at the row that looks different, and the corrected temperature should be $399$ to $400$ K. In (d) credit any physically sensible cause that is consistent with a temperature over-read, but do not credit 'human error' or 'the reading was wrong'; the improvement must address the cause that has been named. A candidate who suggests that the gas leaked should be asked where the gas went, since the syringe is sealed and the other five rows are consistent. A further condonation is worth recording. Some candidates will compute the invariant as $pV$ against $T$ and attempt a gradient through the origin; this is a perfectly good alternative and should be credited in full provided the last row is excluded from the fit and that exclusion is justified, because a best-fit line through all six points is dragged by the outlier and gives an amount of substance about one per cent low. Others will convert volumes to cubic metres at the start; this is more laborious and introduces more rounding, but is not wrong. What should not be credited is a conclusion reached by eye.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: C.3 One recorded line of a grating spectrum is not a genuine order: the angle is right but the intensity is essentially zero, because the first zero of the single-slit envelope falls exactly on the second-order maximum when d = 2a, and the same ratio predicts the intensity of the third order
syllabus_ref: C.3 Wave phenomena (AHL): the diffraction grating equation n lambda = d sin(theta), the single-slit envelope with its minima at a sin(theta) = m lambda, and the orders that are missing when a multiple-slit maximum coincides with a single-slit minimum
title: C.3 One recorded line of a grating spectrum is not a genuine order: the angle is right but the intensity is essentially zero, because the first zero of the single-slit envelope falls exactly on the second-order maximum when d = 2a, and the same ratio predicts the intensity of the third order
a_html:
(a) A grating with 500 lines per millimetre has a slit separation of one millimetre divided by 500 (M1):
$$d = \frac{1.00 \times 10^{-3}}{500} = 2.00 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m} = 2.00\ \mathrm{\mu m} \;(A1).$$
The second order would satisfy $\sin\theta_{2} = 2\lambda/d = \dfrac{2 \times 589 \times 10^{-9}}{2.00 \times 10^{-6}} = 0.589$, giving $\theta_{2} = \arcsin(0.589) = 36.1^{\circ}$ (A1).
(b) The recorded angle of $36.1^{\circ}$ agrees with the expected position of the second order to within the $0.1^{\circ}$ resolution of the scale, so the position alone does not distinguish a genuine order from an artefact (A1). The intensity does: a genuine second order would be comparable with the first, whereas the student records it at 2 against 100 (A1).
The explanation is the single-slit envelope. Its first minimum lies where $a\sin\theta = \lambda$, and the second order lies where $2\lambda = d\sin\theta$. Dividing the second relation by the first eliminates $\sin\theta$ (M1):
$$\frac{d}{a} = 2.$$
So the first envelope minimum falls exactly on the second-order maximum and the second order has zero intensity, which is why the line is missing and only stray light remains. The slit width follows from the same equation, $a\sin\theta_{2} = \lambda$, so
$$a = \frac{\lambda}{\sin\theta_{2}} = \frac{589 \times 10^{-9}}{0.589} = 1.00 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m} = 1.00\ \mathrm{\mu m} \;(A1).$$
This is consistent with $d = 2.00\ \mathrm{\mu m}$, giving $d/a = 2.00$.
(c) The intensity of order $n$ is proportional to the square of the single-slit amplitude at that angle, that is to $[\sin\beta/\beta]^{2}$ with $\beta = \pi a\sin\theta/\lambda$ (M1). At the first order $a\sin\theta_{1}/\lambda = \tfrac{1}{2}$, so $\beta_{1} = \pi/2$ and the factor is $[1/(\pi/2)]^{2} = (2/\pi)^{2}$. At the third order $a\sin\theta_{3}/\lambda = \tfrac{3}{2}$, so $\beta_{3} = 3\pi/2$ and the factor is $[1/(3\pi/2)]^{2} = (2/3\pi)^{2}$. The ratio is
$$\frac{I_{3}}{I_{1}} = \left(\frac{\pi/2}{3\pi/2}\right)^{2} = \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2} = \frac{1}{9} \;(A1),$$
so the third order should be $100/9 = 11$ on the student's scale. She recorded 11, which agrees, and this is the confirmation that the envelope ratio $d/a = 2$ is right rather than a coincidence of the second order alone.
(d) The claim is supported in part and untested in part. The three recorded angles give $d = n\lambda/\sin\theta$ equal to $2.003\ \mathrm{\mu m}$, $1.999\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ and $1.999\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ for the three lines, all consistent with $2.00\ \mathrm{\mu m}$ and hence with 500 lines per millimetre (A1). The agreement is limited by the $0.1^{\circ}$ resolution of the scale: near $62^{\circ}$ an uncertainty of $0.1^{\circ}$ in $\theta$ corresponds to about $0.3\%$ in $\sin\theta$ and hence in $d$, so the experiment confirms the label to a few parts in a thousand rather than exactly (A1).
The anomalous intensity does not weaken the claim; it strengthens it, because a grating with $d/a = 2$ has its second order missing by construction, and the student's record of a faint line at exactly the second-order angle is evidence that the grating is well made rather than badly made (A1). What the experiment does not determine is the slit width $a$ from the label, since the label gives only the line spacing; $a$ had to be inferred from the position of the envelope zero. It also does not determine whether the line spacing is uniform across the 25 mm of the grating, which is the assumption behind treating the envelope ratio as a single number.

Markscheme notes

(a) (M1) for dividing one millimetre by the line density, (A1) for $2.00\ \mathrm{\mu m}$, (A1) for $36.1^{\circ}$. Accept $36.09^{\circ}$ or $36.1^{\circ}$. A candidate who uses $d = 500\ \mathrm{mm}$ or who fails to convert to metres loses (A1) for the separation and may recover the angle mark only if the value is numerically right.
(b) (A1) for noting that the position agrees and therefore does not settle the question, (A1) for identifying the intensity as the anomaly, (M1) for combining $a\sin\theta = \lambda$ with $n\lambda = d\sin\theta$ at $n = 2$, (A1) for $d/a = 2$ and $a = 1.00\ \mathrm{\mu m}$. A candidate who concludes that the line is a genuine second order because the angle is right scores the first (A1) only; the whole point of the part is that the angle is not the test. A candidate who says the order is missing because the grating is faulty scores nothing in this part.
(c) (M1) for the envelope factor and its values at the two orders, (A1) for the ratio $1/9$ and the prediction 11. Condonation: a candidate who obtains the ratio as $1/9$ directly by arguing that the envelope falls as $1/m^{2}$ for odd $m$ scores full marks. A candidate who predicts $1/3$ has used the amplitude rather than the intensity and loses the (A1).
(d) (A1) for the three values of $d$ and the conclusion that they support the label, (A1) for the resolution argument with a numerical consequence, (A1) for the point that the missing order is evidence for a good grating and for naming at least one quantity the experiment does not determine. A candidate who says only that the readings agree with the label scores the first mark and not the other two; the evaluation is expected to say what the experiment cannot establish, not only what it can.
Follow-through: a candidate whose $d$ in (a) is wrong but who then works consistently keeps the method marks in (b) and (c). Forfeits: using the first-order angle to find $a$ without the missing-order argument; treating the residual intensity of 2 as a measurement of the second order; and reporting the slit width as the distance between adjacent slits.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
subtopic: A.2 Forces and momentum
syllabus_ref: A.2 (Forces and momentum: Newton's laws, momentum and impulse, conservation of momentum)
title: A.2 Forces and momentum
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on forces and momentum. Each one stands alone. Use $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and give each answer to three significant figures.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A block of mass $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ rests on a rough horizontal surface and is pulled by a force of $15\ \mathrm{N}$ acting at $30^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. The coefficient of dynamic friction is $0.25$. What is the acceleration of the block?

    (Calculate)
  2. [1 mark](b)

    Two trolleys of mass $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $2.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ are held together on a frictionless track by a compressed spring. The spring is released and the $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ trolley moves off at $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What is the speed of the other trolley?

    (Calculate)
  3. [1 mark](c)

    A force acting on a ball of mass $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ rises uniformly from zero to $60\ \mathrm{N}$ in $0.020\ \mathrm{s}$ and then falls uniformly back to zero over the next $0.040\ \mathrm{s}$. What is the change in speed of the ball?

    (Calculate)
  4. [1 mark](d)

    A lift of mass $400\ \mathrm{kg}$ carries a passenger of mass $60\ \mathrm{kg}$ and accelerates upwards at $1.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. What is the tension in the supporting cable?

    (Calculate)
  5. [1 mark](e)

    A small sphere falling through a viscous liquid reaches a terminal speed $v$. A second sphere of the same material and twice the radius is dropped into the same liquid. The drag force is given by Stokes' law, $F=6\pi\eta r v$. What is the terminal speed of the larger sphere?

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) A. Resolve the pull: the horizontal component is $15\cos30^{\circ}=12.99\ \mathrm{N}$ and the vertical component is $15\sin30^{\circ}=7.50\ \mathrm{N}$ upwards. The normal reaction is therefore $mg-7.50=19.62-7.50=12.12\ \mathrm{N}$, not $mg$. Friction is $0.25\times12.12=3.03\ \mathrm{N}$, so the net horizontal force is $12.99-3.03=9.96\ \mathrm{N}$ and $a=9.96/2.0=4.98\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. (A1) The whole question turns on the normal reaction; B is what you get by taking it as $mg$.

(b) A. The initial momentum is zero and no external horizontal force acts, so $1.5(3.0)+2.5(-v)=0$ and $v=1.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in the opposite direction. (A1) D is the interesting wrong answer: conserving kinetic energy gives $\tfrac12(1.5)(9)=\tfrac12(2.5)v^{2}$, so $v=2.32$, but the spring releases stored energy, so kinetic energy is *not* conserved here.

(c) A. The impulse is the area under the force-time graph. The shape is a triangle of base $0.020+0.040=0.060\ \mathrm{s}$ and height $60\ \mathrm{N}$, so the impulse is $\tfrac12(0.060)(60)=1.8\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ and $\Delta v=1.8/0.50=3.6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (A1) B doubles it by using the rectangle, and C forgets to divide by the mass.

(d) A. Treating the lift and passenger as one body of mass $460\ \mathrm{kg}$: $T-460g=460(1.2)$, so $T=460(11.01)=5065\ \mathrm{N}=5.06\ \mathrm{kN}$. (A1) The mark is for including the passenger in the accelerated mass; D, at $4.99\ \mathrm{kN}$, is the result of accelerating only the lift.

(e) A. At terminal speed, net weight equals drag: $(\rho_{s}-\rho_{l})\tfrac43\pi r^{3}g=6\pi\eta r v$, so $v\propto r^{2}$. Doubling $r$ multiplies $v$ by $4$. (A1) The two scalings are the point: the driving force is cubic in $r$ and the resisting force is linear in $r$, so the ratio grows as $r^{2}$.

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept $4.9$ to $5.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; a candidate who writes the normal reaction as $12.1\ \mathrm{N}$ has the key idea even if the final figure slips. (b) The direction is not asked for and should not be penalised, but a candidate who says the trolleys move in the same direction has not conserved momentum. (c) Accept $3.6$ or $3.60$; watch for the candidate who computes the area correctly but then multiplies by the mass instead of dividing. (d) Accept $5.05$ to $5.07\ \mathrm{kN}$; the distinction between B, C and D is entirely about which mass is accelerated and in which direction, so an unannotated correct figure earns the mark but a wrong figure earns nothing. (e) This is a scaling question and no numerical value is needed; accept any answer that correctly states that the terminal speed is proportional to the square of the radius. Note that the answer would be different for drag proportional to $v^{2}$, which is the more common regime for large spheres in air.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: D.1 Gravitational fields
syllabus_ref: D.1 (Gravitational fields: potential, field strength, escape speed, orbital energy)
title: D.1 Gravitational fields
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on gravitational fields. Each one stands alone. The gravitational potential is taken to be zero at infinity throughout, so the potential at any finite distance from a mass is negative. $G$ is the gravitational constant.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    Two point masses, each of mass $M$, are separated by a distance $2d$. What is the gravitational potential at the midpoint between them?

    (Determine)
  2. [1 mark](b)

    The escape speed from the surface of a planet of radius $R$ is $v$. What is the escape speed from a point at a distance $2R$ from the centre of the same planet?

    (Calculate)
  3. [1 mark](c)

    A satellite of mass $m$ is in a circular orbit of radius $r$ around a planet of mass $M$. What is the total energy of the satellite?

    (Determine)
  4. [1 mark](d)

    A satellite is moved from a circular orbit of radius $R$ to a circular orbit of radius $2R$ around the same planet of mass $M$. What is the change in the total energy of the satellite?

    (Determine)
  5. [1 mark](e)

    A planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$ has a uniform density. Let $g$ be the gravitational field strength at its surface. What is the gravitational field strength at a distance $R/2$ from its centre?

    (Calculate)
a_html:
(a) A. Gravitational potential is a scalar, so contributions add without any direction: each mass is a distance $d$ from the midpoint and contributes $-GM/d$, giving $-2GM/d$. (A1) Option B is the signature error of this subtopic, because it is the field strength that cancels at the midpoint by symmetry, not the potential.

(b) A. Equating kinetic energy to the depth of the potential well, $\tfrac12 mv_{e}^{2}=GMm/r$, gives $v_{e}=\sqrt{2GM/r}$. At $r=2R$ this is $\sqrt{2GM/(2R)}=v/\sqrt{2}=0.707\,v$. (A1) The square root is what B misses.

(c) A. For a circular orbit $\tfrac12 mv^{2}=GMm/(2r)$, so the kinetic energy is $+GMm/(2r)$ and the potential energy is $-GMm/r$; the total is $-GMm/(2r)$. (A1) The result is negative, which is the defining feature of a bound orbit, and the factor of two is the relationship students most often misremember.

(d) A. With $E=-GMm/(2r)$, the energy changes from $-GMm/(2R)$ to $-GMm/(4R)$. The change is $-GMm/(4R)-(-GMm/(2R))=+GMm/(4R)$, an increase. (A1) The sign is the point: raising an orbit requires an input of energy even though the satellite ends up moving more slowly.

(e) A. For a uniform sphere the enclosed mass within radius $r$ is $M r^{3}/R^{3}$, so $g(r)=G(Mr^{3}/R^{3})/r^{2}=GMr/R^{3}$, which rises linearly from zero at the centre to $g$ at the surface. At $r=R/2$ it is $g/2$. (A1) B is the inverse-square law applied where it does not hold.

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept $-2GM/d$; a candidate who explains that the field cancels while the potential does not has demonstrated the key idea even if the sign slips. (b) Accept $0.71\,v$ or $v/\sqrt{2}$; candidates often reach for the inverse-square law here, so credit should follow the square root rather than any particular rounding. (c) The negative sign is part of the answer and a positive magnitude alone does not earn the mark. (d) Accept the modulus with a clear statement of the direction; note the well-known paradox that the satellite slows down while gaining energy, and do not penalise a candidate who flags it. (e) Accept $g/2$ or $GM/(2R^{2})$; this item depends on the uniform-density assumption, which is stated in the stem, and a candidate who objects that real planets are not uniform is right but has not answered the question as set.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: D.3 Motion in electromagnetic fields
syllabus_ref: D.3 (Motion in electromagnetic fields: charged particles in electric and magnetic fields)
title: D.3 Motion in electromagnetic fields
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on the motion of charged particles in electromagnetic fields. Each one stands alone. Unless a question states otherwise, any magnetic field is uniform and the particle enters it travelling at right angles to the field.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field at right angles to the field. Which statement about the particle is correct?

    (State)
  2. [1 mark](b)

    A proton and an alpha particle enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles, both moving at the same speed. What is the ratio of the radius of the alpha particle's path to the radius of the proton's path?

    (Calculate)
  3. [1 mark](c)

    A proton and an alpha particle enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles, this time with the same kinetic energy. What is the ratio of the radius of the alpha particle's path to the radius of the proton's path?

    (Calculate)
  4. [1 mark](d)

    A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude $B$. What is the period of its motion?

    (Determine)
  5. [1 mark](e)

    In a cyclotron, a charged particle is accelerated each time it crosses the gap between the two dees. Which statement is correct?

    (State)
a_html:
(a) A. The magnetic force is $q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$, which is perpendicular to $\mathbf{v}$ by construction, so it does no work and cannot change the speed; it only turns the velocity, producing circular motion. (A1) Every other option in this item attributes some change in speed to the field.

(b) A. Setting $qvB=mv^{2}/r$ gives $r=mv/(qB)$. An alpha particle has mass $4m_{p}$ and charge $2e$, so $r_{\alpha}/r_{p}=(4/1)\times(1/2)=2$. (A1) C, at $4$, is the mass ratio with the charge forgotten.

(c) A. Now the speed is not common, so write $r=\sqrt{2mK}/(qB)$. Then $r_{\alpha}/r_{p}=\sqrt{4}\times(1/2)=2\times0.5=1$: the paths have the same radius. (A1) The contrast with (b) is the whole point of the pair, and B is the answer to the previous question rather than this one.

(d) A. $T=2\pi r/v$ with $r=mv/(qB)$ gives $T=2\pi m/(qB)$; the speed cancels, so the period does not depend on how fast the particle is moving. (A1) B is the reciprocal, the cyclotron frequency, and is the commonest slip here.

(e) A. The magnetic field bends the path and fixes the period; only the electric field in the gap can change the kinetic energy, because only it has a component along the velocity. (A1) C is wrong for a reason worth stating explicitly: the period is independent of speed, which is what makes the cyclotron work at a fixed frequency at all.

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept any wording that separates the change of direction from the constancy of speed. (b) and (c) are a pair and should be marked together in the sense that a candidate who gives the same answer to both has almost certainly not noticed that the controlled quantity changed; accept $2$ and $1$ respectively, and note that an alpha particle is a helium nucleus with mass number four and charge $+2e$. (d) Accept the expression in any equivalent form; a candidate who writes the frequency instead of the period has inverted the quantity and earns nothing unless the inversion is clearly a slip in labelling. (e) Accept any statement that identifies the electric field as the source of the energy gain; credit should not be withheld from a candidate who adds correctly that the magnetic field is what keeps the particle returning to the gap. A candidate who claims that the magnetic field accelerates the particle has misunderstood the direction of the force and should not be credited even if the rest of the description is accurate.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: D.2 Electric and magnetic fields
syllabus_ref: D.2 (Electric and magnetic fields)
title: D.2 Electric and magnetic fields
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on electric and magnetic fields. Each stands alone. Take $k = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-2}}$, $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, $m_{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $m_{p} = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-1}}$ where needed.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A charge of $+4.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ and a charge of $-1.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ are fixed $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ apart. At which point on the line joining them is the resultant electric field zero?

    (Determine)
  2. [1 mark](b)

    What is the electric potential at a distance of $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ from an isolated point charge of $+4.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$?

    (Calculate)
  3. [1 mark](c)

    An electron, initially at rest, is accelerated through a potential difference of $2.5\ \mathrm{kV}$ in a vacuum. What is its final speed?

    (Calculate)
  4. [1 mark](d)

    A proton enters a uniform magnetic field of $0.40\ \mathrm{T}$ at $3.0 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, moving at right angles to the field. What is the radius of its path?

    (Calculate)
  5. [1 mark](e)

    Two long straight parallel wires are $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ apart and each carries $10\ \mathrm{A}$ in the same direction. What is the force per unit length between them?

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) A. Between opposite charges both fields point towards the negative charge, so they add and cannot cancel; the zero therefore lies outside, on the side of the smaller charge. Solving $4.0/x^{2} = 1.0/(x-0.30)^{2}$ gives $x = 0.60\ \mathrm{m}$ from the $+4.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge, that is $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ beyond the $-1.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge. (A1)

(b) A. $V = kQ/r = 8.99\times10^{9} \times 4.0\times10^{-6}/0.30 = 1.20 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}$. (A1) Potential is a scalar and falls as $1/r$, whereas field strength is a vector and falls as $1/r^{2}$; using the wrong power gives $4.0 \times 10^{5}$, which is option B and has the wrong units entirely.

(c) A. Energy conservation gives $eV = \tfrac{1}{2}m_{e}v^{2}$, so $v = \sqrt{2 \times 1.60\times10^{-19} \times 2500/9.11\times10^{-31}} = 2.97 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (A1) The result is about $0.10c$, so the relativistic correction is below one per cent and the classical expression is adequate here.

(d) A. The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction and not the speed, and the path is circular with $Bqv = mv^{2}/r$. Hence $r = mv/Bq = 1.67\times10^{-27} \times 3.0\times10^{6}/(0.40 \times 1.60\times10^{-19}) = 0.078\ \mathrm{m} = 7.8\ \mathrm{cm}$. (A1)

(e) A. Each wire lies in the field of the other, and $F/L = \mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}/(2\pi d) = 2\times10^{-7} \times 10 \times 10/0.050 = 4.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$. (A1) The force is attractive for currents in the same direction and repulsive for opposite directions, and that distinction is worth as much as the magnitude.

Markscheme notes

One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept $0.60\ \mathrm{m}$ from the $+4.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$ charge stated explicitly; a candidate who gives the distance without saying which side has not answered the question. Do not credit option B on the grounds that the algebra works: recognising that the fields must oppose is the physics, and the square root introduces the spurious root precisely to test it. (b) Accept $1.19$ to $1.20 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{V}$; note that the sign is positive because the source charge is positive, and a candidate who worries about sign here is confusing potential with field. (c) Accept $2.9$ to $3.0 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; relativistic correction at this speed is under one per cent and need not be applied. (d) Accept $7.8$ to $7.9\ \mathrm{cm}$ or $0.078\ \mathrm{m}$; the mark is for $r = mv/Bq$, so a candidate who writes the correct expression and then makes an arithmetic slip should be given the benefit of the doubt in bookwork terms. (e) Accept $4.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$ with the direction stated; the direction is half the item and should not be treated as a bonus.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
subtopic: A.4 Rigid body mechanics
syllabus_ref: A.4 (Rigid body mechanics: moment of inertia, rotational dynamics, rolling without slipping)
title: A.4 Rigid body mechanics
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on rigid-body mechanics. Each one stands alone, so you can attempt any of them without the others. Use $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-2}}$ where a numerical value is needed, and give each answer to three significant figures.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A solid cylinder and a thin-walled hollow cylinder have the same mass and the same outer radius. Both are released from rest and roll without slipping down the same incline. What is the ratio of the acceleration of the solid cylinder to the acceleration of the hollow cylinder?

    (Calculate)
  2. [1 mark](b)

    A disc of moment of inertia $0.80\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{2}}$ rotates freely about a fixed vertical axle at $12\ \mathrm{rad\ s^{-1}}$. A lump of clay of mass $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$, initially at rest, is dropped onto the disc and sticks at a point $0.60\ \mathrm{m}$ from the axle. What is the angular speed immediately afterwards?

    (Calculate)
  3. [1 mark](c)

    A solid cylinder is released from rest on a rough incline and rolls down it without slipping, accelerating as it goes. What is the direction of the static frictional force that the surface of the incline exerts on the cylinder?

    (State)
  4. [1 mark](d)

    A light inextensible string is wound around a disc of radius $0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ whose moment of inertia about its axle is $0.30\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{2}}$. The disc turns on a fixed horizontal axle with negligible friction, and a block of mass $1.2\ \mathrm{kg}$ hangs from the free end of the string. What is the tension in the string as the block descends?

    (Calculate)
  5. [1 mark](e)

    A solid uniform sphere of moment of inertia $\frac{2}{5}MR^2$ about its centre rolls without slipping along level ground at a constant speed of $3.0\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$. What fraction of the sphere's total kinetic energy is rotational kinetic energy?

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) For rolling without slipping the acceleration down an incline is $a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + I/(MR^2)}$. The solid cylinder has $I = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$ and so accelerates at $\tfrac{2}{3}g\sin\theta$; the thin-walled hollow cylinder has $I = MR^2$ and so accelerates at $\tfrac{1}{2}g\sin\theta$. The ratio is $\tfrac{2/3}{1/2} = \tfrac{4}{3} = 1.33$. (A1) Option B inverts it, option C assumes every rolling body behaves the same, and option D takes the ratio of the moments of inertia without the denominator.

(b) Angular momentum about the axle is conserved, because neither the axle force nor the weight of the clay exerts a torque about it. Initially $L = 0.80 \times 12 = 9.6\ \mathrm{kg\ m^2\ s^{-1}}$. The clay contributes $mr^2 = 0.50 \times 0.60^2 = 0.18\ \mathrm{kg\ m^2}$, so the final moment of inertia is $0.98\ \mathrm{kg\ m^2}$ and the final angular speed is $9.6/0.98 = 9.80\ \mathrm{rad\ s^{-1}}$. (A1) Option B ignores the clay, option C reports the angular momentum as though it were a speed, and option D adds $mr$ instead of $mr^2$.

(c) The weight acts through the centre of mass and the normal force passes through the contact point, so neither produces a torque about the centre. Only friction can supply the torque that increases the angular speed, and it must act up the incline to do so. (A1) Note that static friction opposes the motion the contact point *would* have, not the motion of the centre of mass.

(d) The string does not slip, so $a = \alpha R$. Then $mg - T = ma$ for the block and $TR = I\alpha$ for the disc, giving $T = Ia/R^2$. Hence $a = \dfrac{mg}{m + I/R^2} = \dfrac{1.2 \times 9.81}{1.2 + 4.8} = 1.96\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-2}}$, and $T = 4.8 \times 1.96 = 9.42\ \mathrm{N}$. (A1) Option B neglects the disc's inertia, option C is the resultant force rather than the tension, and option D uses $I = \tfrac{1}{2}mR^2$ with the block's mass.

(e) With $I = \tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$ and $\omega = v/R$, the rotational term is $\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{5}Mv^2$ and the translational term is $\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2$. The rotational fraction is therefore $\dfrac{1/5}{1/5 + 1/2} = \dfrac{2}{7} = 0.286$. (A1) Option B quotes the coefficient in $I$, option C splits the energy evenly, and option D is the translational fraction.

Markscheme notes

One mark for each correct option. There is no penalty for a wrong answer under the Paper 1A rules, so every question should be attempted, and a student who cannot finish a calculation should eliminate on dimensional or limiting-case grounds and choose. In (a) condone the ratio written as $4:3$ or as $1.33$. In (b) allow follow-through from an incorrect final moment of inertia provided the conservation statement itself is explicit and correct. In (c) accept 'up the slope' or 'up the plane'; the direction must be given relative to the incline, and 'opposite to the motion' is not sufficient because the phrase is ambiguous here. In (d) accept $9.4\ \mathrm{N}$ to two significant figures, and allow an answer obtained by computing the acceleration first. In (e) accept $2/7$ or $0.29$; the fact that the answer has no unit is itself part of what is being assessed. Candidates most often lose these marks not through algebra but by applying a purely translational model to a body that is also rotating; watch for a line of working in which the moment of inertia has quietly disappeared. A calculator is available throughout, so no credit is due for an unreduced surd where a decimal was requested, and values should carry three significant figures.

subject: Physics HL
subtopic: D.4 Induction
syllabus_ref: D.4 (Induction: Faraday's law, Lenz's law, motional emf, self-inductance)
title: D.4 Induction
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on electromagnetic induction. Each one stands alone. In every case the magnetic field is uniform over the region stated and the resistance given is the total circuit resistance.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A rectangular coil of 200 turns and resistance $4.0\ \Omega$ has one side of length $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ inside a uniform magnetic field of $0.80\ \mathrm{T}$. The coil is pulled out of the field at a constant speed of $0.20\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$, with that side remaining perpendicular to the direction of motion. What is the current in the coil while it leaves the field?

    (Calculate)
  2. [1 mark](b)

    A coil of 500 turns and area $0.020\ \mathrm{m^2}$ rotates at a steady frequency of $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ in a uniform magnetic field of $0.10\ \mathrm{T}$, with its axis of rotation perpendicular to the field. What is the maximum emf induced across the coil?

    (Calculate)
  3. [1 mark](c)

    An inductor of inductance $0.40\ \mathrm{H}$ carries a steady current of $3.0\ \mathrm{A}$. How much energy is stored in the magnetic field of the inductor?

    (Calculate)
  4. [1 mark](d)

    A square loop of side $0.10\ \mathrm{m}$ and resistance $2.0\ \Omega$ is pulled at constant speed completely through a region of uniform magnetic field of $0.50\ \mathrm{T}$ directed perpendicular to the plane of the loop. The region is wide enough that the loop enters and leaves separately. What total charge flows past a point in the loop?

    (Determine)
  5. [1 mark](e)

    A conducting rod of length $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ rotates at a steady angular speed of $20\ \mathrm{rad\ s^{-1}}$ about one end, sweeping out a plane that is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of $0.25\ \mathrm{T}$. What is the emf between the two ends of the rod?

    (Calculate)
a_html:
(a) Only the side of length $L = 0.050\ \mathrm{m}$ that lies across the field boundary changes the flux, so $\varepsilon = NBLv = 200 \times 0.80 \times 0.050 \times 0.20 = 1.6\ \mathrm{V}$, and $I = \varepsilon/R = 1.6/4.0 = 0.40\ \mathrm{A}$. (A1) Option B reports the emf, option C puts the coil area where the side length belongs, and option D omits the turn count.

(b) The flux linkage is $N\Phi = NBA\cos(\omega t)$, so $\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin(\omega t)$ with $\omega = 2\pi f = 314\ \mathrm{rad\ s^{-1}}$. Hence $\varepsilon_{\max} = 500 \times 0.10 \times 0.020 \times 314 = 314\ \mathrm{V}$. (A1) Option B uses $\pi f$ for $\omega$, option C uses $f$, and option D gives the flux linkage rather than its rate of change.

(c) $E = \tfrac{1}{2}LI^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.40 \times 3.0^2 = 1.80\ \mathrm{J}$. (A1) Option B omits the half, option C uses $LI$, and option D halves $LI$.

(d) The charge is $Q = \int I\,dt = \dfrac{1}{R}\int \varepsilon\,dt = \dfrac{|\Delta\Phi|}{R}$ over each transition. Entry gives $Ba^2/R = 0.50 \times 0.010/2.0 = 2.5\ \mathrm{mC}$ and exit gives the same again, so $Q = 5.0\ \mathrm{mC}$. (A1) This is the item that separates a student who has memorised a formula from one who knows what charge is: the *net* flux change over the whole motion is indeed zero, but the two currents flow at different times and it is their magnitudes, not their signs, that add.

(e) An element at distance $r$ moves at $\omega r$, so $d\varepsilon = B\omega r\,dr$ and $\varepsilon = \int_0^L B\omega r\,dr = \tfrac{1}{2}B\omega L^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.25 \times 20 \times 0.16 = 0.400\ \mathrm{V}$. (A1) Option B uses the tip speed throughout, option C is dimensionally inconsistent, and option D halves twice.

Markscheme notes

One mark per correct option, no negative marking. In (a) allow an answer reached via the rate of cutting of flux lines provided the length used is the one crossing the boundary. In (b) accept 314 V or 3.1 x 10^2 V, and condone a small discrepancy from rounding omega to 314. In (c) accept 1.8 J. In (d) do not credit an argument from the net flux change alone even if it reaches 5.0 mC by some other route, because the reasoning is what is being rewarded; equally, credit 5.0 mC reached by treating the two transitions separately as intended. In (e) accept 0.40 V and allow the integral form or the mean-speed argument. Note that in (d) the speed at which the loop is pulled does not appear in the answer at all, and that is the point of the item: the charge depends only on the change of flux linkage and on the resistance. In (e) credit the integral form and the mean-speed argument equally, but do not credit B L v applied with the tip speed, which is precisely the error option B exists to catch. In (b) the value 314 V depends on using an angular frequency in radians per second; a candidate working in degrees will reach none of the options, which is a useful diagnostic in itself.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
subtopic: B.5 Current and circuits
syllabus_ref: B.5 (Current and circuits: internal resistance, non-ideal meters, power transfer)
title: B.5 Current and circuits
q_html:
Five independent multiple-choice questions in which a circuit is altered by the act of measuring it, or by the load connected to it. In each case the supply is treated as ideal unless an internal resistance is stated explicitly.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    A cell of emf $12\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $3.0\ \Omega$ is connected to a variable external resistor. What is the greatest power that can be dissipated in that external resistor?

    (Calculate)
  2. [1 mark](b)

    For the cell in the previous question, at the external resistance that gives the greatest power in the external resistor, what fraction of the total power generated by the cell is delivered to that external resistor?

    (State)
  3. [1 mark](c)

    A cell of negligible internal resistance and emf $6.0\ \mathrm{V}$ is connected in series with a $400\ \Omega$ resistor and a $600\ \Omega$ resistor. A voltmeter of resistance $2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ is connected across the $600\ \Omega$ resistor. What does the voltmeter read?

    (Calculate)
  4. [1 mark](d)

    A circuit consists of a $12\ \mathrm{V}$ supply of negligible internal resistance connected to a $100\ \Omega$ resistor. An ammeter of resistance $5.0\ \Omega$ is inserted in series to measure the current. What is the percentage error in the current it reads?

    (Calculate)
  5. [1 mark](e)

    A cell is connected to a $4.0\ \Omega$ resistor and the terminal potential difference is $6.0\ \mathrm{V}$. When the same cell is connected to a $9.0\ \Omega$ resistor the terminal potential difference is $7.2\ \mathrm{V}$. What is the internal resistance of the cell?

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) The power in the load is $P = \dfrac{E^2 R}{(R+r)^2}$, which is greatest when $R = r = 3.0\ \Omega$. Then $I = 12/6.0 = 2.0\ \mathrm{A}$ and $P = I^2R = 4.0 \times 3.0 = 12\ \mathrm{W}$, which is also $E^2/(4r)$. (A1) Option B is $E^2/r$, the power dissipated inside the cell at short circuit, and options C and D come from dropping or doubling the factor of four.

(b) At $R = r$ the same current passes through both resistances, so $I^2R = I^2r$ and exactly one half of the generated power reaches the load. (A1) This is why maximum power transfer and high efficiency are different aims: option B needs an ideal cell, and options C and D correspond to $R = 2r$ and $R = r/3$ respectively.

(c) The voltmeter is in parallel with the $600\ \Omega$ resistor, giving $R_p = \dfrac{600 \times 2000}{2600} = 462\ \Omega$. The circuit total becomes $400 + 462 = 862\ \Omega$, so $I = 6.0/862 = 6.96\ \mathrm{mA}$ and the reading is $I R_p = 3.21\ \mathrm{V}$. (A1) Option B assumes an ideal meter, option C mixes the loaded resistance with the unloaded total, and option D loads the wrong resistor.

(d) True current $I_0 = 12/100 = 0.120\ \mathrm{A}$; with the ammeter in place $I = 12/105 = 0.1143\ \mathrm{A}$. The fractional error is $\dfrac{0.120 - 0.1143}{0.120} = 4.76\%$, which equals $R_A/(R + R_A) = 5.0/105$. (A1) Option B uses $R_A/R$, option C ignores the meter, and option D is the ratio of the two currents rather than the error.

(e) The currents are $I_1 = 6.0/4.0 = 1.5\ \mathrm{A}$ and $I_2 = 7.2/9.0 = 0.80\ \mathrm{A}$. Since $V = E - Ir$, subtracting gives $6.0 - 7.2 = -r(1.5 - 0.80)$, so $r = 1.2/0.70 = 1.71\ \Omega$ and $E = 8.57\ \mathrm{V}$. (A1) Option B inverts the gradient, option C quotes the voltage change, and option D quotes the lost volts.

Markscheme notes

One mark per correct option, no negative marking. In (a) accept 12 W reached by differentiating the power expression or by quoting the maximum power theorem, provided the condition R equals r is stated. In (b) accept 50% or one half; note that a candidate who answers (a) correctly but (b) as two thirds has applied the theorem without understanding it. In (c) accept any value between 3.20 V and 3.22 V from premature rounding of the parallel pair. In (d) accept 4.8% to two significant figures, and credit the exact form 5/105. In (e) accept 1.7 ohms, and allow a graphical solution from a V against I plot provided the gradient is taken with the correct sign. Across the cluster, a candidate who rounds the parallel resistance in (c) prematurely may report anything from 3.20 V to 3.22 V and should be credited; a comparable tolerance applies in (e). In (d) the exact form 5.0 over 105 earns the mark even when left as a fraction. Note that (a) and (b) are formally independent, so a candidate may answer either without the other, and no follow-through between them should be assumed either way.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
subtopic: E.1 / E.2 Photons, the photoelectric effect and matter waves
syllabus_ref: E.1 (Structure of the atom), E.2 (Quantum physics)
title: E.1 / E.2 Photons, the photoelectric effect and matter waves
q_html:
Each question below is self-contained. Take the Planck constant as $6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s, the speed of light in vacuum as $3.00\times10^{8}$ m per second, the elementary charge as $1.60\times10^{-19}$ C, the electron mass as $9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg, and $1\,\mathrm{eV}=1.60\times10^{-19}$ J.

  1. [1 mark](a)

    Light of wavelength 420 nm is incident on a metal surface in a darkened room. What is the energy carried by a single photon of this light, and what is that energy when it is expressed in electron-volts rather than in joules?

    (Calculate)
  2. [1 mark](b)

    A metal has a work function of $2.28$ eV. Light of frequency $8.00\times10^{14}$ Hz is shone on it. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons?

    (Calculate)
  3. [1 mark](c)

    For the metal and the illumination described in the previous question, what stopping potential would be measured?

    (Determine)
  4. [1 mark](d)

    An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of $150$ V. What is its de Broglie wavelength?

    (Calculate)
  5. [1 mark](e)

    A laser emits $2.0$ mW of light at a wavelength of $640$ nm. How many photons does it emit each second?

    (Calculate)
a_html:
(a) $E=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{420\times10^{-9}}=4.74\times10^{-19}$ J, which is option A. (A1) Option B is the same number in electron-volts, so it catches anyone who converts and then forgets which unit they are in; option C comes from multiplying by the wavelength; option D is the frequency, one step short. (a) A

(b) $hf=6.63\times10^{-34}\times8.00\times10^{14}=5.304\times10^{-19}$ J $=3.315$ eV. Subtracting the work function gives $K_{\max}=3.315-2.28=1.035$ eV $=1.66\times10^{-19}$ J, option A. (A1) The trap in option B is subtracting $2.28\times10^{-19}$ J, which is not the same quantity as $2.28$ eV. (b) A

(c) $eV_s=K_{\max}$ in electron-volts, so $V_s=1.035$ V, option A. (A1) The rule is that one electron-volt corresponds to one volt for a singly charged particle, which is why the conversion is trivial once (b) is in eV and impossible if it is left in joules. (c) A

(d) $p=\sqrt{2\,m\,eV}=\sqrt{2\times9.11\times10^{-31}\times1.60\times10^{-19}\times150}=6.61\times10^{-24}$ kg m per second, so $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{p}=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{6.61\times10^{-24}}=1.00\times10^{-10}$ m, option A. (A1) The factor of two is the discriminator here, and it is worth noting that $0.10$ nm is of the order of an atomic spacing, which is why electron diffraction works. (d) A

(e) $E=\dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{640\times10^{-9}}=3.11\times10^{-19}$ J, so the rate is $\dfrac{2.0\times10^{-3}}{3.11\times10^{-19}}=6.4\times10^{15}$ per second, option A. (A1) Option B is the most dangerous distractor in the cluster because the arithmetic is identical and only the prefix differs. (e) A

Markscheme notes

One mark per item and there is no negative marking, so a candidate should be advised to commit to an answer rather than leave a blank. In (a) condone $4.7$ to $4.8\times10^{-19}$ J. In (b) allow the answer in eV provided it is identified as such, and note that a candidate who works entirely in joules must convert the work function first; that conversion is where the mark is actually won or lost. In (d) allow $0.10$ nm or $1.0\times10^{-10}$ m, and credit a candidate who reaches $1.42\times10^{-10}$ m only if they show the factor of two explicitly, since otherwise the working is wrong even though the answer looks close. In (e) accept $6.4\times10^{15}$ to $6.5\times10^{15}$. It is worth telling candidates explicitly that the electron-volt is doing real work in this cluster rather than being decoration: in (b) the subtraction is only possible after the work function has been brought into the same unit as the photon energy, and in (c) the answer in volts is the answer in electron-volts, which is the sense in which the unit simplifies rather than complicates the arithmetic.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
subtopic: B.4 Thermodynamics
syllabus_ref: B.3 Gas laws (ideal gas equation), B.4 Thermodynamics (AHL): first law, work, internal energy, heat engine efficiency
title: B.4 Thermodynamics
q_html:
Stimulus

A fixed amount of monatomic ideal gas is taken round the rectangular cycle ABCDA shown in the table. Each leg is either isochoric (constant volume) or isobaric (constant pressure).

| State | $p$ / Pa | $V$ / m³ | $T$ / K |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | $2.0\times10^{5}$ | $5.0\times10^{-3}$ | $300$ |
| B | $4.0\times10^{5}$ | $5.0\times10^{-3}$ | |
| C | $4.0\times10^{5}$ | $1.0\times10^{-2}$ | |
| D | $2.0\times10^{5}$ | $1.0\times10^{-2}$ | |

For a monatomic ideal gas, $U=\dfrac32 nRT$. The amount of gas is $n=0.40\ \mathrm{mol}$ and $R=8.31\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$.

The cycle runs A → B → C → D → A.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Show that $T_{B}=600\ \mathrm{K}$, $T_{C}=1200\ \mathrm{K}$ and $T_{D}=600\ \mathrm{K}$.

    (Show that)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the net work done by the gas in one complete cycle.

    (Calculate)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Calculate the total thermal energy transferred to the gas during one complete cycle.

    (Calculate)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Determine the efficiency of this cycle as a heat engine, and compare it with the efficiency of a Carnot engine operating between the same maximum and minimum temperatures.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) From $pV=nRT$, with $n$ and $R$ constant, $T\propto pV$.

A → B is isochoric, so $T\propto p$: $\dfrac{T_{B}}{T_{A}}=\dfrac{p_{B}}{p_{A}}=\dfrac{4.0}{2.0}=2 \Rightarrow T_{B}=600\ \mathrm{K}$. (M1)(A1)

B → C is isobaric, so $T\propto V$: $\dfrac{T_{C}}{T_{B}}=\dfrac{V_{C}}{V_{B}}=\dfrac{1.0\times10^{-2}}{5.0\times10^{-3}}=2 \Rightarrow T_{C}=1200\ \mathrm{K}$. (A1)

C → D is isochoric: $\dfrac{T_{D}}{T_{C}}=\dfrac{p_{D}}{p_{C}}=\dfrac{2.0}{4.0}=\dfrac12 \Rightarrow T_{D}=600\ \mathrm{K}$. (A1)

(Consistency check: D → A is isobaric with $\frac{V_A}{V_D}=\frac12$, giving $T_{A}=300\ \mathrm{K}$ as stated.)

(b) Work is done only on the two isochoric-free legs:

B → C: $W=p\,\Delta V=4.0\times10^{5}(1.0\times10^{-2}-5.0\times10^{-3})=4.0\times10^{5}(5.0\times10^{-3})=2000\ \mathrm{J}$ (A1)

D → A: $W=p\,\Delta V=2.0\times10^{5}(5.0\times10^{-3}-1.0\times10^{-2})=-1000\ \mathrm{J}$ (A1)

$$W_{\text{net}}=2000-1000=1000\ \mathrm{J}$$ (A1)

(Equivalently, the area of the rectangle: $(4.0-2.0)\times10^{5}\times(1.0-0.5)\times10^{-2}=1000\ \mathrm{J}$.)

(c) Heat flows in during the two legs where the temperature rises: A → B and B → C.

A → B (isochoric): $W=0$, so by the first law $Q=\Delta U$.

$$Q_{AB}=\tfrac32 nR\,\Delta T=\tfrac32(0.40)(8.31)(600-300)=1.5(0.40)(8.31)(300)=1496\ \mathrm{J}$$ (M1)(A1)

B → C (isobaric): $\Delta U=\tfrac32 nR\,\Delta T=\tfrac32(0.40)(8.31)(1200-600)=2992\ \mathrm{J}$ (A1)

$W=2000\ \mathrm{J}$ from (b), so by the first law $Q=\Delta U+W$:

$$Q_{BC}=2992+2000=4992\ \mathrm{J}$$ (M1)(A1)

$$Q_{\text{in}}=1496+4992=6488\approx6.5\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}$$

(d)

$$\eta=\frac{W_{\text{net}}}{Q_{\text{in}}}=\frac{1000}{6488}=0.154=15.4\%$$ (A1)

A Carnot engine between $T_{\max}=1200\ \mathrm{K}$ and $T_{\min}=300\ \mathrm{K}$ has

$$\eta_{\text{Carnot}}=1-\frac{T_{\min}}{T_{\max}}=1-\frac{300}{1200}=0.75=75\%$$ (M1)(A1)

So this cycle achieves only about one fifth of the Carnot efficiency. (A1) The reason is that heat is taken in over a whole *range* of temperatures — including during the isochoric leg A → B, where the gas is still relatively cool — and rejected over a range as well (C → D and D → A). A Carnot engine takes in all of its heat at the single highest temperature and rejects it all at the single lowest; any engine that absorbs heat while its temperature is changing must do worse.

Markscheme notes

(a) Credit either the ratio argument or direct substitution into $T=pV/nR$. Using $R=8.31$ and $n=0.40$ gives $T_{A}=301\ \mathrm{K}$ rather than exactly $300\ \mathrm{K}$; this is rounding in the data and must not be penalised. Award full marks for temperatures given as 600, 1200, 600 K.

(b) Award (A1) for each leg's work with the correct sign, (A1) for the net. Credit the 'area of the p–V loop' method fully if the area is correctly identified as $(p_{2}-p_{1})(V_{2}-V_{1})$.

(c) The key discrimination is *which* legs to include. Candidates who sum $\Delta U$ over the whole cycle get zero (correctly, since it returns to A) and conclude $Q_{\text{in}}=W_{\text{net}}$, which is wrong — heat is also *rejected*. Award (M1) for applying $Q=\Delta U+W$ on a heating leg. Condone 6.4–6.5 kJ given rounding.

(d) Accept 15%–16%. The Carnot comparison must use the *extreme* temperatures of the cycle (300 K and 1200 K), not the mean. The final (A1) is for an explanation in terms of heat being absorbed/rejected across a temperature range; 'real engines are always less efficient' is not sufficient.

subject: Physics HL
topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
subtopic: A.4 Rigid body mechanics
syllabus_ref: A.4 Rigid body mechanics (AHL): torque, moment of inertia of a disc, torque = I x angular acceleration, rotational kinetic energy
title: A flywheel, a hanging mass, and a brake
q_html:
A uniform solid disc of mass $M=2.4\ \mathrm{kg}$ and radius $R=0.35\ \mathrm{m}$ is mounted on a fixed horizontal axle. A light string is wound round the rim, does not slip, and hangs vertically with a mass $m=0.80\ \mathrm{kg}$ attached to its free end. The disc is released from rest and the mass falls a distance $h=0.90\ \mathrm{m}$ before it reaches the floor.

  1. [5 marks](a)

    Show that the acceleration of the falling mass is $a=\dfrac{mg}{m+M/2}$ and calculate its value.

    (Show that)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the tension in the string while the mass is falling, and explain why it is less than the weight of the mass.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Determine the speed of the mass as it reaches the floor, and verify your answer by comparing the loss of gravitational potential energy with the total kinetic energy gained.

    (Determine)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    After the mass lands the string goes slack. A brake then applies a constant torque of $0.24\ \mathrm{N\,m}$ about the axle. Calculate the number of complete revolutions the disc makes before it stops.

    (Calculate)
a_html:
(a) Let $T$ be the string tension and $a$ the acceleration of the mass; the string does not slip, so the angular acceleration of the disc is $\alpha=a/R$. (M1)

For the hanging mass: $mg-T=ma$ (M1)

For the disc, torque $\tau=TR$ and moment of inertia $I=\dfrac{1}{2}MR^{2}$, so $TR=\dfrac{1}{2}MR^{2}\cdot\dfrac{a}{R}=\dfrac{1}{2}MRa$, giving $T=\dfrac{1}{2}Ma$. (M1)(A1)

Substituting: $mg-\dfrac{1}{2}Ma=ma$, so $a=\dfrac{mg}{m+\dfrac{M}{2}}$. (AG)

Numerically $a=\dfrac{0.80\times 9.81}{0.80+1.2}=\dfrac{7.848}{2.0}=3.92\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. (A1)

(b) $T=\dfrac{1}{2}Ma=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2.4\times 3.924=4.71\ \mathrm{N}$. (M1)(A1)

The weight of the mass is $mg=0.80\times 9.81=7.85\ \mathrm{N}$, so $T<mg$. (A1) The tension is less than the weight because the mass is accelerating downwards: the resultant downward force $mg-T$ is what supplies its acceleration, and if $T$ equalled $mg$ the mass would not accelerate at all.
