If a candidate writes a complete working heap implementation in (b), credit it but do not award extra marks beyond the five available: the part asks for a design, and a long listing is often a way of avoiding the complexity comments that carry the marks. Conversely, a candidate who gives only signatures with no complexity annotation has answered a different question and should be capped at three.

```
subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: Distributed monitoring system — architecture, transmission and schema design
syllabus_ref: A2.2 Network architecture, A2.3 Data transmissions, A2.4 Network security, A3.2 Database design
title: Distributed monitoring system — architecture, transmission and schema design
q_html:
Northreach cold chain

Northreach is a regional health authority that distributes vaccines by road. Its fleet is 140 refrigerated vehicles. Each vehicle carries four temperature probes inside the cargo compartment, and each probe is sampled every 30 seconds throughout the ten-hour delivery window. A reading consists of a probe identifier stored in one byte, a timestamp stored in four bytes, and a temperature stored in two bytes. The authority operates on 300 days each year. Regulatory rules require that any excursion above 8 degrees Celsius is detected and an alert raised within 60 seconds of the reading being taken, and that the full temperature history for any consignment can be produced as evidence for up to six years.

The authority has asked your team to design the monitoring and alerting subsystem. The parameters you need are given in the case study.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate the total volume of data the fleet generates in one operating year, giving your answer in gibibytes, and state what the volume would become if each reading were instead stored as an 80-byte plain-text record.

    (Calculate)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    A junior developer proposes that each probe pushes every reading to the central server the moment it is taken, using a separate secure request per reading. Explain why this is a poor design even though the total payload is small, and explain how placing an edge device in each vehicle changes the trade-off.

    (Explain)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Construct a relational schema, in third normal form, for the part of the system that records vehicles, consignments, probes and excursion alerts. Show the tables with their primary keys, foreign keys and a sensible attribute for each, and state the relationship between consignments and alerts.

    (Construct)
  4. [5 marks](d)

    A second proposal is that each vehicle stores readings locally and uploads the whole day's file once, when it returns to the depot. Evaluate this proposal against the regulatory requirements, considering the alert deadline, the reliability of the evidence trail, and the cost of the system.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Each probe is sampled $\dfrac{10\times3600}{30}=1200$ times per day, so each vehicle produces $4\times1200=4800$ readings per day. (M1)(A1) At 7 bytes each, the fleet produces

$$4800\times7\times140\times300=1.4112\times10^{9}\text{ bytes}$$

per year, which is $\dfrac{1.4112\times10^9}{2^{30}}=1.31$ GiB. (A1) Stored as 80-byte text the same readings occupy

$$4800\times80\times140\times300\div 2^{30}=15.0\text{ GiB},$$

roughly eleven times as much. (A1)

(b) The aggregate payload is only $140\times\dfrac{7}{30}\approx33$ bytes per second, so bandwidth is not the objection. (A1) The objection is per-request cost: each reading would carry its own transport handshake and encryption overhead, so a 7-byte reading could easily be carried inside a request of 800 bytes or more, multiplying the traffic by a factor well over a hundred and adding a fresh handshake every 30 seconds on every vehicle. (M1)(A1) Mobile coverage in a refrigerated vehicle is intermittent, and a per-reading push has no way to buffer across a dropout, so readings would simply be lost when a vehicle passes through a tunnel. (A1) An edge device in the vehicle changes the trade-off decisively: it can buffer readings locally through a coverage gap, batch them into one request every few minutes, evaluate the excursion rule locally so that an alert can be raised within seconds even with no network at all, and forward only alerts plus batched history to the centre. (R1)

(c) Four tables are needed:

VEHICLE(vehicleID PK, registration, depotID FK, commissionedDate)

CONSIGNMENT(consignmentID PK, vehicleID FK, departedAt, returnedAt, productCode)

PROBE(probeID PK, vehicleID FK, positionLabel, calibratedOn)

EXCURSION_ALERT(alertID PK, probeID FK, consignmentID FK, raisedAt, peakTemperature, durationSeconds, acknowledgedBy)

(M1)(A1)(A1) The schema is in third normal form because every non-key attribute depends on the whole of its table's key and on nothing else: probe calibration belongs to the probe, not to the alert, and the depot belongs to the vehicle, not to the consignment. (A1) The relationship between consignments and alerts is one-to-many: one consignment may generate any number of alerts, including none, and each alert belongs to exactly one consignment. (A1)

(d) The depot-upload proposal is cheap and simple, and for the storage requirement alone it would be adequate: the files arrive intact once a day and the six-year archive is straightforward to keep. (A1) It fails the alert deadline outright. A reading taken at the start of a shift would not reach the centre for up to ten hours, against a requirement of 60 seconds, and a spoiled consignment would be delivered before anyone knew. (M1)(A1) It also weakens the evidence trail: a vehicle involved in an accident, or one whose local storage fails, takes the whole day's record with it, and there is no independent copy against which a disputed reading could be checked. (A1) The correct evaluation is therefore that the proposal is acceptable only for the archive tier, not for the alerting tier. A hybrid is justified: the edge device raises alerts immediately over the mobile network, while the full-resolution history is batched opportunistically during the shift and reconciled at the depot. Alerts are small and time-critical; history is large and not. Splitting the two by their deadlines rather than by their size is the whole design. (R1) One further consideration belongs in any real design and is worth raising in an answer: the clock. Timestamps are generated on the vehicle, and if a vehicle's clock drifts then an alert can appear to precede the reading that caused it, which would undermine the evidence trail completely. Synchronising the edge device periodically and recording both the device time and the server receipt time on every alert removes that risk at negligible cost, and a candidate who spots it unprompted is thinking about the system rather than about the question.

Markscheme notes

In (a) award the method mark for the chain of multiplications even if the final conversion is wrong; allow 1.3 GiB to 1.4 GiB and 14.9 to 15.1 GiB, and condone the use of 10^9 rather than 2^30 provided the unit is stated consistently. In (b) the mark is for recognising that per-request overhead, not payload size, dominates; a candidate who simply says 'too much data' should not be credited, because the data is not large. In (c) accept any schema that reaches third normal form and states the keys; do not require the exact attribute names given here, but do require that alert data is separated from probe metadata and that both foreign keys on the alert table are present. In (d) a recommendation is required, not a list of pros and cons: award the highest mark only where the candidate separates the alerting tier from the archive tier and justifies the split by deadline rather than by volume. Candidates may reasonably propose a message queue or a publish-subscribe broker between the vehicle and the centre, and this should be credited where the alert path is separated from the bulk path. Where a candidate argues that the whole system should be edge-only with no central alerting at all, press for how a regulator would inspect the evidence; that question is usually enough to expose the gap.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A2.4 Network security
syllabus_ref: A2.4 Network security, A1.2 Data representation and computer logic (binary, hexadecimal, hashing)
title: A2.4 Network security
q_html:
Wireless smart lock

A smart lock is fitted to a communal entrance. The lock is battery powered and communicates with the resident's phone over a short-range wireless link. The current protocol works as follows. The lock stores a 32-bit shared secret $S$. To unlock, the phone transmits a single frame containing the ASCII text OPEN followed by the 32-bit value $S$ in hexadecimal. The lock compares the received value with its stored $S$ and, if they match, releases the bolt. There is no encryption, no timestamp and no counter. An attacker with a $40\ \mathrm{EUR}$ software-defined radio can capture any frame transmitted within about $15\ \mathrm{m}$ and can later transmit arbitrary bytes. The lock is rated for $25$ operations per day on a $2.4\ \mathrm{Ah}$, $3.0\ \mathrm{V}$ battery. Its microcontroller can compute a keyed hash over $32$ bytes in $4\ \mathrm{ms}$ using $0.90\ \mathrm{mJ}$, whereas transmitting the current static frame costs $0.15\ \mathrm{mJ}$. The round-trip time on the wireless link is $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ and the bolt must be released within $250\ \mathrm{ms}$ of the resident's tap.

You have been asked to redesign the protocol. Use the case study to answer all four parts.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Describe a replay attack against the current protocol. State exactly what the attacker captures, what they transmit, why the lock accepts it, and how long the attack remains available to them.

    (Describe)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Construct a challenge-response protocol that prevents replay. Your answer must specify what the lock sends, what the phone computes, what the phone returns, and what the lock checks.

    (Construct)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Explain how your protocol defeats the replay attack, and state clearly one attack it does not defeat. Quantify the probability that an attacker who has captured a million previous exchanges could still succeed by guessing.

    (Explain)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Evaluate whether the additional cost of your protocol is acceptable for a battery-powered lock. Your answer must include a calculated comparison.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The attacker positions the receiver within range and captures one legitimate frame, which contains the literal text OPEN followed by the 32-bit secret $S$ in hexadecimal. (A1) Because the frame is not encrypted, the attacker reads $S$ directly from the captured bytes; because nothing in the frame varies, no computation is needed at all. (A1)

To unlock later, the attacker retransmits exactly the captured bytes. The lock compares them with its stored $S$, finds them identical, and releases the bolt. (A1)

The attack remains available indefinitely, or until $S$ is changed, because the accepted value never varies and there is no timestamp, counter or expiry. Capturing one frame grants permanent access. (A1)

(b) Protocol:

1. The phone sends a request frame containing HELLO and its device identifier. (A1)
2. The lock generates a fresh 64-bit random value $N$ (a nonce) using its hardware random source, stores it with a short expiry, and transmits CHALLENGE followed by $N$. (A1)(A1)
3. The phone computes $R = H(S \mathbin\| N)$, where $H$ is a keyed hash and $\|$ denotes concatenation, and returns RESPONSE followed by $R$. (A1)
4. The lock computes the same value from its stored $S$ and the $N$ it issued, compares with $R$ using a constant-time comparison, and releases the bolt only if they match and $N$ has not expired or been used before. (A1)

(c) The captured bytes are now useless because each exchange uses a different $N$. A response $R$ valid for one nonce produces a completely different hash for the next, and the phone never transmits $S$ itself, so the attacker who captures a million exchanges has a million $(N_i, R_i)$ pairs but no way to recover $S$ or to compute the response to a nonce they have not seen. (M1)(A1)

It does not defeat an active man-in-the-middle who relays a challenge to the genuine phone and returns the genuine response, because the protocol authenticates the phone to the lock but not the lock to the phone, and it does not defeat physical attacks on the lock or compromise of the phone itself. (A1)

If the attacker instead tries to guess the next nonce, the chance that a 64-bit value repeats one seen before, by the birthday bound after $10^{6}$ exchanges, is approximately (M1)

$$\frac{N^{2}}{2^{65}} = \frac{10^{12}}{3.69\times10^{19}} \approx 2.7\times10^{-8},$$

that is, about one chance in forty million. (A1)

(d) The additional cost is negligible and the protocol is clearly acceptable. (A1) The extra energy per operation is $0.90 - 0.15 = 0.75\ \mathrm{mJ}$ for the hash plus a second transmission of about $0.15\ \mathrm{mJ}$, so about $0.90\ \mathrm{mJ}$ in total. At 25 operations per day that is (M1)

$$0.90\times10^{-3} \times 25 \times 365 = 8.2\ \mathrm{J}\ \text{per year}.$$

The battery stores $2.4\ \mathrm{Ah} \times 3600\ \mathrm{s} \times 3.0\ \mathrm{V} = 25\,920\ \mathrm{J}$, so the extra drain is (A1)

$$\frac{8.2}{25\,920} \times 100\% \approx 0.032\%\ \text{of capacity per year}.$$

On latency, the protocol adds one round trip of $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ to the $250\ \mathrm{ms}$ budget, leaving $210\ \mathrm{ms}$ for the hash and the bolt mechanism against the $4\ \mathrm{ms}$ the hash actually needs. (A1) The conclusion is that the security improvement is effectively free, so there is no engineering justification for shipping the static-token version.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award the marks for capturing the frame, retransmitting it unchanged, the lock's equality check succeeding, and the indefinite lifetime of the attack. The last is the mark most often missed and is the reason the attack is severe rather than merely possible. (b) Accept any challenge-response design in which the lock supplies a fresh unpredictable value and the response depends on both that value and the shared secret. Credit equivalent constructions such as a counter-based scheme, but note that a counter requires synchronised state and ask what happens when it desynchronises. Do not credit a design in which the phone chooses the nonce unless it also signs it, since then the nonce provides no freshness guarantee to the lock. (c) The 'does not defeat' mark requires a specific named attack, not a vague statement that no system is perfectly secure; man-in-the-middle, physical tampering and phone compromise are all acceptable. For the probability, accept the birthday form $N^2/2^{65}$ or a simpler $10^6/2^{64}$ estimate, and accept any value of the order of $10^{-8}$ to $10^{-7}$. (d) The calculation must appear; a qualitative assertion that the cost is small earns nothing. Accept any reasonable energy model that uses the figures given, and credit a candidate who also notes that the hardware random source and the constant-time comparison are implementation requirements rather than automatic consequences of the design.

title: A loop that is linear only while the data keeps moving
q_html:
PulseTrack - steady-run detection

PulseTrack is a wearable heart-rate monitor. It samples the wearer's heart rate once per second and stores each day's readings as a list of integers.

For every reading the device reports the length of the steady run ending at that reading: the number of immediately preceding readings such that every step between consecutive readings in that run differs by no more than a tolerance of 5 beats per minute. A reading with no steady predecessor has run length 0. So for the series [70, 72, 71, 90, 89, 88, 87] the run lengths are [0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3].

A developer wrote the function below and claims it runs in linear time: "the while loop stops as soon as it reaches a reading that differs from the one before it by more than the tolerance, and in a real recording that happens after a step or two."

The device records 86,400 readings per day, one per second for 24 hours, and runs the analysis each night on the day's readings. The analysis must finish within a few seconds.

def steady_runs(readings, tol=5):
    runs = []
    for i in range(len(readings)):
        count = 0
        j = i
        while j > 0 and abs(readings[j] - readings[j - 1]) <= tol:
            count += 1
            j -= 1
        runs.append(count)
    return runs

The readings are stored as a list of integers, one per second. The nightly analysis must finish in a few seconds on the device, and it must report the run lengths exactly.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Explain, by tracing the loop, what steady_runs returns for the readings [70, 72, 71, 90, 89, 88, 87] with the default tolerance of 5.

    (Explain)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Explain why the developer's claim that the function runs in linear time is unsound. State the property of the input that the claim assumes, and describe the input pattern on which the function performs the greatest number of steps.

    (Explain)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Construct a Python function that returns exactly the same result as steady_runs but runs in linear time. You may not import any module and you may not use the abs function. A Java version of this paper requires the same algorithm, so write the algorithm rather than a demonstration of syntax.

    (Construct)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    A colleague proposes to fix the performance by adding a limit inside the while loop so that it stops after at most 1,000 steps. Evaluate this proposal, using your answers to parts (b) and (c).

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Tracing the loop for readings = [70, 72, 71, 90, 89, 88, 87] with tol = 5:

| i | readings[i] | comparisons in the while | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 70 | j = 0, loop does not run | 0 |
| 1 | 72 | $\lvert 72-70 \rvert = 2 \le 5 \rightarrow 1$ | 1 |
| 2 | 71 | $\lvert 71-72 \rvert = 1$, then $\lvert 71-70 \rvert = 1$ | 2 |
| 3 | 90 | $\lvert 90-71 \rvert = 19 > 5$ | 0 |
| 4 | 89 | $\lvert 89-90 \rvert = 1$, then $\lvert 89-71 \rvert = 18 > 5$ | 1 |
| 5 | 88 | $1$, then $2$, then $\lvert 88-71 \rvert = 17 > 5$ | 2 |
| 6 | 87 | $1$, then $2$, then $3$, then $\lvert 87-71 \rvert = 16 > 5$ | 3 |

The function returns [0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3]. (M1) for tracing the loop as a walk backwards while consecutive differences stay within the tolerance, (A1) for the correct values, (A1) for the list as a whole, including the reset to 0 at index 3 and the growing run at the end.

(b) The claim is unsound because the number of steps the inner loop performs is not a constant — it is the length of the steady run, which is a property of the *data*, not of the code. (M1) The claim assumes that consecutive readings almost always differ by more than the tolerance, so that the loop exits after one or two steps. (A1) That assumption is false for this application: heart rate sampled once a second during steady exercise changes by far less than 5 beats per minute between consecutive samples, so long runs are the normal case and the loop walks back a long way. (A1) The greatest number of steps occurs when every consecutive difference is within tolerance — a constant series, or a slow monotonic drift. For each $i$ the loop then runs all the way back to index 0, giving $0+1+2+\dots+(n-1) = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ steps, which is quadratic rather than linear. (A1)

(c)

def steady_runs(readings, tol=5):
    n = len(readings)
    runs = [0] * n
    for i in range(1, n):
        step = readings[i] - readings[i - 1]
        if -tol <= step <= tol:
            runs[i] = runs[i - 1] + 1
    return runs

(M1) for a single pass that keeps no inner loop. (A1) for the observation that makes it work: the steady run ending at i is either empty or it is the run ending at i - 1 extended by exactly one reading, so the answer for i can be read off the answer for i - 1. (A1) for runs[i] = runs[i - 1] + 1 and (A1) for initialising every entry to 0, which is what makes the run reset after a step larger than the tolerance. (A1) for using no library module and no abs, expressing the tolerance as the two-sided test -tol <= step <= tol.

The work done is $n-1$ comparisons and one assignment per reading, so the time is $O(n)$ and the extra memory is $O(n)$ for the output. A Java version of this paper asks for the same algorithm; the translation is a for loop over the array indices and the identical recurrence, so the language is irrelevant to the reasoning.

(d) The proposal should be rejected, for three reasons.

First, it does not change the complexity. The inner loop can still run up to 1,000 steps for every reading, so the worst case is still proportional to $1000n$; capping the loop divides the running time by a constant, and a constant factor is not a change of order. (M1) With 86,400 readings a day the uncapped worst case is $86{,}400 \times 86{,}399 / 2 = 3{,}732{,}436{,}800$ inner steps, the capped version still performs up to $86{,}400 \times 1000 = 86{,}400{,}000$, and the linear version performs 86,399. (A1)

Second, and more seriously, the cap makes the result *wrong* precisely where the app matters. A steady run of 1,500 readings would be reported as 1,000, and a run of 4,000 as 1,000; the error is silent, it is always an under-report, and it is concentrated on the longest runs — which are exactly the steady states the app exists to find. (A1)

Third, the trade is unnecessary, because part (c) already gives an exact linear algorithm. Capping the loop trades a correctness guarantee for a constant factor when a change of order was available at the same cost. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) Accept any trace, as a table or as prose. The essential marks are the mechanism (walk backwards while *each consecutive pair* is within tolerance) and the result. A candidate who compares every earlier reading against the current reading rather than against its own predecessor has misread the function and forfeits the trace marks — this is the single most common error.

(b) The two discriminating marks are the unstated assumption (that consecutive readings usually differ by more than the tolerance) and the worst-case count $n(n-1)/2$. A candidate who writes "it is actually O(n squared)" without naming the assumption earns one mark only. Accept a description of the worst case as "a constant series", "a steady recording" or "a slow drift"; require the recognition that the loop runs to index 0 each time.

(c) Accept any single-pass algorithm that returns the same list, including one that builds the list by appending rather than pre-allocating it. Do not award the linear mark to a candidate who keeps a nested loop, even a faster one — the question is about the order of growth. A candidate who uses abs despite the prohibition should be told the constraint was stated; the reasoning marks may still be awarded. A candidate who uses the csv-style two-pointer scan but does not derive the recurrence should be capped at two marks.

(d) The evaluation must distinguish a constant-factor improvement from a change of order. A candidate who says "1,000 is small enough" has missed that the cap silently corrupts the longest runs, and that those runs are the app's output. Award the final mark only when the answer connects the cap to a correctness loss rather than to performance alone.

title: A constructor that prices every team as a single seat
q_html:
Rowan Software - annual seat pricing

Rowan Software bills teams for a subscription. Every plan has a term in months and an annual fee, and the annual fee is computed once, when the plan object is created, so that invoices can be issued later without recomputing prices.

The code below defines a base class Plan and a subclass SeatPlan, whose price depends on how many seats the team has bought. A seat costs 9 pounds per month. The class attribute seats = 1 is a default for plans that have not specified a seat count.

The developer tested the class with the three tests shown, and all three pass. The service has about 900 team customers; the average team buys 20 seats and signs a 12-month term. The finance team reconciles annual fees once a year and has never queried an individual customer's monthly fee.

class Plan:
    PER_SEAT = 9                      # pounds per seat per month

    def __init__(self, months):
        self.months = months
        self.annual_fee = self.monthly_fee() * months

    def monthly_fee(self):
        return 0

class SeatPlan(Plan):
    seats = 1                         # default for plans with no seat count

    def __init__(self, seats, months):
        super().__init__(months)
        self.seats = seats

    def monthly_fee(self):
        return self.seats * Plan.PER_SEAT

# the developer's tests - all three pass
def test_one_seat():
    assert SeatPlan(1, 12).annual_fee == 108

def test_monthly_fee_scales():
    assert SeatPlan(20, 12).monthly_fee() == 180

def test_seats_are_recorded():
    assert SeatPlan(20, 12).seats == 20

The finance team has asked you to review the pricing code before the catalogue is extended. The reconciliation compares each customer's stored annual_fee with the invoice total.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Explain what annual_fee holds for SeatPlan(20, 12) and why it is not equal to monthly_fee() * months. Refer to the order in which the statements in SeatPlan.__init__ and Plan.__init__ run.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Construct a corrected design in which the annual fee is always computed from the plan's own seat count and no constructor reads a field of an object that is not yet fully initialised. Use composition: a plan must hold a separate pricing object rather than inherit its price. Write the classes and state the annual fee for 20 seats over 12 months.

    (Construct)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Calculate the annual fee that every SeatPlan caches, the fee that a 20-seat 12-month plan should be charged, and the total annual shortfall across all 900 customers. State how many of those customers are billed incorrectly.

    (Calculate)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Evaluate the two ways of removing the bug - patching the inheritance hierarchy so the field is set before the superclass constructor runs, or replacing the hierarchy with composition - and recommend one for a catalogue that will soon combine seats, usage and region.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) For SeatPlan(20, 12) the attribute annual_fee holds 108. (A1) It is not 2160 because of the order in which the two constructors run. The first statement of SeatPlan.__init__ is super().__init__(months), and inside Plan.__init__ the assignment self.annual_fee = self.monthly_fee() * months calls self.monthly_fee(). (M1) Because monthly_fee is overridden, that call dispatches to SeatPlan.monthly_fee, which reads self.seats. At that moment the instance has only months in its attribute dictionary - the statement self.seats = seats has not run yet - so the lookup falls back to the class attribute seats = 1. The fee is therefore computed for a one-seat plan: $1 \times 9 = 9$ per month and $9 \times 12 = 108$ per year. (A1) Only after the superclass constructor returns is the instance attribute set to 20, and by then annual_fee has already been stored and is never recomputed; a later call to monthly_fee() correctly returns $20 \times 9 = 180$, so the live query and the cached value disagree.

(b) The defect is not that a constructor calls a method. It is that a constructor calls a method on an object that is only partly built, so the method can observe a field that does not exist yet. Composition removes the half-built object by making the pricing rule a separate, fully constructed collaborator:

class SeatPricing:
    PER_SEAT = 9
    def __init__(self, seats):
        self.seats = seats
    def monthly_fee(self):
        return self.seats * self.PER_SEAT

class Plan:
def __init__(self, months, pricing):
self.months = months
self.pricing = pricing
self.annual_fee = pricing.monthly_fee() * months

p = Plan(12, SeatPricing(20))
print(p.annual_fee) # 2160
```

(M1) for giving Plan a pricing collaborator instead of a subclass that overrides a price method. (A1) for constructing that collaborator completely before the plan uses it, so no method ever reads a field that has not been set. (A1) for computing the annual fee from the collaborator's result. (A1) for the correct value, $180 \times 12 = 2160$. (A1) for noting that Plan.__init__ still calls a method, but on a different object that is already finished, which is why the same line is now safe.

Two inheritance-preserving fixes also work and are acceptable. Assigning the subclass field before the superclass constructor runs:

class SeatPlan(Plan):
    def __init__(self, seats, months):
        self.seats = seats        # set first
        super().__init__(months)  # monthly_fee() now sees 20

and passing the already-computed fee up to the base constructor, so the base never calls an overridable method at all:

class Plan:
    def __init__(self, months, monthly_fee):
        self.months = months
        self.annual_fee = monthly_fee * months

All three produce annual_fee == 2160. (A1)

(c) During construction self.seats always falls back to the class attribute 1, so every SeatPlan caches $9 \times 12 = 108$ per year, whatever its seat count. (M1) At an average of 20 seats the correct fee is $20 \times 9 = 180$ per month, which is $180 \times 12 = 2160$ per year. (A1) The undercharge is therefore $2160 - 108 = 2052$ per customer per year. (A1) Across 900 customers the shortfall is $900 \times 2052 = 1{,}846{,}800$, and all 900 are billed incorrectly: a customer is billed correctly only if it happens to have exactly one seat, which the 20-seat average rules out. The cached fee is one twentieth of the true fee at 20 seats, which is why 108 looks like a plausible annual price for a small team rather than an obvious error. (A1)

(d) Both remedies remove the bug, so the choice is about the next change rather than this one. Patching the hierarchy - assign seats before super().__init__, or pass the fee up - is a one- or two-line change with no runtime cost, but it leaves the base constructor calling an overridable method, so the trap stays armed for the next subclass whose fields are set after super(). (M1) The composition design removes the trap: Plan depends on a SeatPricing object, so a subclass cannot observe an unset field. Its cost is one small object per plan - 900 SeatPricing objects of 48 bytes each, about 309,600 bytes once their instance dictionaries are counted, or roughly 0.31 MB - against a shortfall of 1,846,800. (A1) That is a ratio of about six to one between the money and the memory, so the memory argument is irrelevant at this scale. (A1) The decisive argument is growth: the catalogue will combine seats, usage and region, and inheritance multiplies subclasses (three independent pricing features give up to $2^3 = 8$ subclasses, and each new feature doubles that), while composition adds one collaborator per feature. Recommend adopting composition for the extended catalogue. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) The mark is for the mechanism, not the number. The candidate must say that super().__init__ runs before self.seats = seats, that the call to monthly_fee() inside the base constructor dispatches to the override, and that the attribute lookup then finds the class attribute seats = 1. A candidate who writes only that the constructor uses the wrong seat count, without the order of the statements, earns at most one mark. Accept a trace table. Do not accept the claim that the class attribute is overwritten: it is not; the instance attribute is created later and shadows it only from that point on.

(b) Accept any design that removes the read of a not-yet-assigned field, including composition, assigning the field before super().__init__, or passing the computed fee into the base constructor; code in Java or another language is acceptable if the syllabus version being sat requires it. The value 2160 must appear. A candidate who keeps the original hierarchy and merely adds a recompute() call after construction has treated the symptom; award at most two marks unless they also explain why the base constructor still calls an overridable method.

(c) Follow through on any consistent seat average; the marks are for the method (a cached 108 against a correct 180 per month, times 12) and for the totals 2052 and 1,846,800. A candidate who forgets that the cached fee is 108 for every plan and uses 20 seats in both terms obtains a shortfall of zero; this forfeits the first mark. Accept all 900, or every customer with more than one seat, for the count, provided the candidate notes the one-seat exception.

(d) This is an evaluate question, so a recommendation is required; a candidate who describes both fixes without choosing earns at most two of the four marks. The memory comparison must be present for the third mark and must be tied to the 1,846,800 figure. The final mark is for the growth argument - combinatorial subclass explosion under inheritance against one collaborator per feature under composition. Do not accept composition is always better without the growth reasoning, and do not accept keep inheritance because it is shorter without acknowledging the fragile base class.

title: A1.3 Operating systems and control systems
q_html:
Parcel packing cells

A fulfilment centre runs four identical packing cells. Each cell processes one parcel per cycle of 45 s. Every parcel must pass through three shared resources, each of which can serve only one cell at a time: a labelling arm, a weighbridge and a dispatch chute. A cell claims the resources one at a time as its control program reaches each stage, holds every resource it has already claimed while it waits for the next, and releases them all only when the parcel has been dispatched. The three resources are attached to the site network so that any cell can request any of them. The centre currently achieves 320 parcels per hour when nothing goes wrong. On average, once in every 40 cycles the four cells deadlock: each holds one or two resources and waits for one held by another. There is no detection, so the deadlock persists until a supervisor notices the queue, walks to the cell, and performs a manual reset taking 6 minutes, which also discards the four parcels in flight. You have been asked to review the design.

Using the case study, answer all four parts. The four cells are named C1 to C4 and the three resources are L (labelling arm), W (weighbridge) and D (dispatch chute).

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Explain, with reference to each of the four conditions required for deadlock, why this system deadlocks. Your answer must name all four conditions and show that each is present.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Construct a resource-allocation scheme that makes deadlock impossible. State the rule, show that it removes at least one of the four conditions you identified, and explain what has to change in the control program of each cell.

    (Construct)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Calculate the average throughput of the centre in parcels per hour given the current deadlock rate, and hence the percentage of capacity lost. Show your working.

    (Calculate)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    An engineer proposes instead to leave the resource requests unchanged and to add a timeout: any cell waiting more than 20 s releases everything it holds, waits 5 s and starts the parcel again. Evaluate this proposal against your scheme in (b).

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) All four Coffman conditions hold.

*Mutual exclusion:* each of L, W and D can serve only one cell at a time, so the resources are non-sharable. (A1)

*Hold and wait:* a cell that has claimed the labelling arm keeps it while it waits for the weighbridge, so processes hold resources while requesting others. (A1)

*No pre-emption:* nothing in the system can take a resource away from a cell; the only way resources are released is by the cell finishing, which is exactly what it cannot do. (A1)

*Circular wait:* with four cells and three resources a cycle is easy to form, for example C1 holds L and wants W, C2 holds W and wants D, and C3 holds D and wants L. Because each cell requests resources in whatever order its stage is reached, and the stages differ between parcels, no ordering prevents that cycle from forming. (A1)

(b) Impose a global ordering on resource acquisition: assign each resource a fixed rank, say L = 1, W = 2, D = 3, and require every cell to request resources in strictly increasing rank order, never requesting a lower-ranked resource while holding a higher-ranked one. (M1)(A1)

This removes the circular-wait condition. (A1) A cycle would require each participant to hold a resource and wait for one of lower or equal rank; since ranks strictly increase along any wait chain, the chain cannot close. Formally, in any cycle the ranks would have to satisfy $r_1 < r_2 < \dots < r_k < r_1$, which is impossible. (A1)

The control program must change in two ways: each cell must determine the full set of resources its parcel will need before claiming any of them, and must then claim them in rank order. Where a parcel genuinely needs them in a different order, the cell must claim all three up front and hold them for the whole cycle, which reduces concurrency but is safe. (A1)

(c) Without deadlock the centre does $4 \times \dfrac{3600}{45} = 320$ parcels per hour. (A1)

In 40 cycles the four cells process $4 \times 40 = 160$ parcels, taking $40 \times 45 = 1800\ \mathrm{s}$. One deadlock adds a 6-minute ($360\ \mathrm{s}$) reset, so 160 parcels take $1800 + 360 = 2160\ \mathrm{s}$. (M1)(A1)

$$\text{throughput} = \frac{160}{2160} \times 3600 = 266.7 \approx 267\ \mathrm{parcels\,h^{-1}}$$ (A1)

$$\text{loss} = \frac{320 - 267}{320} \times 100\% = 16.7\%$$

(d) The timeout does not prevent deadlock; it detects and breaks it. (A1) That is better than an indefinite hang, but it is worse than prevention in three respects. First, every near-deadlock costs 20 s of waiting plus a 5 s backoff plus the wasted work already done on the parcel, so each event costs at least 25 s of cell time against 0 s under ordering. Second, if all four cells time out together and restart together they are likely to re-form the same cycle, an effect known as livelock, which the proposal does nothing to prevent since there is no randomised backoff. (A1) Third, the parcels are discarded either way, so the material loss is unchanged. (A1)

By contrast the ordering scheme in (b) eliminates the events entirely, at the cost of holding all three resources for some parcels and so losing some concurrency. A reasonable evaluation is therefore that the timeout is an acceptable safety net to keep in place, but it should not be the primary mechanism: prevention should be used first and detection second.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award one mark for each condition correctly named and shown to be present; a candidate who names all four but does not apply them to this system earns at most two. The circular-wait mark is the one most often missed and requires an explicit example of a cycle. (b) Accept any consistent global ordering, not necessarily L-W-D, provided the rule is stated as a total order and the reasoning about cycles is given. A candidate who proposes requesting all resources at once (simultaneous acquisition) is also acceptable and should be credited equivalently, since it removes the hold-and-wait condition instead; note in that case that utilisation falls. The final mark is for identifying the change to the control program, which is the practical consequence and is frequently omitted. (c) Accept 266 to 267 parcels per hour and a loss between 16% and 17%. Award the method mark for converting the deadlock rate into an amortised time penalty; a candidate who simply subtracts 6 minutes per hour has the wrong model. (d) The key distinction is prevention versus detection, and candidates who conflate them should not earn the first mark. Credit the livelock observation even if the term is not used, provided the idea that simultaneous restart recreates the cycle is stated. There is no single right conclusion, so award the final marks for a judgement supported by the analysis given.

title: A4.4 Ethical considerations
q_html:
Prioritising housing repairs

A local authority receives repair requests from tenants and must decide which to inspect within 48 hours. It has deployed a model that scores each request and flags those it predicts to be urgent. Urgent means a fault that is dangerous or that will cause rapid deterioration, such as a leaking roof or a failed heating system in winter. The authority covers two areas with very different housing stock. In the North area, of 6 000 requests in the period, 1 500 were genuinely urgent; the model flagged 1 200 as urgent and 1 080 of those were genuinely urgent. In the South area, of 2 000 requests, 400 were genuinely urgent; the model flagged 500 as urgent and 320 of those were genuinely urgent. The authority reports an overall precision of 82% and states that the model is therefore performing well. A tenant in the South area has complained that inspectors call on her neighbours repeatedly for faults that turn out to be minor, while her own leaking roof waited nine days.

Using the case study, answer all four parts.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Explain why the single figure of 82% overall precision is a misleading summary of this model's performance, and state which two quantities must be reported separately for the complaint to be assessed.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Construct the confusion matrix for each area and calculate, for each area separately, the precision, the recall, and the proportion of non-urgent requests that were wrongly flagged.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Discuss what the two sets of figures show, including anything they do not establish. Refer to the tenant's complaint in your answer.

    (Discuss)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Justify one action the authority should take, given that it cannot simultaneously maximise both precision and recall and that inspection capacity is fixed.

    (Justify)
a_html:
(a) An overall figure averages over a population in which the two areas contribute very unequally, 6 000 requests from the North against 2 000 from the South, so the aggregate is dominated by the area where the model performs better. (A1) It says nothing about how the errors are distributed, and it is the distribution that the complaint is about. (A1)

The two quantities that must be reported separately are precision and recall for each area, or equivalently the false-positive rate and the false-negative rate for each area, since precision and recall alone do not determine how many non-urgent requests are wrongly flagged. (A1)(A1)

(b) *North:* flagged 1 200, of which 1 080 urgent, so 120 are not urgent. There are 1 500 urgent in total, so $1500 - 1080 = 420$ urgent requests were missed. Non-urgent requests number $6000 - 1500 = 4500$, of which 120 were wrongly flagged. (M1)(A1)

| North | flagged urgent | not flagged | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| genuinely urgent | 1 080 | 420 | 1 500 |
| not urgent | 120 | 4 380 | 4 500 |
| total | 1 200 | 4 800 | 6 000 |

*South:* flagged 500, of which 320 urgent, so 180 are not urgent. There are 400 urgent in total, so $400 - 320 = 80$ were missed. Non-urgent requests number $2000 - 400 = 1600$, of which 180 were wrongly flagged. (A1)

| South | flagged urgent | not flagged | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| genuinely urgent | 320 | 80 | 400 |
| not urgent | 180 | 1 420 | 1 600 |
| total | 500 | 1 500 | 2 000 |

North: precision $= 1080/1200 = 90.0\%$, recall $= 1080/1500 = 72.0\%$, wrongly flagged $= 120/4500 = 2.67\%$. (A1)
South: precision $= 320/500 = 64.0\%$, recall $= 320/400 = 80.0\%$, wrongly flagged $= 180/1600 = 11.25\%$. (A1)

(c) The figures support the substance of the complaint. A non-urgent request in the South is (M1)
$$\frac{11.25}{2.67} \approx 4.2$$
times as likely to be flagged as one in the North, so South tenants are much more likely to be visited for a fault that turns out to be minor, which is the nuisance she describes. (A1) At the same time the model is not uniformly worse in the South: its recall there is higher, 80% against 72%, so an urgent request in the South is more likely to be caught. That is why her own roof waiting nine days is not necessarily explained by the area statistics and may be a single unfortunate case. (A1)

What the figures do not establish is why the difference exists. The areas differ in housing stock, so the base rate of urgency differs, 25% in the North against 20% in the South, and a model trained on pooled data with one threshold will not behave identically across groups with different base rates even if it is free of bias in its inputs. The data also cannot distinguish a model that is miscalibrated from one that is correctly calibrated but operating at an inappropriate threshold, and they say nothing about whether the features used are themselves proxies for something protected. (A1)

(d) A defensible action is to set the decision threshold separately for each area so that the false-positive rates are equalised, and to publish the resulting precision and recall for both areas. (A1) This directly addresses the complaint, which is about unequal burden rather than about overall accuracy, and it is achievable within fixed inspection capacity because lowering the threshold in the North and raising it in the South reallocates roughly the same number of visits. (A1)

It must be accompanied by a stated decision about which error the authority considers more serious. If a missed urgent repair is the greater harm, the threshold should be set to favour recall and the authority must accept more minor inspections in both areas; if unnecessary visits are the greater harm, the reverse. (A1) What is not defensible is to continue reporting only the aggregate figure, because that suppresses exactly the information needed to make the choice.

Markscheme notes

(a) The mark scheme looks for the idea that an aggregate conceals distribution, and for the identification of precision and recall (or the two error rates) as the disaggregated quantities. A candidate who says only that the model is biased has asserted a conclusion the data do not yet support. (b) Award (M1) for deriving at least one cell correctly from the text, since the numbers are given as counts of flagged and correctly flagged rather than as a matrix. Accept matrices with rows and columns transposed. All six rates must appear; the wrongly-flagged proportion is the one most often omitted and is the rate the complaint is actually about. (c) The comparison mark requires the ratio. Credit the observation that South recall is higher, because it prevents the easy conclusion that the model is simply worse in the South. The 'does not establish' mark is for the point that the statistics cannot separate miscalibration from threshold choice, or for noting that different base rates alone can produce this pattern. (d) Any single action is acceptable provided it is justified against the figures and acknowledges the trade-off. Equalising false-positive rates, equalising recall, or setting thresholds from an explicit cost ratio for the two error types are all creditable. An answer that proposes collecting more data or retraining without addressing the threshold question has not engaged with the fact that the trade-off is irreducible at fixed capacity.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A1 Computer fundamentals
syllabus_ref: A1.1 Computer hardware and operation (A1.1.4 the role of cache memory, A1.1.5 the machine instruction cycle, A1.1.6 the effect of clock speed and cache on performance)
title: Where the cycles actually go
q_html:
A processor whose clock speed is not the problem

An embedded vision system processes a stream of images. Measurements on the running system give the following. Of all memory accesses, $95\%$ are satisfied by the level-1 cache in $1$ clock cycle. Of the accesses that miss in level 1, $80\%$ are satisfied by the level-2 cache, and the whole level-2 path, including the level-1 miss, takes $12$ clock cycles. An access that misses in both caches goes to main memory, and that path takes $200$ clock cycles in total. The instruction mix is fixed, and apart from memory accesses the processor completes one instruction per clock cycle.

Two upgrade proposals are on the table. Both are advertised with a large number on the box, and neither number is the one the system will actually see.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate the average number of clock cycles spent on memory per instruction, showing how each level of the hierarchy contributes.

    (Calculate)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    A hardware accelerator can execute $40\%$ of the workload five times faster than the processor does now. Calculate the overall speedup of the system, and state the largest speedup that could ever be obtained by accelerating this same $40\%$, however fast the accelerator is made.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    A second proposal is to raise the clock frequency by $25\%$. The memory chips are unchanged, so their latency stays the same number of nanoseconds and therefore becomes a larger number of clock cycles. Calculate the resulting average cycles per instruction and hence the real speedup, and explain why it falls so far short of $25\%$.

    (Explain)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Evaluate which of the two proposals is the better use of the engineering budget, referring to your answers to (b) and (c) and to one further consideration that the numbers do not capture.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Work through the hierarchy from the fastest level outwards. An access hits in level 1 with probability $0.95$ and costs $1$ cycle. It misses level 1 with probability $0.05$; of those, $0.80$ are satisfied by level 2 at $12$ cycles and $0.20$ go to main memory at $200$ cycles. (M1)(A1)
$$\text{average cycles} = 0.95(1) + 0.05\bigl[0.80(12) + 0.20(200)\bigr]$$
$$= 0.95 + 0.05\bigl[9.6 + 40\bigr] = 0.95 + 0.05(49.6) = 0.95 + 2.48 = 3.43$$ (A1)(A1)
So the processor spends about $3.43$ clock cycles per instruction, of which only $0.95$ is the level-1 access itself. The tail dominates: level-2 hits add $0.48$ cycles in total, while main-memory accesses add $2.00$ cycles, so the $1\%$ of all accesses that miss in both caches accounts for $2.00$ of the $3.43$, which is more than half the average and more than twice what the level-1 hits contribute.

(b) Amdahl's law gives the speedup as (M1)
$$S = \frac{1}{(1-f) + \dfrac{f}{s}} = \frac{1}{0.60 + \dfrac{0.40}{5}} = \frac{1}{0.60 + 0.08} = \frac{1}{0.68} = 1.47$$ (A1)(A1)
The limiting case is $s \to \infty$, which gives $S_{\max} = 1/(1-0.40) = 1.67$. (A1) However fast the accelerator becomes, the remaining $60\%$ of the workload is untouched, so the system can never be more than $1.67$ times faster by this route.

(c) With the clock $25\%$ faster, a fixed nanosecond latency corresponds to $1.25$ times as many clock cycles, so the level-2 path becomes $12 \times 1.25 = 15$ cycles and the main-memory path becomes $200 \times 1.25 = 250$ cycles. (M1)
$$\text{average cycles} = 0.95(1) + 0.05\bigl[0.80(15) + 0.20(250)\bigr] = 0.95 + 0.05\bigl[12 + 50\bigr] = 0.95 + 3.10 = 4.05$$ (A1)
Execution time is cycles divided by frequency, so with the new frequency $1.25$ times the old one, (M1)
$$\frac{T_{\text{new}}}{T_{\text{old}}} = \frac{4.05/1.25}{3.43/1.00} = \frac{3.24}{3.43} = 0.945,\qquad \text{speedup} = 1.06$$ (A1)
The speedup is about $6\%$ rather than $25\%$ because the extra cycles are being spent waiting, and waiting does not get faster when the clock does. As the clock rises, the proportion of time spent stalled on memory grows, so the gap between the advertised figure and the delivered figure widens.

(d) The accelerator is the better buy on these numbers: $1.47$ against $1.06$, and the accelerator's figure is also closer to its own ceiling of $1.67$, whereas the clock increase delivers under a quarter of what its name promises. (A1)(A1) One thing the numbers do not capture is cost and risk: an accelerator is new hardware, new drivers and a new failure mode in a system that already works, while a clock change is a configuration setting. If the accelerator's development cost is more than a few times the cost of the clock change, the safer option may be worth its smaller return, and a decision that rests only on the two ratios above would be incomplete. (A1)

It is worth stating what the $3.43$ means before using it in later parts: it is an average over the whole instruction stream, so it already includes the instructions that hit in level 1 and cost almost nothing. Any proposal that changes the miss rates or the path latencies changes this average, and that is the only way an upgrade can help.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1) for the weighted-sum structure and (A1) for each of the three contributions; accept $3.4$ to $3.5$. A candidate who adds $1 + 12 + 200$ weighted by $0.95$, $0.04$ and $0.01$ has understood the structure but has applied the level-2 probability to all accesses rather than to level-1 misses, and should lose one of the accuracy marks. (b) Accept $1.46$ to $1.48$ and $1.67$; the ceiling mark is separate and is for understanding that the limit comes from the unaccelerated fraction. Do not credit a speedup of $5$ or of $1.40$ obtained by multiplying the fraction by the speedup. (c) Accept average cycles $4.0$ to $4.1$ and speedup $1.05$ to $1.07$; the mark is for dividing by $1.25$ as well as for recomputing the cycles, and a candidate who reports $4.05/3.43 = 1.18$ as a slowdown has forgotten the frequency change entirely. (d) Accept either proposal if it is argued from the calculations and names a non-numerical factor; the comparison must be made, not merely asserted. A candidate who computes $3.43$ correctly and then describes the main-memory contribution as small has misread their own arithmetic and should be corrected in feedback, since the tail is the dominant term and the rest of the question depends on noticing that.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B2 Programming
syllabus_ref: B2.4 Programming algorithms (B2.4.1 the complexity of an algorithm, B2.4.2 searching and sorting algorithms, B2.4.3 the suitability of an algorithm for a given task)
title: The algorithm that wins on paper and loses on the machine
q_html:
Two ways to find one record

A library catalogue holds $n$ records sorted by accession number, stored contiguously in memory. Two search routines are available. Linear search examines records in order from the start of the list; in the worst case it makes $n$ comparisons. Binary search repeatedly compares against the middle of the remaining range; in the worst case it makes $\lfloor \log_{2} n \rfloor + 1$ comparisons. Profiling on this machine gives a realistic cost model rather than a comparison count: a linear-search comparison costs $3\ \mathrm{ns}$, because consecutive records are already in the cache, while a binary-search comparison costs $30\ \mathrm{ns}$, because each probe lands far from the last one and usually misses the cache. A binary search also pays a one-off $400\ \mathrm{ns}$ of setup before its first comparison.

The table appears to settle the matter. This question asks whether it does.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Determine the worst-case number of comparisons binary search makes for each value of $n$ in the table, showing how $\lfloor \log_{2} n \rfloor + 1$ gives the stated figures, and state the complexity class of each algorithm.

    (Determine)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Using the cost model in the stimulus, calculate the worst-case time taken by each algorithm for each value of $n$ in the table. Hence determine the smallest value of $n$ for which binary search is the faster of the two, showing your method.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Explain why the comparison counts in the table give the opposite ranking to the timings for small $n$, referring to the cost model and to the way each algorithm accesses memory.

    (Explain)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Evaluate whether a programmer should implement a hybrid routine that uses linear search below the crossover value and binary search above it, giving one reason for and one reason against.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) For $n = 16$, $\lfloor\log_{2} 16\rfloor + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5$; for $n = 256$, $8 + 1 = 9$; for $n = 65\,536$, $16 + 1 = 17$; for $n = 16\,777\,216$, $24 + 1 = 25$. (A1) for the method, (A1) for the four values. Linear search is $\mathrm{O}(n)$ and binary search is $\mathrm{O}(\log n)$. (A1)

(b) Linear search takes $3n$ nanoseconds. Binary search takes $400 + 30(\lfloor\log_{2} n\rfloor + 1)$ nanoseconds. (M1)

| $n$ | linear search | binary search |
|---|---|---|
| $16$ | $48\ \mathrm{ns}$ | $400 + 30(5) = 550\ \mathrm{ns}$ |
| $256$ | $768\ \mathrm{ns}$ | $400 + 30(9) = 670\ \mathrm{ns}$ |
| $65\,536$ | $196\,608\ \mathrm{ns}$ | $400 + 30(17) = 910\ \mathrm{ns}$ |
| $16\,777\,216$ | $50\,331\,648\ \mathrm{ns}$ | $400 + 30(25) = 1150\ \mathrm{ns}$ |

(A1) for each column. For the crossover, note that between $n = 128$ and $n = 255$ the binary-search comparison count is fixed at $8$, so the binary-search time is constant at $400 + 30(8) = 640\ \mathrm{ns}$ across that range. (M1) Solving $3n = 640$ gives $n = 213.3$, so (M1) at $n = 213$ linear search takes $639\ \mathrm{ns}$ and binary takes $640\ \mathrm{ns}$, and at $n = 214$ linear takes $642\ \mathrm{ns}$ and binary still takes $640\ \mathrm{ns}$. The smallest $n$ for which binary search is faster is therefore $n = 214$. (A1)

(c) The comparison count measures one cost, and it is not the cost that dominates for small $n$. Binary search has a fixed setup of $400\ \mathrm{ns}$, which at $n = 16$ is more than eight times the entire cost of the linear search, and each of its comparisons costs ten times as much because the probes jump around the array and usually miss the cache. (A1)(A1) Linear search walks along the array, so after the first access every subsequent record is already in a cache line that has been fetched, and each comparison costs $3\ \mathrm{ns}$. (A1) Complexity classes describe how the time grows as $n$ becomes large, and they deliberately discard constant factors; for $n$ below a few hundred the constants here decide the outcome, and the asymptotically worse algorithm wins. (A1)

(d) In favour: the hybrid takes the better of the two routines at every size, so it is never worse than either, and the crossover is a single comparison against a constant, which is almost free. (A1) Against: it is two code paths to write, test and maintain instead of one, and the crossover of $214$ is specific to this machine's cache behaviour and this record size — on different hardware the threshold moves, so the constant becomes a tuning parameter that someone has to keep valid. (A1) Whether it is worth it depends on how often the routine runs: in a loop executed millions of times the gain is real, and in a function called once per user action it is not worth the complexity. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) Accept the four values with or without the working; the complexity classes must be stated in big-O form. (b) Accept the table entries to two significant figures. For the crossover, credit any systematic method — tabulation, bisection or solving $3n = 640$ on the correct interval — and accept $214$; a candidate who solves $3n = 400 + 30(\log_{2} n + 1)$ treating the logarithm as continuous gets about $n = 200$ and should not be penalised provided the method is shown, since the floor function is what makes the true answer a little higher. (c) The explanation must refer to the fixed setup cost and to the per-comparison cost difference; a candidate who says only that binary search has overhead has not used the model. The cache explanation is the more valuable of the two and should be credited generously. (d) Credit a reason for and a reason against; a candidate who argues only one side cannot reach the top mark. The point that the threshold is machine-specific is the strongest objection and should be looked for. Do not accept 'binary search is O(log n) so it is always faster' as an answer to any part: the item exists to show that this is false, and a candidate who restates it has not engaged with the model at all.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A1.1 Redundancy in a block storage array: the parity block of a stripe is the exclusive OR of that stripe's data blocks, so exactly one lost block per stripe can be rebuilt, and the number of failures tolerated does not grow with the number of disks in the stripe
syllabus_ref: A1.1 Computer hardware and operation (secondary storage, and the use of redundancy across an array of disks), with A1.2 Data representation and computer logic (the exclusive OR operation and its use in a parity bit)
title: A1.1 Redundancy in a block storage array: the parity block of a stripe is the exclusive OR of that stripe's data blocks, so exactly one lost block per stripe can be rebuilt, and the number of failures tolerated does not grow with the number of disks in the stripe
q_html:
One stripe of a redundant array of independent disks

The array divides its address space into stripes and writes each stripe across several disks. A stripe consists of four data blocks followed by one parity block, and the parity block holds the bitwise exclusive OR of the four data blocks of that stripe. The array rotates the position of the parity block from stripe to stripe, so that no single disk stores the parity of every stripe. The table gives the four data blocks of one stripe as they were written.

The array divides its address space into stripes. A stripe consists of four data blocks and one parity block, and the parity block holds the bitwise exclusive OR of the four data blocks of that stripe. The position of the parity block rotates from stripe to stripe, so that no single disk holds the parity of every stripe. When the array reads a block it reads that block alone; the parity block is consulted only when a block is found to be unreadable. The table gives the four data blocks of one stripe as they were written. The figure shows that stripe together with a neighbouring stripe, and marks one unreadable block in each of the two stripes. The two unreadable blocks are in different stripes, and the controller has not yet had to rebuild two blocks that lie in the same stripe.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the parity block of the stripe given in the table, and state the fraction of the array's total block capacity that remains available for data when every stripe carries one parity block for four data blocks.

    (Calculate)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Show that the value of the block D3 can be rebuilt from the parity block and the three surviving data blocks of the stripe, and determine the value that is rebuilt.

    (Show that)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Explain why the array can rebuild the two unreadable blocks marked in the figure at the same time, even though it could not rebuild two unreadable blocks that lay in the same stripe.

    (Explain)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Determine how many simultaneous block failures the array can survive within a single stripe, and state what a second parity block in every stripe would change.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) The parity block is the exclusive OR of the four data blocks, so it is computed by combining them two at a time.

0x5A XOR 0x3C = 0x66
0x66 XOR 0xF0 = 0x96
0x96 XOR 0x27 = 0xB1

The parity block is 0xB1. The exclusive OR is associative and commutative, so the order in which the four blocks are combined does not matter.

A stripe that holds four data blocks and one parity block occupies five blocks in order to store four blocks of data. The fraction of the array's capacity available for data is therefore 4/5 = 0.80, that is eighty per cent. The remaining twenty per cent is the cost of the redundancy: one block in every five is spent on the parity and holds no data of its own.

(b) When the block D3 is unreadable, the array knows the parity block 0xB1 and the three surviving data blocks 0x5A, 0x3C and 0x27. The parity block was formed as the exclusive OR of all four data blocks, and the exclusive OR is its own inverse: a value exclusive ORed with itself gives zero, and a value exclusive ORed with zero is unchanged. Combining the parity block with the three surviving blocks therefore cancels those three and leaves the missing one.

0xB1 XOR 0x5A = 0xEB
0xEB XOR 0x3C = 0xD7
0xD7 XOR 0x27 = 0xF0

The rebuilt value is 0xF0, which is the value the table records for D3. The same computation works whichever of the four blocks is lost, because the parity block is symmetric in the four of them; a rebuild of D1 would combine 0xB1 with 0x3C, 0xF0 and 0x27 and return 0x5A.

(c) Each stripe contributes exactly one equation. For the stripe in the table the equation is D1 XOR D2 XOR D3 XOR D4 = P, in which the only unknown is the one block that has been lost, so the equation can be solved. The two unreadable blocks marked in the figure lie in different stripes, so each of the two stripes supplies its own equation, and each of those equations contains one unknown. The two equations are independent of one another, because the stripes are computed separately when the data is written, so they can be solved at the same time and the two blocks can both be rebuilt.

If two blocks of the same stripe were lost, that stripe would supply one equation containing two unknowns, and one equation in two unknowns does not determine either unknown. Every assignment of values to the two missing blocks that keeps the exclusive OR equal to the parity block would satisfy the equation equally well, so the array would have no way to tell which assignment was the original. The stripe's single equation is one constraint, and one constraint removes one unknown.

(d) A stripe with one parity block carries one equation and can therefore absorb exactly one lost block. That number does not depend on how many data blocks the stripe holds: a stripe of four data blocks and a stripe of twelve data blocks each carry one equation and each tolerate exactly one failure. Widening the stripe raises the fraction of the array available for data, since the parity overhead falls from one block in five to one block in thirteen, but it does not raise the tolerance at all. The tolerance is set by the number of parity blocks in the stripe and not by the number of disks in it, which is the point that a candidate who reasons by analogy with the disk count will miss.

A second parity block in every stripe would give each stripe two equations instead of one. Two equations in two unknowns can be solved, so such an array would tolerate two simultaneous block failures within the same stripe, and it would also be able to rebuild a block even when the parity block itself is one of the two failures. The cost is a second block of overhead: a stripe of four data blocks would then occupy six blocks, so the fraction available for data would fall from 4/5 to 4/6, that is from eighty per cent to about sixty-seven per cent.

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark for the method of combining the blocks with the exclusive OR, one mark for the value 0xB1, and one mark for the fraction 4/5 or eighty per cent. A candidate who writes 0xB1 but gives the capacity as five quarters, or as one hundred per cent because the parity is 'not data', forfeits the third mark.

(b) One mark for stating that the exclusive OR is its own inverse or that combining the parity with the survivors cancels them, one mark for a correct sequence of combinations, one mark for the value 0xF0, and one mark for showing the check that the rebuilt value reproduces the parity block. Follow-through is allowed from a wrong parity block in (a) provided the method in (b) is sound, since a candidate who computes 0x00 in (a) and then rebuilds 0xF0 by the correct method has demonstrated the same understanding.

(c) One mark for saying that each stripe supplies its own independent equation, one mark for saying that each of those equations contains one unknown, and one mark for the contrast, that one equation in two unknowns does not determine either unknown. The phrase 'different stripes' alone earns nothing; the reason must be the independence of the equations.

(d) One mark for exactly one failure per stripe, one mark for the statement that this number is independent of the number of data blocks, and one mark for the effect of a second parity block, namely two failures per stripe at the cost of a second block of overhead. An answer that says the tolerance grows with the number of disks scores zero for this part, however well the earlier parts are done.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A1.2 A weighted check digit modulo a prime detects every interchange of two digits, because the change it makes to the total is a product of two factors each smaller than the modulus; an unweighted digit sum detects none, because the change is zero
syllabus_ref: A1.2 Data representation and computer logic (check digits and the detection of errors in stored or transmitted data), with A2.3 Data transmissions (why an error must be detected before it can be corrected)
title: A1.2 A weighted check digit modulo a prime detects every interchange of two digits, because the change it makes to the total is a product of two factors each smaller than the modulus; an unweighted digit sum detects none, because the change is zero
q_html:
The catalogue's check on the codes it stores

A book catalogue stores ten-digit ISBN codes. Each code consists of nine identifying digits followed by a check digit. The check digit is chosen so that, with the digits weighted from ten down to one, the weighted total is a multiple of eleven. When a code is typed in, the catalogue runs a validation routine. The routine adds the ten digits together and accepts the code if that total is a multiple of ten. The routine was written by a volunteer who believed that a check digit is simply a digit chosen to make the digits add up to a round number. The table shows one record, the code as it was typed, and the routine's verdict.

The nine identifying digits of record R-4471 are 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 1 and 5, and the check digit is the final 2, so the code as the publisher printed it is 0306406152. The code held in the catalogue is 0306406512: the eighth and ninth digits have been interchanged somewhere between the publisher's list and the catalogue's keyboard. The catalogue's routine accepted the code, and the record has stood in the catalogue for two years. The correct rule for a ten-digit ISBN weights the first digit by ten, the second by nine, and so on down to the tenth digit weighted by one, and requires the weighted total to be a multiple of eleven. A rival scheme weights each digit by its own position, counting the first digit as position one, and requires the total to be a multiple of ten. The catalogue's routine is a third scheme again: it weights every digit by one.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the check digit that the weighted rule requires for the nine identifying digits 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 1 and 5, and hence state whether the code held in the catalogue satisfies the rule.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Determine the weighted total of the code held in the catalogue, and state what its remainder on division by eleven shows about the interchange of the two digits.

    (Determine)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Explain why the catalogue's routine accepted a code that the weighted rule rejects, referring to the effect that interchanging two digits has on the sum of those digits.

    (Explain)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    The rival scheme that weights each digit by its position and works modulo ten is not equivalent to the weighted rule. Deduce, from the change that interchanging two digits makes to a weighted total, one interchange that the rival scheme fails to detect, and explain why the weighted rule modulo eleven cannot fail to detect any interchange of two digits.

    (Deduce)
a_html:
(a) The weighted rule weights the digits from ten down to one. For the nine identifying digits 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 1 and 5 the weights are 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3 and 2, so the weighted total of the identifying digits is

10(0) + 9(3) + 8(0) + 7(6) + 6(4) + 5(0) + 4(6) + 3(1) + 2(5)
= 0 + 27 + 0 + 42 + 24 + 0 + 24 + 3 + 10
= 130.

The check digit carries weight one, so it must satisfy 130 + d = 0 (mod 11). Now 130 = 11 x 11 + 9, so 130 is 9 more than a multiple of eleven, and the check digit must make up the difference: d = 11 - 9 = 2. The check digit is 2, which agrees with the final digit of the publisher's code 0306406152.

The code held in the catalogue is 0306406512, which has the same ten digits in a different order. Its weighted total is 136, and 136 = 11 x 12 + 4, so the total is 4 more than a multiple of eleven. The code held in the catalogue therefore does not satisfy the rule, and the check digit it carries, 2, is not the check digit for the nine digits that precede it in that order.

(b) The weighted total of the code held in the catalogue is

10(0) + 9(3) + 8(0) + 7(6) + 6(4) + 5(0) + 4(6) + 3(5) + 2(1) + 1(2)
= 0 + 27 + 0 + 42 + 24 + 0 + 24 + 15 + 2 + 2
= 136.

The remainder on division by eleven is 4, and a valid code would leave a remainder of zero. The remainder is not zero, so the interchange is detected: the code held in the catalogue is not a valid ISBN under the weighted rule, and the nonzero remainder is the evidence. Comparing the two totals, the publisher's code gives 132 and the catalogue's code gives 136, so interchanging the eighth and ninth digits raised the total by 4. That increase is not an accident of these particular digits; it is the difference between the two weights, 3 and 2, multiplied by the difference between the two digits, 1 and 5.

(c) The catalogue's routine adds the ten digits together and tests whether the total is a multiple of ten. The ten digits of the publisher's code are 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 1, 5 and 2, which add to 27. The ten digits of the catalogue's code are 0, 3, 0, 6, 4, 0, 6, 5, 1 and 2, which also add to 27. Addition does not care about the order of its terms, so interchanging two digits leaves the sum of the digits exactly as it was. The routine therefore computes the same total for both codes, finds 27 in each case, and accepts both, because 27 has the same remainder on division by ten, namely 7, as itself.

The routine is not merely weaker than the weighted rule; it is blind to the whole class of errors to which keyboard entry is most prone. Interchanging two adjacent digits is the commonest mistake made when a long number is copied by hand, and the routine's weighting, which is to say a weight of one on every position, makes every interchange invisible. A check that cannot see the commonest error is not a check that has been weakened; it is a check that is not doing the job it was written for.

(d) Consider a weighted total in which the digit at position i carries weight w_i. Interchanging the digits at positions i and j replaces the contribution w_i d_i + w_j d_j with w_i d_j + w_j d_i, so the total changes by

(w_i d_j + w_j d_i) - (w_i d_i + w_j d_j) = (w_i - w_j)(d_j - d_i).

For the rival scheme the weight of a digit is its position, so w_i = i and w_j = j, and the change is (i - j)(d_j - d_i). The rival scheme accepts the corrupted code when this product is a multiple of ten. Take the digits at positions 1 and 3, and suppose they are 0 and 5. Then i - j is 1 - 3 = -2 and d_j - d_i is 5 - 0 = 5, so the change is -2 x 5 = -10, which is a multiple of ten, and the rival scheme does not notice the interchange. The interchange of a 0 and a 5 two positions apart is therefore one that the rival scheme misses. The reason the miss is possible is that ten is not prime: the factor of five that the digit difference supplies can be paired with the factor of two that the position difference supplies to make a multiple of ten.

For the weighted rule the weights are ten, nine, eight and so on down to one, and the change made by an interchange is (w_i - w_j)(d_j - d_i). The digits are between 0 and 9, so d_j - d_i lies between -9 and 9, and the positions are between 1 and 10, so w_i - w_j also lies between -9 and 9. Neither factor can be a multiple of eleven, because eleven is larger than nine, and neither factor is zero when the digits differ and the positions differ. Since eleven is prime, a product is a multiple of eleven only if one of its factors is, and neither factor is. The change is therefore never a multiple of eleven, so the total of a code with two digits interchanged can never be a multiple of eleven, and the interchange is always detected. Choosing a prime modulus larger than the largest possible value of either factor is what makes the guarantee hold.

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark for the weighted total 130 of the nine identifying digits, one mark for the check digit 2 with the reasoning 130 = 9 (mod 11) so d = 2, and one mark for the verdict that the catalogue's code does not satisfy the rule. A candidate who computes 132 and then reports the code as valid has used the wrong digit order and forfeits the third mark.

(b) One mark for the total 136, one mark for the remainder 4, and one mark for the conclusion that the interchange is detected because the remainder is not zero. Accept the remainder as 4 or as -7; accept the observation that the interchange changed the total by 4 only if it is attached to the weights 3 and 2.

(c) One mark for stating that the sum of the digits is 27 in both orders, one mark for the reason, that addition does not depend on the order of its terms, and one mark for drawing the consequence, that the routine is blind to every interchange and not merely to this one. A candidate who says only that the routine 'checks the wrong thing' without referring to the invariance of the digit sum scores at most one mark.

(d) One mark for the expression (w_i - w_j)(d_j - d_i) or its equivalent, one mark for a correct specific interchange such as the 0 and the 5 at positions 1 and 3 with the product -10, one mark for the argument that eleven is prime and larger than both factors, and one mark for completing it, that a product is a multiple of a prime only when one factor is. Follow-through is allowed from a wrong expression in the first mark provided the prime argument is made correctly.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A2.2 Network architecture: device roles, subnets and broadcast domains
syllabus_ref: A2.1 Network fundamentals, A2.2 Network architecture (the structure of a network, the roles of switches and routers, subnets and broadcast domains)
title: A2.2 Network architecture: device roles, subnets and broadcast domains
q_html:
The figure shows the network of a small company. A router is connected to two switches, and three personal computers are connected to each switch. The two subnets are labelled in the figure, and the two addresses shown on the links from the router are the addresses of the router's own interfaces, one in each subnet. The company has been allocated the block 192.168.10.0/24 and has decided to use only the first half of it.
