```
title: A forty-gigabyte file that will not fit in memory twice
q_html:
Northwind Climate Archive ingestion

A weather service ingests a daily archive from a national network of 500 stations. The archive is a single text file of 40 GB. Each record is one line of about 100 bytes holding four comma-separated fields: station code, timestamp, temperature and humidity.

The file arrives as a compressed stream over a socket. The stream cannot be rewound and the raw file is never written to disk, because the service has no room for it. The machine that runs the ingestion has 8 GB of RAM.

The service must produce, for each station, the number of valid readings, the minimum and maximum temperature and the mean temperature. It must also report every malformed record to the provider so that the archive can be corrected, and the provider needs the line number of each bad record. The provider has warned that a corrupt upload can contain millions of malformed lines.

def ingest(stream):
    data = stream.read()                      # 40 GB, held in memory
    errors = []
    summary = {}
    for lineno, line in enumerate(data.split("\n"), start=1):
        fields = line.split(",")
        if len(fields) != 4:
            errors.append((lineno, line))     # keeps every bad line
            continue
        station, timestamp, temp, humidity = fields
        ...
    return summary, errors

The ingestion runs once a night on a single machine, must not exhaust memory, and must finish before the next upload arrives.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Explain why stream.read() cannot be used here, referring to the size of the file and the memory available, and state what a streaming implementation does instead.

    (Explain)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Explain why data.split("\n") followed by line.split(",") produces errors that the developer would not see when testing on a small file. Describe how a record containing a comma inside a quoted field must be parsed.

    (Explain)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Construct a Python function ingest(stream, max_errors) that consumes the stream exactly once and returns a summary, an error report and an error count. stream is a file-like object that supports iteration and cannot be rewound. The summary must give, for each station, the count, minimum, maximum and sum of temperatures. The error report must hold the line number and a reason for at most max_errors malformed records, and the count must be the exact total of malformed records. You may not import any module, and you may not call stream.read() or stream.seek(). A Java version of this paper requires the same algorithm.

    (Construct)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Evaluate the decision to keep only the first max_errors malformed records while still counting all of them, against the provider's requirement to receive the line number of every malformed record. State what is given up and recommend a design.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The file is 40 GB and the machine has 8 GB of RAM, so stream.read() tries to build a string five times larger than the memory available; the process would be killed before any summary was produced, and the failure would happen after the whole file had been transferred. (M1) The stream also cannot be rewound: it arrives compressed over a socket and the raw file is never written to disk, so the program cannot read part of it, release the memory and then return to the beginning. (A1) A streaming implementation reads one record at a time and keeps only the running state it needs — for each station a count, a minimum, a maximum and a running total — so its memory use is proportional to the number of stations, not to the size of the file, and 500 stations need only a few tens of kilobytes. (A1)

(b) There are two faults, and neither is visible on a small test file.

The first is data.split("\n"). It splits the entire 40 GB string and, because a text file normally ends with a newline character, it produces a final empty element. That empty element is counted as a malformed record, so the reported error count is wrong by one before any real error is found. (M1)(A1) Iterating the file object directly avoids this, because a text stream yields one line per record and never yields a phantom line at the end.

The second is line.split(","), which splits on every comma, including a comma that is inside a quoted field. A record such as ST04,"North, West",4.0,60 contains four fields, but split(",") returns five pieces, so a perfectly valid record is rejected and the field boundaries of the following fields are wrong. (M1)(A1) A correct parser scans the line character by character, keeps a flag for whether it is inside a quoted field, treats a doubled quote as a literal quote character, and splits only on commas seen outside quotes.

(c)

def ingest(stream, max_errors):
    summary = {}
    errors = []
    total_errors = 0

for lineno, raw in enumerate(stream, start=1):
line = raw.rstrip("\r\n")
if line == "":
total_errors += 1
if len(errors) < max_errors:
errors.append((lineno, "empty line"))
continue

fields = split_csv(line)
if len(fields) != 4:
total_errors += 1
if len(errors) < max_errors:
errors.append((lineno, "field count %d" % len(fields)))
continue

station, timestamp, temp, humidity = fields
try:
t = float(temp)
except ValueError:
total_errors += 1
if len(errors) < max_errors:
errors.append((lineno, "non-numeric temperature"))
continue

if station in summary:
count, low, high, total = summary[station]
summary[station] = (count + 1, min(low, t), max(high, t), total + t)
else:
summary[station] = (1, t, t, t)

return summary, errors, total_errors

def split_csv(line):
fields, current, in_quotes = [], [], False
i = 0
while i < len(line):
ch = line[i]
if ch == '"':
if in_quotes and i + 1 < len(line) and line[i + 1] == '"':
current.append('"')
i += 2
continue
in_quotes = not in_quotes
elif ch == "," and not in_quotes:
fields.append("".join(current))
current = []
else:
current.append(ch)
i += 1
fields.append("".join(current))
return fields
```

(M1) for consuming the stream exactly once, with enumerate supplying the line number, and never calling read() or seek(). (A1) for holding only bounded state per station — a count, a minimum, a maximum and a running total — so memory is proportional to the number of stations. (A1) for capping errors at max_errors while total_errors still counts every malformed record, so the exact scale of the corruption is preserved. (A1) for the quoted-field parser, which is what makes the field count correct for records such as ST04,"North, West",4.0,60. (A1) for validating the numeric field and continuing rather than crashing, so that one bad record does not abandon the remaining 400,000,000.

The time is $O(n)$ in the number of records and the memory is $O(S)$ for $S$ stations plus at most max_errors small tuples. A Java version of this paper asks for the same algorithm: a BufferedReader read line by line, a HashMap of running statistics, and the identical two-state parser.

(d) The requirement and the cap are in direct conflict. The provider must receive the line number of *every* malformed record, and a corrupt upload can contain millions of them, so an in-memory list capped at max_errors will be full almost immediately and the line numbers beyond the cap are lost. (M1) The cap does bound memory — max_errors tuples of an integer and a short string is a few tens of kilobytes, which is safe on an 8 GB machine — so the design trades completeness for a memory guarantee. (A1)

That trade is unnecessary, because the error report does not have to live in memory. Each malformed record can be written to a second output stream as it is found: memory stays bounded at one record, and the provider receives every line number. (A1) The costs are a second output to manage and the throughput the writes consume, but the error file is normally tiny — it is only large when the upload is genuinely corrupt, which is exactly when the provider needs it in full. The running total_errors count should be kept regardless, so that the summary can state the scale of the corruption even if the provider's tooling truncates the error file.

The recommendation is therefore to stream the errors out, and to fall back to a capped in-memory list only when no second output is available. In that fallback the report must say so: it must state that line numbers beyond the cap are missing while the total count remains exact, so that the provider knows how much of the report is absent rather than believing the report is complete. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) Require either the arithmetic (40 GB against 8 GB, a factor of five) or an equivalent statement of impossibility. A candidate who proposes adding RAM or using a bigger machine has not engaged with the design and should be redirected; credit is not awarded for hardware. "Streaming" must be described as reading one record at a time with bounded state, not merely as "using a loop".

(b) Each fault needs its mechanism. For the trailing-newline fault, accept a description of the phantom final empty element; a candidate who says only "split is wrong" earns nothing. For the quoting fault, accept a prose description or code. A candidate who says "use the csv module" earns the description mark only if they also say what a CSV parser must do about quoted delimiters.

(c) The marks are for structure, not for library knowledge. Accept any single-pass function returning equivalent summary, error and count objects; a dictionary of tuples, a dictionary of lists, or a small class are all acceptable. Do not award the capped-list mark to a candidate who stores every malformed line, and do not award the parser mark to a candidate who still calls split(",") on a raw line. try/except, an explicit numeric test, or a regular expression are all acceptable for the validation mark. A candidate who reads the stream twice loses the single-pass mark even if the results are correct.

(d) The evaluation must name the conflict and then choose. A candidate who says "increase max_errors" has not engaged with the memory bound and should be capped at one mark. The strongest answers propose the second output stream; a candidate who defends the cap can still earn two marks if the loss of line numbers is stated explicitly and the exact count is retained. Do not accept "store the errors in a database" as a free answer — it is a second output stream in disguise, and it should be credited only if the candidate says that the writes are streamed rather than batched.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B4.1 Binary search trees: traversal, insertion, deletion and search cost
syllabus_ref: B4.1 Fundamentals of ADTs (HL only), B2.2 Data structures (binary search trees: traversal, insertion, deletion, search cost)
title: B4.1 Binary search trees: traversal, insertion, deletion and search cost
q_html:
A public library is building a catalogue system. Each book is identified by a numerical accession number, and the catalogue must support three operations: finding the record for a given accession number, adding a new accession number, and printing the whole catalogue in ascending order of accession number. The system designer decides to hold the accession numbers in a binary search tree. The figure shows two binary search trees, A and B, that were built from the same five accession numbers, with the insertion order used for each tree given above it. The height of a tree is taken to be the number of nodes on the longest path from the root to a leaf. Answer all parts with reference to the figure, and justify each answer.

  1. [2 marks](a)

    State the in-order traversal of tree A, and explain why an in-order traversal of any binary search tree returns its keys in ascending order.

    (State)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Determine where the accession number 40 would be inserted in tree A, and state the height of the tree after that insertion.

    (Determine)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Describe the steps needed to delete a node that has two children from a binary search tree, and apply your description to the deletion of the node holding 45 from tree A.

    (Describe)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    The library's catalogue will eventually hold 200 000 accession numbers. Compare the greatest number of comparisons a search might need in a tree shaped like tree A with the greatest number it might need in a tree shaped like tree B, and comment on the practical significance of the difference.

    (Compare)
  5. [3 marks](e)

    A colleague suggests replacing the tree with a hash table, which would give constant-time lookup. Explain whether a hash table could satisfy all three of the operations the catalogue must support.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) An in-order traversal visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree, and applied to tree A it yields 20, 30, 35, 45, 50. (A1) The traversal is ascending because of the ordering property of a binary search tree: every key in the left subtree of a node is smaller than the node's key, and every key in the right subtree is larger. (M1) Visiting left, then node, then right therefore emits each key only after every smaller key in its subtree, and before every larger one, so the output is sorted whatever the shape of the tree.

(b) Insertion compares the new key with each node from the root downwards and moves left when the key is smaller and right when it is larger. Starting at 30, the key 40 is larger, so it goes right; at 45 it is smaller, so it goes left; at 35 it is larger, so it goes right, and the position is empty. (M1)(A1) The key 40 therefore becomes the right child of 35. (A1) That path visits four nodes, 30, 45, 35 and 40, so the height of the tree rises from 3 to 4.

(c) A node with two children cannot simply be removed, because the two subtrees would have to be reattached. The standard method is to replace the key being deleted with its in-order successor, which is the smallest key in its right subtree, and then delete that successor from the right subtree, where it is guaranteed to have at most one child. (M1)(A1) For tree A, the in-order successor of 45 is 50, since 50 is the only key in 45's right subtree and is therefore its smallest. (A1) The key at the node is overwritten with 50, and the original node holding 50, which is a leaf, is then removed. The resulting tree has root 30, left child 20, and right child 50 with left child 35, so its height is 3. (A1)

(d) In a tree shaped like A the height grows with the logarithm of the number of keys, because each comparison halves the range still to be searched. (M1) For 200 000 keys the height is about log2(200000), which is 17.6, so a search visits at most 18 nodes and needs at most 18 comparisons. (A1) In a tree shaped like B, each node has only one child, so the tree is a chain and a search may have to visit every node. (M1) For 200 000 keys that is 200 000 comparisons, which is roughly 11 000 times as many as the balanced shape needs. The practical significance is that the degenerate shape offers no improvement over scanning a list, so the choice of a tree delivers nothing unless the shape is controlled. (A1)

(e) A hash table computes the position of a key from the key itself, so lookup, insertion and deletion are all constant-time on average, and the three operations would be fast. (M1) However, the keys in a hash table are stored in an order determined by the hash function, not by the keys, so the third operation, printing the catalogue in ascending order of accession number, cannot be done without retrieving every key and sorting it, which costs O(n log n) each time. (A1) The hash table is therefore the better structure only if the ordered listing is not required, or if it is produced once and cached; as specified, it does not satisfy the third requirement. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) A1 for the correct sequence 20, 30, 35, 45, 50; M1 for the reason, which must refer to the ordering property and to visiting left, node, right. A candidate who lists the keys in the order they were inserted has not performed a traversal and scores 0 of 2. (b) M1 for comparing with 30, 45 and 35 in the right order; A1 for identifying 40 as the right child of 35; A1 for the height of 4. Accept a correct route that reaches the same position by a different description. A candidate who answers 3 has not noticed that the new path is longer than the old longest path, and scores 2 of 3. (c) M1 for the idea of replacing the deleted key with another key rather than removing the node; A1 for naming the in-order successor, or the equivalent predecessor, as the replacement; A1 for identifying 50 as the successor of 45 in this tree; A1 for the resulting tree and its height. A candidate who instead promotes 35 and reattaches 50 correctly should be given the last A1, since the predecessor method is equally valid. (d) M1 for the logarithmic height of a balanced tree; A1 for about 18 comparisons; M1 for the linear height of the chain; A1 for 200 000 comparisons together with a comment that recognises the practical consequence. Accept any answer that gives the two orders of growth correctly even if the arithmetic is approximate. (e) M1 for recognising that a hash table gives constant-time access; A1 for identifying that it provides no ordering; A1 for the conclusion that the ordered listing cannot be produced efficiently, with the cost stated. Do not accept an answer that rejects the hash table without a reason.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A3.2 Database design
syllabus_ref: A3.2 Database design, A3.3 Database programming, B1.1 Approaches to computational thinking
title: A3.2 Database design
q_html:
Migrating a policy administration system

An insurer administers 18 million policy records on a forty-year-old mainframe system written in COBOL, with data held in flat files and indexed by a bespoke access method. The system processes 240 000 transactions per night in a batch window and about 3 200 payment instructions per hour during the day. It is reliable but there are four staff in the country who can maintain it, all within ten years of retirement. The board has approved a migration to a relational database behind a service interface. Two proposals are on the table. Proposal A is a big-bang cutover on a single weekend: the new system is built in full, the old one is switched off, and if the new system fails the fallback is to restore the mainframe from the previous night's backup, which takes 14 hours. Proposal B is an incremental migration in which a facade routes each function either to the old or the new system, functions are moved one at a time, and both systems run in parallel until the last one is moved. The migration team estimates that dual running costs EUR 14 000 per month in additional infrastructure and that a reconciliation mismatch rate of 0.02% is achievable, each exception taking an average of 6 minutes to investigate. Analyst time is costed at EUR 65 per hour.

Using the case study, answer all four parts. Assume a month is 30 nights of batch processing.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Explain why a big-bang cutover is a poor choice for this system, referring to specific figures in the case study rather than to general principles.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Construct an incremental migration plan. State the mechanism that routes each request, the order in which you would move functions and why that order, and how the two systems are kept consistent while both are live.

    (Construct)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Calculate the total cost of nine months of dual running, including the analyst time spent on reconciliation. Show your working.

    (Calculate)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Evaluate the two proposals. If a failed big-bang cutover causes an 8-hour outage in which 3 200 payments per hour are missed and each missed payment costs EUR 120 in penalties and remediation, compare that with your answer to (c) and state which proposal you recommend.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The decisive figure is the fallback: restoring from the previous night's backup takes 14 hours, during which roughly $14 \times 3200 \approx 45\,000$ payment instructions are not processed. (A1) A single failed cutover therefore risks a full working day of missed payments on a book of 18 million policies. (A1)

The staff position removes the option of a leisurely recovery. Only four people can maintain the old system, so if the new system fails and the old one must be restored and then kept running, there is almost no capacity to diagnose and fix the new one. (A1)

There is also no way to validate the new system at full scale before committing: 240 000 transactions per night cannot be simulated faithfully enough to be confident, and the first genuine run would also be the production run. (A1)

(b) *Mechanism:* place a facade in front of both systems. Every request arrives at the facade, which inspects the function being invoked and routes it either to the mainframe or to the new service. Callers never know which is serving them, so functions can be moved one at a time and moved back if necessary. (M1)(A1)

*Order:* move the read-mostly reference functions first, then simple queries, then writes, and leave the nightly batch and the payment instruction generation until last. (A1) The reason is that a read that goes wrong is visible immediately and is cheap to reverse, whereas a write that goes wrong corrupts data that may not be discovered for weeks; and the batch window is the most complex and least reversible part of the system, so it should be migrated only when everything feeding it is already new. (A1)

*Consistency while both are live:* run both systems for each migrated function and compare their outputs automatically every night, logging any disagreement as an exception for an analyst. The mainframe remains the system of record until a function has run clean for a sustained period, at which point the new system becomes the record for that function and the old one stops being authoritative for it. (A1)

(c) Infrastructure: $9 \times 14\,000 = \text{EUR }126\,000$. (A1)

Exceptions per night: $0.02\% \times 240\,000 = 48$. (M1)
Time per night: $48 \times 6 = 288$ minutes $= 4.8$ hours. (A1)
Over nine months, $9 \times 30 = 270$ nights: $270 \times 4.8 = 1296$ hours, at EUR 65 per hour:
$$1296 \times 65 = \text{EUR }84\,240$$
Total: $126\,000 + 84\,240 = \text{EUR }210\,240$. (A1)

(d) A failed cutover misses $8 \times 3200 = 25\,600$ payments, costing (M1)
$$25\,600 \times 120 = \text{EUR }3\,072\,000.$$
Comparing with the EUR 210 240 for nine months of dual running, a single failure costs about (A1)
$$\frac{3\,072\,000}{210\,240} \approx 15$$
times as much as the entire incremental programme. (A1)

Recommendation: Proposal B. Even if one assumed a failure probability for the big-bang cutover as low as one in ten, its expected cost would be about EUR 307 000, still above the full cost of dual running, and the incremental route has the further advantages of keeping the old system available as a live fallback for every function not yet moved, of building operational confidence gradually, and of allowing the four remaining experts to be consulted steadily rather than in a crisis. The one real drawback is the nine-month cost of running both, which the calculation shows to be small relative to the risk avoided.

Markscheme notes

(a) The marks are for using the figures; general assertions about risk earn nothing. The 14-hour restore and the four maintainers are the two that matter most, and a candidate who cites only the size of the dataset has missed the point, since size alone is not the difficulty. (b) Award (M1) for the facade concept regardless of the name used; a candidate who proposes a hard switch per function without a routing layer has not solved the problem. The order mark requires a reason, and the reason must be about reversibility or blast radius rather than convenience. The consistency mark is for dual-running with automated comparison and a defined point at which authority transfers; a candidate who says the two databases are kept synchronised by replication should be asked how, given that the schemas differ. (c) Accept a total between EUR 200 000 and EUR 220 000 depending on the assumption about nights per month; award the method marks for the mismatch count and the conversion to cost. (d) The comparison must be quantitative. Credit a candidate who goes further and computes an expected value or a break-even failure probability, since that is the strongest form of the argument. A recommendation of Proposal A is not creditable given these figures, but a candidate who argues for a shorter dual-running period, say four months, on the grounds that the mismatch rate would fall as the new system stabilises, should be credited.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A4.2 Choosing a scaling method when one outlier dominates the range
syllabus_ref: A4.2 Data preprocessing (HL only) (normalisation, standardisation, outlier handling)
title: A4.2 Choosing a scaling method when one outlier dominates the range
q_html:
A hospital logistics team is building a machine-learning model to predict delivery times.
One of the features is the loading time, in minutes, for the ten most recent deliveries:

$$10,\ 11,\ 12,\ 13,\ 14,\ 15,\ 16,\ 17,\ 18,\ 1400$$

The final value, $1400$ minutes, is a data-entry error: the true value was $14.00$ and the
decimal point was lost. The team has not yet cleaned the data and is comparing two ways of
scaling the feature before clustering.

(a) Calculate the mean and the standard deviation of the ten values as recorded. \tag{3}

(b) Determine the min–max scaled values of $10$, $18$ and $1400$, and calculate the scaled gap
between consecutive typical values. \tag{4}

(c) Determine the standardised (z-score) values of $10$, $18$ and $1400$, calculate the
corresponding scaled gap, and compare the two methods. \tag{5}

(d) Hence explain which scaling method the team should prefer for this data set. \tag{3}

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the mean and the standard deviation of the ten values as recorded.

    (Calculate)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Determine the min-max scaled values of 10, 18 and 1400, and calculate the scaled gap between consecutive typical values.

    (Determine)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Determine the standardised values of 10, 18 and 1400, calculate the corresponding scaled gap, and compare the two methods.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Hence explain which scaling method the team should prefer for this data set.

    (Explain)
a_html:
(a) The nine typical values are the integers $10$ to $18$, whose sum is
$\frac{9(10 + 18)}{2} = 126$; adding $1400$ gives $1526$ and the mean is

$$\bar{x} = \frac{1526}{10} = 152.6 \tag{A1}$$

Note that the mean already sits far above every genuine reading: the true centre of the nine
typical values is $14$, and the single error has moved it by $138.6$.

The sum of squared deviations is most safely found from
$\sum x^{2} - n\bar{x}^{2}$ (M1). Here

$$\sum x^{2} = 100 + 121 + \cdots + 324 + 1960000 = 1824 + 1960000 = 1961824$$

and $n\bar{x}^{2} = 10 \times 152.6^{2} = 10 \times 23286.76 = 232867.6$, so

$$\sum (x - \bar{x})^{2} = 1961824 - 232867.6 = 1728956.4 \tag{A1}$$

The outlier contributes $1247.4^{2} = 1556006.8$ of that, which is $90.0\%$ of the whole
total. The population variance is $\frac{1728956.4}{10} = 172895.6$ and

$$\sigma = \sqrt{172895.6} = 415.8 \tag{A1}$$

(b) Min–max scaling maps $x$ to $\frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}$, and here
$x_{\min} = 10$ and $x_{\max} = 1400$, so the divisor is $1390$ (M1):

$$\frac{10 - 10}{1390} = 0.000, \qquad \frac{18 - 10}{1390} = 0.00576, \qquad
\frac{1400 - 10}{1390} = 1.000 \tag{A1}$$

The typical values therefore occupy the interval $[0,\ 0.00576]$ — the bottom $0.58\%$ of the
range — and the outlier sits alone at $1.000$ (A1). The scaled gap between consecutive typical
values, which are one minute apart in the original data, is

$$\frac{1}{1390} = 0.000719 \tag{A1}$$

(c) Standardising maps $x$ to $\frac{x - \bar{x}}{\sigma}$ (M1):

$$\frac{10 - 152.6}{415.8} = -0.343, \qquad \frac{18 - 152.6}{415.8} = -0.324, \qquad
\frac{1400 - 152.6}{415.8} = 3.00 \tag{A1}$$

The typical values occupy $[-0.343,\ -0.324]$ and the outlier sits at $3.00$ (A1). The scaled
gap between consecutive typical values is

$$\frac{1}{415.8} = 0.00241 \tag{A1}$$

which is $\frac{0.00241}{0.000719} = 3.34$ times the min–max gap (A1). Standardisation
therefore preserves about three and a third times as much resolution among the typical readings
as min–max does, even though it is far from ideal: the outlier still inflates $\sigma$ from
about $2.4$ to $415.8$ and drags the mean to $152.6$, more than ten times the largest genuine
reading. Note also that $3.00$ is the largest z-score any value in a data set of ten can have,
so the outlier is pressing against the ceiling that the sample size allows.

(d) Neither method should be used on the raw data (A1). The right first step is to correct or
remove the erroneous $1400$, since it is a known data-entry fault rather than a genuine
observation; with it removed the range is $8$, the mean is $14$ and the choice of scaler barely
matters (A1). If the value must be retained, standardisation is preferable to min–max because
the mean and standard deviation are less sensitive to a single extreme value than the minimum
and maximum are — the outlier moves $\sigma$ but does not set it, whereas it sets $x_{\max}$
directly (A1). Better still is a robust scaler based on the median and interquartile range,
which for this data gives a scaled gap of $\frac{1}{5} = 0.2$, about $278$ times the min–max
resolution.

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for the sum or the mean $152.6$. (M1) for setting up the sum of squared
deviations. (A1) for the outlier's squared deviation $1556006.76$. (A1) for
$\sigma = 415.8$; accept $[415, 416]$. Allow the sample standard deviation ($s = 438.3$)
provided it is identified as such, with full marks.

(b) (M1) for the divisor $1390$. (A1) for the three scaled values. (A1) for identifying that
the typical values fall in the bottom fraction of the range. (A1) for the gap $0.000719$.

(c) (M1) for the standardisation formula. (A1) for the three z-scores. (A1) for the interval
occupied by the typical values. (A1) for the gap $0.00241$. (A1) for the ratio $3.34$.

Forfeiture: a candidate who uses the *cleaned* mean or standard deviation in (c) has answered a
different question and earns at most the first (M1) — the item is explicitly about what happens
before cleaning.

(d) (A1) for recommending cleaning first. (A1) for the consequence of cleaning. (A1) for
comparing the sensitivity of the two scalers, or for proposing a robust alternative with the
figure $0.2$.

Note: a candidate who simply states that min–max is "affected by outliers" has not used the
quantitative work from (b) and (c) and earns at most one mark.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A2 Networks
syllabus_ref: A2.1 Network fundamentals, A2.2 Network architecture (A2.1.6 the role of IP and MAC addresses, A2.2.2 the structure of a network, subnetting)
title: Fitting four departments into one /24
q_html:
One /24 and four departments

A school has been allocated the block $192.168.40.0/24$ and must divide it between four departments and two router links. The required numbers of hosts are: science $60$, humanities $28$, administration $12$, and the library $6$. In addition, two point-to-point links between the department routers each need exactly two usable addresses. Addresses are assigned from the start of the block upwards, and no two subnets may overlap.

There is more than enough address space for all six requirements, but only if the block is divided unevenly. Design the division, then justify it.

  1. [5 marks](a)

    Design a subnetting scheme using variable-length subnet masks. For each of the six requirements give the network address in dotted decimal, the prefix length, and the number of usable host addresses it provides.

    (Design)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Determine how many addresses in the /24 block remain unused by your scheme, and compare this with the number that would remain if the block had instead been divided into four equal subnets.

    (Determine)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Explain how a host uses its own address and subnet mask to decide whether a destination address is on its own subnet, and what it does if it is not.

    (Explain)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Evaluate one advantage and one disadvantage of the variable-length scheme compared with using four equal subnets, in a network that may grow.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Work downwards in size so that each block starts on a boundary its own prefix length divides. A prefix that leaves $h$ host bits provides $2^{h} - 2$ usable addresses. (M1)

| requirement | network address | prefix | usable hosts |
|---|---|---|---|
| science, needs 60 | $192.168.40.0$ | $/26$ | $62$ |
| humanities, needs 28 | $192.168.40.64$ | $/27$ | $30$ |
| administration, needs 12 | $192.168.40.96$ | $/28$ | $14$ |
| library, needs 6 | $192.168.40.112$ | $/29$ | $6$ |
| WAN link 1, needs 2 | $192.168.40.120$ | $/30$ | $2$ |
| WAN link 2, needs 2 | $192.168.40.124$ | $/30$ | $2$ |

(A1) for each correct prefix, (A1) for the complete set of addresses, (A1) for the usable-host counts. The blocks occupy $0$–$63$, $64$–$95$, $96$–$111$, $112$–$119$, $120$–$123$ and $124$–$127$ with no overlap, because each block begins at an address divisible by its own size.

(b) The six blocks consume $64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 4 = 128$ addresses, so $256 - 128 = 128$ addresses remain free for growth. (M1)(A1) Four equal subnets would each be a $/26$, giving $4 \times 64 = 256$ addresses and leaving none at all; in that scheme $62 + 30 + 14 + 6 = 112$ required hosts are spread across $248$ usable addresses, so $136$ are wasted inside the subnets, and the two WAN links would not fit. (M1)(A1)

(c) The host performs a bitwise AND between its own address and its subnet mask to obtain its network address, then does the same to the destination address using its own mask. (M1) If the two network addresses are equal, the destination is local and the host sends the frame directly, using ARP to find the destination's MAC address. (A1) If they differ, the host sends the frame to its default gateway instead, addressing the frame to the gateway's MAC address while leaving the destination IP address untouched; the gateway then routes the packet onwards. (A1)

(d) The advantage is that the variable-length scheme leaves $128$ addresses free and can absorb growth in any department by allocating from that pool, or by renumbering only the department that has outgrown its block. (A1) The disadvantage is that it is harder to manage and harder to read: the six prefixes have to be recorded in the routing table individually rather than summarised, and a technician who sees a $/29$ and a $/30$ side by side has more to hold in their head than one who sees four identical entries. (A1) If the network is expected to grow unevenly, or to need small links like these, the extra complexity is worth it; if all four departments are likely to grow at the same rate, the simpler scheme is the better choice. (A1)

A useful check on any scheme is to write the blocks out in order and confirm that each one finishes exactly where the next one begins: $0$ to $63$, $64$ to $95$, $96$ to $111$, $112$ to $119$, $120$ to $123$ and $124$ to $127$. A scheme that leaves a gap or overlaps two blocks has placed a block on a boundary its own size does not divide, and the check takes seconds.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award the method mark for allocating in descending order of size. Accept any scheme that meets every requirement without overlap, provided each block starts on a boundary divisible by its own size; a scheme that places the /27 at .96 and the /28 at .64 is invalid because a /27 cannot start at .96 and should lose the address mark even though the sizes are right. Do not require the dotted-decimal subnet masks to be written out if the prefix lengths are given. (b) Accept $128$ and any figure from $120$ to $140$ for the equal-subnet comparison depending on how the candidate treats the two WAN links, which do not fit in that scheme at all; the observation that the WAN links cannot be accommodated is worth a mark on its own. (c) The AND operation must be named; 'it compares the first three octets' is not sufficient because it is false for these prefixes. (d) Credit only advantages and disadvantages that follow from the design rather than from networking in general. That adjacency check is worth teaching explicitly, because it catches the boundary error immediately and does not depend on remembering a rule.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A2.4 A security incident caused by a legitimate account with excessive privilege, where the control that would have prevented it conflicts with the requirement that clinical staff must not be blocked out of records in an emergency
syllabus_ref: A2.4 Network security, with A4.4 Ethical considerations and A3.2 Database design
title: A2.4 A security incident caused by a legitimate account with excessive privilege, where the control that would have prevented it conflicts with the requirement that clinical staff must not be blocked out of records in an emergency
q_html:
An incident at a three-site hospital trust

A hospital trust runs one patient-records system across three sites, with six clinical departments. Access is granted through roles. In the year of the incident the trust operated forty roles; the largest was TechSupport, held by thirty-four members of the IT service desk, which carried the union of every permission any of its holders had ever asked for, including read and write access to the full records of every department at every site. The trust's written policy is that no member of staff may be denied access to a record they need in order to treat a patient, and that any access outside a member's own department must be visible in the audit log within one working day.

The incident: a service-desk analyst whose employment was being terminated copied the records of $1{,}180$ patients from four departments he had never worked in and had never had a legitimate reason to view. The copy was made over eleven days using his own account and his own credentials during normal working hours. It was found two months later during a routine audit. Nothing he did required an exploit, a stolen password or a disabled control, and every copy operation was recorded in the log. The log had $4.2$ million entries for the year and was reviewed by one auditor two days a week.

The proposal on the table is to replace the forty roles with a strict role-based scheme in which a role exists for every combination of site, department and job function that the trust employs, and in which any access outside a member's own role is refused by the system and escalated to a manager. The trust employs six departments, five job functions and three sites. The trust's information-governance officer has objected, on the grounds that the strict scheme will create an administration burden the trust cannot carry and that a refused request in a clinical emergency is a patient-safety event.

The trust's board has asked for an analysis of the incident against the three components of the CIA triad, a design for a replacement role-based access-control scheme, the working arithmetic of the current audit coverage and the proposed quarterly permission review, and an evaluation of the information-governance officer's objection.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Analyse the incident against the three components of the CIA triad, identifying for each component whether it was breached and giving the specific evidence from the case that supports your answer.

    (Analyse)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Design a role-based access-control scheme for this trust, stating how many roles the strict scheme described in the case would need and explaining how your design resolves the conflict between the trust's policy on emergency access and the principle of least privilege.

    (Design)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    The auditor reviews $4.2$ million log entries a year in two days a week. Determine what fraction of the log is currently reviewed, and determine the review workload the proposed scheme implies if each role must be reviewed quarterly at fifteen minutes per role.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Evaluate the proposal against the information-governance officer's objection, and state which of the two requirements -- least privilege or unblocked clinical access -- your design sacrifices and why.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) *Confidentiality* was the component actually breached, and the breach was large and deliberate: $1{,}180$ patients' records were copied by someone who had no legitimate reason to see any of them. The evidence is the volume, the four departments outside his own and the eleven days over which he worked (A1).

*Integrity* was not breached on the evidence given. Every operation was a copy out of the system; the case records no modification, deletion or insertion of records, and none of the $1{,}180$ records is stated to have been altered. It is worth saying plainly that the absence of an integrity breach is a fact about this incident and not a property of the design -- the same account carried write access to the full records of every department, so integrity was equally exposed and was simply not attacked (A1).

*Availability* was not breached either. The systems remained available to the clinicians who needed them throughout, and nothing in the case suggests service loss. The relevant observation is that the compromise was found two months late, which is a failure of detection rather than of availability; the log contained the evidence from the first day (A1).

The interesting finding is that two of the three components were untouched and the third was breached completely, by a user whose permissions were only what the trust had given him. In a CIA-triple analysis of this incident the useful output is not the tally but the reason each answer comes out as it does.

(b) The strict scheme described in the case needs a role for every combination of site, department and job function:
$$3 \times 6 \times 5 = 90 \ \text{roles} \;\; (A1).$$
Against the forty roles in use now, that is a little over twice the number of roles and it is what the governance officer means by an administration burden -- part (c) puts a figure on it.

The design should keep least privilege as the default and treat emergency access as an explicitly-granted, self-expiring exception (M1). Concretely:

1. Roles are the union of department and job function, not the cross product with site. A ward nurse is a ward nurse at any of the three sites; the site is an attribute of the *record*, not of the person. That reduces the role count to $6 \times 5 = 30$ and leaves the site as a condition evaluated at request time (A1).
2. Emergency access is a break-glass grant, not a role. A clinician who needs a record outside their role requests it, states a reason code, and is given time-limited access -- an hour is long enough for a clinical decision -- with notification to the responsible manager and an entry in the log that is machine-flagged. The clinical requirement is met in seconds, and the exception is narrow, time-bound and attributable (A1).
3. The audit becomes targeted. What matters for detection is the small set of accesses outside a member's usual pattern, not the $4.2$ million entries. Flagging break-glass grants, out-of-own-department reads and reads at volume per user per day reduces the reviewer's queue to something a human can actually read (A1).

(c) The auditor works two days a week, which is $2 \times 52 = 104$ working days a year, or about $\dfrac{104}{5} = 20.8$ working weeks (M1). Reviewing $4.2$ million entries at, say, one entry per second would take
$$\frac{4{,}200{,}000}{3600 \times 7} = 166.7 \ \text{seven-hour days},$$
against the $104$ days available; so even at one entry per second the log cannot be read in the time the trust gives it, and the true coverage is a small fraction of a per cent (A1). The practical statement is that the log as configured is not a control at all: it is a record that exists so that a breach can be reconstructed afterwards, which is exactly how this incident was found.

The proposed scheme's review workload is a different quantity and it is small by comparison. Ninety roles reviewed quarterly at fifteen minutes each:
$$90 \times 15 = 1{,}350 \ \text{minutes} = 22.5 \ \text{hours per quarter},$$
or $7.5$ hours a month (A1). Under the reduced design of part (b), with thirty roles, the same review costs $30 \times 15 = 450$ minutes $= 7.5$ hours per quarter, a third of the strict scheme's burden. Note the direction of the comparison: the *permission review* is affordable under either scheme and the *log review* is not affordable under either, so the governance officer's objection is about the wrong quantity.

(d) The objection is half right. The administration burden of ninety roles is real but small in absolute terms -- $22.5$ hours a quarter is a fraction of one person's time -- and it is not the reason the strict scheme should be rejected. The patient-safety objection is the serious one, because a system that refuses a clinician access to a record in an emergency has converted a security control into a clinical hazard, and no audit finding justifies that (A1).

My design sacrifices something, and it is least privilege in the strict sense: a break-glass grant means that for a short period a member of staff holds access their role does not include. What is preserved is the part of least privilege that matters -- that the excess access is bounded in time, requires a stated reason, is attributable to a person and is reported rather than discovered (A1). The alternative, refusing the request, protects the principle absolutely and harms patients; the alternative of granting standing access to everyone who might ever need it, which is what the trust actually did, is what produced this incident. Sacrificing a strict reading of the principle in favour of an auditable exception is the trade the case is designed to force, and the mark is for saying which side of it the design comes down on and why.

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for each component with evidence. The marks are for the *evidence*, not the verdict: "confidentiality breached because 1,180 records were copied by someone with no reason to see them" scores, "confidentiality was breached" does not. A candidate who claims integrity or availability was breached must point to a modification or an outage in the case; the case contains neither and claiming one forfeits that component's mark.

(b) (A1) for $3 \times 6 \times 5 = 90$, (M1) for a design that separates the two requirements rather than trading one away, (A1) for the site-as-attribute reduction, (A1) for the break-glass mechanism with its time limit, reason code and notification, (A1) for the targeted audit. Full marks do not require all four design elements; a candidate who gives the role count, the site attribute and the break-glass mechanism has the substance. A design that answers "give everyone less access" without saying what happens in an emergency scores (A1) and (M1) only.

(c) (M1) for converting the auditor's time into days or weeks, (A1) for the conclusion that the log cannot be read at any realistic rate, (A1) for $22.5$ hours per quarter from the ninety roles. A candidate who computes $90 \times 15$ and stops has the third mark; the first two require the comparison. Accept $104$ days, $20.8$ weeks or a "small fraction of a per cent" as the statement of coverage.

(d) (A1) for separating the two objections and treating the clinical one as the serious one, (A1) for naming what the design gives up, (A1) for tracing a consequence of that choice -- what bounds the relaxation (its lifetime, its reason code, its reportability) or what fails clinically if the request is refused instead. A candidate who says "both requirements can be satisfied" without saying which is relaxed in the emergency case scores at most the first mark.

Forfeits: describing the incident as an external attack, which the case explicitly denies; proposing encryption as the primary control, which does nothing about an authorised user; proposing to remove the technical-support account, which leaves the support function unable to work. Condonation: role counts of $30$ or $90$ are both accepted in (b) provided the scheme described matches the number given.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A3.2 A relation that satisfies third normal form because the attribute on the right of the offending dependency is prime, and therefore fails Boyce-Codd normal form, so that no decomposition of it can be lossless, in Boyce-Codd normal form and dependency preserving at the same time
syllabus_ref: A3.2 Database design (functional dependencies, candidate keys, and normalisation to third normal form), with A3.1 Database fundamentals
title: A3.2 A relation that satisfies third normal form because the attribute on the right of the offending dependency is prime, and therefore fails Boyce-Codd normal form, so that no decomposition of it can be lossless, in Boyce-Codd normal form and dependency preserving at the same time
q_html:
A timetabling relation

A school keeps a single relation of the classes it runs. Each row records a student, a subject that the student is taking, and the teacher who takes that student for that subject. The relation is called Enrolment and has the attributes Student, Subject and Teacher. Two rules hold. First, a student is taught a given subject by exactly one teacher. Second, each teacher teaches exactly one subject, although a subject may be taught by more than one teacher. The table shows part of the relation. The school has found that when a teacher changes the subject they teach, many rows must be changed, and that it cannot record the fact that a teacher teaches a subject unless at least one student is taking that subject from that teacher.

The relation Enrolment has the attributes Student, Subject and Teacher, and the school has stated two rules. A student is taught a given subject by exactly one teacher, so Student together with Subject determines Teacher. Each teacher teaches exactly one subject, so Teacher determines Subject, although a subject may be taught by more than one teacher. The school has observed two problems in practice. When a teacher changes the subject they teach, many rows have to be changed together, and a change that touches only some of them would leave the relation contradicting its own rule. The school also cannot record that a teacher teaches a subject unless some student is taking that subject from that teacher, so a newly appointed teacher who has not yet been assigned a student cannot be entered at all. The head of computing has proposed splitting the relation into two relations, one over Student and Teacher and one over Teacher and Subject, and has asked whether that proposal solves the problems.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Determine every candidate key of the relation Enrolment, and justify each one by naming the attributes that it determines.

    (Determine)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Show that the relation satisfies third normal form but does not satisfy Boyce-Codd normal form, naming the functional dependency that makes the difference and explaining why it is tolerated by one normal form and not by the other.

    (Show that)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Determine whether the proposed decomposition into the relations (Student, Teacher) and (Teacher, Subject) is lossless and whether it preserves every functional dependency, justifying each answer.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Evaluate whether the school should adopt the proposed decomposition or leave the relation in third normal form, given the two problems the school has already observed.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The attribute set is {Student, Subject, Teacher}. The given dependencies are {Student, Subject} -> Teacher and Teacher -> Subject.

The pair {Student, Subject} determines Teacher by the first dependency, so its closure is the whole attribute set {Student, Subject, Teacher} and the pair is a superkey. Neither Student alone nor Subject alone determines anything else, so no proper subset of the pair is a superkey, and {Student, Subject} is a candidate key.

The pair {Student, Teacher} determines Subject by the second dependency, since Teacher alone determines Subject, so its closure is also the whole attribute set and the pair is a superkey. Neither Student alone nor Teacher alone determines the other, so {Student, Teacher} is a candidate key as well.

There are exactly two candidate keys, {Student, Subject} and {Student, Teacher}. The prime attributes, which are the attributes belonging to at least one candidate key, are therefore Student, Subject and Teacher: all three attributes of the relation are prime.

(b) Third normal form requires that for every functional dependency X -> A, either X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute. Take the first dependency, {Student, Subject} -> Teacher. The determinant {Student, Subject} is a candidate key and therefore a superkey, so this dependency satisfies the condition. Take the second, Teacher -> Subject. The determinant Teacher is not a superkey, because the closure of Teacher is {Teacher, Subject}, which does not contain Student. The dependent, Subject, is a prime attribute, since Subject belongs to the candidate key {Student, Subject}. The dependency therefore satisfies the condition through its second clause, and the relation is in third normal form.

Boyce-Codd normal form requires that for every functional dependency X -> A, X is a superkey, with no alternative clause for prime attributes. The dependency Teacher -> Subject fails this test, because Teacher is not a superkey. The relation is therefore not in Boyce-Codd normal form.

The difference between the two normal forms is exactly the clause that third normal form adds and Boyce-Codd normal form removes. Third normal form allows a determinant that is not a superkey provided the attribute it determines is part of some candidate key. That allowance exists because removing such a dependency can cost more than it saves, which is what part (c) shows. Here the dependent, Subject, is prime, so the allowance applies and the relation is in third normal form but not in Boyce-Codd normal form.

(c) The proposed decomposition replaces Enrolment with R1 over {Student, Teacher} and R2 over {Teacher, Subject}.

The decomposition is lossless. A binary decomposition is lossless when the common attribute set determines at least one of the two relations, that is, when the common attributes form a superkey of at least one of them. The common attribute here is Teacher, and Teacher determines Subject, so Teacher is a superkey of R2 over {Teacher, Subject}. The condition holds, so the join of R1 and R2 reproduces exactly the rows of Enrolment, with no spurious rows and no lost rows.

The decomposition is not dependency preserving. A decomposition preserves the dependencies when the union of the dependencies that hold within the separate relations implies every dependency of the original relation. R2 over {Teacher, Subject} carries Teacher -> Subject, so that dependency survives. R1 over {Student, Teacher} carries no non-trivial dependency at all, because neither Student alone nor Teacher alone determines the other in the original relation. The dependency {Student, Subject} -> Teacher has Student and Subject in different relations, since Student appears only in R1 and Subject only in R2, so it cannot be enforced by either relation and cannot be recovered by joining them. That dependency is lost.

The proposal therefore buys Boyce-Codd normal form and losslessness at the price of the dependency that made {Student, Subject} a key. Losing it means the database can no longer prevent a student from being recorded with two different teachers for the same subject, because no single relation in the schema holds enough information to detect it.

(d) The school faces a genuine choice, because no decomposition of this relation is lossless, in Boyce-Codd normal form and dependency preserving at the same time. The proposed decomposition and the original relation each give up one of the three.

Leaving the relation in third normal form keeps the dependency {Student, Subject} -> Teacher enforceable by the relation itself, so the database can still reject a row that gives one student two teachers for one subject. It keeps the update anomaly the school has observed, because Teacher -> Subject is a dependency between two attributes of the same relation, and changing a teacher's subject means changing every row in which that teacher appears. It also keeps the insertion anomaly, because a row is a class and a teacher with no students cannot be represented.

Adopting the decomposition removes both anomalies. R2 over {Teacher, Subject} holds one row per teacher, so a teacher's subject is recorded once and a newly appointed teacher can be entered before any student is assigned, which also removes the insertion anomaly. The cost is that the lost dependency has to be enforced outside the schema, by a constraint or a check in the application that verifies a student has only one teacher per subject.

The better choice is to adopt the decomposition, because both of the problems the school has actually observed are cured by it and the guarantee that is given up can be replaced by a single constraint that is easy to state and cheap to enforce. The anomalies are present today and cause work every time a teacher changes subject; the lost dependency is a guarantee the school can rebuild in one place. A school with a large and changing timetable will feel the anomalies far more often than it will be inconvenienced by the extra constraint. The judgement is a judgement, however, and an answer that keeps the relation in third normal form and argues that an enforceable dependency is worth more than the convenience of one-row updates is defensible, provided the trade is stated.

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark for each candidate key correctly identified with a closure argument, and one mark for stating that the prime attributes are all three of them. A candidate who identifies only {Student, Subject} and misses {Student, Teacher} has missed the dependency Teacher -> Subject and scores at most one mark.

(b) One mark for the statement that third normal form holds, one mark for the reason, that Subject is prime, one mark for the statement that Boyce-Codd normal form fails, and one mark for naming Teacher -> Subject as the offending dependency with the reason that Teacher is not a superkey. A candidate who says the relation fails both normal forms has not used the prime attribute and scores at most two marks.

(c) One mark for lossless with the reason that Teacher is a superkey of (Teacher, Subject), one mark for not dependency preserving, and one mark for naming the lost dependency as {Student, Subject} -> Teacher with the reason that its two attributes cannot lie in the same relation. An answer that claims the decomposition preserves all dependencies scores zero for this part.

(d) No mark for the choice itself; one mark for correctly describing what each option gives up, one mark for connecting the choice to the two anomalies the school has actually observed, and one mark for a reasoned recommendation with its cost stated. Either recommendation can earn full marks if the trade is stated accurately; a recommendation with no mention of the lost dependency cannot exceed two marks.

subject: CS HL
topic: Theme A: Concepts of computer science
subtopic: A1.4 Compilation against interpretation on a stated cost model, where the one-off compilation cost is the whole of the decision and the per-run comparison points the wrong way
syllabus_ref: A1.4 Translation (HL only), with B1.1 Approaches to computational thinking and B2.3 Programming constructs
title: A1.4 Compilation against interpretation on a stated cost model, where the one-off compilation cost is the whole of the decision and the per-run comparison points the wrong way
q_html:
A configuration language for a mail-order catalogue

A retailer maintains a small configuration language, catcfg, used to describe how a printed catalogue's pages are built from a product database. A script is about $12\,000$ tokens long, is stored as a text file, and is run once each weekday morning to generate that day's catalogue layout. When a price band changes, an editor edits the script by hand and the next morning's run uses the edited version. The engineering team is deciding between two ways of running it: an interpreter that reads the script and executes it directly on every run, and a compiler that translates the whole script into an intermediate form which is then executed. Measured on the retailer's server, the interpreter consumes $1.5\ \mu\mathrm{s}$ per token on each run, and the compiler consumes $60\ \mu\mathrm{s}$ per token once when it translates the script and $0.25\ \mu\mathrm{s}$ per token on each run of the translated form. For this question you may ignore the cost of starting either program and the cost of reading the file from disk.

The engineering team has asked for a recommendation on how to run catcfg, grounded in the costs given in the stimulus. Identify which stage of translation detects each of the three faulty fragments, explain one advantage the compiled form has for this particular workflow, determine when the two approaches cost the same across a sequence of runs, and comment on whether that figure should decide the choice.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Three faulty fragments of a catcfg script are given below. For each one, identify the stage of translation that detects it -- lexical analysis, syntax analysis or semantic analysis -- and justify your choice.
    (i) price + 1@5 (ii) if price > 100 then total = total + price with no closing keyword (iii) pagewidth = priceband * 2 where priceband is a text value and pagewidth is declared as an integer.

    (Identify)
  2. [2 marks](b)

    Explain one advantage that the compiled form has over the interpreted form for this particular workflow, referring to the number of times the script is run and to what changes between runs.

    (Explain)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Determine the total time in milliseconds taken by each of the two approaches for a single run, and determine the number of executions at which the two totals become equal. Show your working.

    (Determine)
  4. [2 marks](d)

    Comment on whether the equality you found in part (c) should decide the choice, referring to what the workflow does between executions.

    (Comment)
a_html:
(a)

(i) 1@5 is lexical: the tokeniser's rules define a number as a run of digits and @ is not a character that can appear in one, so the scanner fails to form a valid token before any grammar is considered (A1). The characters are individually fine; it is the sequence that no token can cover.

(ii) The missing closing keyword is syntax. Every token so far is valid -- if, an identifier, a relation, a number, the keyword then, an assignment -- and it is the arrangement of those tokens that the grammar rejects, because the rule for a conditional requires a terminator (A1). No meaning has been examined yet.

(iii) priceband * 2 with a text operand is semantic. The statement is grammatically well formed and every token is valid; what fails is the check that the types of the operands are compatible with the operator and with the declared type of the target (A1). This check needs the symbol table of declarations, which is why it cannot be done during scanning or parsing.

(b) The compiled form pays the translation cost once and then runs cheaply, and on this workflow the script is executed roughly $260$ times a year -- once each weekday -- against a small number of edits. The number of executions is large and the number of *different* versions is small, so the one-off cost is amortised over many runs (M1).

What changes between runs is normally nothing at all: the environmental data comes from the product database, not from the script. The edit that follows a price-band change is the exception, and it does invalidate the translated form; but even if the script were edited once a month, the translation would be repeated twelve times a year against two hundred and sixty executions (A1).

(c) One run of the interpreter:
$$12\,000\ \text{tokens} \times 1.5\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 18\,000\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 18\ \mathrm{ms} \;\; (A1).$$

One *first* run of the compiled route:
$$12\,000 \times 60\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 720\,000\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 720\ \mathrm{ms} \;\; (A1\text{ for the translation}) ,$$
and each subsequent run costs
$$12\,000 \times 0.25\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 3\,000\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 3\ \mathrm{ms} \;\; (A1).$$

Let $n$ be the number of executions. The interpreted total is $18n$ milliseconds and the compiled total is $720 + 3n$ milliseconds, both measured from the first run and including it. Setting them equal:
$$18n = 720 + 3n, \qquad 15n = 720, \qquad n = 48 \;\; (A1).$$
After $48$ executions both routes have consumed $864\ \mathrm{ms}$. Under the compiled route the script is executed about $260$ times a year, so the crossover is passed in the tenth week of the first year, and the compiled route is decisively cheaper thereafter: at $260$ executions the interpreted total is $4\,680\ \mathrm{ms}$ against $1\,500\ \mathrm{ms}$ for the compiled one, a saving of about $3.2$ seconds a year.

(d) The equality should not decide the choice on its own, because it is derived from a model whose central assumption is that the same script is executed many times unchanged (M1).

The workflow does edit the script: whenever a price band changes, the editor changes the file, and a compiler must then translate the whole thing again at a cost of $720\ \mathrm{ms}$. If the script were edited before every run, the compiled total for $n$ runs would be $n(720 + 3)$ milliseconds against $18n$ for the interpreter, and the compiler would never win. Between the two extremes the answer turns on the edit rate, which the stimulus does not fix. What can be said without that number is that the crossover of $48$ is the edit-free case and therefore the *most favourable* figure the compiler can claim; the real crossover is higher, by $48$ executions for every extra retranslation, and the decision should be taken on a measured edit rate rather than on the model alone (A1).

The model also ignores two things that favour the interpreter: the compiled intermediate form has to be stored and kept in step with its source, which is a real operational cost, and in this workflow the run takes place once a day, so a saving of sixteen milliseconds per run is not visible to anybody. If the only consideration were time, the case for compiling would rest on the tenth week of each year; if the consideration is engineering effort and the risk of a stale translated file, the interpreter may still be the better answer.

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for each of the three with a reason. The reason must refer to the stage's own job, not restate the error: "lexical because it is a character that cannot start a token" scores, "lexical because it is a typo" does not. A candidate who places (iii) at syntax has confused a grammar rule with a type rule and scores two of three.

(b) (M1) for using the ratio of executions to distinct versions, (A1) for connecting it to what changes between runs. A candidate who says "compiled code runs faster" without referring to the number of runs scores nothing: the mark is for the amortisation argument, which is the only thing that distinguishes the two approaches here.

(c) (A1) for $18\ \mathrm{ms}$, (A1) for $720\ \mathrm{ms}$ of translation, (A1) for $3\ \mathrm{ms}$ per subsequent run, (A1) for $n = 48$ with the working. A candidate who writes $18n = 720 + 3(n-1)$ obtains $n = 47.8$ and should be given the final mark if they state that $48$ executions is the first at which the compiled total is lower; the difference is whether the first run is counted in both totals, which it should be. A candidate who answers with the per-run ratio ("six times faster") forfeits the last mark; that is exactly the comparison the item is testing.

(d) (M1) for identifying the assumption of an unchanged script, (A1) for a consequence that changes the decision -- a higher crossover, or a crossover that does not exist if the edit rate is high enough. A candidate who says only "the script is edited sometimes" scores the first mark and not the second, because the mark requires the effect of the edit to be traced into the arithmetic.

Condonation: speeds may be quoted in microseconds throughout with the conversion to milliseconds made at the end; the arithmetic is identical. A candidate who states the crossover as "about fifty executions" scores the last mark in (c), provided the exact value is also shown. Forfeits: including the disk read or the process start-up in the totals, which the stem excludes; treating the $12\,000$ tokens as $12\,000$ lines, which changes the arithmetic by a factor the candidate cannot justify.

topic: Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving
subtopic: B3.2 Two independent classification axes modelled with inheritance, where the obvious hierarchy multiplies out and the correct design uses composition to keep the two axes separate
syllabus_ref: B3.2 Fundamentals of OOP for multiple classes (HL only), with B3.1 Fundamentals of OOP for a single class and B2.2 Data structures
title: B3.2 Two independent classification axes modelled with inheritance, where the obvious hierarchy multiplies out and the correct design uses composition to keep the two axes separate
q_html:
A media catalogue for a school library

A library system stores entries for its collection. Each entry has a format, which is one of four: Print, Audio, Video or Download. Each entry also has a genre, which is one of five: Fiction, Reference, Biography, Poetry or Periodical. Format and genre vary independently: the library holds every combination except Download with Periodical, which it has decided never to stock, so there are nineteen combinations in use out of a possible twenty. Every entry also has a title, an author or creator, a shelf location and a loan period.

Behaviour depends on both axes. A format dictates how a copy is lent (a print copy can be recalled, a download expires, an audio copy has a play count), and a genre dictates how the entry is catalogued and which subject headings apply. A later release will add a fifth format, Microform, and a sixth genre, Drama.

A junior developer has proposed a class hierarchy with one abstract class MediaEntry and a concrete subclass for each combination: PrintFiction, PrintReference, PrintBiography, and so on.

The library must decide whether to accept the junior developer's hierarchy. Identify the two axes of classification and the data and operations that belong to each, explain how many concrete classes the proposal contains in use and in full, design an alternative structure that keeps the axes separate, and justify a situation in which the multiplicative hierarchy would nevertheless be the better choice.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Identify the two axes of classification in this system and, for each, state one piece of data and one operation that depends on it rather than on the other axis.

    (Identify)
  2. [2 marks](b)

    Explain how many concrete classes the proposed hierarchy contains in use and how many it would contain if it covered every possible combination including the one the library has decided never to stock.

    (Explain)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Design an alternative class structure that keeps the two axes separate, state how many classes it contains, and state what it costs to add the proposed fifth format.

    (Design)
  4. [2 marks](d)

    Justify a situation in which the junior developer's multiplicative hierarchy would be the better choice despite the larger class count.

    (Justify)
a_html:
(a) The two axes are format ('Print', 'Audio', 'Video', 'Download') and genre ('Fiction', 'Reference', 'Biography', 'Poetry', 'Periodical') (A1).

A datum that depends on format rather than on genre: the media type stored with a copy, or a play count or an expiry date -- all of these are properties of how the thing is carried, and none of them changes when a biography is reclassified as reference (A1). An operation that depends on format: renew(), which behaves differently for a print copy that can be recalled and a download that expires. A datum that depends on genre: the list of subject headings, or the Dewey-class code. An operation that depends on genre: catalogue(), or suggestSimilar(), which works on subject matter and is indifferent to whether the item is a download or a video (A1).

The test in each case is whether a change on the *other* axis would force a change here. Reclassifying a novel as poetry changes the subject headings and changes nothing about how it is lent; converting the same title from print to audio changes how it is lent and changes nothing about its subject headings.

(b) In use the library holds every combination except 'Download' with 'Periodical', so the proposal needs
$$4 \times 5 - 1 = 19 \ \text{concrete classes} \;\; (A1).$$
It also needs at least one method to differ between them, or the subclasses are empty shells that exist only to carry a name.

Covering every combination gives
$$4 \times 5 = 20 \ \text{concrete classes} \;\; (A1),$$
one more than the number in use. The difference is worth noticing in the other direction: the proposal is already nineteen classes and the library intends to add a fifth format and a sixth genre, which takes the in-use count from nineteen to
$$5 \times 6 - 1 = 29,$$
an addition of ten classes for two changes to the specification.

(c) A design that keeps the axes apart uses two small hierarchies and lets each entry hold one of each:

  • a Format hierarchy with an abstract Format and four subclasses (Print, Audio, Video, Download), each implementing lend() and renew() (A1);
  • a Genre hierarchy with an abstract Genre and five subclasses (Fiction, Reference, Biography, Poetry, Periodical), each implementing headings() (A1);
  • a single MediaEntry class holding a title, a creator, a location, a loan period, one Format object and one Genre object, and delegating the format-specific and genre-specific operations to whichever objects it holds (A1).

The class count is $2$ abstract bases $+\ 4$ formats $+\ 5$ genres $+\ 1$ entry $= 12$ classes in total, of which the two abstract bases carry no instances and the concrete working classes number ten. The library's existing nineteen combinations are expressed as nineteen *objects* of MediaEntry, not as nineteen classes.

Adding Microform means writing one new subclass of Format and changing nothing else: the count of classes goes up by one, no MediaEntry code changes, and the combination of Microform with each of the five genres works immediately. Under the proposal the same change would add five classes, each of which would need its own lend() and renew() implementations even though they would be identical.

(d) The multiplicative hierarchy is the better choice when the two axes do not merely coexist but interact, that is when the behaviour of a combination is not the sum of what the two axes would do separately (A1).

A concrete case from this system: a DownloadPeriodical may be barred from the collection, and a PrintPeriodical must be lent with a shorter period than other print material. If a rule of that kind applies to one cell of the grid and to no other, then the cell has behaviour of its own, and the cleanest place for it is a subclass that exists to hold it. Composition would express the same thing with a conditional inside MediaEntry, and a conditional that tests the pair of axes is exactly a hard-coded combination in a different place (A1).

The general statement is worth giving: composition is preferred when the axes can be combined freely and their behaviour composes; inheritance is preferred when the combinations have their own behaviour. Here nineteen of the twenty cells behave as the composition of their row and column, so composition is right, and a candidate who says so and identifies the one cell that would justify the other design has understood the distinction rather than the rule of thumb.

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for naming both axes, (A1) for a format-dependent datum or operation, (A1) for a genre-dependent one. The two examples must be *different in kind* or the mark is not awarded twice for the same idea: a candidate who gives playCount for format and shelfLocation for genre scores the first two marks only if the shelf location is shown to be genre-independent, which it is not -- location is a property of neither axis and is a generic attribute. A candidate who gives headings() for genre and lend() for format scores all three.

(b) (A1) for nineteen, (A1) for twenty, with the reason for the difference stated or implied. A candidate who writes twenty twice has not read the exception and scores one mark.

(c) (A1) for the format hierarchy, (A1) for the genre hierarchy, (A1) for a single entry class that holds one of each. The class count is not itself marked in this part, but a candidate who produces two hierarchies and no entry class has not designed a structure that can hold the nineteen combinations and cannot score the third mark. Counting the classes as ten, twelve or "nine concrete plus one entry" is all accepted provided the arithmetic matches the structure described.

(d) (A1) for the general criterion -- the axes interact, or some cells have behaviour of their own -- (A1) for a specific example from this system. "When the combinations are genuinely different" without an example scores the first mark only.

Condonation: a candidate who uses an interface rather than an abstract class scores the same; so does one who makes Format and Genre enumerations with a strategy object per value, provided the two axes remain separate. Forfeits: proposing a single class with a format field and a genre field and a long if-else chain over both, which does express the two axes but puts all the behaviour in one class -- a candidate who explains that the behaviour is still separated by dispatching on the held objects scores full credit, and one who simply nests the conditionals does not.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 6.6 Decision trees and 6.7 Descriptive statistics
syllabus_ref: Unit 6: 6.6 Decision trees and 6.7 Descriptive statistics (the SL Toolkit). P2 Section B.
title: A mean that says grow and a spread that says do not
q_html:
Foxglove Bakery

Foxglove Bakery runs a single shop in a market town and is considering a second outlet. Two sites are available on the same high street: a small kiosk, which would cost EUR 40,000 to fit out, and a large cafe, which would cost EUR 120,000. Both would be financed by a bank loan at 6% a year, and the directors compare annual profit after interest.
