The directors have two sets of profit forecasts, before interest, for each option. If demand is high, the kiosk would make EUR 40,000 a year and the cafe EUR 120,000. If demand is low, the kiosk would still make EUR 10,000, but the cafe would lose EUR 60,000 a year.

The finance director has assumed a 0.6 probability of high demand, based on her reading of the local economy. The marketing director disagrees. She has collected the daily customer numbers from a trial stall that traded in the same high street, with the same opening hours, for twelve months. Her figures are in the table, and she defines a high-demand month as one in which the stall served more than 80 customers a day.

The directors of Foxglove Bakery must decide whether to open a kiosk or a cafe as the second outlet.

  1. [5 marks](a)

    Using the table, calculate the mean, the median and the range of daily customers, and comment on how well the mean represents a typical month.

    (Calculate)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Estimate the probability of a high-demand month from the trial data. Then calculate the expected annual profit after interest of each option using the finance director's probability and using your estimate.

    (Calculate)
  3. [6 marks](c)

    Evaluate which option Foxglove Bakery should choose. Justify your answer with reference to your decision tree and to the descriptive statistics.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The twelve monthly figures are 40, 45, 38, 42, 120, 130, 125, 44, 41, 118, 135 and 46, giving a total of 924 customers a day across the months. (M1)

Mean = 924/12 = 77 customers a day. (A1)

Ordered, the two middle values are 45 and 46, so the median = (45 + 46)/2 = 45.5 customers a day. (A1)

Range = 135 - 38 = 97 customers a day. (A1)

The mean is a poor summary of a typical month. It is 31.5 customers a day above the median, and no month was close to it: five months clustered near 42 and five near 125, with the remaining two between. The distribution is bimodal, not symmetrical, so the mean describes a month that never happened. (A1)

(b) High-demand months are those above 80 customers a day: months 5, 6, 7, 10 and 11, so five of twelve. The trial estimate of the probability of high demand is 5/12 = 0.417. (M1)(A1)

Using the finance director's 0.6: kiosk = 0.6 x 40,000 + 0.4 x 10,000 = EUR 28,000; cafe = 0.6 x 120,000 + 0.4 x (-60,000) = EUR 48,000. (M1)(A1)

Interest: kiosk loan 40,000 x 6% = EUR 2,400; cafe loan 120,000 x 6% = EUR 7,200. Net expected profit: kiosk EUR 25,600; cafe EUR 40,800. (A1)

Using the trial estimate of 5/12: kiosk = (5/12) x 40,000 + (7/12) x 10,000 = EUR 22,500; cafe = (5/12) x 120,000 + (7/12) x (-60,000) = EUR 15,000. After interest: kiosk EUR 20,100; cafe EUR 7,800. (A1)

The two probabilities therefore rank the options differently.

(c) Indicative evaluation. On the finance director's probability the decision is straightforward. The cafe's expected profit of EUR 40,800 is more than half as much again as the kiosk's EUR 25,600, and the upside, EUR 120,000 in a good year, is the kind of return that would justify the larger loan. A decision tree drawn on a 0.6 chance of high demand points clearly to the cafe.

The descriptive statistics undermine the probability the tree uses. The mean of 77 customers a day is not a typical month: it sits between two clusters, and the median of 45.5 is the better guide to what most months look like. Five of the twelve months were high-demand, so the empirical probability is 0.417, not 0.6. Rerun with 5/12, the ranking reverses: the kiosk earns EUR 20,100 against the cafe's EUR 7,800. The kiosk is also the more robust choice, because its worst case is a profit of EUR 10,000 while the cafe's is a loss of EUR 60,000, half the size of the whole investment.

The evaluation therefore turns on the probability, and the probability is the one thing the directors cannot observe. If the town's economy really does deliver high demand six years in ten, the cafe is right; if the trial stall is representative, the cafe destroys value in most years and the interest payment makes the bad case worse. The strongest answers note that a decision tree is only as good as its probabilities, that the trial was one stall in one year, and that opening the kiosk first keeps the option open. Credit any supported conclusion. (A1)(A1)(A1)(A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1)(A1) for the mean, (A1) for the median and (A1) for the range. The comment mark requires the candidate to notice that the mean is well above the median and that the data are bimodal; a candidate who says only that the mean is 77 forfeits it. Accept 45.5 for the median.

(b) Award (M1)(A1) for identifying the five high-demand months and the probability of 5/12; accept 0.42 or 41.7%. Award (M1)(A1) for the two expected profits on the 0.6 probability and (A1) for the interest and net profits; then (A1) for the two expected profits on 5/12 and their net values. Follow through on arithmetic slips, but a candidate who omits the interest in one option and not the other cannot reach the evaluation marks.

(c) The discriminating marks are for rerunning the expected values with the empirical probability and for noticing that the ranking reverses. A candidate who reports the mean of 77 and recommends the cafe cannot earn more than two marks. Credit a conclusion that chooses the cafe only if it is justified by evidence about the local economy rather than by the finance director's assumption. Do not credit answers about the cafe's menu or staffing.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 5.2 The output of a flow line is set by its slowest stage, so adding capacity anywhere else produces nothing, and the choice between buying capacity at the bottleneck and buying overtime at the bottleneck is a choice between a fixed cost and a variable one
syllabus_ref: Unit 5: 5.2 Operations methods (flow production and the capacity of a line of dependent stages), with 3.3 Costs and revenues and 5.1 The role of operations management
title: 5.2 The output of a flow line is set by its slowest stage, so adding capacity anywhere else produces nothing, and the choice between buying capacity at the bottleneck and buying overtime at the bottleneck is a choice between a fixed cost and a variable one
q_html:
A four-stage flow line

A manufacturer makes a single product on a flow line of four stages, in the order cutting, welding, assembly and finishing. Each stage is worked by one machine, and the product passes through all four stages in that order. Each machine is available for 2 400 minutes in a working week. The table gives the time each stage takes to process one unit. The machines are not shared, so a machine that is idle at one stage cannot be used to relieve a stage that is behind. Demand is steady at 600 units a week and the manufacturer is currently unable to meet it, which is costing sales.

The manufacturer's four-stage line has one machine at each stage, and each machine is available for 2 400 minutes a week. The times per unit are given in the table. Demand is steady at 600 units a week and the manufacturer cannot meet it, so it is losing sales that it could otherwise make. The operations manager has two proposals. The first is to buy a second welding machine at a cost of 85 000 dollars, which would halve the time the welding stage takes per unit, and which would be depreciated over five years. The second is to work overtime at whichever stage is limiting output, at an overtime rate of 36 dollars an hour, which is available whenever it is needed and can be stopped at any time. The operations manager has also considered buying a second assembly machine and has asked what difference that would make, since assembly takes four minutes a unit and is the stage the manager believed to be the problem.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the weekly capacity of each of the four stages, and state which stage has the smallest capacity.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Determine the maximum number of units the line can produce in a week at present, and the shortfall against the weekly demand of 600 units.

    (Determine)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Determine the effect on the line's weekly output of installing a second assembly machine, showing the capacity of every stage after the change.

    (Determine)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Determine the effect on the line's weekly output of installing a second welding machine, and explain why the two answers in (c) and (d) differ.

    (Determine)
  5. [3 marks](e)

    Evaluate whether the manufacturer should buy the welding machine or pay for overtime, using the weekly costs of each and considering the manufacturer's circumstances.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The weekly capacity of a stage is the minutes available divided by the minutes each unit takes at that stage. With 2 400 minutes available at every stage:

Cutting: 2 400 / 3.0 = 800 units a week.
Welding: 2 400 / 5.0 = 480 units a week.
Assembly: 2 400 / 4.0 = 600 units a week.
Finishing: 2 400 / 2.5 = 960 units a week.

The welding stage has the smallest capacity, at 480 units a week.

(b) A unit must pass through all four stages, so the line can produce no more units in a week than its slowest stage can pass. Welding is the slowest stage at 480 units a week, so the maximum weekly output is 480 units. Demand is 600 units a week, so the shortfall is 600 - 480 = 120 units a week, and those 120 units of sales are lost every week.

The other stages are not working at their limit. At an output of 480 units a week, cutting is using 480 x 3.0 = 1 440 of its 2 400 minutes, which is sixty per cent of its capacity; assembly is using 480 x 4.0 = 1 920 minutes, which is eighty per cent; and finishing is using 480 x 2.5 = 1 200 minutes, which is fifty per cent. Welding is using all 2 400 minutes, which is one hundred per cent.

(c) A second assembly machine halves the time assembly takes per unit, from 4.0 minutes to 2.0 minutes, so the capacity of assembly becomes 2 400 / 2.0 = 1 200 units a week. The capacities of the four stages are then 800 at cutting, 480 at welding, 1 200 at assembly and 960 at finishing.

The slowest stage is still welding, at 480 units a week, so the output of the line does not change. It remains 480 units a week and the shortfall remains 120 units a week. The money spent on the second assembly machine buys no additional output at all, because assembly was not limiting the line; the 120 extra units a week that the second machine could pass through cannot reach it, since welding cannot send them on.

(d) A second welding machine halves the time welding takes per unit, from 5.0 minutes to 2.5 minutes, so the capacity of welding becomes 2 400 / 2.5 = 960 units a week. The capacities of the four stages are then 800 at cutting, 960 at welding, 600 at assembly and 960 at finishing.

The slowest stage is now assembly, at 600 units a week, so the output of the line rises to 600 units a week, which is exactly the demand. The shortfall is closed. Welding is no longer the constraint and has spare capacity of 360 units a week; cutting is now the next tightest stage after assembly, at 800 units a week.

The two answers differ because output is governed by the slowest stage and by nothing else. In (c) the stage that was improved was not the slowest stage, so the line's output was still set by welding and did not move. In (d) the stage that was improved was the slowest stage, so the constraint moved to assembly and the output rose until it reached the new limit. Improving a stage that is not the constraint does not raise output; it only adds idle capacity to a stage that already had some. This is why the operations manager's belief that assembly was the problem was mistaken: assembly takes four minutes a unit, which is longer than cutting and longer than finishing, but welding takes five, and it is the longest time per unit that sets the pace.

(e) Either route closes the 120-unit shortfall, and the choice turns on the shape of the cost rather than on the size of it.

Overtime at the welding stage costs 36 dollars an hour. To make 120 extra units at 5.0 minutes a unit requires 120 x 5.0 = 600 minutes, which is 10 hours a week. At 36 dollars an hour that is 360 dollars a week, or 18 720 dollars a year. Overtime is a variable cost: it is paid only when the extra output is wanted, and it can be stopped in a week in which demand falls.

The welding machine costs 85 000 dollars depreciated over five years, which is 17 000 dollars a year, or about 326.92 dollars a week. It is a fixed cost: it is incurred every week whether the extra 120 units are made or not, and it commits the manufacturer for five years.

On cost alone the machine is slightly cheaper, at about 326.92 dollars a week against 360 dollars a week, which is about 2.72 dollars per extra unit against 3.00 dollars. Over five years the saving is roughly 1 720 dollars a year, about 8 600 dollars in total, which is small against an outlay of 85 000 dollars, and the payback on the machine is very long if it is justified only by the shortfall. The machine does have advantages beyond the weekly cost. It raises welding capacity to 960 units a week, so it leaves room for demand to grow to 600 units without any further spending, whereas overtime has to be paid for every extra unit and becomes more expensive if demand rises. It also removes the dependence on staff being willing to work overtime week after week, which is difficult to sustain and which raises the risk of absence and of poor quality on a tired shift.

Against that, the machine is a commitment. If demand falls, the 85 000 dollars is spent and the depreciation continues, while overtime can be cancelled. The manufacturer's position is not stated in the case, and the recommendation has to turn on it.

On the information given, the manufacturer should pay the overtime in the first instance, and revisit the machine if demand rises or proves to be permanent. The shortfall is 120 units a week, which is twenty per cent of demand, and the cost difference between the two routes is small enough, about 33 dollars a week, that it does not by itself justify an 85 000-dollar commitment. Overtime keeps the manufacturer flexible while it establishes whether the extra demand is durable, and it can be replaced by the machine once the demand has been shown to be permanent. The machine becomes the better choice as soon as demand is expected to rise towards the new welding capacity of 960 units, or as soon as the overtime proves difficult to staff; at that point the fixed cost is being spread over a larger output and the flexibility that overtime buys is no longer worth its price.

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark for the correct method, minutes available divided by minutes per unit, one mark for the four capacities 800, 480, 600 and 960, and one mark for identifying welding as the smallest. Follow-through is allowed from one arithmetic slip if the identification is consistent with the candidate's own figures.

(b) One mark for the output of 480 units a week, one mark for the shortfall of 120, and one mark for the reason, that output is limited by the slowest stage. A candidate who adds the stage capacities or takes the average has not understood the line and scores zero for this part.

(c) One mark for the new assembly capacity of 1 200 units a week, one mark for the statement that output is unchanged at 480 units a week, and one mark for the reason, that welding is still the slowest stage. An answer that reports a rise in output because assembly capacity has risen scores zero for this part, however correct the arithmetic.

(d) One mark for the new welding capacity of 960 units a week, one mark for the new output of 600 units a week with assembly as the new constraint, and one mark for the explanation that improving the constraint moves the constraint while improving any other stage changes nothing. Accept 600 units as the output because it matches demand; a candidate who states that assembly now limits the line at 600 units a week has the point even if the answer is expressed as 'up to 600'.

(e) No mark for naming a route. One mark for the correct weekly costs, overtime at 360 dollars a week or 18 720 dollars a year and the machine at about 326.92 dollars a week or 17 000 dollars a year, one mark for identifying the machine as the fixed cost and overtime as the variable one and drawing the consequence for flexibility, and one mark for a recommendation that states what would change it. A candidate who recommends the machine because it is cheaper per week takes two marks only if the flexibility argument is also addressed; the cost difference alone, at about 33 dollars a week, does not settle the question.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 5.4 / 3.8 / 6.3 Reshoring decision with landed cost and working capital effects
syllabus_ref: 5.4 (Location), 3.8 (Investment appraisal), 6.3 (STEEPLE analysis)
title: 5.4 / 3.8 / 6.3 Reshoring decision with landed cost and working capital effects
q_html:
Vantar

Vantar makes technical outdoor clothing. It currently manufactures 180 000 units a year in a low-wage economy and sells them online and through a small number of independent retailers at a retail price of €59. The lead time from placing an order to having stock available is 62 days, which forces Vantar to commit to its whole season's production before it knows what will sell. The operations director has costed a move to a domestic factory: the unit production cost would be higher, but the lead time would fall to 9 days, which would allow the company to make small reorders during the season. The finance director has calculated that the average value of finished-goods stock would fall from €2.10m to €0.72m, and the company's annual cost of holding stock is 18% of its value. Vantar's marketing manager estimates that 4% of units are currently sold at an average markdown of 35% because the wrong sizes were committed to. The cost data are given below.

Using the case study and the cost data, answer all three parts.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate the total landed cost per unit for the offshore option and for the domestic option, and calculate the increase in annual production cost if Vantar reshores.

    (Calculate)
  2. [6 marks](b)

    Evaluate whether Vantar should move production to the domestic factory, taking into account the effect on stockholding and the markdowns described in the case study.

    (Evaluate)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    To what extent do factors other than cost determine the right decision for Vantar? Refer to at least two external factors in your answer.

    (To what extent)
a_html:
(a) Offshore: $\text{CIF}=14.00+1.20=\unicode{8364}15.20$; the tariff is $12\%$ of $\unicode{8364}15.20=\unicode{8364}1.82$; adding $\unicode{8364}0.30$ handling gives a landed cost of $\unicode{8364}17.32$ per unit. (M1)(A1) Domestic: $21.50+0.25=\unicode{8364}21.75$ per unit. (A1) The increase is $\unicode{8364}4.43$ per unit, so across $180\,000$ units the annual production cost rises by $4.426\times180\,000=\unicode{8364}796\,680$, about $\unicode{8364}797\,000$. (M1)(A1)

(b) On unit cost alone the move looks wrong: $\unicode{8364}4.43$ is a $25.5\%$ increase in the cost of every item. (A1) Two effects work against that conclusion. First, average stock falls from $\unicode{8364}2.10$ m to $\unicode{8364}0.72$ m, a release of $\unicode{8364}1.38$ m, and at an annual holding cost of $18\%$ that saves $1.38\times0.18=\unicode{8364}248\,400$ a year. (M1)(A1) Second, a nine-day lead time allows reorders during the season rather than a single pre-commitment, so the markdown problem largely disappears: $4\%$ of $180\,000$ units is $7\,200$ units, currently discounted by $35\%$ of $\unicode{8364}59$, which is about $\unicode{8364}148\,700$ of lost margin a year. (M1)(A1) Together these recover about $\unicode{8364}397\,000$, so the net additional cost is roughly $\unicode{8364}797\,000-\unicode{8364}397\,000=\unicode{8364}400\,000$ a year, or $\unicode{8364}2.22$ per unit — about $3.8\%$ of the $\unicode{8364}59$ retail price, not the $25\%$ headline figure. (A1)

Against that residual cost must be set a shorter cash cycle, far less risk of being left with a season's worth of unwanted stock, and the marketing value of being able to promote a domestic supply chain. (A1) A balanced evaluation is that the move is financially defensible if Vantar can recover $\unicode{8364}2.22$ per unit through a modest price rise or through the higher full-price sell-through that reordering makes possible, and it is not defensible if the market will not bear any increase at all. The decisive question is therefore not cost but price elasticity, which the data do not give. (R1)

(c) To a considerable extent, because the cost gap after the stock and markdown effects is small enough that external factors can easily dominate it. (A1) *Political:* the offshore option depends on a $12\%$ tariff that a trade dispute could raise overnight; a five-point increase would add about $\unicode{8364}0.76$ to every unit and close a third of the remaining gap by itself, and this risk is entirely outside Vantar's control. (M1)(A1) *Environmental and ethical:* the company sells technical outdoor clothing to customers who are unusually attentive to provenance, and a domestic supply chain with a much shorter transport leg is a marketing asset that does not appear in the cost comparison at all; conversely, moving production offshore to a jurisdiction with weaker labour protections would carry reputational risk that could cost more than $\unicode{8364}400\,000$. (M1)(A1) *Economic:* a domestic factory removes exposure to freight-cost volatility and to currency movement on a $\unicode{8364}2.52$ m annual import bill. (A1) The counter-argument is that $\unicode{8364}400\,000$ a year is real money and that none of these factors is certain, so the decision remains finely balanced; but where the quantified gap is under four per cent of retail price, factors that cannot be quantified will usually decide it. (R1)

Markscheme notes

In (a) allow €17.30 to €17.35 and €21.70 to €21.80, and credit the tariff calculation shown even if the final addition is wrong. The annual increase should be about €797,000; allow €795,000 to €800,000. In (b) the evaluation mark requires the candidate to bring in both the stockholding saving and the markdown saving; an evaluation based on unit cost alone is capped at three, and one based on unit cost plus stockholding but not markdowns is capped at four. Allow a range of about €390,000 to €410,000 for the net cost, since candidates may treat the markdown recovery differently. In (c) any two of the STEEPLE factors are acceptable provided each is applied to Vantar specifically rather than described in the abstract; a generic list of external factors with no application earns at most two marks. In (b) a candidate may reasonably question the 18% holding cost or the assumption that the whole stock reduction is achieved in the first year; both are fair challenges and should be credited where they are explained, since the case study presents them as estimates rather than facts. Do not, however, credit a rejection of the markdown saving on the grounds that it is uncertain: it is quantified in the stimulus and is the whole reason the lead-time reduction has value.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 3.8 Unequal asset lives, a replacement chain, and a common cost that cancels only in part
syllabus_ref: 3.8 Investment appraisal (payback period, average rate of return, net present value); 3.2 Sources of finance
title: 3.8 Unequal asset lives, a replacement chain, and a common cost that cancels only in part
q_html:
Vastra Teknik must choose between two machines for a four-year contract. The contract will
generate net cash inflows of $\pounds 90{,}000$ a year for each of the four years whichever machine
is used, so the choice turns entirely on the costs. The company's cost of capital is $10\%$ per
year and all cash flows arise at the ends of years.

Machine P costs $\pounds 120{,}000$ and has a working life of two years, so it must be replaced
by an identical machine at the end of year 2 at the same price. It is decommissioned at the end of
year 2 and again at the end of year 4.

Machine Q costs $\pounds 230{,}000$ and has a working life of four years, so it is not replaced.
It is decommissioned once, at the end of year 4.

The decommissioning charge is $\pounds D$ on each occasion it arises, and is the same for both
machines. Assume initially that $D = 20{,}000$.

(a) Calculate the payback period for each machine. \tag{3}

(b) Calculate the net present value of each machine over the four years, and state which machine
should be chosen on this basis. \tag{5}

(c) The finance director argues that the decommissioning charge can be ignored, because both
machines incur it and it will therefore cancel. Explain, with a calculation, why this is only
partly correct. \tag{4}

(d) Determine the value of $D$ at which the recommendation would change. \tag{4}

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the payback period for each machine, taking no account for now of the replacement that machine P requires at the end of year 2.

    (Calculate)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Calculate the net present value of each machine over the four years, and state which machine should be chosen on this basis.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    The finance director argues that the decommissioning charge can be ignored, because both machines incur it. Justify, with a calculation, why this is only partly correct.

    (Justify)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Determine the value of $D$ at which the recommendation would change.

    (Determine)
a_html:
(a) Machine P returns $\pounds 90{,}000$ a year against an outlay of $\pounds 120{,}000$, so

$$\text{payback}_{P} = \frac{120{,}000}{90{,}000} = 1.33 \text{ years}$$

which is about one year and four months (A1). Machine Q recovers $\pounds 230{,}000$ at the same
rate, so

$$\text{payback}_{Q} = \frac{230{,}000}{90{,}000} = 2.56 \text{ years}$$

or roughly two years and seven months (A1). On payback, P is the clear winner, recovering its cost
more than a year sooner (A1). Note that payback ignores the second purchase P must make at the end
of year 2, which is one reason the ranking it produces should not be trusted on its own.

(b) The four-year annuity factor at $10\%$ is

$$\frac{1}{1.1} + \frac{1}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{1}{1.1^{3}} + \frac{1}{1.1^{4}} = 3.1699$$

so the present value of the inflows, identical for both machines, is

$$90{,}000 \times 3.1699 = \pounds 285{,}288 \tag{A1}$$

For P the outflows are the purchase at $t = 0$, the replacement at $t = 2$, and decommissioning at
$t = 2$ and $t = 4$ (M1):

$$120{,}000 + \frac{120{,}000}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{20{,}000}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{20{,}000}{1.1^{4}}
= 120{,}000 + 99{,}174 + 16{,}529 + 13{,}660 = \pounds 249{,}363 \tag{A1}$$

For Q the outflows are the single purchase at $t = 0$ and decommissioning at $t = 4$ (M1):

$$230{,}000 + \frac{20{,}000}{1.1^{4}} = 230{,}000 + 13{,}660 = \pounds 243{,}660 \tag{A1}$$

Hence

$$\text{NPV}_{P} = 285{,}288 - 249{,}363 = \pounds 35{,}925, \qquad
\text{NPV}_{Q} = 285{,}288 - 243{,}660 = \pounds 41{,}628 \tag{A1}$$

Both are positive, so both are worth undertaking; on net present value Q should be chosen, by
$\pounds 5{,}702$ (A1). This reverses the payback ranking in (a), and it also reverses the average
rate of return, which favours P at $16.7\%$ against $12.0\%$ for Q precisely because P is measured
against a much smaller capital base.

(c) The director is right about one of the two payments and wrong about the other. Both machines
pay $D$ at the end of year 4, and that payment is multiplied by the same discount factor
$\frac{1}{1.1^{4}}$ in both columns, so it is common and does cancel (A1). Machine P, however, also
pays $D$ at the end of year 2, and Q pays nothing at that date; this payment has no counterpart to
cancel against (A1). Its present value is

$$\frac{20{,}000}{1.1^{2}} = \pounds 16{,}529 \tag{A1}$$

so the decommissioning charge contributes $\pounds 16{,}529$ to the difference between the two
machines — not zero, and not the $\pounds 33{,}058$ that a candidate who doubled it would report. The
claim is therefore only partly correct: the charge is irrelevant to the comparison in year 4 and
decisive in year 2 (A1).

The practical consequence is that the charge is not a detail. Without it the two machines would
differ by

$$(120{,}000 + 99{,}174) - 230{,}000 = -\pounds 10{,}826$$

in P's favour, and P would be chosen. It is the year-2 payment alone, worth $\pounds 16{,}529$, that
overturns a gap of $\pounds 10{,}826$ and turns the decision round.

(d) Let the decommissioning charge be $D$. The year-4 payments cancel as before, so the difference
between the present values of the two cost streams is

$$\left(120{,}000 + \frac{120{,}000}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{D}{1.1^{2}} + \frac{D}{1.1^{4}}\right)
- \left(230{,}000 + \frac{D}{1.1^{4}}\right) = -10{,}826 + \frac{D}{1.1^{2}} \tag{M1}$$

where the two $\frac{D}{1.1^{4}}$ terms have been cancelled (A1). Q is preferred while this is
positive and P while it is negative, so the recommendation changes where

$$-10{,}826 + \frac{D}{1.21} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad D = 10{,}826 \times 1.21
= \pounds 13{,}100 \tag{A1}$$

At $D = 13{,}100$ the two machines are exactly equivalent, and the firm is indifferent (A1). Since
the actual charge of $\pounds 20{,}000$ exceeds $\pounds 13{,}100$, Q is confirmed as the better
choice — but the margin is $\pounds 5{,}702$, and a decommissioning quote that came in under
$\pounds 13{,}100$ would switch the decision to P.

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark for each payback figure, one for the comparison. Accept 1.3 and 2.6 years or the equivalent in months. Allow follow-through to (b) from a payback error. (b) One mark for the present value of the inflows, one for identifying the four outflow terms for P, one for the P total, one for the Q total, one for the two NPVs and the recommendation. Do not award the recommendation mark without both NPVs. Condone rounding to the nearest pound throughout; the exact totals are 249,362.75 and 243,660.27. A candidate who omits the replacement purchase should lose the term mark but may still earn the method mark for discounting. (c) One mark for saying the year-4 payment cancels, one for saying the year-2 payment does not, one for the figure 16,529, one for the conclusion that the claim is partly right. Credit the figure even if the candidate describes it as 'the extra cost of P'. (d) One mark for setting up the difference with the year-4 terms cancelled, one for the equation, one for D = 13,100, one for stating which machine wins on either side of it. A candidate who cancels both D terms gets -10,826 and should be held at the first mark: the point of the part is precisely that the cancellation is only partial.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 5.5 Break-even with a stepped fixed cost: two break-even points and a region of loss above the first
syllabus_ref: 5.5 Break-even analysis (contribution, break-even output, margin of safety, profit targets); 3.3 Costs and revenues
title: 5.5 Break-even with a stepped fixed cost: two break-even points and a region of loss above the first
q_html:
Kestrel Assembly makes a single product which it sells for $\pounds 14$. Variable cost is
$\pounds 6$ per unit.

Fixed costs are $\pounds 60{,}000$ a year for output up to and including $8{,}000$ units. Above
$8{,}000$ units a second shift is required, and fixed costs rise to $\pounds 85{,}000$ a year. The
step applies to the whole year's output, not only to the units above $8{,}000$, and there is no
change in selling price or variable cost.

(a) Calculate the break-even output on the assumption that fixed costs remain at
$\pounds 60{,}000$. \tag{3}

(b) Show that profit at an output of $8{,}000$ units is $\pounds 4{,}000$, while profit at an output
of $8{,}001$ units is $-\pounds 20{,}992$. \tag{5}

(c) Determine the output at which the business breaks even for the second time. \tag{4}

(d) Evaluate whether the business should plan an output of $10{,}000$ units, supporting your
answer with a calculation of the minimum selling price required. \tag{4}

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the break-even output on the assumption that fixed costs remain at $60{,}000$.

    (Calculate)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Show that profit at an output of $8{,}000$ units is $4{,}000$, while profit at an output of $8{,}001$ units is $-20{,}992$.

    (Show that)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Determine the output at which the business breaks even for the second time.

    (Determine)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Evaluate whether the business should plan an output of $10{,}000$ units, supporting your answer with a calculation of the minimum selling price required.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Contribution per unit is

$$\pounds 14 - \pounds 6 = \pounds 8 \tag{A1}$$

and break-even output is fixed cost divided by contribution per unit (M1):

$$\frac{60{,}000}{8} = 7{,}500 \text{ units} \tag{A1}$$

This lies below $8{,}000$ units, so the $\pounds 60{,}000$ figure is the right one to use and the
answer is consistent.

(b) At $8{,}000$ units the higher fixed cost has not yet been triggered, so

$$\text{profit} = 8 \times 8{,}000 - 60{,}000 = 64{,}000 - 60{,}000 = \pounds 4{,}000 \tag{M1A1}$$

At $8{,}001$ units the step applies to the whole year's output, so fixed costs are
$\pounds 85{,}000$ and not $\pounds 60{,}000$ (M1):

$$\text{profit} = 8 \times 8{,}001 - 85{,}000 = 64{,}008 - 85{,}000 = -\pounds 20{,}992 \tag{A1}$$

The two figures differ by $\pounds 24{,}992$ even though output has risen by a single unit (A1). Of
that, $\pounds 8$ is the contribution earned by the extra unit and $\pounds 25{,}000$ is the step in
fixed cost, so almost the entire movement is the step and not the unit. A profit-and-loss account
drawn up for any output from $8{,}001$ units upwards must therefore use $\pounds 85{,}000$, and the
$7{,}500$-unit figure from (a) tells the business nothing about that region.

(c) In the upper band, fixed costs are $\pounds 85{,}000$ and contribution per unit is unchanged at
$\pounds 8$ (M1):

$$\frac{85{,}000}{8} = 10{,}625 \text{ units} \tag{A1}$$

At $10{,}625$ units contribution is $8 \times 10{,}625 = \pounds 85{,}000$, which exactly covers the
higher fixed cost, so profit is zero (A1). Because $10{,}625 > 8{,}000$ the answer lies inside the
band to which it applies and is self-consistent, exactly as in (a) (A1).

The business therefore breaks even twice, at $7{,}500$ units and again at $10{,}625$ units, and
makes a loss at every output in between, with the single worst point being $8{,}001$ units. Any
output from $10{,}626$ units upward is profitable. The margin of safety at a planned output of
$12{,}000$ units is $12{,}000 - 10{,}625 = 1{,}375$ units, or $11.5\%$ — measured against the second
break-even point, not the first, which would give a meaningless $37.5\%$.

(d) At $10{,}000$ units the business is in the upper band, so fixed costs are $\pounds 85{,}000$
(M1). Let the selling price be $p$; contribution per unit is $p - 6$ (M1). Break-even requires

$$10{,}000(p - 6) = 85{,}000 \tag{A1}$$

so

$$p = \frac{85{,}000}{10{,}000} + 6 = 8.50 + 6 = \pounds 14.50 \tag{A1}$$

The current price of $\pounds 14.00$ gives a contribution of $\pounds 80{,}000$ against fixed costs
of $\pounds 85{,}000$ and a loss of $\pounds 5{,}000$, so the required increase is $\pounds 0.50$,
or $3.6\%$. Two cautions are worth recording. The answer is the break-even price at this output, not
a recommended price: at $\pounds 14.50$ the business makes exactly nothing on $10{,}000$ units, and a
price below $\pounds 14.50$ loses money. And the answer is specific to $10{,}000$ units, because the
$\pounds 85{,}000$ is spread over whatever volume is actually produced; at $12{,}000$ units the
break-even price would be only $\pounds 13.08$.

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark for the contribution, one for dividing fixed cost by contribution, one for the figure 7,500. Award the final mark only if the candidate states or implies that 7,500 is below 8,000 and therefore consistent. (b) One mark for using 60,000 at 8,000 units, one for the 4,000, one for switching to 85,000 at 8,001 units, one for the -20,992, one for noting that the whole step and not just the extra unit drives the change. A candidate who applies 85,000 to only the units above 8,000 gets 3,992 and should lose the third and fourth marks. (c) One mark for using 85,000, one for dividing by 8, one for 10,625, one for checking that the answer lies in the band to which it applies. Allow 10,625 or 10,626; do not allow 7,500 as the only answer. (d) One mark for using 85,000 rather than 60,000, one for setting up the equation, one for 14.50, one for the interpretation. Accept a correctly argued answer in pence. Follow-through applies throughout: a candidate who misreads the step but is otherwise consistent should not be penalised twice.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 2.1 Labour turnover as a weighted aggregate: recovering a missing department and targeting the right one
syllabus_ref: 2.1 Introduction to human resource management (workforce planning, labour turnover, absenteeism); 6.7 Descriptive statistics
title: 2.1 Labour turnover as a weighted aggregate: recovering a missing department and targeting the right one
q_html:
Haldane Logistics employs $250$ staff in three departments. The workforce plan records
the number of staff who left during the year, but the entry for department B has been lost.

| Department | Number employed | Number leaving during the year |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 120 | 9 |
| B | 80 | not recorded |
| C | 50 | 11 |

The company's overall labour turnover for the year is known to have been $14.4\%$. Each leaver
costs the business $\pounds 3{,}500$ to replace, covering recruitment, training and lost output.

Labour turnover is calculated as

$$\text{labour turnover} = \frac{\text{number of staff leaving during the year}}
{\text{number of staff employed}} \times 100.$$

(a) Calculate the number of staff who left department B during the year. \tag{3}

(b) Calculate the labour turnover rate for each department and confirm the overall rate of
$14.4\%$. \tag{5}

(c) Show that the overall rate is not the average of the three departmental rates, and explain why
the difference arises. \tag{4}

(d) The human resources director proposes an overall target of $10\%$ and must choose between two
interventions: reducing department A's turnover to $5\%$, or reducing department C's turnover to
$10\%$. Evaluate which should be prioritised. \tag{4}

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the number of staff who left department B during the year.

    (Calculate)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Calculate the labour turnover rate for each department and confirm the overall rate of $14.4$ per cent.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Show that the overall rate is not the average of the three departmental rates, and explain why the difference arises.

    (Show that)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    The human resources director proposes an overall target of $10$ per cent and must choose between reducing department A turnover to $5$ per cent and reducing department C turnover to $10$ per cent. Evaluate which should be prioritised.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Overall turnover of $14.4\%$ on $250$ staff gives a total of

$$0.144 \times 250 = 36 \text{ leavers} \tag{M1}$$

of which $9$ came from A and $11$ from C, so department B accounts for (M1)

$$36 - 9 - 11 = 16 \text{ leavers} \tag{A1}$$

(b) Applying the formula to each department in turn (M1):

$$\text{A}: \frac{9}{120} \times 100 = 7.5\%, \qquad
\text{B}: \frac{16}{80} \times 100 = 20.0\%, \qquad
\text{C}: \frac{11}{50} \times 100 = 22.0\% \tag{A1A1A1}$$

The overall rate is the total leaving divided by the total employed, not the average of the three
percentages:

$$\frac{9 + 16 + 11}{120 + 80 + 50} \times 100 = \frac{36}{250} \times 100 = 14.4\% \tag{M1A1}$$

which confirms the figure given.

(c) The simple average of the three departmental rates is

$$\frac{7.5 + 20.0 + 22.0}{3} = \frac{49.5}{3} = 16.5\% \tag{M1A1}$$

against a true overall rate of $14.4\%$, so the average overstates turnover by $2.1$ percentage
points (A1). The reason is that the departments are not the same size. The average gives each
department's rate a weight of one third, but department A actually employs $48\%$ of the workforce
and department C only $20\%$ (A1). The overall rate is a weighted mean in which each department's
rate is weighted by its headcount:

$$\frac{120(7.5) + 80(20.0) + 50(22.0)}{250}
= \frac{900 + 1{,}600 + 1{,}100}{250} = \frac{3{,}600}{250} = 14.4\%$$

The $7.5\%$ earned by the largest department pulls the figure down more than the $22\%$ earned by
the smallest pulls it up, which is exactly the effect the unweighted average discards.

(d) Reducing department A to $5\%$ means $0.05 \times 120 = 6$ leavers, a saving of $3$ (M1). Total
leavers fall to $33$ and the overall rate becomes

$$\frac{33}{250} \times 100 = 13.2\% \tag{A1}$$

an improvement of $1.2$ percentage points, at a saving of $3 \times 3{,}500 = \pounds 10{,}500$.

Reducing department C to $10\%$ means $0.10 \times 50 = 5$ leavers, a saving of $6$ (M1). Total
leavers fall to $30$ and the overall rate becomes

$$\frac{30}{250} \times 100 = 12.0\% \tag{A1}$$

an improvement of $2.4$ percentage points, at a saving of $6 \times 3{,}500 = \pounds 21{,}000$.

Department C should be prioritised. It delivers twice the reduction in the overall rate and twice
the cost saving, from $20\%$ of the workforce rather than $48\%$ (A1). The reason is that the
improvement depends on two things multiplied together — the size of the department and the size of
the cut — and department C's cut is $12$ percentage points against department A's $2.5$.

Two qualifications belong in a full answer. Neither intervention reaches the $10\%$ target on its
own: both together give $12.0\%$, and hitting $10\%$ would require $25$ leavers in total, so a
further five must come from somewhere. And the arithmetic is silent on why people leave. Department
C's $22\%$ may reflect working conditions, pay or management, and if the underlying cause is not
addressed the reduction may prove temporary; conversely, if department A's low turnover reflects a
genuinely well-managed operation, cutting it further may be the cheapest of all. The numbers say
where the leverage is, not what to do about it (A1).

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark for converting 14.4% of 250 to 36 leavers, one for subtracting the known leavers, one for the figure 16. (b) One mark for applying the formula, one for each of the three departmental rates, one for dividing total leavers by total employed. Do not award a rate calculated as an average of the others. Accept rates to one decimal place. (c) One mark for the average of 16.5%, one for the comparison with 14.4%, one for explaining that the departments differ in size, one for the weighted-mean calculation or an equivalent explanation in words. A candidate who says only 'the average is wrong' without saying why should be held at two marks. (d) One mark for the 3 leavers saved in A, one for 13.2%, one for the 6 leavers saved in C, one for 12.0%. The evaluation mark is awarded for a supported choice of C; allow A only if a cost or feasibility argument is given. Credit the 10,500 and 21,000 figures even if the candidate backs the other option. Follow-through: a candidate who finds 16 in (a) by a different route should not be penalised again in (b), provided the method is consistent.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 3.5 Two transactions that move the liquidity ratios in opposite directions, and the cancellation inside the acid test
syllabus_ref: 3.5 Profitability and liquidity ratio analysis (gross, operating and net profit margins, ROCE, current ratio, acid test); 3.4 Final accounts
title: 3.5 Two transactions that move the liquidity ratios in opposite directions, and the cancellation inside the acid test
q_html:
Marlowe Supplies: extract from the final accounts for the year ended 31 March

The income statement for the year shows revenue of $\pounds 480{,}000$ and cost of goods sold of $\pounds 300{,}000$. Operating expenses were $\pounds 120{,}000$, interest payable was $\pounds 12{,}000$ and tax was $\pounds 9{,}600$.

The statement of financial position at the year end is summarised below. All figures are in pounds, and there are no other current assets and no other current liabilities.

Marlowe Supplies is a single-product wholesaler. The figures above are taken from its final accounts for the year just ended. Before those figures are finalised the business is considering two transactions: paying a supplier $\pounds 10{,}000$ in cash, and then buying $\pounds 30{,}000$ of inventory on credit.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the gross profit margin, the operating profit margin and the net profit margin.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the return on capital employed, stating which figure you have used as the numerator and which as the denominator.

    (Calculate)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Calculate the current ratio and the acid test ratio at the position shown.

    (Calculate)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    The business pays a supplier $\pounds 10{,}000$ in cash. Show that both the current ratio and the acid test ratio rise, and explain why a payment that reduces current assets and current liabilities by the same amount improves both ratios.

    (Show that)
  5. [4 marks](e)

    The business then buys $\pounds 30{,}000$ of inventory on credit. Show that the acid test ratio falls to 0.81, and evaluate whether the two transactions together leave Marlowe Supplies in a stronger or a weaker liquidity position than it began in.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Gross profit is revenue less cost of goods sold, so (M1)

$$\pounds 480{,}000 - \pounds 300{,}000 = \pounds 180{,}000 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{180{,}000}{480{,}000} = 37.5\% \tag{A1}$$

Operating profit deducts the operating expenses: $\pounds 180{,}000 - \pounds 120{,}000 = \pounds 60{,}000$, so the operating profit margin is $60{,}000/480{,}000 = 12.5\%$ (A1).

Net profit also deducts interest and tax: $\pounds 60{,}000 - \pounds 12{,}000 - \pounds 9{,}600 = \pounds 38{,}400$, so the net profit margin is $38{,}400/480{,}000 = 8.0\%$ (A1).

The three margins fall by design: each one deducts a further layer of cost, so the sequence $37.5\%$, $12.5\%$, $8.0\%$ is a description of where the revenue goes. The largest single deduction is the $\pounds 120{,}000$ of operating expenses, which takes 25 percentage points of revenue and is the reason the gross margin is three times the operating margin.

(b) Capital employed is the long-term money in the business, which here is equity plus non-current liabilities (M1):

$$\pounds 200{,}000 + \pounds 100{,}000 = \pounds 300{,}000$$

Return on capital employed is operating profit divided by capital employed (M1):

$$\frac{60{,}000}{300{,}000} = 20.0\% \tag{A1}$$

The numerator must be operating profit, not net profit. Using net profit would give $38{,}400/300{,}000 = 12.8\%$, which understates the return on the assets because it charges the capital employed with interest that has already been deducted in arriving at net profit. Using equity alone as the denominator would give $60{,}000/200{,}000 = 30.0\%$, which overstates it by leaving the non-current liabilities out of the capital they helped to fund.

(c) Current assets are inventory, receivables and cash (M1):

$$\pounds 45{,}000 + \pounds 60{,}000 + \pounds 15{,}000 = \pounds 120{,}000$$

The current ratio is current assets over current liabilities (A1):

$$\frac{120{,}000}{60{,}000} = 2.00$$

The acid test removes inventory from the numerator, because inventory is the current asset least likely to convert to cash at its book value (A1):

$$\frac{120{,}000 - 45{,}000}{60{,}000} = \frac{75{,}000}{60{,}000} = 1.25$$

(d) Paying $\pounds 10{,}000$ in cash reduces cash to $\pounds 5{,}000$, so current assets become $\pounds 110{,}000$ and current liabilities become $\pounds 50{,}000$ (M1).

$$\text{current ratio} = \frac{110{,}000}{50{,}000} = 2.20 \qquad \text{acid test} = \frac{110{,}000 - 45{,}000}{50{,}000} = \frac{65{,}000}{50{,}000} = 1.30 \tag{A1}$$

Both ratios rise, from 2.00 to 2.20 and from 1.25 to 1.30, even though the business is now smaller by $\pounds 10{,}000$ of cash (A1).

The reason is that the same amount leaves the top and the bottom of the fraction. Writing the current ratio as $a/b$ with $a > b$, the new ratio is $(a-x)/(b-x)$, and

$$\frac{a-x}{b-x} > \frac{a}{b} \iff b(a-x) > a(b-x) \iff ab - bx > ab - ax \iff a > b$$

so the ratio rises whenever the transaction removes equal amounts from both and the ratio was above one. The size of the payment does not matter, and neither does the fact that it is a payment: any transaction that reduces current assets and current liabilities by the same amount has this effect. The same algebra run in reverse shows that adding equal amounts to both *lowers* a ratio above one, which is what part (e) does.

(e) Buying $\pounds 30{,}000$ of inventory on credit raises inventory to $\pounds 75{,}000$ and current liabilities to $\pounds 80{,}000$, so current assets become $\pounds 140{,}000$ (M1).

$$\text{current ratio} = \frac{140{,}000}{80{,}000} = 1.75 \tag{A1}$$

The acid test numerator is unchanged, because the $\pounds 30{,}000$ added to inventory is subtracted again (M1):

$$\frac{140{,}000 - 75{,}000}{80{,}000} = \frac{65{,}000}{80{,}000} = 0.8125 \approx 0.81 \tag{A1}$$

The two transactions together have moved the current ratio from 2.00 to 1.75 and the acid test from 1.25 to 0.81, so on balance the liquidity position is weaker, not stronger (A1).

The acid test is the ratio that should be read here, and the current ratio is the one that flatters. At 1.75 the current ratio still looks comfortable, and it has fallen by less than the acid test because inventory is doing the work: inventory is now $\pounds 75{,}000$ of $\pounds 140{,}000$ of current assets, so more than half of what the business counts as liquid is stock that has to be sold before it becomes cash. The acid test has crossed below 1.00, which means the business cannot settle its current liabilities from the assets it already holds in near-cash form. It would have to sell inventory, and selling inventory is what generates the receivables and cash in the first place, so the position is circular rather than merely tight.

The evaluation is not one-sided, however. The $\pounds 30{,}000$ of inventory was bought to be sold, and if it turns over as the existing stock does it will convert into receivables and then cash within the working capital cycle, restoring the acid test without any new financing. The $\pounds 10{,}000$ paid to the supplier also released credit and may have earned a settlement discount. So the transactions weaken the *reported* liquidity position while leaving the *underlying* trading position intact, and the honest conclusion is that the ratios have moved in a way the business should monitor rather than a way that shows it is in difficulty. What the figures cannot settle is how quickly the new inventory will turn over, and that is the question a lender would ask next.

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark each for 37.5%, 12.5% and 8.0%, with the working shown for at least one. Award the marks for the three percentages even if the candidate does not comment on the pattern; the comment is offered in the answer and is not required.

(b) One mark for capital employed of 300,000, one for the ROCE of 20.0%, and one for using operating profit rather than net profit in the numerator. A candidate who uses net profit and obtains 12.8% should be awarded the first mark only, and the same applies to a candidate who uses equity alone and obtains 30.0%, because in both cases the denominator or the numerator has been chosen wrongly rather than miscalculated.

(c) One mark for current assets of 120,000, one for 2.00, one for 1.25 with inventory removed from the numerator. A candidate who divides inventory by current liabilities, or who includes inventory in the acid test, scores the first mark only.

(d) One mark for the revised figures, one for both ratios and the direction of change, one for the explanation that equal amounts leave the top and bottom of a fraction above one. The explanation mark requires the condition that the ratio exceeds one; a candidate who says "paying a debt always improves liquidity" has stated a rule that is false for a ratio below one and earns no marks for the explanation.

(e) One mark for the revised current assets and liabilities, one for 1.75, one for the observation that the acid test numerator is unchanged, one for 0.81. The evaluation mark is awarded for a conclusion that distinguishes the reported ratio movement from the underlying trading position; a bare "liquidity is worse because the acid test fell" scores 0 for the evaluation, because it does not engage with the fact that the inventory was bought to be sold.

Forfeits: treating the acid test numerator as unchanged in part (d), which happens if the candidate applies the cancellation rule to the wrong transaction and obtains 1.25 again; reporting the acid test as 0.83 by adding the inventory to current assets without adjusting the denominator. Condonation: a candidate who writes the ratios as fractions rather than decimals, or who rounds 0.8125 to 0.81 or 0.813, should be given full credit.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 5.5 A break-even output above the capacity ceiling: a negative margin of safety and the three single levers that would close the gap
syllabus_ref: 5.5 Break-even analysis (contribution, break-even output, margin of safety, target profit); 3.3 Costs and revenues
title: 5.5 A break-even output above the capacity ceiling: a negative margin of safety and the three single levers that would close the gap
q_html:
Ridgeway Ceramics makes a single product on one kiln line. The selling price is $\pounds 40$ per unit and the variable cost is $\pounds 24$ per unit. Annual fixed costs are $\pounds 200{,}000$. The kiln line can produce at most $10{,}000$ units in a year, and there is no way to add a second line within the year.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the contribution per unit and the break-even output.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Determine the margin of safety in units and as a percentage of capacity, and explain what a negative margin of safety means for this business.

    (Determine)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Show that the best result Ridgeway Ceramics can achieve in a year is a loss of $\pounds 40{,}000$.

    (Show that)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Determine the value of the selling price at which the business would exactly break even at its current capacity, and state the corresponding value for the annual fixed costs and for the variable cost per unit, taking each of the three on its own.

    (Determine)
  5. [4 marks](e)

    Evaluate which of the three changes in part (d) the management of Ridgeway Ceramics is most likely to be able to make, and justify your answer.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Contribution per unit is the selling price less the variable cost per unit (M1):

$$\pounds 40 - \pounds 24 = \pounds 16 \tag{A1}$$

Break-even output is fixed costs divided by contribution per unit (A1):

$$\frac{200{,}000}{16} = 12{,}500 \text{ units}$$

(b) The margin of safety is the amount by which the planned output exceeds the break-even output, so with output at the capacity ceiling (M1):

$$10{,}000 - 12{,}500 = -2{,}500 \text{ units}$$

As a percentage of capacity (A1):

$$\frac{-2{,}500}{10{,}000} \times 100 = -25\%$$

A negative margin of safety means the business cannot reach break-even at any output it is able to produce (A1). Every unit it makes sells for $\pounds 16$ more than its variable cost, and that contribution is never enough to cover $\pounds 200{,}000$ of fixed costs, so the business makes a loss in every year in which it operates. The negative figure is not a shortfall to be made up by selling harder; it is a statement that the break-even point lies outside the set of outputs the business can reach.

(c) At full capacity the total contribution is (M1)

$$10{,}000 \times \pounds 16 = \pounds 160{,}000$$

and the loss is the fixed costs less that contribution (A1):

$$\pounds 160{,}000 - \pounds 200{,}000 = -\pounds 40{,}000$$

Because contribution per unit is positive, each additional unit sold reduces the loss by $\pounds 16$, so profit increases with output throughout the feasible range (M1). The largest output the line can produce is therefore the least unprofitable one, and $\pounds 40{,}000$ is a loss at the best point rather than at a poor one: there is no output at which Ridgeway Ceramics makes a profit, so the maximum profit it can achieve in a year is a loss of $\pounds 40{,}000$.

(d) Each change is found by setting the total contribution at capacity equal to the fixed costs.

For the selling price, let it be $p$ (M1):

$$10{,}000(p - 24) = 200{,}000 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p - 24 = 20 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p = \pounds 44.00 \tag{A1}$$

For the annual fixed costs, with contribution per unit still $\pounds 16$:

$$10{,}000 \times 16 = \pounds 160{,}000 \tag{A1}$$

For the variable cost per unit, let it be $v$:

$$10{,}000(40 - v) = 200{,}000 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 40 - v = 20 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \pounds 20.00 \tag{A1}$$

So the three thresholds are a price of $\pounds 44.00$ (a rise of $\pounds 4.00$, or 10%), fixed costs of $\pounds 160{,}000$ (a cut of $\pounds 40{,}000$, or 20%) and a variable cost of $\pounds 20.00$ (a cut of $\pounds 4.00$, or 16.7%). Each figure is a threshold and not a target: at exactly that value the business breaks even at full capacity and makes nothing, so any of the three has to be bettered before a profit appears.

(e) The three changes are not equally available, and the comparison has to be made on two axes: how large the change is, and whether the business controls it.

The price rise is the smallest proportional change and it requires no investment, no renegotiation and no new equipment, which makes it attractive on paper. It is also the least likely to hold. Ridgeway sells a single product into a market it does not control, and a 10% rise has to be accepted by every customer for the arithmetic to work; if it is accepted by fewer, the contribution gain on the remaining units does not compensate for the volume lost, and at a price of $\pounds 44$ the business needs *all* 10 000 units to break even, leaving no room for any loss of demand at all. The remedy that looks cleanest is the one with the narrowest margin for error.

The fixed-cost cut is the largest change in absolute terms, $\pounds 40{,}000$, and it is the one the business controls most directly, since fixed costs are largely internal commitments. But the kiln line is the fixed cost that matters, and it cannot be halved; a 20% reduction in a single-line ceramics business means cutting maintenance, staffing or the second shift, and cutting the second shift is precisely what would reduce capacity and make the position worse. A fixed-cost cut that lowers the ceiling lowers the output the business can sell, and the break-even output would have to be recalculated against the smaller capacity rather than assumed unchanged.

The variable-cost cut is the one most likely to be achievable. $\pounds 4.00$ per unit is a 16.7% reduction in the cost of materials and power, and variable costs are the category a manufacturer can most often attack: renegotiating a clay or glaze contract, reducing kiln waste, buying in larger quantities. It requires no change to the price the customer sees and no reduction in capacity, so it does not trade one problem for another. The difficulty is that a 16.7% cut is substantial for a business whose inputs are commodity-like, and any saving is likely to arrive in stages rather than at once.

Taken together, the most likely single change is the variable-cost reduction, and the strongest reason is not that it is the largest or the smallest but that it is the only one that leaves the capacity ceiling and the selling price untouched. The most reliable answer, however, is not to rely on any single lever: a smaller price rise combined with a smaller variable-cost reduction reaches the same threshold while exposing the business to less risk on either one, and a management that pursues only one of the three is betting the whole recovery on the assumption that is hardest to verify. What the figures cannot show is how the market would respond to a price rise or how far a supplier would move, and those are the questions that decide between the options.

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark for the contribution of 16, one for dividing fixed costs by contribution, one for 12 500 units. A candidate who computes 200 000/24 scores no marks, because 24 is the variable cost rather than the contribution.

(b) One mark for subtracting the break-even output from capacity, one for -25%, one for the meaning. The meaning mark requires the candidate to say that break-even is unreachable at any feasible output; "the margin of safety is low" does not earn it, because the sign is the point.

(c) One mark for the total contribution at capacity, one for the loss of 40 000, one for the observation that positive contribution per unit makes the largest output the least unprofitable. A candidate who computes the loss at some other output, or who reports a profit, cannot score the third mark.

(d) One mark for setting total contribution equal to fixed costs in the price case, and one mark for each of the three thresholds: 44.00, 160 000 and 20.00. Follow-through applies: a candidate who used the wrong contribution in (a) but applies a consistent method should be given the method marks.

(e) The evaluation mark is awarded for a judgement that names one change as most likely and supports it with a reason that distinguishes the three. The remaining marks are for engaging with at least two of the three in terms of feasibility rather than arithmetic -- for example that the price rise has the least margin for error because it needs full volume, or that a fixed-cost cut may reduce capacity. A response that lists the three percentage changes without judging between them scores 0 for the evaluation.

Forfeits: computing the margin of safety as 12 500 - 10 000 = 2 500 and reporting it as positive, which reverses the entire item; treating 12 500 units as achievable and reporting a profit at that output. Condonation: a candidate who expresses the fixed-cost threshold as a 20% reduction rather than as 160 000, and who shows the working, should be given full credit.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 4.5 A revenue-positive, profit-negative price cut: price elasticity of demand governs turnover, but contribution per member governs profit once a variable cost sits under the price
syllabus_ref: Unit 4: 4.5 The seven Ps of the marketing mix (pricing strategies and price elasticity of demand); 3.3 Costs and revenues. Toolkit: descriptive statistics.
title: 4.5 A revenue-positive, profit-negative price cut: price elasticity of demand governs turnover, but contribution per member governs profit once a variable cost sits under the price
q_html:
A members' gym considering a price cut

Highfield Fitness is a single-site gym with a maximum capacity of $500$ memberships. It currently charges $£40$ per month and has $300$ members, so it is running at three-fifths of its capacity. The variable cost of serving a member is $£6$ per month, covering cleaning, utilities and consumables, and the gym's fixed costs are $£8{,}000$ per month, covering rent, staff salaries and equipment leases regardless of how many members it has.

The manager is concerned that the gym is not full and proposes cutting the monthly fee by $15\%$ to $£34$. A trial in a neighbouring town suggested that such a cut raises membership by about $20\%$, a figure the manager believes would hold here. The manager's argument is that revenue would rise because the gym would sell a fifth more memberships, and that this on its own makes the proposal worthwhile. The gym can admit up to $500$ members without any increase in fixed costs.

The manager of Highfield Fitness wants to fill the gym by cutting the monthly fee, and argues that the extra memberships will raise revenue. Using the figures in the stimulus, calculate the present revenue, contribution and profit; calculate the price elasticity of demand implied by the proposal; show what the cut would do to revenue and to profit; determine the membership the gym would actually need to hold profit where it is; and evaluate whether the cut should be made.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the gym's current monthly revenue, its contribution per member, its total monthly contribution and its monthly profit.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the price elasticity of demand implied by the manager's figures, and state whether demand is price-elastic or price-inelastic over this price range.

    (Calculate)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Show that the price cut raises monthly revenue to $£12{,}240$ but reduces monthly profit to $£2{,}080$, and comment on why revenue and profit move in opposite directions.

    (Show that)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Determine the number of members the gym would need at the new monthly fee to leave its monthly profit unchanged, and compare that number with the $360$ members the manager expects.

    (Determine)
  5. [4 marks](e)

    Evaluate whether Highfield Fitness should cut its monthly fee, referring both to the figures you have calculated and to the assumptions behind the manager's expectation.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Current monthly revenue:
$$300 \times \u00a340 = \u00a312{,}000 \;\; (A1).$$
Contribution per member is the price less the variable cost of serving that member:
$$\u00a340 - \u00a36 = \u00a334 \;\; (A1).$$
Total monthly contribution is $300 \times \u00a334 = \u00a310{,}200$, and after fixed costs the monthly profit is
$$\u00a310{,}200 - \u00a38{,}000 = \u00a32{,}200 \;\; (A1).$$
Note that the $£6$ per member is a *variable* cost: it is incurred only for members the gym actually has, which is why it is deducted from the price rather than lumped with the rent.

(b) The proposal changes the price by $-15\%$ and, on the manager's own figure, changes the quantity demanded by $+20\%$. So
$$\text{PED} = \frac{\text{percentage change in quantity demanded}}{\text{percentage change in price}} = \frac{+20\%}{-15\%} = -1.33 \;\; (M1)(A1).$$
The *magnitude* is greater than one, $|{-1.33}| > 1$, so demand is price-elastic over this range $(A1)$. That is exactly the condition the manager is relying on: with elastic demand, a fall in price raises total revenue. The candidate should be able to state that conclusion and it is correct.

(c) At the new fee the gym has $300 \times 1.20 = 360$ members and charges $\u00a340 \times 0.85 = \u00a334$, so
$$\text{new revenue} = 360 \times \u00a334 = \u00a312{,}240,$$
a rise of $\u00a3240$ a month on the $£12{,}000$ in part (a) $(A1)$.

Profit falls, however, because the contribution per member falls with the price while the variable cost does not. The new contribution per member is $\u00a334 - \u00a36 = \u00a328$, so
$$\text{new total contribution} = 360 \times \u00a328 = \u00a310{,}080,$$
and
$$\text{new profit} = \u00a310{,}080 - \u00a38{,}000 = \u00a32{,}080 \;\; (A1).$$
That is $\u00a3120$ *less* than the present profit of $\u00a32{,}200$.

Revenue and profit move in opposite directions because they are governed by different quantities $(A1)$. Revenue depends only on price times volume, and elasticity is precisely a statement about revenue; profit depends on the *contribution* each member makes, and the six-pound cut in price cuts contribution per member by the same six pounds, from $\u00a334$ to $\u00a328$, a fall of $17.6\%$. A $20\%$ rise in volume cannot offset a fall of that size in contribution per unit, so the total contribution falls even though the revenue rises. Elasticity is silent about profit because it works with revenue alone; the variable cost is what breaks the coincidence between the two.

(d) To hold profit where it is, the new total contribution must still be $\u00a310{,}200$, so the gym needs
$$\frac{\u00a310{,}200}{\u00a328} = 364.3 \;\; (M1)(A1).$$
Membership comes in whole numbers, so the gym would need $365$ members $(A1)$. The manager expects $360$ members, which is five short of the membership required, and at $360$ members the profit is the $\u00a32{,}080$ of part (c). The comparison to state is that the proposal misses its own break-even point by about five memberships, not that it is close to it: five members is a small number of people but it is the whole of the margin.

(e) On the figures given, the gym should not cut the fee. The decision is not close: every member the gym gains at $\u00a334$ adds $\u00a328$ of contribution, and the fee cut removes $\u00a36$ of contribution from each of the $300$ members who would have paid $\u00a340$ anyway. The gain from fifty more members (about $360 - 300 = 60$ extra, worth $60 \times \u00a328 = \u00a31{,}680$) is outweighed by the $300 \times \u00a36 = \u00a31{,}800$ given up on the members who were already there $(A1)$, and the two figures have been arranged so that this is exactly the $\u00a3120$ shortfall. A cut of this size cannot pay for itself unless almost every existing member stays and the new members arrive in numbers the trial does not promise.

The weaknesses in the manager's expectation should be identified rather than assumed away $(A1)$. The $20\%$ figure comes from a *neighbouring town*, so it is evidence about a different location, a different competing set of gyms and a different population; the manager's belief that it would hold here is an assumption, not a measurement $(A1)$. The trial also tells the manager what happened to membership when the price was cut elsewhere, with no indication of how long the effect lasted; a promotional price often attracts members who leave when it rises, which would raise the variable-cost base without building the membership the gym wants.

A judgement is required, and it should be a clear one $(A1)$. The strongest honest case for the cut is not in the figures but beside them: if the extra members raise the gym's utilisation, its classes fill, its atmosphere improves and its retention improves, then part of the benefit would appear *later* in lower turnover among existing members, which the item's numbers do not capture. That argument is real, but it is not what the manager offered, and it would have to be large enough to close a gap of at least $\u00a3120$ a month and probably much more. On the arithmetic presented, the recommendation is to keep the fee at $\u00a340$ and look elsewhere for the members: the gym has $200$ memberships of headroom and the cheapest way to fill them is not to reduce the contribution of the members it already has.

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for revenue $£12{,}000$, (A1) for contribution per member $£34$, (A1) for profit $£2{,}200$ (the total contribution of $£10{,}200$ may be shown as working). A candidate who treats the $£6$ as a fixed cost and deducts it after fixed costs will be wrong and forfeits the profit mark; the mark is for recognising that it is variable.

(b) (M1) for forming the ratio of the two percentage changes, (A1) for $-1.33$ or $-4/3$, (A1) for stating elastic with the magnitude test $|\text{PED}| > 1$. A candidate who writes $1.33$ without the sign and then calls it elastic has the substance and should keep the marks.

(c) (A1) for new revenue $£12{,}240$, (A1) for new profit $£2{,}080$, (A1) for the explanation that the contribution per member has fallen faster than the volume has risen. The explanation mark needs the per-member contribution, not "costs went up": a candidate who says only "revenue rose but costs rose more" without naming the $£28$ contribution has the first two marks and not the third.

(d) (M1) for setting the new total contribution equal to $£10{,}200$, (A1) for $364.3$, (A1) for rounding up to $365$ and comparing with $360$. Accept a candidate who works from the contribution lost on existing members and the contribution gained on new ones; the answer is the same. A candidate who answers $360$ because that is the forecast has not answered the question.

(e) (A1) for a reasoned recommendation against the cut, supported by the shortfall computed in (d). (A1) for identifying the transferability of the trial as an assumption. (A1) for identifying at least one further assumption (the duration of the trial's effect, or retention, or the absence of any change in variable cost per member). (A1) for a defensible judgement that weighs the qualitative case against the arithmetic rather than ignoring it. Full marks do not require the candidate to agree with the model answer: a clear case *for* the cut built on stated qualitative benefits, with the $£120$ gap acknowledged and argued, can score the fourth mark.

Forfeits: using $£40 - \u00a36$ as the new contribution per member after the cut, which double-counts the price change; computing elasticity from $£40$ and $£34$ directly rather than as a percentage change (that gives $-6/40 = -15\%$, which is the price change and no elasticity); stating the profit effect as positive because revenue rose. Condonation: contribution may be called "unit contribution" or "contribution per member"; $£2{,}080$ may be shown as $£2{,}080$ or "about $£2{,}100$" provided the exact figure appears once.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 2.1 The cost of labour turnover against the cost of a retention pay rise, where the wrong comparison is total recruitment spend against total salary increase rather than the saving the proposal actually buys
syllabus_ref: Unit 2: 2.1 Introduction to human resource management (workforce planning, labour turnover, absenteeism); 3.3 Costs and revenues. Toolkit: descriptive statistics.
title: 2.1 The cost of labour turnover against the cost of a retention pay rise, where the wrong comparison is total recruitment spend against total salary increase rather than the saving the proposal actually buys
q_html:
A call centre weighing a pay rise against recruitment costs

Brightline Support operates a single call centre employing $400$ staff. The average salary is $£22{,}000$ a year. In the year just ended the labour turnover rate was $30\%$, and the finance function calculates that it costs $£2{,}500$ to recruit and train one replacement, covering advertising, agency fees, induction and the lost productivity of the new starter's first weeks.

The directors are worried about retention and propose raising pay by $4\%$ for every member of staff, from the start of the next financial year. The human resource manager expects this to halve the turnover rate, from $30\%$ to $15\%$, on the grounds that pay is the reason most leavers give in their exit interviews, and argues that a pay rise which halves turnover would save a great deal on recruitment and training. The directors have asked for the arithmetic before deciding. They have not asked about anything other than the effect on recruitment and salary costs.

The directors of a call centre are considering a pay rise in order to keep staff. Using the figures in the stimulus, calculate the present turnover rate and the present annual recruitment cost; calculate the annual cost of the proposed pay rise; show what the pay rise would save and what it would add; determine how many leavers it would have to prevent to pay for itself; and evaluate whether the pay rise should be approved.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the number of staff who left in the year just ended, the present annual cost of recruitment and training, and express the turnover rate as it is normally stated.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the annual cost of the proposed $4\%$ pay rise across the whole workforce.

    (Calculate)
  3. [3 marks](c)

    Show that if the pay rise did halve the turnover rate it would save $£150{,}000$ a year in recruitment and training, and that against its own cost this increases the call centre's total annual costs by $£202{,}000$.

    (Show that)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Determine how many leavers the pay rise would have to prevent in a year in order to pay for itself, and compare that number with the total number of leavers at the present turnover rate.

    (Determine)
  5. [4 marks](e)

    Evaluate whether the directors should approve the pay rise, referring to the figures you have calculated and to the assumptions on which the human resource manager's expectation rests.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) A turnover rate of $30\%$ on a workforce of $400$ means
$$400 \times 0.30 = 120 \;\; (A1)$$
staff left during the year. At $£2{,}500$ to recruit and train one replacement, the present annual cost of turnover is
$$120 \times \u00a32{,}500 = \u00a3300{,}000 \;\; (A1).$$
The turnover rate is already stated as a percentage of the workforce, so it is $30\%$; it may also be expressed as $120$ leavers against an average workforce of $400$, which is the same figure $(A1)$. It is worth noting that the $£300{,}000$ is money the call centre is *already* spending, not a new cost, and that nothing in the pay rise changes it except by changing the number of leavers.

(b) A $4\%$ rise on an average salary of $£22{,}000$ is
$$\u00a322{,}000 \times 0.04 = \u00a3880 \;\; (M1)$$
per member of staff per year. Across $400$ staff this is
$$400 \times \u00a3880 = \u00a3352{,}000 \;\; (A1).$$
The whole of that $\u00a3352{,}000$ is a new, recurring cost $(A1)$: it is paid every year for as long as the pay rate stands, and it is paid to all $400$ staff, not only to the ones the rise is meant to keep.

(c) If turnover halved, from $30\%$ to $15\%$, the number of leavers would fall from $120$ to $400 \times 0.15 = 60$. The saving is the cost of the $60$ replacements the call centre no longer needs:
$$(120 - 60) \times \u00a32{,}500 = \u00a3150{,}000 \;\; (A1).$$
The pay rise costs $\u00a3352{,}000$. The change in the call centre's total costs is therefore
$$+\u00a3352{,}000 - \u00a3150{,}000 = +\u00a3202{,}000,$$
a rise of $\u00a3202{,}000$ a year $(A1)$, not a saving. Put as totals: recruitment and training would fall to $60 \times \u00a32{,}500 = \u00a3150{,}000$, and with the new salary bill of $\u00a3352{,}000$ sitting on top of it the two costs together come to about $\u00a3502{,}000$ against the present $\u00a3300{,}000$ $(A1)$.

The essential point is which quantity changes. The present turnover cost of $\u00a3300{,}000$ does not become zero when turnover halves; it becomes $\u00a3150{,}000$. The proposal buys a *reduction* of $\u00a3150{,}000$, and it must be set against a cost of $\u00a3352{,}000$, not against the $\u00a3300{,}000$ that was being spent anyway.

(d) To pay for itself, the recruitment saving must equal the cost of the rise, so the number of replacements the rise must prevent is
$$\frac{\u00a3352{,}000}{\u00a32{,}500} = 140.8 \;\; (M1)(A1),$$
that is $141$ leavers must be prevented. But at the present turnover rate only $120$ staff leave in a whole year, so there are not $141$ leavers to prevent: even a turnover rate of zero would remove only $120$ replacements and save $120 \times \u00a32{,}500 = \u00a3300{,}000$, which is $£52{,}000$ short of the cost of the rise $(A1)$. The conclusion is sharp and worth stating plainly: on the figures given, the pay rise cannot pay for itself at any turnover rate, because its maximum possible saving is smaller than its cost.
