(e) On the arithmetic, the directors should not approve the rise as a way of saving money, because it does the opposite: it adds $\u00a3202{,}000$ a year to costs even while delivering the halving of turnover the manager expects $(A1)$. The maximum saving available from the whole of the call centre's turnover problem is $\u00a3300{,}000$, and the rise costs $\u00a3352{,}000$, so the retention case cannot be made on recruitment savings at all -- the manager's mechanism fails before any assumption is tested.

The assumption should then be examined on its own terms $(A1)$. Halving turnover from $30\%$ to $15\%$ is a very large change to attribute to a pay rise of $4\%$, and the evidence for it is that pay is what leavers *say* in exit interviews; what people say when they leave is not the same as what would have kept them. A $4\%$ rise is below the level of inflation in most years, so it may not even be felt as a real improvement. If the manager is optimistic and turnover falls by less than half, the saving shrinks further while the $\u00a3352{,}000$ does not.

A judgement is still required, and there is an honest case on the other side $(A1)$. The figures only cover salary and recruitment, and the directors explicitly did not ask about anything else; turnover also carries a cost in service quality, in the loss of experienced agents, and in the morale of the staff who remain, none of which is in the $£2{,}500$ figure. If those costs are large, a pay rise could be justified as a *service* investment rather than a *recruitment* saving -- but that is a different argument from the one the manager made, and it would have to be supported by evidence the call centre has not gathered.

The recommendation should be direct $(A1)$. Approve no pay rise on the case as put, because the retention argument is arithmetically impossible: a rise costing $\u00a3352{,}000$ cannot recover more than $\u00a3300{,}000$ in avoided recruitment even if nobody left. If the directors want to reduce turnover, a smaller, targeted measure -- a retention bonus paid only to staff who stay, or an increase confined to the roles that actually leave -- would cost less than a rise paid to all $400$ and would not repeat every year for the staff it is not needed for.

Markscheme notes

(a) (A1) for $120$ leavers, (A1) for $£300{,}000$, (A1) for stating the rate as $30\%$. A candidate who gives $120$ and $£300{,}000$ without restating the percentage has the substance and keeps the third mark if the rate appears in the working.

(b) (M1) for the per-head increase of $£880$, (A1) for $£352{,}000$, (A1) for noting that it is recurring and paid to the whole workforce. A candidate who applies the $4\%$ to the $120$ leavers only, or to the recruitment cost, has misread the proposal and forfeits the marks.

(c) (A1) for the $£150{,}000$ saving, (A1) for the net increase of $£202{,}000$ (accept $£502{,}000$ against $£300{,}000$ as the statement of totals), (A1) for explaining that the comparison is against the *reduction* in recruitment cost, not the total. The third mark is for the reasoning, not the arithmetic: a candidate who computes both figures but writes that the rise "saves $£150{,}000$" without saying it costs $£352{,}000$ has not earned it.

(d) (M1) for dividing the cost of the rise by the cost per replacement, (A1) for $140.8$ or $141$, (A1) for the comparison with the $120$ leavers available and the conclusion that the maximum saving of $£300{,}000$ is still short. A candidate who answers "140 leavers" and stops, without noticing that only 120 exist, forfeits the third mark. The point of the part is that the target is unattainable.

(e) (A1) for refusing the rise as a cost-saving measure with the shortfall as the reason, (A1) for examining the assumption that a $4\%$ rise halves turnover, ideally with the observation that the evidence is what leavers say rather than what would have kept them, (A1) for identifying the costs the figures exclude (service quality, experience, morale of stayers), (A1) for a judgement that either proposes a cheaper targeted alternative or explains why the excluded costs could justify the rise despite the arithmetic. Full marks do not require the model answer's recommendation: a candidate who approves the rise on clearly stated service grounds, with the $£202{,}000$ acknowledged, can score the fourth mark.

Forfeits: comparing $£300{,}000$ with $£352{,}000$ and calling the difference the cost, which is the error the item is built to catch; assuming the whole $£300{,}000$ disappears if turnover halves; treating the pay rise as a one-off cost. Condonation: $140$ leavers instead of $141$ loses the second mark in (d) but not the first or third, since the comparison with $120$ is unaffected; the net figure may be given as $£202{,}000$ or $£200{,}000$ if the exact value is shown once.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 4.4 Purchase-intent research read with 6.7 weighted and standardised rates
syllabus_ref: 4.4 Market research (sampling, bias); 6.7 Descriptive statistics
title: 4.4 Purchase-intent research read with 6.7 weighted and standardised rates
q_html:
Purchase intent by age band, waves 1 and 2

Positive responses are respondents who said they would definitely or probably buy. Note that the two waves did not interview the same number of people in each band.

Nordvik Drinks commissions two waves of purchase-intent research for a new low-sugar cordial. Respondents are asked whether they would definitely or probably buy the product at its intended price.

Wave 1 is an in-store intercept survey carried out at weekends. Wave 2 is an online panel carried out on weekdays.

The company's target market for the launch is 900 000 adults, split 30% / 40% / 30% between the 18–34, 35–54 and 55+ bands. Each buyer is expected to make one purchase in the launch year, and the gross margin is £1.40 per unit.

  1. [3 marks](a)

    Calculate the overall positive response rate for each wave.

    (Calculate)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Calculate the positive response rate within each of the three age bands for each wave, and state what your results show that the comparison in part (a) conceals.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Using the target market mix of 30% / 40% / 30%, show that the age-standardised positive rate is 25.0% for wave 1 and 30.0% for wave 2.

    (Show that)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    The marketing director proposes to forecast launch-year sales using the wave 2 overall rate from part (a). Evaluate this proposal, quantifying its effect on the launch decision.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Wave 1: $\dfrac{118}{400} \times 100 = 29.5\%$. Wave 2: $\dfrac{153}{600} \times 100 = 25.5\%$. On this comparison purchase intent appears to have fallen by $4.0$ percentage points between the two waves.

(b) Wave 1. 18–34: $\dfrac{80}{200} = 40.0\%$. 35–54: $\dfrac{30}{120} = 25.0\%$. 55+: $\dfrac{8}{80} = 10.0\%$.

Wave 2. 18–34: $\dfrac{54}{120} = 45.0\%$. 35–54: $\dfrac{54}{180} = 30.0\%$. 55+: $\dfrac{45}{300} = 15.0\%$.

Intent rose in every single band — by 5.0, 5.0 and 5.0 percentage points respectively. The overall comparison in part (a) conceals this completely, because the two waves did not interview the same mix of people: wave 2 drew 300 of its 600 respondents from the 55+ band, against 80 of 400 in wave 1, and that band has the lowest intent in both waves. The headline fall is an artefact of who was asked, not a change in what people think.

(c) Applying the target mix to the wave 1 band rates: $0.30(40.0) + 0.40(25.0) + 0.30(10.0) = 12.0 + 10.0 + 3.0 = 25.0\%$. Applying it to the wave 2 band rates: $0.30(45.0) + 0.40(30.0) + 0.30(15.0) = 13.5 + 12.0 + 4.5 = 30.0\%$. Both waves are therefore reweighted onto the same population, and on that like-for-like basis intent rose by $5.0$ percentage points.

(d) The proposal should be rejected. The wave 2 overall rate of 25.5% is computed on a sample that is not representative of the target market: it over-weights the 55+ band by a factor of roughly five relative to the target mix. Applying it gives $900\,000 \times 0.255 = 229\,500$ buyers. Applying the standardised wave 2 rate of 30.0% gives $900\,000 \times 0.30 = 270\,000$ buyers. The difference is $40\,500$ units, and at a gross margin of £1.40 that is $40\,500 \times 1.40 = £56\,700$ of margin left out of the forecast. That is large enough to change the decision if the launch has a fixed cost close to the projected margin — a project that looks marginal at 229 500 units may clear its threshold at 270 000. Against this, the standardised figure is not free of doubt: wave 2 was an online panel taken on weekdays, so it may under-represent people who shop in stores at weekends, and stated purchase intent reliably overstates actual buying. The defensible conclusion is that the director's method is wrong in a known direction and by a known amount, and that the forecast should use the standardised rate while being presented as an upper estimate.

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark for each rate and one for the comparison. Accept rates given to one decimal place. Do not penalise a candidate who comments that the two rates are not comparable — that is creditworthy here and is developed in later parts.

(b) One mark for each wave's set of three band rates (two marks total), one for the observation that intent rose in every band, and one for identifying the differing age mix as the cause. A candidate who computes the band rates but does not draw the conclusion earns the first two marks only.

(c) One mark for setting up the weighted sum with the target mix, one for each standardised rate, and one for the resulting comparison. Candidates may use either the percentages or the counts; both are acceptable. Follow-through applies from part (b).

(d) This is an AO3 part: marks are for the judgement and its support, not for the arithmetic alone. Award one mark for rejecting the proposal, one for each of the two forecasts (four marks total across the set), one for the quantified difference in units and one for the money figure. A candidate who reaches the correct numbers but does not say what they mean for the decision is capped at three. Conversely, a candidate who rejects the proposal with sound reasoning but whose arithmetic slips may still earn three, provided the direction of the error is identified. Credit the counter-argument about stated intent overstating actual purchase where it is developed rather than merely listed.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 3.5 When the ratios improve and the cash position does not: a financing decision the numbers cannot settle
syllabus_ref: 3.5 Profitability and liquidity ratio analysis
title: 3.5 When the ratios improve and the cash position does not: a financing decision the numbers cannot settle
q_html:
Ravensworth Ltd is a wholesaler. Extracts from its accounts for two years are shown below, together with the figures for a proposed expansion.

| | Year 1 (\$000) | Year 2 (\$000) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Revenue | 2 400 | 3 200 |
| Gross profit | 900 | 1 120 |
| Net profit before interest and tax | 288 | 352 |
| Capital employed | 1 800 | 1 920 |
| Inventory | 300 | 420 |
| Other current assets | 320 | 280 |
| Current liabilities | 310 | 500 |

The directors propose an expansion costing \$180 000, which would be financed entirely by an increase in the bank overdraft. The expansion would increase inventory by \$180 000 and is expected to raise annual net profit before interest and tax by \$46 000. No other figure in the table would change immediately.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    For each of Year 1 and Year 2, calculate the gross profit margin, the net profit margin, the return on capital employed and the current ratio. Give ratios to two decimal places and percentages to one decimal place.

    (Calculate)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Calculate the acid test ratio for each year. Hence analyse whether the financial performance of Ravensworth Ltd improved in Year 2.

    (Analyse)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Calculate, for the proposed expansion: the annual percentage return on the \$180 000 invested, the payback period, and the current ratio and acid test ratio immediately after the expansion is financed by the overdraft.

    (Calculate)
  4. [3 marks](d)

    Evaluate whether the directors should proceed with the expansion on the terms described. There is no single correct answer: marks are awarded for the reasoning, including the use of the figures you have calculated.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Year 1 (A1 for the year):

  • Gross profit margin $= 900 \div 2400 = 37.5\%$
  • Net profit margin $= 288 \div 2400 = 12.0\%$
  • Return on capital employed $= 288 \div 1800 = 16.0\%$
  • Current ratio $= (300 + 320) \div 310 = 620 \div 310 = 2.00$

Year 2 (A1 for the year):

  • Gross profit margin $= 1120 \div 3200 = 35.0\%$
  • Net profit margin $= 352 \div 3200 = 11.0\%$
  • Return on capital employed $= 352 \div 1920 = 18.3\%$
  • Current ratio $= (420 + 280) \div 500 = 700 \div 500 = 1.40$

One mark is available for each of the four ratios being correct in both years (A1 each).

(b) The acid test ratio is $320 \div 310 = 1.03$ for Year 1 and $280 \div 500 = 0.56$ for Year 2 (A1).

The assessment has to be given in two directions, and a candidate who gives only one of them has not finished (A1). Profitability as a return on the resources employed improved: ROCE rose from $16.0\%$ to $18.3\%$ and absolute net profit rose from \$288 000 to \$352 000 (A1). But profitability as a margin, and liquidity, both deteriorated: gross margin fell from $37.5\%$ to $35.0\%$, net margin from $12.0\%$ to $11.0\%$, the current ratio from $2.00$ to $1.40$, and the acid test ratio from $1.03$ to $0.56$ (A1).

The acid test figure is the one that matters. At $0.56$ the business cannot cover its current liabilities out of current assets without selling inventory, and the fall from $1.03$ to $0.56$ means it has moved from comfortable to exposed in a single year. The most likely explanation is that rapid revenue growth of $33\%$ has been financed by current liabilities, which rose from \$310 000 to \$500 000, rather than by new capital.

(c) Annual return $= 46 000 \div 180 000 = 25.6\%$ (A1). Payback period $= 180 000 \div 46 000 = 3.9$ years (A1).

After the expansion, financed by the overdraft: other current assets stay at \$280 000, inventory rises to $420 + 180 = \$600 000$, so current assets total \$880 000; current liabilities rise to $500 + 180 = \$680 000$.

  • Current ratio $= 880 \div 680 = 1.29$ (A1)
  • Acid test ratio $= (880 - 600) \div 680 = 280 \div 680 = 0.41$ (A1)

(d) A developed answer distinguishes the project from the method of finance, and that is the insight the item is built around (A1).

The project looks sound on its own terms. A return of $25.6\%$ exceeds the current ROCE of $18.3\%$, so the expansion would raise the average return on capital employed, and a payback period of $3.9$ years is reasonable for a wholesaler investing in stock-holding capacity. On the quantitative evidence alone the expansion earns more than it costs.

The method of finance does not. Overdraft finance is repayable on demand and is a current liability, so it pushes the current ratio down from $1.40$ to $1.29$ and the acid test ratio from $0.56$ to $0.41$ (A1). At $0.41$ the business would be holding \$600 000 of inventory against \$680 000 of liabilities falling due within the year, and the additional inventory is precisely the asset the acid test excludes. Financing a three-to-four-year investment with money that can be recalled at short notice is a maturity mismatch, and the ratios are right to flag it.

The conclusion candidates should reach is that the expansion should proceed but should not be financed this way. If the same \$180 000 were raised as a long-term loan, current liabilities would stay at \$500 000 and the current ratio would be $880 \div 500 = 1.76$, with the acid test ratio unchanged at $0.56$ -- that is, the expansion would improve the current ratio rather than damage it. The objection is to the overdraft, not to the investment (A1).

A candidate who reaches the opposite conclusion -- that the business should not expand at all -- can still be credited fully if the judgement is supported by the figures, for example by arguing that an acid test ratio of $0.56$ before any expansion is already too low to take on further fixed commitments, and that the business should rebuild liquidity first. What earns no credit is letting the $25.6\%$ return settle the question on its own, because that number is silent about when the money has to be repaid.

Markscheme notes

(a) Award one (A1) for each of the five ratios calculated correctly for BOTH years, up to a maximum of five marks. Ratios to two decimal places and percentages to one decimal place, as instructed; condone a correctly calculated ratio given to a different number of decimal places. Accept ROCE calculated on capital employed as given. Do not award a mark where one year is correct and the other is not.
(b) Award (A1) for recognising that the answer is two-directional, (A1) for the improvement in ROCE and in absolute profit, (A1) for the deterioration in the two margins and in the two liquidity ratios. A candidate who says only 'it improved' or only 'it deteriorated' is capped at one mark regardless of how many correct figures are quoted.
(c) Award (A1) for 25.6 per cent, (A1) for 3.9 years (accept 3.91), (A1) for the current ratio 1.29 and (A1) for the acid test ratio 0.41. Follow-through: a candidate who wrongly leaves current liabilities at 500 obtains 1.76 and 0.56 and should still be awarded the two marks for the ratios if the arithmetic on their own figures is correct, but loses the marks if inventory was not added to current assets.
(d) This is an evaluative response marked on the quality of the reasoning rather than on the conclusion. Award (A1) for a judgement that is supported by at least two of the calculated figures; (A1) for distinguishing the project from the method of finance, or for an equivalent insight such as recognising the maturity mismatch; (A1) for a developed conclusion -- including the alternative of long-term finance, or a coherent contrary case supported by the figures.
Accept any reasonable conclusion provided it is supported. Do NOT award the final mark for an answer that simply restates that 25.6 per cent is greater than 18.3 per cent and advises proceeding.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 3.8 Investment appraisal
syllabus_ref: Unit 3: 3.8 Investment appraisal (payback period, average rate of return, net present value); 3.2 Sources of finance. Toolkit: decision trees are not required here.
title: Two projects, three appraisal methods, three different answers
q_html:
Kestrel Leisure plc

Kestrel Leisure plc operates forty indoor climbing centres and is considering two mutually exclusive investment projects. Each requires an immediate investment of €400 000 and each has an expected life of four years, after which it will have no residual value.

The company will finance whichever project it chooses with a bank loan at an interest rate of 10% per year. Project B would also require €50 000 of working capital at the start of Year 1, which the company expects to recover in full at the end of Year 4. This amount is not included in the cash flows shown below.

The two projects are mutually exclusive, so Kestrel Leisure can accept at most one of them.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate the payback period of each project, giving your answers in years to two decimal places.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the average rate of return of each project, using average annual profit as a percentage of the initial investment.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Using the discount factors provided, calculate the net present value of each project.

    (Calculate)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Recalculate the net present value of Project B to include the working capital requirement, and then recommend which project Kestrel Leisure should accept. Justify your recommendation using all of your calculations.

    (Recommend)
a_html:
(a) Project A. Cumulative cash flow: after Year 1, €120 000; after Year 2, €280 000; after Year 3, €460 000. The investment of €400 000 is recovered during Year 3, when €120 000 of the €180 000 inflow is still needed. (M1)

Payback $=2+\dfrac{120\,000}{180\,000}=2.67$ years. (A1)

Project B. Cumulative cash flow: after Year 1, €60 000; after Year 2, €160 000; after Year 3, €320 000; after Year 4, €560 000. The investment is recovered during Year 4, when €80 000 of the €240 000 inflow is still needed. (M1)

Payback $=3+\dfrac{80\,000}{240\,000}=3.33$ years. (A1)

(b) Project A: total net cash flow is $120\,000+160\,000+180\,000+80\,000=540\,000$, so total profit is $540\,000-400\,000=140\,000$ and average annual profit is $\dfrac{140\,000}{4}=35\,000$. (M1)

ARR $=\dfrac{35\,000}{400\,000}\times 100=8.75\%$. (A1)

Project B: total net cash flow is €560 000, so total profit is €160 000 and average annual profit is $\dfrac{160\,000}{4}=40\,000$. ARR $=\dfrac{40\,000}{400\,000}\times 100=10.00\%$. (A1)

(c) Project A: the present values of the inflows are $120\,000(0.909)=109\,080$; $160\,000(0.826)=132\,160$; $180\,000(0.751)=135\,180$; and $80\,000(0.683)=54\,640$. The total present value is €431 060. (M1)(A1)

NPV of A $=431\,060-400\,000=+€31\,060$. (A1)

Project B: the present values are $60\,000(0.909)=54\,540$; $100\,000(0.826)=82\,600$; $160\,000(0.751)=120\,160$; and $240\,000(0.683)=163\,920$, totalling €421 220. NPV of B $=421\,220-400\,000=+€21\,220$. (A1)

(d) Project B also requires €50 000 of working capital at the start, an immediate outflow that must be discounted at the Year 0 factor of 1.000, and it recovers €50 000 at the end of Year 4, whose present value is $50\,000(0.683)=34\,150$. (M1)

Revised NPV of B $=421\,220-400\,000-50\,000+34\,150=+€5\,370$. (A1)

Recommendation: accept Project A. (A1)

Justification: Project A is superior on two of the three methods. It pays back in 2.67 years against 3.33, which matters because the loan is being serviced at 10% and a shorter payback shortens the period during which the company carries the risk of the cash flows not materialising. Its NPV is €31 060 against €5 370 for Project B once the working capital is included, and since the money is borrowed at exactly the 10% used to discount, the NPV is the method that measures the effect on shareholder wealth directly. Project B is only superior on ARR, at 10.00% against 8.75%, and that measure is misleading here because it ignores the timing of the cash flows and, as presented, ignores the working capital entirely. (A1)

Markscheme notes

Parts (a) to (c): award the method marks for a correct cumulative total and the accuracy marks for the final figure; accept answers given in years and months if the conversion is correct. Part (b): accept an alternative ARR that uses average annual profit as a percentage of average investment, provided the formula is stated, but do not allow a candidate to mix the two formulae across the two projects. Part (c): candidates who discount the €400 000 investment should be corrected but not penalised twice, since the investment is at Year 0 where the discount factor is 1.000 anyway; credit their NPV if the arithmetic is otherwise correct. Part (d): the working-capital treatment is the discriminating mark. A candidate who subtracts €50 000 but forgets to add back the discounted recovery will obtain €21 220 − €50 000 = −€28 780 and conclude that B should be rejected; award the method mark and the recommendation mark, but not the accuracy mark. The justification marks require reference to at least two of the three methods and to the 10% cost of borrowing; a recommendation that rests on payback alone is incomplete. Follow-through applies throughout: a candidate whose NPVs are both wrong but who reasons consistently from their own figures should still earn the justification mark.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 5.4 Location
syllabus_ref: Unit 5: 5.4 Location (quantitative and qualitative factors, cost comparison and crossover output); 5.5 Break-even analysis.
title: Two sites, one crossover point, and a forecast that will not commit
q_html:
Tarn Valley Preserves

Tarn Valley Preserves makes jams and chutneys and has outgrown its current premises. Two sites are available and the company must choose one of them; it cannot afford both.

Marketing estimates a 0.6 probability that demand for the company's products will be 220 000 units per year and a 0.4 probability that it will be 120 000 units per year. The production cost structure differs between the two sites, and the qualitative differences are set out in the table.

Tarn Valley Preserves must commit to one site, and the choice will be difficult to reverse because the lease runs for ten years.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate the total annual cost at each site if demand is 220 000 units, and state which site is cheaper.

    (Calculate)
  2. [3 marks](b)

    Calculate the output at which the total annual costs of the two sites are equal.

    (Calculate)
  3. [4 marks](c)

    Using the probabilities given, calculate the expected annual cost at each site and comment on what your answer means for the decision.

    (Comment)
  4. [4 marks](d)

    Recommend which site Tarn Valley Preserves should choose, justifying your answer with reference to your calculations and to two qualitative factors.

    (Recommend)
a_html:
(a) Site X: total cost $=280\,000+1.80(220\,000)=280\,000+396\,000=€676\,000$. (M1)(A1)

Site Y: total cost $=140\,000+2.60(220\,000)=140\,000+572\,000=€712\,000$. (A1)

Site X is cheaper by €36 000 per year at this level of demand. (A1)

(b) Setting the two total costs equal: $280\,000+1.80q=140\,000+2.60q$. (M1)

So $140\,000=0.80q$ and $q=175\,000$ units. (M1)(A1)

Site Y is cheaper below this output and Site X above it, because Site X trades higher fixed costs for a lower variable cost per unit.

(c) Site X: $0.6(676\,000)+0.4(496\,000)=405\,600+198\,400=€604\,000$. (M1)(A1)

Site Y: $0.6(712\,000)+0.4(452\,000)=427\,200+180\,800=€608\,000$. (A1)

The expected costs differ by only €4000 per year on a commitment of more than half a million euros per year, which is well under 1% of the total. (A1) The expected-value calculation therefore does not settle the question: whichever site is chosen, the company is making almost the same bet on cost, and the decision will be decided by which risk the management team is more willing to carry rather than by the arithmetic. It is also worth noting that the expected value conceals the shape of the risk: Site Y is cheaper in the low-demand outcome and more expensive in the high-demand outcome, so choosing Y is choosing to be relatively safe if demand disappoints, while Site X is choosing to be better off if demand materialises.

(d) Recommendation: choose Site X, the city centre. (A1)

The quantitative case is narrow but consistent: Site X is €36 000 per year cheaper at the higher demand level, it has the lower expected cost at €604 000 against €608 000, and its crossover point of 175 000 units sits well below the 220 000 units that marketing considers more likely than not. Since the lease runs for ten years and the higher-demand outcome is the one the company's growth plan depends on, the cheaper variable cost is the more valuable characteristic to lock in. (A1)

The decisive qualitative factor is space. Site X has no room to expand at any price, so if demand exceeds 220 000 units the company would have to acquire a second site and duplicate management, which would destroy most of the cost advantage it has just calculated. Site Y has a large plot available now, which gives the business the option to grow without a second location. (A1)

The counter-argument is labour. Site X has a large local pool of skilled production staff, while Site Y would require training, which adds cost and time and creates a dependency on retaining the staff it trains. A preserves manufacturer depends on consistent product quality, so the availability of experienced staff reduces operational risk. On balance the expected cost difference is too small to decide the matter, and the choice between the two risks comes down to which the company fears more: a permanent capacity ceiling on a growing product, or an operating cost it cannot control. (A1)

Markscheme notes

Part (a): award the method mark for the linear cost structure and the accuracy marks for the two totals; a candidate who omits the fixed cost entirely should be corrected, because the whole point of the comparison is the trade-off between fixed and variable cost. Part (b): accept the answer obtained by any correct method, including a graphical one, provided the crossover output is identified. Part (c): accept an answer rounded to the nearest thousand, but require the two expected costs to be compared rather than merely stated. The comment mark depends on the candidate noticing how small the difference is relative to the size of the commitment; a candidate who simply says 'Site X is cheaper' has not commented. Part (d): the recommendation mark is independent of which site is chosen, provided the reasoning is internally consistent. The two justification marks require one qualitative factor handled well rather than two factors listed, and a candidate who merely quotes from the table without explaining the consequence for the business does not reach them. Do not accept a recommendation that ignores the expansion constraint, since it is the factor that makes the ten-year lease relevant.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 5.2 Operations methods
syllabus_ref: Unit 5: 5.2 Operations methods (job, batch and flow production; capital and labour intensity; factors influencing the choice of method). Toolkit: descriptive statistics and decision trees.
title: A flow line that is cheaper per bench and dearer per year
q_html:
Hartswood Garden Furniture

Hartswood Garden Furniture makes wooden garden benches, tables and chairs at a workshop in Somerset. It produces 120 000 units a year across twelve product variants and sells them through garden centres and a mail-order catalogue. All of the products are currently made by batch production.

The best-selling product is a two-seat bench, which accounts for 48 000 units of the annual output. Sales of the bench are highly seasonal: 80% of the annual volume is sold in April, May and June, and the remaining 20% is spread evenly over the other nine months. The company's marketing manager estimates a 0.6 probability that annual bench sales will be 48 000 units next year and a 0.4 probability that they will be 30 000 units, depending on the weather.

A consultant has proposed that Hartswood install a flow production line for the bench. Under the present batch system the bench has annual fixed costs of EUR 180 000 and a variable cost of EUR 18.25 a unit. The proposed flow line would have annual fixed costs of EUR 480 000 and a variable cost of EUR 10 a unit, and would cost EUR 600 000 to install. It would have a capacity of 8 000 benches a month. It could make only the bench; the other eleven products would stay on batch production.

Because the flow line cannot be expanded, any output needed above 8 000 benches in a month would have to be made in advance and stored. Hartswood's warehouse can hold the finished benches, but storing them costs EUR 3 per bench per month, and the consultant expects benches to be held for an average of four months. The finance director has also pointed out that a flow line is difficult to change over, so any design change to the bench would be expensive and slow.

Hartswood Garden Furniture must decide whether to invest EUR 600 000 in a flow production line for its best-selling bench.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Explain two reasons why the consultant believes flow production would be suitable for the bench, and one reason why the company's other eleven products make flow production difficult.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Calculate the mean monthly demand for the bench and the demand in a peak month. Calculate the unit cost of the bench under batch production and under flow production at an annual volume of 48 000 units, and comment on the difference.

    (Calculate)
  3. [6 marks](c)

    Using descriptive statistics and a decision tree, evaluate whether Hartswood should invest in the flow production line. Justify your answer with reference to capacity, storage cost and the product range.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) The consultant's case for flow production rests on volume and cost. The bench is a single, standardised product made in large numbers - 48 000 units a year - and flow production is designed for exactly this: a continuous sequence of operations with little or no changeover, which spreads a high fixed cost over a large output and gives a low variable cost. Second, demand for the bench is predictable in total, and the consultant argues that a dedicated line would remove the batch changeovers that currently interrupt production. (A1)(A1)

The eleven other products are the problem. Flow production is only economic when a line can run for long periods without being stopped and altered. Hartswood makes twelve variants in total, and a flow line for the bench cannot make tables, chairs or the other bench designs. Those products must stay on batch production, so the investment would improve the cost of one product out of twelve while leaving the rest of the factory unchanged. (A1)(A1)

(b) Mean monthly demand $= 48 000 / 12 = 4 000$ benches. (A1)

Peak demand: 80% of 48 000 $= 38 400$ benches are sold in three months, so peak monthly demand $= 38 400 / 3 = 12 800$ benches. (M1)(A1)

Unit cost at 48 000 units:

Batch: fixed cost per unit $= EUR 180 000 / 48 000 = EUR 3.75$; plus variable cost EUR 18.25, giving EUR 22.00 per bench. (M1)(A1)
Flow: fixed cost per unit $= EUR 480 000 / 48 000 = EUR 10.00$; plus variable cost EUR 10.00, giving EUR 20.00 per bench. (A1)

Comment: at 48 000 units flow production is EUR 2.00 a bench cheaper, a saving of EUR 96 000 a year, and the crossover point at which flow becomes cheaper is $(EUR 480 000 - EUR 180 000) / (EUR 18.25 - EUR 10.00) = 36 364$ benches. Since annual demand is 48 000, the arithmetic appears to favour flow - but this comparison ignores the constraint that the flow line's capacity of 8 000 benches a month imposes on a seasonal product.

(c) Indicative evaluation, using descriptive statistics and a decision tree.

The descriptive statistics show why the annual average is the wrong basis for the decision. Mean monthly demand is 4 000 benches, but peak monthly demand is 12 800 and off-season demand is about 1 067. The range is therefore about 11 733 benches a month. The flow line can make only 8 000 a month, so in each of the three peak months it is short by $12 800 - 8 000 = 4 800$ benches. Over the three months the shortfall is 14 400 benches, all of which must be made in advance and stored. (M1)(A1)

Storage costs EUR 3 a bench a month, and the consultant expects an average holding period of four months: $14 400 \times EUR 3 \times 4 = EUR 172 800$ a year. The EUR 96 000 saving from flow production is therefore more than wiped out, leaving flow production EUR 76 800 a year more expensive than batch at the higher demand level. (A1)

The decision tree makes the same point under uncertainty. Marketing estimates a 0.6 probability that demand is 48 000 and a 0.4 probability that it is 30 000.

Batch production: at 48 000, cost $= EUR 180 000 + EUR 18.25 \times 48 000 = EUR 1 056 000$; at 30 000, cost $= EUR 180 000 + EUR 547 500 = EUR 727 500$. Expected cost $= 0.6 \times EUR 1 056 000 + 0.4 \times EUR 727 500 = EUR 924 600$. (M1)(A1)

Flow production: at 48 000, cost $= EUR 480 000 + EUR 10 \times 48 000 = EUR 960 000$, plus storage of EUR 172 800, giving EUR 1 132 800. At 30 000, peak monthly demand is $0.8 \times 30 000 / 3 = 8 000$, which exactly equals the line's capacity, so no storage is needed and cost $= EUR 480 000 + EUR 300 000 = EUR 780 000$. Expected cost $= 0.6 \times EUR 1 132 800 + 0.4 \times EUR 780 000 = EUR 991 680$. (M1)(A1)

Batch production has the lower expected cost, by EUR 67 080, and the conclusion does not depend on the probabilities: flow is more expensive in the high-demand state and also more expensive in the low-demand state, so no plausible weighting reverses it.

The flow line would also commit EUR 600 000, would be difficult to change over, and could not make the other eleven products. Conclusion: Hartswood should not invest in the flow line. A stronger answer will note that the same analysis would justify revisiting flow production if the company could smooth demand, reduce the product range, or add a second line to raise peak capacity.

Markscheme notes

(a) Two marks for the consultant's reasoning (high volume of a standardised product; low unit cost) and two for the constraint created by the other eleven products. A candidate who says only 'flow production is cheaper' has not explained why it would be suitable and earns one mark.

(b) Award (A1) for the mean and (M1)(A1) for the peak monthly demand. The peak is the discriminating figure: a candidate who divides 48 000 by 12 and uses 4 000 as the monthly requirement has not understood the seasonality. Award (M1)(A1) for the batch unit cost and (A1) for the flow unit cost. The comment must note that flow is cheaper on unit cost alone and identify the crossover, but that the comparison ignores capacity.

(c) Award (M1)(A1) for the pre-build quantity of 14 400 benches and the storage cost of EUR 172 800; a candidate who omits the storage cost cannot earn the evaluation marks, because that omission is exactly the error the question is testing. Award the decision-tree marks for the two expected costs. A candidate who computes the expected costs without the storage cost will obtain EUR 888 000 for flow against EUR 924 600 for batch and conclude, wrongly, that flow is cheaper; award the method marks but not the evaluation marks, and credit the candidate if they notice the capacity constraint in words even without the full calculation. Credit any supported conclusion.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 6.1 SWOT analysis and 6.3 STEEPLE analysis
syllabus_ref: Unit 6: 6.1 SWOT analysis and 6.3 STEEPLE analysis (the SL Toolkit). P1 Section A.
title: A strength the outside world is quietly converting into a threat
q_html:
Calderbank Print & Packaging

Calderbank Print & Packaging is a family printing firm in a market town, employing 40 people. For eighteen years it has printed the weekly leaflets of a supermarket chain under a rolling annual contract that is renewed each spring. Each year the directors write a SWOT: they have again listed the supermarket contract as the business's greatest strength and 'no experience of packaging design' as a weakness, and they propose to spend EUR 60,000 on a faster leaflet press to protect the contract.

Around the firm, however, the market is moving. Shoppers increasingly use supermarket apps instead of paper leaflets, and a rival has installed a digital press that prints short runs cheaply. The government has introduced a tax on virgin paper and placed extended producer responsibility for packaging waste on producers. Energy costs for the presses have risen by about 40% in two years, and trade customers now ask for recyclable cardboard cartons rather than plastic film. Local environmental groups have publicly praised firms that cut paper use.

The table shows how the firm's revenue has actually moved across its three service lines over the last three years.

The directors of Calderbank Print & Packaging must decide whether to spend EUR 60,000 on a faster leaflet press or to invest in packaging capability instead.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Explain how a SWOT analysis and a STEEPLE analysis differ in what they can tell the directors, using one example of each from the case.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Using the table, calculate each service line's share of total revenue in 2023 and in 2025, the change in total revenue over the period, and revenue per employee in each year. Comment on what the figures show.

    (Calculate)
  3. [6 marks](c)

    Evaluate whether Calderbank should follow the SWOT and spend EUR 60,000 on the leaflet press, or act on the STEEPLE findings instead. Justify your answer.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) SWOT is an audit of the firm's own position. It sorts factors into strengths and weaknesses, which are internal and controllable, and opportunities and threats, which are external, and it is used to match the firm's resources to its environment. STEEPLE examines the external environment alone, across social, technological, economic, environmental, political, legal and ethical factors, and is used to identify change that the firm does not control. (A1)(A1)

The difference matters here. The case example for SWOT is the supermarket leaflet contract, which the directors call a strength because it is long-standing and gives a predictable order book. The case example for STEEPLE is the social and technological shift away from printed leaflets towards supermarket apps, which is outside the firm's control and is shrinking the market for the product it prints. (A1)(A1)

(b) Total revenue: 2023 = 900 + 250 + 150 = EUR 1,300k; 2025 = 590 + 610 + 170 = EUR 1,370k. (M1)(A1)

Shares of total: leaflet printing falls from 900/1,300 = 69.2% to 590/1,370 = 43.1%; packaging rises from 250/1,300 = 19.2% to 610/1,370 = 44.5%; signage rises from 150/1,300 = 11.5% to 170/1,370 = 12.4%. (A1)

Total revenue rose by EUR 70k, or 5.4%, so the business looks as though it is growing. Revenue per employee: 2023 = 1,300,000/40 = EUR 32,500; 2025 = 1,370,000/40 = EUR 34,250. (M1)(A1)

The comment mark is for seeing that the headline is misleading. The total is up only because packaging has grown by 144%, from EUR 250k to EUR 610k, while the line the directors are defending has fallen by EUR 310k, or 34.4%, and is now smaller than packaging. The firm's future is already being decided by the line its SWOT calls a weakness. (A1)

(c) Indicative evaluation. The SWOT points one way. The leaflet contract is the firm's oldest relationship and its largest single order, and losing it would remove about 43% of revenue at a stroke. Spending EUR 60,000 on a faster press lowers the unit cost of the work the contract needs and may make Calderbank the cheapest bidder when the contract is next renewed. On this reading the EUR 60,000 protects the core of the business.

The STEEPLE reading contradicts it. The fall in leaflet revenue is not caused by anything inside the firm: readers are moving to apps, the supermarket has begun cutting print volumes, and the tax on virgin paper and extended producer responsibility raise the cost of the very product the press would print. A faster press makes Calderbank better at producing something its customer is buying less of. The weakness the SWOT admits, no packaging design experience, sits in the one line that is growing, and packaging faces rising demand because of the same environmental and legal pressures that are hurting leaflets. (A1)(A1)

A defensible answer can still support the press, because it buys time and cash while packaging capability is built. But the strongest answers notice that the two tools classify the same contract differently, as a strength internally and a threat externally, and recommend using the leaflet cash flow to fund packaging rather than to defend the declining line. Credit any supported conclusion. (A1)(A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark for each of the two tool descriptions and one for each correctly applied example. A candidate who describes SWOT and STEEPLE accurately but uses no case example earns at most two. Do not credit a SWOT that lists only internal factors or a STEEPLE that includes the firm's own capabilities.

(b) Award (M1)(A1) for the two totals and (A1) for the shares; accept shares to one decimal place. Award (M1)(A1) for revenue per employee. The comment mark requires the candidate to contrast the falling leaflet line with the rising packaging line; a candidate who reports only that total revenue grew forfeits it. Follow through on arithmetic slips.

(c) The two discriminating marks are for recognising that the decline is externally driven and that the admitted weakness sits in the growing line. A candidate who simply repeats the SWOT and recommends the press cannot earn more than two marks, however well written. Credit a conclusion that keeps the press only if it is justified by timing or cash flow, not by the claim that leaflets will recover. Do not credit generic statements about the internet that are not tied to the case.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 6.2 Ansoff matrix and 6.4 Boston Consulting Group (BCG) matrix
syllabus_ref: Unit 6: 6.2 Ansoff matrix and 6.4 Boston Consulting Group (BCG) matrix (the SL Toolkit). P1 Section A.
title: Two matrices, one product, opposite instructions
q_html:
Brackenwood Pet Foods

Brackenwood Pet Foods is a family-owned manufacturer of dry dog food, based in one factory and selling through pet shops and a small number of garden centres. The directors use the BCG matrix each year to decide where to invest, measuring market share within the premium dog-food segment, and they use the Ansoff matrix whenever they consider a new product or a new market.

The premium segment is worth EUR 150 million a year. Supermarket own-label dog food, which Brackenwood does not supply, is a separate value segment three times larger. Against the whole dog-food market, Brackenwood's best-selling product, Adult Complete, has a share of 11%, while the value-segment leader has 13%.

The directors treat market growth of 10% or more a year as high, and a relative market share of 1.0 or more as high. The table gives the four main products.

The directors of Brackenwood Pet Foods must decide where to invest over the next three years.

  1. [5 marks](a)

    Using the table, calculate the relative market share of each of the four products and classify each one using the BCG matrix. Show your working.

    (Calculate)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Explain how the Ansoff matrix would classify two growth options open to Brackenwood, using examples from the case.

    (Explain)
  3. [6 marks](c)

    Evaluate whether Brackenwood should follow the BCG recommendation to harvest Adult Complete. Justify your answer with reference to the Ansoff matrix and to the market data.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Relative market share = own share divided by the largest rival's share. Puppy Complete 22/20 = 1.10; Adult Complete 34/18 = 1.89; Senior Care 7/26 = 0.27; Grain-Free Fresh 9/24 = 0.38. (M1)(A1)(A1)

Growth: Puppy Complete 14% (high), Adult Complete 3% (low), Senior Care 2% (low), Grain-Free Fresh 16% (high).

Classification: Puppy Complete is a star, with high growth and high relative share. Adult Complete is a cash cow, with low growth and high relative share. Senior Care is a dog, with low growth and low relative share. Grain-Free Fresh is a question mark, with high growth and low relative share. (A1)(A1)

(b) Ansoff classifies growth by whether the product and the market are existing or new. Market development means an existing product sold into a new market: Adult Complete sold through the supermarket value channel, which Brackenwood does not currently supply. The product already exists; only the market is new. (A1)(A1)

Market penetration means more of an existing product sold into the existing market: winning more shelf space for Adult Complete in the pet shops and garden centres it already uses. (A1)

Also creditable: product development, such as new Grain-Free recipes for existing premium customers, and diversification, a new product for a new market, which is the riskiest quadrant. (A1)

(c) Indicative evaluation. The BCG reading is clear. Adult Complete has a relative market share of 1.89 and market growth of only 3%, so it is a classic cash cow: the matrix says take its cash and invest it in the star, Puppy Complete. On the premium-segment numbers this is textbook, and harvesting means withdrawing promotion and product development from Adult Complete rather than reinvesting in it.

Ansoff contradicts that instruction. The lowest-risk growth available to Brackenwood is market development: taking the existing Adult Complete product into the supermarket value segment. That is a new market for an existing product, the second-least-risky quadrant, and it needs investment, which is exactly what harvesting removes. So the BCG instruction to take cash out of Adult Complete would close the one low-risk growth option the firm has.

The data make the clash worse. The classification depends on how the market is defined. Measured against the premium segment, Adult Complete has a relative share of 1.89; measured against the whole dog-food market, its share is 11% against the value leader's 13%, a relative share of 0.85, which is a dog, not a cash cow. The same product carries opposite BCG labels. The tool cannot settle the question until the directors decide which market they intend to compete in, and that is a strategic choice, not a calculation.

A defensible answer can still harvest: the firm is small, Puppy Complete is the star, and cash is scarce. The strongest answers notice that harvesting Adult Complete would destroy the Ansoff option the same product makes possible, and recommend funding market development of the cash cow instead. Credit any supported conclusion. (A1)(A1)(A1)(A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1) for the relative-share method and (A1)(A1) for the four correct figures. Award (A1)(A1) for the four correct classifications; a candidate who misclassifies one product but applies the 10% and 1.0 rules consistently earns one of the two. Accept 0.38 or 0.375 for Grain-Free Fresh and 0.27 for Senior Care. A candidate who computes relative share as the largest rival divided by the firm's own share reverses the matrix and cannot earn the classification marks.

(b) Two marks for market development correctly identified and applied to the supermarket channel; one mark for a correctly applied market penetration example; one further mark for either product development or diversification correctly applied. Do not credit new product, new market as market development.

(c) The discriminating marks are for seeing that the Ansoff market-development option requires the very investment that BCG harvesting removes, and for noticing that the cash-cow label depends on the premium-segment definition. A candidate who simply repeats the BCG classification and recommends harvesting cannot earn more than two marks. Credit a conclusion that harvests only if it is justified by the firm's lack of funds, not by the claim that Adult Complete has no growth left.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 6.5 Business plan and 6.8 Circular business models
syllabus_ref: Unit 6: 6.5 Business plan and 6.8 Circular business models (the SL Toolkit). P1 Section A.
title: A circular plan that pays back only at a reuse rate the trial never reached
q_html:
Dale & Vale Dairy

Dale & Vale Dairy delivers milk and cream to 3,000 households on five rounds. Each household receives five bottles a week, fifty-two weeks a year. The milk is currently sold in single-use plastic bottles that cost EUR 0.12 each; the bottles are not collected.

The founders, Ravi and Meg, want to switch to returnable glass bottles as part of a circular business model and have written a business plan to raise the money. The plan assumes that each glass bottle will be used twenty times before it is broken or lost. Glass bottles cost EUR 0.60 each, and a bottle washer, crates and a chilled store would cost EUR 180,000. Collecting, washing and handling a returned bottle would cost EUR 0.03 each time it is used. The plan presents the switch as a cost saving and shows a payback period the bank will accept.

The bank lends to the dairy only if the investment pays back within four years.

Before committing, Ravi and Meg ran a three-month trial with 200 households. In the trial each glass bottle was used, on average, six times before it was broken or lost. The founders believe the rate would improve once customers were used to the system, because the trial households were told about the scheme only a week before it began. Ravi argues that the plan's figures are the right ones because they describe how the scheme will work once it is established, and that the dairy has a public commitment to remove single-use plastic. Meg is not sure the dairy can afford to be wrong.

The founders of Dale & Vale Dairy must decide whether to commit to the returnable glass scheme in the business plan.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Explain two ways in which a circular business model such as returnable glass bottles could reduce Dale & Vale's costs, and one way in which it could increase them.

    (Explain)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Using the figures, calculate the cost per delivery and the total annual cost of bottles and washing under plastic, under the plan's assumption of twenty uses, and under the trial's six uses. State the break-even number of uses and the payback period the plan implies.

    (Calculate)
  3. [6 marks](c)

    Evaluate whether the business plan's proposal to switch to returnable glass bottles is sound. Justify your answer with reference to the trial, the bank's lending rule and the founders' objectives.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) A circular business model keeps materials in use rather than disposing of them after one cycle. Two ways it could cut Dale & Vale's costs. First, a glass bottle that is reused replaces many single-use bottles, so the dairy stops buying a new EUR 0.12 plastic bottle for every delivery. Second, it avoids the waste-disposal and packaging charges attached to single-use plastic and reduces exposure to future levies on single-use packaging. (A1)(A1)

One way it increases costs: the model needs reverse logistics. Bottles must be collected from households, returned to the depot, washed and refilled, which adds handling cost and requires the EUR 180,000 washer and store. The dairy also bears the cost of bottles that are broken or never returned. (A1)(A1)

(b) Annual deliveries = 3,000 households x 5 bottles x 52 weeks = 780,000 deliveries. (M1)(A1)

Plastic: cost per delivery EUR 0.12; annual cost = 780,000 x 0.12 = EUR 93,600. (A1)

Plan (20 uses): cost per delivery = 0.60/20 + 0.03 = EUR 0.03 + EUR 0.03 = EUR 0.06; annual cost = 780,000 x 0.06 = EUR 46,800. (M1)(A1)

Trial (6 uses): cost per delivery = 0.60/6 + 0.03 = EUR 0.10 + EUR 0.03 = EUR 0.13; annual cost = 780,000 x 0.13 = EUR 101,400. (A1)

Break-even uses: 0.60/u + 0.03 = 0.12 gives u = 0.60/0.09 = 6.67, so a glass bottle must be used at least seven times to be cheaper than plastic. (A1)

Payback on the plan's figures: annual saving = 93,600 - 46,800 = EUR 46,800; payback = 180,000/46,800 = 3.8 years. (A1)

(c) Indicative evaluation. The plan is internally consistent and looks attractive on its own assumptions. At twenty uses a bottle, glass costs EUR 0.06 a delivery against EUR 0.12 for plastic, a saving of EUR 46,800 a year, and the EUR 180,000 is repaid in 3.8 years, inside the bank's four-year rule. The bank's condition is therefore satisfied on the plan's numbers, and the circular model also delivers the founders' environmental objective.

The trial contradicts the assumption on which the whole plan rests. At six uses, glass costs EUR 0.13 a delivery, more than the plastic it replaces, and the annual cost rises to EUR 101,400, about EUR 7,800 a year worse than doing nothing. The break-even is seven uses, so the trial is not close: it falls below the point at which the investment stops destroying value. On the trial evidence the payback never arrives, and the bank's four-year rule is not met.

The evaluation therefore turns on a judgement about the trial. Ravi's argument has some force, because the trial lasted only three months and customers were told about the scheme a week before it began, so six uses may understate a mature scheme. Meg's argument is that the dairy cannot afford to be wrong, and the shortfall is a recurring EUR 7,800 a year, not a one-off. The strongest answers note that the plan should be rewritten with a range of reuse rates, that the scheme should be re-trialled with proper notice, and that the founders' zero-waste objective could be pursued at a smaller scale before EUR 180,000 is committed. Credit any supported conclusion. (A1)(A1)(A1)(A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) One mark for each of the two cost reductions and one for the cost increase, each correctly explained; naming reuse without explaining the saving earns at most one. Credit avoided bottle purchases, disposal charges and future levies. Do not credit the claim that it is good for the environment as a cost reduction.

(b) Award (M1)(A1) for the 780,000 deliveries, (A1) for the plastic cost, (M1)(A1) for the plan's cost per delivery and annual cost, (A1) for the trial cost, (A1) for the break-even of seven uses and (A1) for the 3.8-year payback. Follow through on arithmetic slips. A candidate who uses 0.60/20 without adding the EUR 0.03 washing cost cannot reach the evaluation marks, because the omission is the error the question tests.

(c) The discriminating marks are for the trial cost of EUR 0.13 and the recognition that six uses is below the break-even of seven. A candidate who accepts the plan's twenty uses and concludes that the switch is clearly worthwhile cannot earn more than two marks. Credit a conclusion that proceeds with the scheme only if it is justified by the trial's weakness or by a staged rollout, not by the claim that customers will return bottles out of goodwill.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 5.5 Break-even analysis; 3.3 Costs and revenues
syllabus_ref: 5.5 Break-even analysis (Unit 5); 3.3 Costs and revenues; 3.2 Sources of finance (not required); Toolkit: decision trees
title: 5.5 Break-even analysis; 3.3 Costs and revenues
q_html:
Verdana Foods Ltd (VF)

VF produces chilled plant-based ready meals at a single factory in Porto, Portugal, and sells through two channels: to supermarket chains, and directly to consumers through its own website. The two channels carry very different cost structures — supermarket orders leave the factory in full pallets, while online orders are picked, packed and delivered chilled to individual households.

VF's marketing director has proposed a campaign to shift the sales mix towards the online channel, which she describes as "obviously better, because the contribution per unit is higher and it must therefore lower our break-even". The finance director is less sure. She estimates a 0.6 probability that total volume remains at 620 000 units and a 0.4 probability that it falls to 480 000 units, because some supermarket buyers may delist VF if it starts promoting its own website to their customers.

All figures below are for the year ended 31 March 2026. Total sales volume was 620 000 units and total fixed costs were €486 000.

The proposed campaign would add €54 000 per year to fixed costs and is expected to change the sales mix to 60% supermarket / 40% online.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Calculate VF's weighted average contribution per unit at the current sales mix, and hence its break-even level of output.

    (Calculate)
  2. [5 marks](b)

    Calculate the break-even level of output and the margin of safety at a volume of 620 000 units if the campaign achieves the expected 60 / 40 mix. Comment on why this result differs from the marketing director's claim.

    (Calculate)
  3. [6 marks](c)

    Using the finance director's probabilities, calculate the expected annual profit both with and without the campaign. Evaluate, with reference to one stakeholder group and one non-financial factor, whether VF should launch the campaign.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Contribution per unit = selling price − all variable costs.

Supermarket: $3.20-1.85-0.00=\textbf{€1.35}$ (A1)

Online: $5.00-1.85-1.10=\textbf{€2.05}$ (A1)

Weighted average contribution $=0.78(1.35)+0.22(2.05)=1.053+0.451=\textbf{€1.504 per unit}$ (M1)

$$\text{Break-even output}=\frac{\text{fixed costs}}{\text{contribution per unit}}=\frac{486\,000}{1.504}=323\,138\approx\textbf{323 000 units}$$ (A1)

(b) New weighted average contribution $=0.60(1.35)+0.40(2.05)=0.81+0.82=\textbf{€1.63 per unit}$ (M1)

New fixed costs $=486\,000+54\,000=\textbf{€540 000}$ (A1)

$$\text{New break-even output}=\frac{540\,000}{1.63}=331\,288\approx\textbf{331 000 units}$$ (A1)

$$\text{Margin of safety}=\frac{620\,000-331\,288}{620\,000}\times100=\textbf{46.6\%}$$ (A1)

The marketing director is right that contribution per unit rises, from €1.504 to €1.63. She is wrong that break-even falls: it rises, from about 323 000 to about 331 000 units, because fixed costs increase by 11.1% while weighted contribution increases by only 8.4%. The margin of safety also falls, from 47.9% to 46.6%. (A1)

(c) Profit = (volume × weighted contribution) − fixed costs.

*Without the campaign (contribution €1.504, fixed €486 000):*

  • at 620 000 units: $620\,000(1.504)-486\,000=932\,480-486\,000=\textbf{€446 480}$
  • at 480 000 units: $480\,000(1.504)-486\,000=721\,920-486\,000=\textbf{€235 920}$

$$\text{EV}=0.6(446\,480)+0.4(235\,920)=267\,888+94\,368=\textbf{€362 256}$$ (M1)(A1)

*With the campaign (contribution €1.63, fixed €540 000):*

  • at 620 000 units: $620\,000(1.63)-540\,000=1\,010\,600-540\,000=\textbf{€470 600}$
  • at 480 000 units: $480\,000(1.63)-540\,000=782\,400-540\,000=\textbf{€242 400}$

$$\text{EV}=0.6(470\,600)+0.4(242\,400)=282\,360+96\,960=\textbf{€379 320}$$ (M1)(A1)

The campaign has the higher expected profit by €17 064, about 4.7% of the expected profit without it. (A1)

*Evaluation.* On expected value the campaign is justified, and it is more robust than the margin of safety suggests: because the campaign is better in both states of the world (€470 600 > €446 480, and €242 400 > €235 920), the decision does not actually depend on which probability is correct. The break-even volume *of the change itself* is $54\,000\div(1.63-1.504)=428\,571$ units, and both volume scenarios exceed it. (A1)

However the expected-value calculation hides a step change rather than a smooth one. Supermarket buyers are the stakeholder group at risk: they supply 60% of volume even after the shift, and their reaction to a supplier promoting direct-to-consumer sales is not a 40%-chance event — it is a decision they either make or do not. If delisting removed the supermarket channel entirely, the 480 000-unit scenario would be optimistic. Set against that, a non-financial factor pulls the other way: chilled single-household delivery carries a markedly higher carbon footprint per unit than palletised supermarket distribution, which sits awkwardly with the sustainability positioning of a plant-based brand and could damage the very customers the campaign targets.

Conclusion (AO3): a supported recommendation. The expected gain of €17 064 is thin relative to a channel-specific risk that the model does not capture, so a full campaign is hard to justify on these numbers; the stronger recommendation is to test the online offer in a limited region, or to grow online volume without advertising it to supermarket customers, so that the contribution gain is captured without triggering the delisting risk. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) Award (M1) only if the two channel contributions are *weighted* by the sales mix; an unweighted mean of €1.70 is a common error and forfeits the method mark. Accept answers in the range 322 000–324 000.

(b) The final (A1) is for the comment, and it must identify the *relative* size of the two changes — 'contribution went up but fixed costs went up more' in words is sufficient, a bare 'she is wrong' is not. Candidates who compute the margin of safety at 480 000 units should be followed through if stated.

(c) Award the method marks for weighting both outcomes by their probabilities; a candidate who weights the two volumes by their probabilities (564 000) and then computes a single profit figure at that volume has not used the decision tree and forfeits both method marks. The evaluation mark requires a *supported* recommendation — credit any reasonable conclusion, including 'launch', provided it is justified with reference to the figures and to at least one stakeholder or non-financial factor. Do not credit generic factors ('the weather', 'the economy') or a stakeholder named without an explanation of their interest.

Note on Toolkit use: the expected-value calculation is the decision-tree tool applied with the branches implicit. Candidates who draw the tree explicitly should be credited equally.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 3.5 / 1.5 / 1.4 Ratio analysis applied to a growth decision
syllabus_ref: 3.5 (Profitability and liquidity ratio analysis), 1.5 (Growth and evolution), 1.4 (Stakeholders)
title: 3.5 / 1.5 / 1.4 Ratio analysis applied to a growth decision
q_html:
Maren & Daughters

Maren & Daughters is a family-owned chain of twelve bakery cafés in a medium-sized European city. It is owned entirely by the founder's three children, who work in the business and take all major decisions between them. The chain has grown steadily by opening one new café roughly every eighteen months, each funded from retained profit and a bank loan. The bank has now indicated that it will not lend further without additional security. Two of the three owners want to grow by franchising; the third wants to continue opening company-owned cafés and is prepared to bring in an outside investor. Extracts from the most recent accounts are given below, together with the projections prepared by each camp.

Using the case study and the figures provided, answer all three parts.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Analyse the recent financial performance and position of Maren & Daughters using ratio analysis. Your analysis must include calculations.

    (Analyse)
  2. [6 marks](b)

    Evaluate whether Maren & Daughters should expand by franchising or by opening company-owned cafés, using the projections in the case study.

    (Evaluate)
  3. [5 marks](c)

    Discuss the likely impact of the expansion on two different stakeholder groups, and explain why their interests may conflict.

    (Discuss)
a_html:
(a) Gross profit is $8.40-3.78=\unicode{8364}4.62$ m, so the gross margin is $\dfrac{4.62}{8.40}=55.0\%$. (M1)(A1) Operating profit is $4.62-3.36=\unicode{8364}1.26$ m, an operating margin of $15.0\%$, and the net margin is $\dfrac{0.756}{8.40}=9.0\%$. (A1) Return on capital employed is $\dfrac{1.26}{6.30}=20.0\%$, which is strong for a retail food business and suggests the existing estate is being used well. (A1) Liquidity looks comfortable: the current ratio is $\dfrac{1.68}{0.84}=2.0$, well above the usual benchmark of $1.5$. (A1) Gearing is $\dfrac{2.52}{6.30}=40\%$, which is not alarming in itself but matters here because the bank has already refused further lending without security. (A1) The overall picture is a profitable, liquid business whose constraint is access to capital rather than the quality of its trading. (R1)

(b) Franchising generates $\unicode{8364}1.0$ m in upfront fees $(40\times\unicode{8364}25\,000)$ and $\unicode{8364}1.44$ m a year in royalties $(40\times6\%\times\unicode{8364}600\,000)$. (M1)(A1) It requires almost no capital, it sidesteps the bank's refusal entirely, and it transfers most of the operating risk to the franchisees. (A1) Against that, the royalty stream is only as good as the franchisees: sixty per cent of the chain's future profit would depend on people the family does not employ and cannot directly manage, and one café cutting corners on hygiene would damage a brand built over twenty years. The $\unicode{8364}1.0$ m of fees is also one-off, so the recurring benefit is the $\unicode{8364}1.44$ m royalty, not the headline $\unicode{8364}2.44$ m. (A1)

The company-owned option costs $8\times\unicode{8364}450\,000=\unicode{8364}3.6$ m and adds $8\times\unicode{8364}90\,000=\unicode{8364}0.72$ m a year before depreciation, or about $\unicode{8364}0.36$ m after charging depreciation over ten years. (M1)(A1) Payback is $\dfrac{3.6}{0.72}=5$ years, and the return on the new capital is roughly $10\%$, which is half the $20\%$ the business currently earns. (A1)

On the figures, franchising dominates: it produces more annual income, needs a fraction of the capital, and avoids diluting ownership. (R1) The qualification is that the comparison is not purely financial. Franchising converts a business the family controls into one it licenses, and the loss of control over standards is the genuine cost, not the lost margin. A balanced evaluation therefore recommends franchising but with a contractual and operational framework — approved suppliers, inspection rights, a training requirement — that protects the brand, and possibly a small number of company-owned cafés retained as a benchmark and a training base. (R1)

(c) *The three owner-directors.* Under franchising they keep full ownership and receive fees and royalties without new borrowing, so income rises and personal financial risk falls. (M1)(A1) However, the third sibling's objection is not about money but about control, and two of them will get their way over the third, which risks a family relationship as well as a business one. (A1)

*Employees.* Under franchising the existing staff keep their jobs but the new outlets' staff are employed by franchisees, probably on different terms and without the informal culture of a family firm; there is also no longer a clear promotion ladder into new cafés. Under the company-owned route about eighty new jobs are created inside the business with the same terms and progression. (M1)(A1)

The interests conflict because owners benefit from franchising's lower risk and faster income while employees benefit from the company-owned route's job creation and internal promotion. (A1) A candidate might also note that customers gain from faster expansion under either option but lose if franchise standards slip, which links the stakeholder analysis back to the brand risk identified in (b). (R1)

Markscheme notes

In (a) award one mark per correctly calculated and interpreted ratio, up to a maximum of four; candidates must calculate rather than describe. Accept other valid ratios such as the acid test or the gearing ratio expressed against equity, provided they are computed from the figures given. The ROCE figure is the one that matters most, because the whole question turns on whether new capital earns the 20% the business currently earns. In (b) the evaluation mark requires a supported judgement; a balanced list of advantages with no conclusion is capped at four. Candidates who prefer the company-owned route should not be penalised provided they engage with the 10% versus 20% return and the capital constraint imposed by the bank, since the bank's refusal is what makes the option difficult rather than impossible. In (c) any two stakeholder groups are acceptable, but the conflict must be identified explicitly rather than left implicit in two separate descriptions. Candidates who argue for a mixed strategy — a small core of company-owned cafés retained for training and benchmarking alongside a franchised estate — should be credited, and arguably deserve credit above a pure recommendation, because it addresses the control objection without abandoning the capital advantage. Where a candidate raises the outside investor as a third option, allow it on its merits; the case study does not quantify it, which is a legitimate point to make rather than an omission to be penalised.

subject: BM SL
subtopic: 1.2 Types of business entities; 1.4 Stakeholders; 1.5 External environment
syllabus_ref: Unit 1: 1.2 Types of business entities; 1.3 Business objectives; 1.4 Stakeholders; 1.5 External environment. Toolkit: STEEPLE analysis
title: 1.2 Types of business entities; 1.4 Stakeholders; 1.5 External environment
q_html:
Marisol's Kitchen

Marisol's Kitchen is a bakery in a city centre, owned and run by Marisol as a sole trader. It has traded for nine years, employs fourteen staff, and is consistently profitable, with annual revenue of about €780 000 and net profit of about €94 000. Nearly all profit is reinvested in the shop.

Marisol works six days a week and has turned down two offers to open a second site because, she says, "the moment I'm not there, it stops being my bakery". She has no written business plan and funds everything from retained profit, having avoided borrowing since a difficult first year.

A former customer, Dev, has offered to invest €250 000 for a 40% share, on condition that the business becomes a private limited company and opens three more sites within two years. Dev's stated aim is to build the business and sell it to a regional chain within five years. Marisol would remain a director and keep 60%.

Two of Marisol's longest-serving staff have said they would like to become supervisors in the new sites. Her current landlord has indicated that the lease on the original shop will not be renewed beyond next year.

Marisol must decide whether to accept Dev's investment.

  1. [4 marks](a)

    Explain two features of a private limited company that would help the business expand, compared with Marisol remaining a sole trader.

    (Explain)
  2. [4 marks](b)

    Using STEEPLE analysis, analyse one external factor from the case that could affect Marisol's decision.

    (Analyse)
  3. [6 marks](c)

    Evaluate whether Marisol's objectives and Dev's objectives can be reconciled if she accepts the investment.

    (Evaluate)
a_html:
(a) Award two explained features:

  • Access to finance through share capital. As a private limited company the business can raise capital by issuing shares to new investors (and, unlike a sole trader, does not depend on Marisol's personal savings or retained profit). This matters because three new sites require far more than the €94 000 of annual profit Marisol currently reinvests. (A1)(A1)
  • Separate legal personality and limited liability. The company is a legal person in its own right, so it can own property, sign leases and borrow in its own name, and the shareholders' liability is limited to what they have invested. This matters because expansion into three leased sites would otherwise expose Marisol personally to unlimited liability for those commitments. (A1)(A1)
  • Also creditable: continuity of existence (the business survives changes in ownership, which matters given Dev's plan to sell), and the ability to bring in non-executive expertise through the board.

(b) Award up to four marks for one factor, analysed. For example:

  • Legal (or Economic) — the landlord's refusal to renew the lease. STEEPLE identifies the *legal* environment as an external constraint on property and tenancy. If the original site — the source of all current profit and the brand's home — must close next year, then Marisol's implicit objective of preserving the business she built is unachievable by doing nothing. This *strengthens* the case for accepting investment, because a second site would be needed simply to survive. (A1)(A1)(A1)(A1)
  • Alternatively: Social — changing consumer demand for independent bakeries, or the expectations of her staff, who want promotion opportunities; or Economic — the cost of fit-out and the interest rate environment affecting any borrowing. Credit any factor that is genuinely external, named as a STEEPLE category, and linked to the decision.

(c) Indicative evaluation:

The conflict is real. Marisol is a sole trader for reasons that are not financial: she has repeatedly declined expansion, and her own words ("it stops being my bakery") show that control and identity are her objectives. Dev's objective is explicit — build and sell within five years. These are different definitions of success: Marisol wants to keep a business, Dev wants to exit one. (A1)(A1)

Where they overlap. Both want the business to grow and be more profitable; three more sites would give her two supervisors the promotion they want and would solve the lease problem; and Marisol's 60% holding means she is not a passive minority — she retains majority control of ordinary decisions, and as a director she would shape how expansion happens. On a narrow reading, growth and profitability are compatible with both objectives for the first few years. (A1)(A1)

Why the reconciliation is fragile. The 60/40 split protects Marisol only until Dev decides to sell: a buyer would want control, and Dev's five-year exit plan means that in five years Marisol's 60% sits inside a business someone else has chosen. Objectives also diverge on *how* to grow — Marisol avoids borrowing and grows from retained profit, while three sites in two years requires exactly the speed and risk she has spent nine years avoiding. And if the new sites fail, limited liability protects her personal assets but not the business she identifies with. (A1)

Conclusion. The objectives can be reconciled *only* if the terms change: a shareholders' agreement giving Marisol a veto over any sale of the business, or an agreed timetable that ties the exit to her own retirement. Without such protections, accepting the investment means trading an objective she actually holds (independence) for one she has never expressed (capital growth). On the evidence of the case, Marisol should either negotiate control over the exit, or decline and seek a smaller, debt-funded second site that lets her keep both the business and her independence. (A1)

Markscheme notes

(a) The feature must be *explained* and *contrasted with the sole trader form* — 'a company has limited liability' with no explanation of why that matters here is capped at one mark per feature. Do not credit 'it sounds more professional'.

(b) The mark is for the analysis, not for listing STEEPLE. A candidate who names all six categories but analyses none earns at most one mark. The factor must come from the case (lease, staff ambitions, Dev's offer is *internal* to the decision and not a STEEPLE factor — watch for this confusion).

(c) Six marks require: (i) identification of the two conflicting objectives with evidence, (ii) genuine analysis of where they coincide, (iii) analysis of why the coincidence is limited (the exit plan is the key), (iv) a supported conclusion. Candidates who simply list stakeholder groups without comparing objectives are capped at two. There is no single correct conclusion — 'accept with protections' and 'decline' are equally creditworthy if argued from the case.

Note on Toolkit use: STEEPLE in (b) is the required Toolkit application. Candidates who produce a full STEEPLE table but do not use it to reach a conclusion about the decision should be credited for the tool but not for the analysis marks.
